en: Imperial Edict: The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs takes the awakening to one’s own mind as its foundation. Those who speak thus are said to possess correct knowledge and correct view.
When this is employed to benefit others and engage with the world, leading people directly to the source of the mind, only then can one be called a true descendant of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
As for what are called the paths of externalists and demons, they too possess knowledge and views; however, because they falsely identify [with that which is not the mind], [they are excluded].

Taking the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*) as the root of birth and death and regarding it as the ultimate principle, they mistakenly identify this with Buddha-nature and slander the precepts and practices;
for these reasons, they are termed followers of external paths or demonic paths. I have examined the *Recorded Sayings* of Miyun Wu and Tianyin Xiu;

their words and pedagogical applications single-mindedly uphold the "Upward" direction and point directly to the human mind, thereby acceding to the intent transmitted from the West and attaining the essence of Caoxi.
Regarding the "Zhengmo" (Correct Pulse): Upon examining the *Miyun Wu Lu* (Record of Miyun’s Enlightenment), it shows him refuting the false claims of his disciple Fazang.
Among the citations from Fazang’s own words, [Miyun] was appalled by his total delusion regarding the fundamental nature and his ignorant, reckless assertions.
Not only was Fazang ignorant of the essential tenets of the Buddha-dharma, but he had not even caught a glimpse of the realization attained by his own master. Thus, he gave rein to his...
This is groundless fabrication that deceives the world and deludes people; it is truly the insight of an external demon.

Thus, although his master [Huiyuan] refuted it once and again, and Tianyin Xiu also wrote the *Shiyi pusa* (The Universal Discourse Dispelling Doubts) to condemn its errors, the demon’s mind did not cease at the time.
His writings were either not circulated or destroyed; such was the case with his successor, Hongren, who was poisoned by this influence.

Furthermore, there are five treatises that attempt to defend [the aforementioned views], which have been circulated together with the hope that these demonic teachings will endure and that demonic karma will be produced without end.
Those in the world and future generations who possess the discerning eye are few; they do not recognize this harm.
Even those who recognize it and seek to refute it may possess virtue but lack official rank, such that their single voice is not believed for lack of corroboration. This will lead to...
Those who seek the ultimate Zen school harbor doubts and do not know where it leads; yet those who propagate its doctrines claim that the essence of Zen lies therein.
Thus, they first give rise to false faith, and subsequently develop false views. When false faith arises, right faith is severed;
when false views are formed, right view is extinguished. Consequently, demonic seeds will inevitably appear everywhere among people.
People have inherited these demonic teachings; their own inherent nature-principle (xingzong) remains unclarified, while the proliferation of verbal branches and twining vines spreads unchecked.

Now, these demonic offspring and grandsons go so far as to not sit in incense meditation and not observe the retreat period, even to the point of drinking wine, eating meat, violating precepts, and breaking the Vinaya, devoting themselves solely to composing poetry and essays to flatter and please the scholar-officials.
Regarding these courtesans, performers, and entertainers, would they not defile the ancestral temple?
If they are not eliminated, then the Dharma-eye of all Buddhas and the life-force of wisdom of sentient beings will be affected by no small degree.

As the sovereign of the realm, I concentrate my mind on the Mean to carry out the affairs of self-cultivation, family regulation, state governance, and world peace. Residing outside the monastic sphere, I am not one who presides over a hall to preach the Dharma.
What relevance does this have for awakening and cultivation? Furthermore, what relevance does it have for the *pitakas* and the *kṣāntis*?

However, since I have thoroughly mastered the essential principles of the Chan school, clearly understood the nature of demons and heterodoxies, keenly perceived the magnitude of demonic activities in the present, and foreseen the depth of demonic afflictions in the future, I truly cannot help but speak; I cannot bear not to speak. As for the Chan school, it is the teaching...
The Outer Separate Transmission: It may be expressed through silence; it may be expressed through speech. An ancient worthy said:
"To exhaust all fundamental discernment is like placing a single hair in the great void; to exhaust the pivotal mechanisms of the world is like casting a single drop into the vast ocean.
Such words flow naturally from within the original nature, just as the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures [flow from the Buddha]. Thousand...
Among the seven hundred koans, which one does not flow spontaneously from the original nature? Not a single real dharma binds those in the realms of humans and devas.

Now, Mōzang establishes the sign of "one zero" (0) as the ancestor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas, taking the thread-by-thread of the *kāṣāya* robe as the binding point for his school’s fundamental tenet. There are four dharmas, there are two heads, and there is the small...
The Dharma is the Great Dharma; there is the Great Dharma of the Great Dharma, which is termed the subtle essence of the secret intent.

There is transmission and bestowal. Now, as for the demonic successor Hongren: when Saṃghanandin encountered the youth holding a mirror and walking straight forward, it was to demonstrate that there has always been an elephant to be shown.
This proves that the image of the demonic teacher’s "one zero" is not contradictory. Furthermore, because of many...
The single matter of the robe encircling the patriarch’s stupa serves as clear evidence that making a robe is bound up with the fundamental purpose [of the Way].
Furthermore, Linji’s striking of Kefu Puhua is carved out as a symbolic representation of Huangbo’s three blows of the staff;
such various acts treated as substantial dharmas are beyond counting. All of these derive from intellectual speculation and forced interpretation, thereby losing sight of the true essence.
Regarding one's own mind, Huangbo said: "People nowadays only desire to know much and understand much; instead, this results in congestion and blockage.
They only know how to give their children plenty of butter to eat, yet they have no idea at all whether it will digest or not. This is the case for those who study the Path of the Three Vehicles."

All are of this same nature; they are all termed "undigested food. Thus one knows that what is not digested is entirely poisonous medicine, all of which is grasped within the realm of arising and ceasing. Within True Suchness (Tathatā), none of these things exist at all.
Now, while those who suffer from indigestion are many, the father and son Mañjuśrī and Mārajit are those who have already been satiated by the poison. The Buddha-dharma is not...
2. How can you insist upon the fixed numbers three and four, yet further claim to possess a secret transmission regarding the principles of those same three and four?

You extensively cite the words and phrases of ancient worthies from ages past that appear similar [to your own views] as footnotes, only to use them for comparison while claiming not to establish verbal teachings.
Thus, you single-handedly uphold the orthodox lineage that points directly upward, yet you spit at the clouds above and instead soil your own face. Zhaozhou.
The Master said: "In this place, I receive people using only the matter of our fundamental nature.
If I were to receive people according to their individual capacities, there are already the Three Pitakas and Twelve Divisions of the Canon to do that for them.

To merely speak of 'no marks of right and wrong or discrimination' is already not the fundamental matter; how much more so to explicitly produce such marks of right and wrong and discrimination?"—the World-Honored One.
The teachings spoken over forty-nine years, and the seventeen hundred ancient cases of the "ancient sages," are all merely words and letters.
If you do not recognize this very point, then even if you replicate every character and phrase like a clay gourd, it will be the teaching of a demon;
it will be a slander against the Buddha. Even if you could memorize the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures as taught by the Buddhas and Patriarchs, [it would still be of no avail].
The seventeen hundred *gong'an* are, word for word and phrase for phrase, without error; yet they are truly nothing more than mud and silt within the ocean of luminosity.
Moreover, once one has fallen into the realm of verbal expression, it is identical to the characteristics of the teachings (*jiaoxiang*).

If it is identical to the characteristics of the teachings, then the Three Baskets and Twelve Divisions of the Canon are already present; why then establish the principle of a "separate transmission outside the teachings"? Let him say whatever he pleases.
To speak of "ability" (néng): can one transcend the Three Piṭakas and the Twelve Divisions of the Canon? Sages possess many abilities, and Buddhas possess many supernormal powers (abhijñā).
Yet ability is not the fundamental nature of a sage, nor are supernormal powers the primary tenet of a Buddha. How could Zhongni (Confucius) ever have known the Sanskrit language of the West?
And how could the Tathāgata produce the Tang language of Zhendan (China)? Ability and supernormal powers each have their own respective domains.

Exhausted! What connection does this have with that? And what need is there to mention the matter of written characters? The father and son of the Māra-treasury (Mozang) arbitrarily mocked Miyun for being illiterate, implying that he was not their equal in scholarship.
If one wishes to engage in exegesis or compose literary works, there are naturally scholars available for that; what use are they to the followers of the School?

Whether one knows how to read or not, it has no bearing upon this— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the philosophical context of Chan/Zen discourse regarding the relationship between literacy and spiritual realization.*
What does this have to do with the individual? One who is widely versed in the Classics and Histories is like cutting out colored paper to add artificial blossoms to a tree;
one who cannot recognize a single character (*dīng*) likewise does not need to borrow fire or water from a neighbor when the rice is cooked.
As for the likes of Mazu and his son, their great underlying ailment lies precisely in their ability to recognize characters while failing to recognize *this*. Now, as for these Mongolians...
When a Mongol arrives, we receive them; when a Russian arrives, we receive them;
when those from Siam, Sulu, Ryukyu, or Japan arrive, we receive those from Siam, Sulu, Ryukyu, and Japan.
If one must wait until they have mastered written characters before receiving them, then the Buddha-dharma would be unable to cover heaven and earth.
The demonic treasury of heterodox and external views considers its own words to be based on antiquity and its characters to be derived from the scriptures;

yet how could it know that [the truth] encompasses the entirety of the Tripiṭaka and the Twelve Divisions of the Canon, even unto the Thirteen Classics, the Twenty-one Histories, and the various masters and hundred schools of thought?
All the texts contained within the four libraries of the world have been thoroughly integrated and harmonized with this, until every edge is smoothed away and every seam is obliterated.
Since the Buddha’s advent, one has been unable to open one's mouth; it is precisely at such a time that even the appearance of a Buddha cannot save you.
For thirty years Ānanda served as the Buddha’s attendant, yet he was constrained solely by his extensive learning and wisdom.

The Buddha rebuked him, saying: "Even if you study wisdom for a thousand days, it is not equal to studying the Way for a single day. If one does not study the Way, even a drop of water will be difficult to digest;
how much more so when Māgandika uses the heterodox and external views of devils to rashly intrude upon the matters that transcend the Buddhas and Patriarchs?"
How could there even be room for rebuke? It merely deceives those who have eyes but lack the pupils.
Before those with clear vision, the demonic form reveals itself. Zhaozhou said, "The teachers of today produce branch upon branch upon branch;
they are all far removed from the Sages. One generation is not equal to the next. It is just as Nanquan usually said:

"You must practice among those of different kinds. But how do you understand this? Nowadays, these young children with yellow mouths go about the crossroads weaving webs of sophistry, eating their fill for the sake of a meal, seeking prostrations, and gathering three or five hundred followers while claiming, "I am a good spiritual friend;
you are students. You should know that such people are the demonic forms of the Dharma-treasury and his son. From the beginning...
A hundred years ago, Zhaozhou had already reached a definitive judgment; there was no need to wait until it met the eye before knowing it.
Regarding both awakening and cultivation, Linji’s single blow was used to point people toward the truth. Mazu Daoyi criticized this, calling it "one-sided Zen" and a "shallow pit for evasion.
If one were to discuss this matter, neither wondrous words nor clever phrases would be of any use—not even a single blow.
"Ha! This too is a superfluous teaching. That the ancients were compelled to employ the staff and the shout was originally intended to cut off emotional views and directly point to the human mind.
If one interprets them through emotional views, it is a profound error. Did the ancients not say:
"A single blow of the staff or a single shout is not used as a mere blow of the staff or a mere shout"? How could they have been attached to this one shout or one blow?

The intent of this demon is merely to reject and obstruct the "stick and shout," hoping to gain a sensational victory by using the "one-circle" (*iō*) sign he has falsely established and the "real dharma" of the "double-headed four dharmas.
He fails to realize that this greatly contradicts the essential principle of the "special transmission outside the teachings," which holds that there is no dharma to be transmitted.
Furthermore, regarding awakening and cultivation, it has never been said that a single blow of the staff constitutes [the goal].
The patriarch of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas—yet the Māra-treasury falsely fabricates the sign of "one-zero" (10) as the patriarch of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas.

Is this not merely a case of evading the essential point and falling into a stagnant pitfall? If one uses the sign of "one-zero" as a staff or a shout, it is still evading the essential point and falling into a stagnant pitfall.
If one takes the sign of "one-zero" to be the patriarch of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas, it is nothing less than...
This is the den of Māra’s household. National Teacher Zhong showed the ninety-seven circles to Tan-yuan; Tan-yuan showed them to Wei and Yang.
This was a fabrication by Mo-zang, which he claimed was a "secret seal" with no written record prior to Dīpaṃkara.
On that day, when Tan-yuan showed it to Yang-shan, Yang-shan saw it and immediately burned it. Later, when Tan-yuan questioned Yang-shan about it, Yang-shan [replied]: [The text provided ends here.]
I have compiled this single volume and presented it to Yuan; nothing has been omitted or lost.
Furthermore, when Guishan drew a circle (○) with a character for "one day" (日) inside, Yangshan drew a circle on the ground with a character for "one day" inside, then wiped it away with his foot.
Guishan laughed heartily. Mazang merely marveled at how Yangshan was able to remember [the details] upon seeing him just once, deeming it a miraculous wonder;
yet he failed to discern the point in Guishan’s hearty laughter, nor did he realize it in Yangshan’s burning of the documents and his wiping of his feet.
This is what is called "Hanlu the hound chasing after clods of earth. If you say that the ninety-seven marks [of a Buddha] are extraordinary, then as for me now—
It is thus reduced from eighty-four thousand marks to eight thousand three hundred and ninety-seven marks;
again, it is reduced to seven hundred and ninety-one marks; again, to ninety-five marks; again, to ninety marks;
and finally, it is reduced to ten marks. It is just like entering the ocean to count its sands, yet continuing to traverse [the path].
What is so extraordinary about this single set of the *Huayan* (Flower Treasury) as a play?

As for the Three Essentials and Three Principles, since their proclamation by Linji, there has been no master, ancient or modern, who has not taken them up and discussed them; yet none were able to present them with clear precision.
Mazu Zhang then took the three blows of the staff from Huangbo to provide a forced interpretation, arranging them through his own fabrications. This is...
Thus, they are entirely ignorant of the Three Essentials and the Three Keys. Did not Linji say:
"In general, when expounding the School of the Patriarchs, every single phrase must embody the Three Gates; within each Essential, there must be the Three Keys.

He first mentions the two words "expounding" (*yanchang*), for expounding cannot be without words and phrases. To understand words and phrases, one must recognize the Essentials and Keys; only then can they become living phrases.

Thus, within the One Origin (*yuan*), the Three Essentials (*yao*) are inherently present; within the Three Origins, the Nine Essentials are fully contained. This is represented by the diagrams: [○@(一/(三*二))] [○@(二/(三*一))] [○@(三/(二*一))].

It is thus that the Origins establish the Essentials, and the Essentials permeate the Origins. Without the Nine Essentials, one cannot permeate the Three Origins; only upon attaining the Nine Essentials do the Three Origins become complete.
They are undivided yet divided, and divided yet undivided; such is the nature of the Origins and the Essentials.
This Dharma encompasses all phenomena without exception. Just as a single blow of the staff is not used merely as a "blow of the staff," it is clear and manifest.
Furthermore, the method of the Four Selections (*si liao jian*) is like the four seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter;
though the cold scenery changes, it never transcends this one year. This one year is precisely the blow of the staff. (Caodong)
These five ranks are also like the mutual presence of the Five Elements; they do not transcend this single breath of qi. This single breath of qi is precisely the staff and the shout.
As for Fushan’s Nine Baskets, I maintain that within a single phrase one must possess all nine baskets, and within those nine baskets, one must possess the fifty-five bundles.
Furthermore, regarding Fenyang’s Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality, I maintain that...
Within a single phrase, one must possess the ten wisdoms that accord with reality (*jñāna-satya-samprayukta*). Within this single accord with reality, one must possess the fifty-five realities.
If it is thus, how does it differ from the essential principle of the origin? To pile them up and expand upon them would be difficult to enumerate exhaustively.
In short, although the patriarchs of successive generations have changed their outward appearances to guide worldly beings, they never departed from the World-Honored One.
The meaning of the "Flower-Holding" [episode] and the "Staff and Shouting" (zhīdà) of Linji—anything departing from this is the teaching of a demon.
Moreover, these staffs and shouts can embody all dharmas and can dissolve all dharmas; how could these staffs and shouts have any fixed characteristics?
How could a single blow or shout be used as merely a single blow or shout? Mōzàng did not recognize this and labeled it "one-stump Chan. If one speaks of Chan in this way, [it is true Chan].
Even with a single wedge already belonging to many, Māra’s intention was still not satisfied; one does not know how many wedges he would have required before his demonic intent would be fulfilled.
As for the three blows of the staff and the three days of deafness—could there possibly be any other meaning?
What connection could there possibly be? Furthermore, in the preface to his *Record of the Five Schools* (*Wuzong lu*), Mo-zang employs the analogy of a *stūpa*:
he takes the nine tiers to represent the teachings of the five periods; the place where the spire is joined to the top to represent Tathāgata-dhyāna;

the thousand-foot sandalwood pillar emerging from space to pierce the summit to represent the Chan of the Patriarchs; and the five-colored lights and samādhis to represent the schools of the Five Houses.
Furthermore, they boastfully claim that their own words are like adding a single handful of sand to the pinnacle of a stūpa. Such are their various demonic doctrines.

Indeed, all aspects of the teachings belong to the category of the "trap" (quán) and the "snare" (tí)—the means to capture the meaning. When one digs the earth to plant melons, the melons that grow are not the earth itself;
when gold is extracted from ore, the ore is certainly not the gold. Thus, it is said that when the stages of the teaching are exhausted, the point where they culminate is precisely the Tathāgata.
Chan is nothing more than a dream or a delirium. Furthermore, the Great Meaning of the Westward Transmission is precisely the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*.
The five houses and their branches are all truly returning to the source; how can one divide them into Buddhas and Patriarchs, and further divide them into five houses?
Even though the Two Vehicles and the Mahāyāna are like skin, flesh, bone, and marrow—with their stages clearly distinct—they cannot be split apart.

It does not open [this matter]; how much less could it address the matter of the "Single Precept" (Dantika) that transcends all? What connection is there between the Five Radiances and the Five Schools?
It is very much like the pedantic Confucians of the Han dynasty who claimed that the twenty-eight chapters of the *Shangshu* corresponded to the twenty-eight generals of the Cloud Terrace.
The Māra’s intention was merely to cast aspersions on the Five Houses as being those who transcend Buddhas and Patriarchs;
yet, by grasping a handful of sand and placing it upon his head, he has already surpassed them. This is what the Tathāgata calls the fulfillment of a great falsehood.

Furthermore, the Māra conceals the fact that Caoxi’s “originally there is not one thing” is not the falling into the void of an externalist path; even Huineng at Huangmei had not yet [reached such a state].

The single phrase "seeing one's nature" causes one to die under its words. Now, if we discuss it solely in terms of the line "originally there is not a single thing," it certainly seems like a view of self-realization;
yet, since it subsequently says, "Where could dust and grime cling? this may also be called transcending all achievements and merit, reaching directly for that which lies above.
Even Huangmei had not yet seen his nature—the single phrase [of seeing nature] caused him to die under its words.
Let us not discuss this for now. To say that [the Master] was merely "covering people's eyes and ears" is also incorrect. How could Huangmei have intended to mislead sentient beings?
As for the response regarding "white rice without a sieve," how could Caoqi have been practicing the worldly custom of modesty?

Although the judgment regarding awakening and cultivation may seem somewhat vague, he directly rebuked those who conceal their ignorance as being "nihilistic externalists"—a point which becomes even more evident [in the following].

This is unacceptable; it can be seen that [Hongren] himself had not yet attained full realization, for he regarded the various conditioned phenomena as merely substantial entities, which is nothing but false knowledge and false views.

Furthermore, Hongren criticized Miphan (Miyun) for claiming that "sentient and insentient beings are suddenly revealed in their brilliance" as something belonging to the private sphere of the inner chambers.
He cited Yunmen’s statement, "The entire earth has not a single hair's breadth of affliction," as a turning phrase (*zhuǎnjù*), rather than [accepting it as the ultimate].
To see a single form as "half-carrying" (ban-ti) requires one to know that there is also a time for "full-carrying" (quan-ti) to serve as proof.
Little do they realize that the finality of Míyún’s single blow is precisely the full-carrying at every point;
it is the power by which both the sentient and the insentient are suddenly and radiantly manifested. Since they have not yet reached Míyún’s place of awakening, they merely cite [the words of] Yún.

Regarding the phrases of the gates, they are joined together and covered over, like a fox relying on a city wall or a rat taking refuge in a village shrine. This causes people not to dare to burn or smoke them out;
yet in the end, the city wall and the shrine remain simply the city wall and the shrine, while the fox and the rat remain simply the fox and the rat.
How could one ever confuse the fox and the rat with the city wall and the shrine? Hongren further said: "Master Sanfeng was a teacher of Tiantong; he followed his source and lineage."

"Our master was Sanfeng; he was indeed our 'Dharma-milk' (the one who nourished us with the Dharma). We do not need to ask about our karmic offenses, for we have already confessed them of our own accord.

Is this not because, having never met with reality, there is not a single dharma to be attained? Thus it is called the 'source and stream. Since what has been obtained is based on evidence and proof, how could one falsely claim it to be 'Dharma-milk'?
When one's practice reaches full penetration and one recognizes one’s own mind, the way of teacher and disciple merges like a needle meeting its eye."
They accord with one another; like the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching, this seal of the mind from of old is simply to say:
"You are thus, and I am also thus. How could there ever have been a single dharma to transmit? Moreover, in reality, not a single dharma can be obtained.

That which is transmitted and received in a single word—only such as this may be called the milk of the Dharma. If one harbors the false knowledge and false views of the Mara of Concealment and Endurance, [it is not so].
The external teachers and their disciples take secret oral transmissions as "milk," yet this is actually "poisonous milk. How can it be called the "Dharma-milk"?
I, the Emperor, maintain that these demonic hoards are not entirely devoid of knowledge; they simply left their masters too early, resulting in afflictions and deluded thoughts.
Arrogant and conceited, they seek only to triumph, desiring to stand alone at the head of the Dharma gate.
They disregard the fact that their own feet have not yet touched the ground, wishing instead to display the artifice of "wisdom exceeding that of the teacher.

They fixate on technical names and categories such as the "One-Pointed Mind" and the "Four Dharmas of the Double Head," intending to compose works that surpass their masters. Thus, they constantly establish one delusion after another.
He then compiled and excerpted from literary and historical records, weaving together the words and phrases of ancient masters to substantiate his point.
This is just as Yongming said: "With a limited mind, one gives rise to a view of partiality; one restricts the vastness of the great void and defines the boundaries of the Dharma-realm.
Consequently, the emotions of discrimination do not transcend the realm of manifold dust, and thus [one fails to enter] the realm of True Suchness."
Above, the mental mechanism is stirred; within the ocean of quiescent extinction, the waves of consciousness surge. Within the confines of the sensory channels, views are maintained;

through a crack in the wall, one steals a glimpse of light. One establishes the duality of subject and object, gives rise to interpretations of superior and inferior, and aligns the phrasing to fixate upon the ultimate meaning.
To analyze each point according to its school: how could the wing-beats of a gnat ever rival those of the great Peng? How could the glow of a firefly compare to the brilliance of the sun?
As for the words and writings of the Magu (Māgha) father and son, a few sentences from Yongming are sufficient to judge them exhaustively.

At that time, Magu sought to please the scholar-officials and secured their protection, causing the monastic community to vie with one another like dogs chasing clods of earth, thereby leading [to these consequences].

They constitute a distinct lineage; their followers remain widely dispersed among the populace to this day. It is due to this that the School of the Lineage (Zongmen) has declined and fallen into ruin.

If I do not now suppress and expel them, when will the demonic teachings be extinguished? Order that all woodblocks for the *Tengyur* (Bka’-’gyur), the *Collected Works of Tsongkhapa* (Tsong-kha-pa’i gsung-’bum), the *Origins of the Five Schools* (Gzhan-stong dang rang-stong sogs kyi grub-mtha’i rtsa-ba), the *Defenses of the Five Schools* (Grub-mtha’ lnga’i bsrung-ba), and other such texts be destroyed. [Monks...]

It is strictly forbidden for anyone to privately collect [these texts]. Should anyone be found in violation of this decree by concealing them, they shall be apprehended and prosecuted under the law of irreverence (*agaurava*).
Furthermore, a treatise titled *Wujia jiuyi shu* (A Book on Rescuing the Five Schools) has been composed, which refutes [erroneous views] point-by-point;

it is now carved and included within the Canon so that those of future generations possessing correct knowledge and vision may recognize these demonic heterodoxies and harbor no further doubts. — By Tian Tong Mi Yun Wu.
Regarding the branch of the Lower Dharma Treasury (Xià Fǎzàng), all its followers shall be investigated in detail by the Provincial Governors and Viceroys of their respective jurisdictions.
All of its lineages shall be completely eliminated, and they shall never again be permitted to enter the ancestral monasteries.

Only those who are able to study under other masters elsewhere, attain correct insight and views, and subsequently inherit another lineage shall be permitted to hold the whisk (act as a master). On the day this edict arrives, [it shall be enforced] at all ancestral monasteries throughout the empire.
If the person presiding over the opening of the hall is a descendant of the Fa-zang lineage, the bells and wooden clappers must be removed immediately, and he is not permitted to preach the Dharma.
The local official shall then select someone from another branch of the Tiantong lineage to succeed as the Abbot. All ancestral temples have been renowned monasteries since ancient times.
Furthermore, monastic properties (chángzhù) originally belong to the ten directions. I have merely expelled the heterodox followers of Xu;
this has no original connection with monastic properties, nor does it concern those who study under the ten directions. Let local officials not misunderstand my intent.
Not a single blade of grass or a single tree within monastic properties shall be disturbed, and the disciples who come to study shall not be startled or troubled.

To practice what is unwholesome is itself a violation of my will. For instance, the monastics under Master Yi stubbornly cling to demonic teachings, claiming that their "Dharma-milk" is unerring and that they perfectly accord with the intent of the "Separate Transmission" and have truly attained the lineage of Linji.

Yet, they refuse to submit with sincere hearts or to awaken from their dream and sober up from their intoxication. Let them come to see me so that they may present their case face-to-face. I—[the Emperor]—[shall hear them].

I shall personally compare their teachings with those of the Buddha-dharma. If they are found to surpass my own views and their discourse proves even more sublime, I shall immediately withdraw my original decree and re-establish the Sanfeng school.

However, if they have exhausted their skillful means and remain defiant, refusing to submit despite my appeals through secular law, I shall punish them severely according to the laws of the world; do not leave a legacy of regret for future generations.

I regret this. Heretical doctrines have long been prone to deluding the human mind; yet, distinguishing between the inner and outer paths, as well as what is right or wrong, correct or false, is not difficult.
That which takes the self-nature (*svabhāva*) as its basis for practice and exposition is called "inner";

that which does not take the self-nature as its basis, but consists of deluded practice and deluded exposition, is called "outer. The tradition of the Śākya school has always opened the gateway to the fundamental source.

As for the "External" (Wai) [section]: it is like the Purple Yang True Man (Ziyang Zhenren), who, following his *Wuzhen Pian* (Treatise on Realizing the Truth), separately authored an "External Collection" (*Waiji*) that did not contain a single word concerning the Daoist school, but instead expounded the Chan school from the standpoint of the original nature in every instance.
Among the masters of the ancestral Chan school, there have been few who were as lucid and unimpeded as he, encompassing such insights within only a few chapters.
To see [them] and designate them as "external"—is this not permissible? As for those like the True Man, they are those who internalize the external.
As for those like the followers of Māgandika, who plundered the Buddha-dharma and destroyed the Buddha-dharma, they are those who externalize the internal. This is the pure lineage of Caoxi.
How can such turbid currents be tolerated? All the more so this demonic teaching, which has been disseminated among humans by the progeny of Māra.

Those of later generations have received its inexhaustible lingering poison; as it concerns the very faculty of the Dharma-eye and the life-force of wisdom, how could I, the Emperor, bear not to discern right from wrong?
To all under heaven and future generations, there shall surely be those who receive my profound grace, like eyebrows trailing down to the ground.
One must know that this demon must be discerned, for it is a demon within the realm of the Buddha;
one must distinguish this anomaly, for it is a deviation within the midst of sameness. The Transmission says: "To cease heterodox teachings and rectify the human heart.
Indeed, to eliminate the heterodox and support the orthodox is something I cannot help but do. Let us examine the Three Teachings...

The designation [of these two traditions] began during the Jin and Wei dynasties. Later generations, bound by the hollow reputation of venerating Confucianism, consequently harbored the intent to disparage and reject the two [other] schools.

I, the Emperor, reflect that Laozi was a contemporary of Confucius; his purpose in inquiring about the rites and the praise of him as "a dragon" are recorded in the historical annals, proving he did not belong to a different teaching from Confucius. As for the Buddha, he was born in the Western Regions before Confucius.
For several decades, had Śākyamuni and Confucius appeared together in the same era, they would surely have exchanged mutual salutations and respect.
For the Five Canons, the Nine Classics, the Three Substances, and the Six Acts of Conduct constitute the great axes and minor cords for governing the world;
these were indeed established by the Two Emperors and Three Kings, yet were fully synthesized by our Most Sage. Nevertheless, one must necessarily be liberated from all conceptual signs (*lakṣaṇa*).
Only after this can the mind then penetrate the nature and principle of all things and phenomena; this is an absolute certainty.
In later generations, some have compared the sun, moon, and stars to the three teachings, asserting that one is the sun and another is the moon.
To designate such-and-such as a "star" is not, in my view, necessary; one need not harbor such restrictive views.
It is sufficient to take the sun, moon, and stars—which are fundamentally of the same light—as a metaphor for how the three teachings differ in their applications while sharing the same essence.

By examining the *Waiji* (External Collection) of the Real Man Ziyang, one will naturally have no doubts regarding the principle that the Way of the Immortals and the Buddha are one and the same. The Way.
Since they are thus unified, one can all the more be free from doubt regarding the teaching that the three religions coexist without contradiction.

I have therefore appended this note here, so that those in future generations who seek the true and ultimate principles of nature may cast aside sectarian boundaries and broaden their understanding; of this, I hold high expectations. This is a special edict.
The Fourth Day of the Fourth Month in the Eleventh Year of the Yongzheng Era. An Imperial Composition:
*Jianmo Bianyi Lu* (Record of Selecting Demons and Discerning Heresies), Volume One.
The Demon Ren said: "Does not the Buddha say: 'I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the Wondrous Mind of Nirvana, and the Reality-Body without..."

This is the mark. This subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate is entrusted to Mahākāśyapa. Now, the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* is precisely the vast and fundamental essence of the mind possessed by all of us.
The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is the adamantine eye that clarifies both light and darkness, and which shares equally in death and birth.
Mind is the eye; the eye is the mind. It is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) that is devoid of marks (*alakṣaṇa*). As it is said:
It is like the seal of a nation: it has no beginning, no end, and no middle; yet within that single seal, its patterns and lines are fully complete.

If one wishes to investigate the mind, then even if one searches through the three periods of time vertically and across the ten directions horizontally, the investigation would still not be exhaustive. How could this be?
Have you read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* regarding the investigation of the mind in its seven locations?

It is a pity that within an assembly of hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, the World-Honored One held up a flower—neither inside, nor outside, nor in between—directly pointing to the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha.
Yet we have been rendered utterly dull by the demon of "endurance," which has stifled the vast mind-body inherently possessed by us.
"The entire earth is a single eye"—this is the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the adamantine eye of simultaneous clarity and obscurity, and of simultaneous death and birth.
How could it merely be a case of mistaking a servant for a master? Furthermore, how can clarity and obscurity, or life and death, be anything other than this?
"Vajra-eye! Vajra-eye! How can there still be light and darkness, birth and death?
To speak of a 'bright vajra-eye' is already unattainable, let alone a 'dark vajra-eye. To speak of a 'born vajra-eye' is already unattainable, let alone a 'dead vajra-eye.
No matter how Meng Babang goes about it, he is much like Han Lu chasing a clod of earth. Even if one could speak of it,"
If there were even a hair’s breadth of difference, then heaven and earth would be as far apart.

As for the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana, the signless reality-essence, and this subtle and wonderful Dharma gate—if they could be explained or annotated through words, why would it have been necessary for Kāśyapa alone to be worthy of receiving the entrustment?
Furthermore, the Three Pitakas and Twelve Divisions of the Canon have long ago been expounded so exhaustively that they are as leak-proof as a vessel filled to the brim with water.
Why, then, did he single out a flower at the very end? Two people facing one another, feigning strangeness, to deceive men and women throughout the world and for all generations.

He further claimed that "the mind is the eye, and the eye is the mind. If this were so, would it not follow that apart from the eye there is no mind, and apart from the mind there is no eye? To the full extent of...
Regarding the "ground" (dharma-realm): what within it could be said not to be mind? Regarding the "entirety of the earth": what within it could be said not to be the eye?
To take this very mind and eye and claim them to be the "Dharma King’s Treasure Seal" is exactly like forging an official seal; how could it be a true imperial seal?

Furthermore, a single seal possesses both its pattern and its texture, and it grasps and upholds the three periods of time. Now, as for these "three periods," they are the ultimate reality of no-boundary.

The reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is without limits. If one were to liken it to a single seal in which both the pattern and the grain are complete, one might say it has no prior limit or posterior limit;

yet this is still merely a vague approximation. How can it be said that there is no middle limit? Furthermore, before the sealing there is the prior limit, and once sealed there is the posterior limit;
so what could be meant by "no prior or posterior limits"? How does this differ from the discourse on the three time-periods (*traiyadhvika*)?
Regarding the discussion:
Mōnin said, "When it reached its degeneration, intellectual understanding arose perversely; therefore, it could not help but transform into 'sparks' (kikō) and 'staffs and shouts' (bōkatsu).

Furthermore, when that too reached its degeneration, it could not help but transform into the establishment of core tenets (shūshu). Once the core tenets were established, [it became] like the three..."
The rites and music of this era are complete; even if a thousand sages were to appear in succession, they could not alter them.
Now, the corruption of discourse lies in its obsession with mind and nature (*cittatā*), while the corruption of the "staff and shout" (*bōhé*) lies in its disruption of the lineage.

Therefore, those who seek awakening through the staff and shout must recognize the malady of disrupting the lineage, establish the four types of shouts to harmonize them, discern the fundamental essentials, and provide a comprehensive seal that cuts off the stream.
The fundamental principles for those who attain awakening through the words of the master’s responsive activity include the four prohibitions,
the five ranks, the six aspects, and various gates of samādhi; the fundamental principles of the Caodong, Guiyang, and Fayan schools are such as these.
From the patriarchs of old until now, they spoke all day long yet never spoke at all. How could a single word ever deviate from the fundamental principle?

If it deviates from the fundamental principle, what is there in such speech worth saying? It is said that when things first degenerated, [the masters] employed "critical edges" (jīfēng) and "staffs and shouts" (bàng hè);
when they degenerated further, they established fixed principles (dìng zōngzhì). Once the principles were fixed, it was as if the rites and music of the Three Dynasties were fully restored; even so—

That thousands of sages have appeared in succession yet could not alter it—how could one rashly plagiarize the residual dregs of Zhuangzi and presume to confront the matters that transcend the Buddhas and patriarchs?
If this were so, then what are called "pithy words," "staffs," "shouts," and the "essential tenets" would be nothing other than substantial dharmas.
This is indeed false speech; this is indeed a fabrication of the bizarre; this is merely dragging through mud and water, unable to save even oneself.
Such is the reason why a demon is called a demon. It is thus, it is thus. Furthermore, it is said that Linji and Yunmen established the fundamental tenets such as "building" and "shouting."
Caoshui, Shishuang, and Fayan established the "Four Prohibitions" and other fundamental principles; yet they dogmatically asserted their own positions and arbitrarily created distinctions.
Like owls and rats that relish excrement, they dragged down the phoenix to share a single pit with them for food, thereby burying and killing the Five Houses of Chan.
Mozhu said: "The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye—how easy it would be to speak of! Precisely because it is not easy to speak of, the former sages kept it secret and allowed for its awakening.
Precisely because it is not easy to awaken to, it has remained submerged until now, never being brought forth."
Now, since these [teachings] have long been submerged, there must surely be Great Beings who return by virtue of their vows to arise and rescue them.
Yet, in the process of such rescue, it is inevitable that one will encounter taboos; thus, there are those who harbor doubts and those who engage in slander.

It has even reached the point where they have been poisoned, cast into prison, branded on the face, and flogged on the back—conditions that were unavoidable even for the ancients, let alone in our own day. As the saying goes:
When a string is too taut, it snaps; this is the natural course of things. The Elder of Sanfeng encountered such an inevitable calamity and ultimately escaped it.
As for those things that cannot be avoided, must they not depend on oneself?
Now, as for this one great matter, even Śākyamuni Buddha could not keep it secret, nor could Śākyamuni Buddha hold it back.
Having preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, the Three Piṭakas and Twelve Divisions of the Canon remain intact; how then could he have kept it secret?
Furthermore, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the empty space of the ten directions all remain present; how could he have taken them up and kept them secret? Nevertheless...
For forty-nine years he preached the Dharma—the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures—yet he never spoke a single word. How can one grasp this?
Mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the empty space of the ten directions are preaching in every dust mote and in every land, preaching with blazing intensity.
Yet those who awaken do so of themselves; those who are deluded remain deluded of themselves. How, then, could one take hold of this and grasp it? Mazu then said: "Precisely because..."
It is not easily spoken of; therefore, the former sages kept it secret and waited for one’s own awakening.

Precisely because it is not easily awakened to, it has remained submerged and failed to be brought forth, serving as nothing more than a drowsy prattle in broad daylight. Within this, there is primordial purity; this land is primordially the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
How could there ever have been a scene of hurried confusion, of disheveled hair and the binding of a cap? Yet such is what they call their teacher.
Māgūi buried this matter and did not mention it; yet [Dongshan] brought it up, thereby offending a taboo and leaving the calamity unresolved.
Māgūi, knowing full well he could not escape it, stood forth courageously to accept the responsibility and brought it up. How pitiable, how pitiable!
What suffering, what suffering!
Māra Ren said: "Now, as for the writing of the world, one gathers dots and strokes to form characters; one gathers characters to form phrases;
and one gathers phrases to form chapters. In the formation of a chapter, there must necessarily be traces of sequence, beginning, and conclusion."
Only with a seal is there none [of this]. It is the same with the study of the Way: there is small awakening and there is great awakening. Great awakening is like a seal;

small awakening is like a collection of written characters. At such a time, unless one has ascended into the hall of a master of vast caliber, there is no one who does not find satisfaction in the dots, strokes, characters, and phrases.
For this reason, Xinghua, through Dajue, came to see the late Master Linji; so it was with Luopo.
It was through Jia Shan’s single phrase that pierced the secure barrier that Huanglong inspired Wen Yue, and Yunmen refined his realization at Xuefeng.
As for Guankui’s journey to Moshan and Miaoxi’s following of Foguo, these were all cases of awakening once and then awakening again, even reaching the point of eighteen great awakenings.
Yet what else could this be? It was simply a matter of diligent cultivation and following after the truth.
The seals above merely join their patterns and stop there. Fengxue said: "The Mind-Seal of the Patriarchs resembles the mechanism of an iron ox:
when it departs, it is sealed; when it stays, it is broken. Even when sealing mud, sealing water, or sealing space, it leaves no trace.
I have often contemplated this deeply: from the Plucking of the Flower until Mazu and Linji, there were thirty-nine transmissions. And...
This seal was recast; its radiance and sharpness spread in all directions, such that one would lose their eyesight upon even a sidelong glance at it—this is what is meant by "the seal of water.
From Xinghua to Yuanwu, Dahui, Huqiu, and Ying’an, there were eleven further transmissions.

Yet these elders sang ever more loftily and reached ever more unfathomable heights, like dragons transforming and tigers crouching, or like wind rushing and lightning flashing. This is what is meant by...
This is the seal of emptiness. After reaching the Flower Treasury World (Huazang), this seal gradually vanished. Alas!

Our late master Sanfeng excavated it from deep within the springs, polished its luster, scraped away its grime, and restored it to its original appearance for use in our own day—this is what is meant by "sealing the mud.
Why is this so? Because the Great Dharma of Linji had been extinguished for seven hundred years when the Master appeared.
After [the clay] was exhausted, he called out once, but there was no response. He called out a second time, but there was still no response.
He called out a third time; his voice choked and his breath failed him. He looked around in every direction, wandering about, yet there was no one to harmonize with him.
Thus, having no choice, he had to imprint [his words] upon the clay to await those of future generations throughout the world. How bitter his heart must have been! As for what is called...
What is "mud" (ni)? It refers to the inability of the seal-impression to transform. It is not that the seal-impression cannot transform; it is that the mud cannot transform. Alas!

Our lifelong ultimate essentials and those who fail to penetrate the pinnacle of these essentials differ from one another by no more than a hundred paces—just as one who strikes with a staff until the end differs from another. How can we not be cautious? How can we not be cautious?
Be cautious! Be on guard—be cautious! Conceal it and protect it, awaiting the one who is destined for it. Should someone like Linji appear, he shall burn the talisman and split the seal;
he will take the five-colored patterns drawn upon the void and bring them into dark, perfect harmony with the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma).
This is the vow of Sanfeng, and it is also the vow of the successive patriarchs of old.
The Three Seals are: first, the Seal of Space; second, the Seal of Water; third, the Seal of Mud. Regarding these, masters of antiquity and today have proclaimed:
"When mountains, rivers, and the great earth all vanish away, and the past and future limits are severed, this is called the Seal of Space.

When seeing mountains as still being mountains, and seeing water as still being water, this is called the Seal of Water. When at the final, secure barrier, one’s feet tread upon solid ground, this is called the Seal of Mud."

Some say: "To see emptiness or see existence, while a 'view' still persists, is called 'sealing the mud. To be neither empty nor existent, yet still falling into the extremes of middle and side, is called 'sealing the water.

If one reaches the point where even 'one' is not established, where ground and position are not set up, and where both middle and side are discarded—such as it is for a Tathāgata, such as it is—this is called 'sealing the sky. Others say: "The three seals are not three barriers; they are all..."
The ultimate limit is such that if emptiness comes, it is like emptiness, which is called "sealing the sky"; if existence comes, it is like existence, which is called "sealing the mud";

and if that which is neither empty nor existent comes, it is like that which is neither empty nor existent, which is called "sealing the water. Although these three explanations differ in appearance, they are identical in essence.
In essence, this never departs from right knowledge and right view; it is not something to be known or understood through intellectual consciousness or speculative calculation.
Regarding the "Patience of Mara" (māra-kṣānti), it is said that from the "Plucking of the Flower" [by Vimalakīrti] down to Linji, this seal was recast—this is what is called "sealing the water.

From Xinghua down to Yuanwu, the song grew ever higher and became increasingly unfathomable—this is what is called "sealing the sky. By the time of Huayan, the seal was lost; by the time of Mazu, it was further obscured.
Furthermore, having recovered it from the depths of the deep spring, one polishes its luster and scrapes away its grime, suddenly restoring it to its former appearance so that it may seal the clay.

This suggests that this seal is identical to the seal of a royal decree; it clarifies that within one’s own hand there is the Buddha’s Imperial Seal of State, and that one is truly the legitimate heir of the King of Awakening. In terms of worldly law, such a person would be considered a traitor.
As for those who speak of the supramundane Dharma, they may indeed be called mad and deluded. Now, even the succession of emperors depends upon serving Heaven and receiving its Mandate;
it does not depend on the presence or absence of the Imperial Seal. How much more so for the true decree of the Awakened King—how could there be any seal or stamp to be transmitted?
If there were such a thing, it would imply that phenomena are established as substantial entities. Such a view belongs to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
A demonic obstruction. He confessed and admitted it himself. Mochizuki Ryōin said:

"The various patriarchs—four, seven, two, and three—manifested many principles according to the capacities of their audiences. However, the use of the staff, the shout, and the sharp point of the encounter began with Mazu.
The various elder masters failed to discern Sanpō’s true intention; instead, they harbored resentment toward him for being different from themselves. To this point...
You wish to obliterate the Dharma-seal transmitted from antiquity, claiming that "one blow reaches the bottom" and that you do not establish any fixed patterns;
yet you alone fail to consider from whom this staff and shout originally originated. If you claim that this staff directly connects back to Mazu, [you must acknowledge its source].
Thus, from Mazu upward, the use of the staff and the shout had never been employed.

If one were to claim that this staff still derives from Mazu’s lineage, then from Mazu downward, there has never been a lack of a fundamental teaching (zongzhi). Which of these two positions is correct?

If one claims to have established one's own school independently, without receiving it from another, what does this do for the staff and the shout? Examining the matter from every angle, it truly lacks any foundational basis.
On the contrary, you wish to refute those who support and rescue the wisdom-life, labeling them as having no teacher, as heterodox, or as deviant.
Who could say that such claims are credible? Now that Sanfeng has passed away, yet your refutations have arrived once more;
how then can my own defense cease? This is not for the sake of debate, but for the sake of salvation.
As for "the savior": when a person encounters hardship, I rescue them; when a person is facing death, I restore them to life.

Now, as for following the fundamental principle of the Buddhas and Patriarchs from above—the fact that there was no birth prior to Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja and no extinction after Maitreya—this is not even a supramundane dharma, so how could there be mundane conventions? What suffering or hardship could there be? What could be gained or lost?
It is lost. Furthermore, by what means could one rescue it? The minds of sentient beings have no place where they do not take as an object;
only that they cannot take Prajñā as an object. Now, amidst the clear blue sky and bright sun, suddenly wild flowers arise;

one falsely gives rise to a mind of rescue, falsely establishes the appearance of rescue, falsely utters words of rescue, and falsely creates the realm of rescue. Setting aside for a moment that there is no need for rescue, in truth, it is also not received.
"Save me! Yet this great lie is established, and one falls into the Avīci Hell; then, though one wishes to save oneself, it cannot be done.
Furthermore, is there a duality between the fundamental teaching (zongzhi) and the staff and shout (banghe), or is there no duality?

For example, with Sanfeng Fazang, the staff and shout are Sanfeng, and the fundamental teaching is Fazang. Thus, one might wish to affirm Fazang while rejecting Sanfeng, thereby extinguishing Sanfeng."

When Shishuang [Zhuan] sought to rescue the Dharma-treasury, his breath was gasping and his composure utterly ruined; with hair disheveled and his cap’s sash hanging loose, one could not help but call him a madman.
Yet, when it comes to the "staff and shout" (banghe), he took Mazu as his own model—how could he have known that these had existed even before the time of Dīpaṃkara?
Furthermore, consider the World-Honored One holding up a flower: was holding up a flower not a staff and a shout? Kāśyapa’s smile: was that smile not a staff and a shout?
Extending this principle further: Heaven has the four seasons—spring, autumn, winter, and summer; wind, rain, frost, and dew are the *kan* (staff) and *ge* (shout) of Heaven.

The earth sustains the divine breath; wind and thunder give form to things, and all creatures emerge into life; these are the *kan* and *ge* of Earth. The hawk soars to the heavens and the fish leap in the deep abyss;
these are the *kan* and *ge* of the myriad things. The fingernails grow and the hair lengthens; the pulses throb and the vital energy circulates; [the act of] eating...
The inner [attire] passes through it, while the outer is wrapped in clothing; this is the "staff and shout" (banghe) of the person. How can it be said that these first appeared only after Mazu?

Furthermore, the staff and shout are merely names and forms (*nāma-rūpa*). They are like the *guān* (cap): in the Xia dynasty it was called *shōu*, in the Yin it was called *xǔ*, in the Zhou it was called *biàn*, and from the Qin and Han dynasties onward it was called *guān*.
It was only after the Wei and Jin dynasties that the name *mào* (hat) first appeared. Today, then, as for the *guān* and...
Caps and hats are all given names, yet those called *shou*, *xu*, and *bian* have no such designations.
To discuss the matter in essence, they are nothing more than implements for warming the head and adorning the head; what need is there to inquire whether their names differ?

The staff and the shout (*banghe*) are likewise nothing more than a single mechanism for establishing all phenomena and dissolving all phenomena, intended to cause people to realize the fundamental principle for themselves. As for their falling [upon one],...

While the state [of realization] does not involve the fundamental principle (zongzhi), its functioning never departs from it. How could one possibly weigh the use of staff and shouts against the fundamental principle?
What difference is there between this and weighing a crown against the head? It would not be unreasonable to call such a person ignorant.
To speak of the "fundamental principle" once and then again of the "fundamental principle"—is this not what is meant by the so-called "school" (zong)?
The gist is this: these are the teachings of Māra and not the true intent of our school. To take the teachings of Māra as the true intent—how could one avoid severing the life-force of human wisdom?

Māraruci said: "For forty-nine years he preached the Dharma, all of it a provisional shielding according to the capacities of beings; it was only upon reaching the 'Plucking of the Flower' that [the truth] finally..."

This is the principle of being uniquely honored throughout all heavens and the world below. My late teacher said that the single flower was brought forth to perfectly realize the vastness of the mind-dharma within our own hearts;

this is no mere speculative talk. Your letter claims that taking "a single blow" as the total presentation of the uniquely honored state implies that anything else besides this is the teaching of demons.
How could this be the principle of the total presentation of the uniquely honored state that I speak of? As for what I have...

This refers to being uniquely honored. Just as the Son of Heaven is the sole sovereign over the myriad states, what I call "the total presentation" (quanti) is like all the myriad states being within the transformative influence of the Son of Heaven: a single edict brings order to the world;
a single word is responded to by the world; appointing one official or assigning one office, and the world receives its grace. This is the teaching of the world.

All who are transformed through teaching and transformation return to this; therefore, it is called "the Solely Honored. It is not that there exists something else, outside of the world, that is the Solely Honored, nor that there exists a world separate from the Solely Honored.
The same applies to the Dharma of the Mind. In the Caodong (Dong) school, there are five ranks, among which the position of the Sovereign is honored.
In the Linji school, there are four categories of guest and host, among which the "Host within the Host" is esteemed. In the Yunmen school, there is the "Whole... [text fragment ends].
*Dibandhi*. Taking the *quandi* (total raising) as the ultimate, there is within the teachings the "Ocean-Seal Samādhi" (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).
This means that the myriad phenomena, including all things in the universe, are entirely within the radiance of the ocean; without beginning or end, they all manifest simultaneously.
This is what is called the "solely honored total raising. As for the single blow from the staff that opens the scriptures, it is called the "mind beyond the Dharma," and it is called...
"Dry Wisdom" (śuṣka-vipaśyanā) refers merely to being solitary; it is acceptable to be solitary. However, I do not know what it means to be "venerable.
When the World-Honored One was first born, he pointed one hand toward heaven and one hand toward the earth, walked seven steps, and declared: "In the heavens above and on the earth below..."
"I alone am honored. Yunmen said, "If I, this old monk, had seen him, I would have struck him dead with one blow and fed him to the dogs, just to ensure peace in the world.
Xuedou said, "Yunmen’s words contain two points of failure: one point where no one can bear his enmity, and one point where his kindness is too great to be repaid.
When the ancient masters raise these themes for proclamation, what exactly is their ultimate meaning?
This is a matter of mental activity. Furthermore, according to the records of the Western Heavens (India), what kind of mental activity is this?
If you cannot understand it, you will enter hell as swiftly as a shot arrow; if you can understand it, you will likewise enter hell as swiftly as a shot arrow.
Whether you understand it or not, all under heaven is at peace. Why is this? Because above the heavens and below the heavens, I alone am honored. Thus said Miphan (Miyun).
To claim that "a single blow is the total presentation" (*quan-ti*) and the sole honored truth is still merely a vague approximation, like a distorted melody;
it is truly like the parable of the demon and the patience, where the characters "wu" (烏) and "an" (焉) are mistaken for "ma" (馬). What end can there be to such confusion?

Furthermore, you have arbitrarily conflated the Five Ranks of Ruler and Subject with the Four Guests and Hosts, asserting that among the Five Ranks, the position of the Ruler is supreme, while among the Four Guests and Hosts, the "Host within the Host" is most noble. This not only contradicts the principle of the "Sole Honored One"...
This has no connection whatsoever with the intent of the Venerable One. Furthermore, within the five ranks, could there be four who are lowly and one who is honored?
Within the four guest-host relationships, could there be three who are base and one who is noble? The five ranks are like the five fingers of a single hand;

the four guest-host relationships are like the four corners of a single room. Is it not the case that looking east makes it west, and observing south results in north? Within the same [reality], there is...
Within diversity there is sameness; how could one truly take one, two, three, four, or five and attempt to synthesize them?

As for characterizing Yunmen’s "one blow" as "dry wisdom" (qianhui) and as the "solitude of the solitary," this is nothing less than a burning defiance of the heart, a reckless and arrogant denunciation of one's own ancestor—there is simply nothing more to be said.
The words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are all but direct mind and direct action. It is only...

This was spoken directly to the person; those who understand will understand of themselves, while those who do not understand will simply not understand. When has there ever been any accommodation or concealment according to circumstances?

Mozhen said: "Whenever the former sages manifested such a circle (○) or such a dot (●), it was like the hexagram drawings of Fu Xi;
though they lacked written characters, the principles of heaven, earth, and the myriad things were fully contained therein.
The dharma-verses transmitted by the seven Buddhas and the patriarchs are like the 'Appended Phrases' (Xici) of King Wen; as for what is called the 'double-headed single-knot,' there is none..."

Regarding the *mun* (text) and *mim-in* (seal-mudrā), are they not like the lines and images of a hexagram? It is because one uses this ○-sign to encompass verbal expression, and through verbal expression enters this ○-sign;
thus, they do not conflict with one another. Formerly, when Great Master Linji first resided at Zhenzhou, he said to Puhua and Ke Fu:

When Renbing asked about the meaning of the Master’s intent, Linji responded with three segments and two blows, clarifying them through the four critical examinations (*si liaojian*).
Thereupon, the fundamental tenets of Yuan, Yao, Guest and Host, and Shining and Function were established. Indeed, it was Huangbo who received Linji.
Yet, after three blows of the heavy staff, Nanquan established himself in such a manner; was this not the very image and judgment (*xiàngtuàn*) of those three blows?

However, the hexagram has no image or judgment; the principle of the hexagram remains as it is. If one were to know the image and judgment by means of the hexagram, [the principle would remain unchanged].
By means of the *xiang* (images) and *tuan* (judgments), one comes to know the hexagrams; yet the principle of the hexagrams remains as it ever was.

Suppose there were a person today who took a single day to represent *Qian* (Heaven). Would such a person truly understand *Qian*?

During the time of Fuxi, there were no written characters. That which is referred to as "Qian" (乾) was not this symbol drawn by Fuxi, nor was it the character that King Wen later annotated with the words "Qianyuan, heng, li, zhen. As for the circle (○), what kind of written character could it possibly be?
Furthermore, how could it be understood as being on the side of written characters? Although the Book of Changes concerns the heavens, the earth, and the myriad things...
The principles thereof are complete. However, these are merely secondary matters. If one discusses their essential purport, they all serve to perfect human relations (*renlun*).
Within the sphere of human relations, myriad things are not uniform; each must change according to the times to ensure that what is appropriate is attained.
There must certainly be a way [to understand this]. The Sage wished to categorize it point by point, as is done in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-vinaya*, yet he could not exhaust its profound intricacies.
Consequently, he employed various metaphors to encompass it. Each of the Four Sages composed their own *Yi* (Changes);
while the Way remains the same, their meanings do not overlap. When compared with the Buddhist gate, this is most evident in the Vinaya gate.

This is similar [to what follows], yet it is not clearly understood here; often, one is led to employ facile language as if it were the "special transmission outside the teachings" of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

These are the assertions of those who have never even set foot within the gateways of these two schools. For example, regarding the Vinaya texts within the Tripiṭaka, which specific articles would obstruct the fundamental tenets?

They have fashioned diagrams of hexagrams, using the dharma-transmission verses of the Seven Buddhas and Patriarchs as the *Xici* (Appended Phrases), while taking the "double-headed single-knot" and "textless secret seals" fabricated by their own masters as the *yaoxiang* (hexagram lines and images). This is truly like striking a sounding board in the dark or feeling one's way with a candle;
it is groundlessly to defame the Sages and corrupt the Worthies, even to the point of claiming that Linji struck Kefu and Puhua used the Four Kinds of Teachings.
To simplify it: thus, doctrines such as "Original Essence and Function," "Guest and Host," and "Illumination and Application" were established.

The ancestral masters' *jiyuan* (opportune encounters) are like a cool breeze or a great mass of fire; they cannot be grasped and cannot be approached. How could there be any "blows of the staff" today?
"Ho! On the following day, I composed several lines of verse to clarify and verify this: "To know this Patriarch, even the command to wash one's feet is unnecessary.

Now, to take the fourfold critical examination (*si liaojian*), the primary and secondary, guest and host, and illumination and function as the fundamental tenet—this is not merely mistaking the head for a reflection;
it is mistaking the shadow of the feet for the head. This is not merely a tangle of words regarding the "fundamental essentials" (*yuanyao*);

even the Three Baskets and Twelve Divisions of the Canon could not possibly be the fundamental tenet of Gautama. To claim that Gautama took these as his fundamental tenet would be to slander the Buddha.

The *Mozang Song* regarding the public case of the World-Honored One ascending the seat: Mañjuśrī strikes the gavel. It is said that everyone attempts to grasp this before the World-Honored One has even ascended the seat;
they have already missed it. Furthermore, he offers this verse: "The rain has passed, the mountain waters flow, and the sound of the water mill rings.
Where could Mañjuśrī have struck his gavel? There is no need to inquire about head or foot; let the precious seat descend as it may."

[The Master] ascends with [the assembly]. The World-Honored One ascends the seat. Mañjuśrī strikes the gavel and says: "Observe closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King; the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One descends from the seat. Now, since he has already ascended the seat, the Dharma of the Dharma-King is entirely without concealment. Mañjuśrī having thus announced it...

The striking of the gavel is finished. Having reached the point of complete clarity, he again performs the "many-mouthed" *āpavarga* (concluding ritual), earnestly entrusting [the teaching] by saying:
"Contemplate the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King. That which is enacted is for the sake of compassion; thus there are these words spoken in the weeds.
Since Māgasa already knows that the mountain water mill is Mañjuśrī’s striking of the gavel, why does he not [recognize it] again?
Face the place where the World-Honored One ascended the seat; look clearly with wide-open eyes. Yet it is said: "What need is there to ask about the top of the feet or the bottom of the feet?
Whether he descends from or ascends the jeweled throne is up to him. Is this not to falsely gauge the World-Honored One with the wiles of an outsider?
If this is so, would it not still be a matter of seeking understanding before the World-Honored One had ascended the seat?
Yet, that which is called "the empty mountain and the water mill" is worlds apart from Mañjuśrī’s striking of the gavel; the empty mountain remains clearly before one's eyes.
When has one ever beheld the wondrous seeing that is devoid of seeing? When the sound of the pestle is in one's ears, when has one entered the perfect hearing that is devoid of hearing?
In the *Mozang* (Magong) verse on the public case of the Flower-holding at Vulture Peak, it says: "The great earth blooms with the spring of the Victorious Land; the azure pond gazes..."
Laughing heartily, they recognize one another. Since the moment the warbling of the swallows and orioles was provoked, the story has reached the present day and become increasingly distorted.
Regarding the "Plucking the Flower" koan: the warbling of the swallows and orioles precisely expresses it; the warblers and orioles are themselves the flower, and their speech is itself the plucking.

There is no duality and no distinction. Yet Sanfeng Zang said: "Since the moment the warbling of the swallows and orioles was provoked, the story has reached the present day and become increasingly distorted."
This is a distortion. Even the perception of a swallow or a nightingale has not yet attained even one semblance of reality. To speak of whether something is true or not true—Magu Ren said:
"When the Sixth Patriarch entered the chamber of Huangmei, he too was surrounded by his monastic robes, and [Huangmei] tested him for his prior realization."
He reached the point where he should give rise to his mind by dwelling nowhere; upon hearing these words, he attained great enlightenment. He then said: "All phenomena do not depart from self-nature.
How unexpected it is that self-nature is fundamentally pure! How unexpected it is that self-nature is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished!
How unexpected it is that self-nature is fundamentally immovable! How unexpected it is that self-nature can give rise to all phenomena! Huangmei recognized his thorough realization.
Wu then entrusted him with his robes and alms bowl. The former master said that every stitch of the *kāṣāya* clearly reveals the numerical principles of the Dharma;
it was not for nothing. Indeed, from the single-layered robe up to the twenty-five-layered robe, each layer consists of five strips, each being four lengths long and one length short.
Through their inversion, interlacing, opening, and closing, they silently seal the vastness inherently possessed by all people.
The essence of the mind is both perfectly interfused and sequentially arrayed, never stagnating in one-sidedness; only then does one exhaustively fathom the profundity of this mind and this Dharma.
It is not that there is some so-called "esoteric transmission" existing apart from the mind. As the Sixth Patriarch’s verse says: "Bodhi originally has no tree;
the bright mirror is likewise not a stand. Originally there is not a single thing; where could dust gather? Is this not, however, still lingering in the realm of purity?
Is there perhaps something regarding the mental dharmas that has not yet been perfected? Please attempt to explain this.

If this verse were already the ultimate realization, then there should have been no further mention of "great penetration beneath a word" upon entering the room after the third drum. Since such expressions do exist, [it follows that there is more].
