That people of today fail to realize this and consequently claim that the First Patriarch fixed the core teaching (zongzhi) upon the robe—is this not an extreme deception of the world?
Moreover, the First Patriarch himself said: "Internally, the Dharma-seal is transmitted to accord with and verify the mind; externally, the kāṣāya is bestowed to establish the core teaching."

If one were to use the robe to represent the essential meaning (宗旨), such that the essential meaning resided upon the robe, then when Lingyun saw the peach blossoms, or when Shuilao was kicked by Mazu, the enlightenment of these two masters would have to reside in the treetops or beneath the heels of their sandals.
This is because they were unwilling to contemplate deeply. Why is this? Please observe the moment the World-Honored One held up the flower and universally addressed the great assembly.
The assembly said: "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvana, which I entrust to Mahākāśyapa.
At that time, among the hundreds of thousands of humans and devas, none had yet raised a point of contention like that of Master Xiù.

Why was it that the World-Honored One did not immediately bestow the golden-threaded robe at that moment, but instead added another layer of kōan before the Many-Sons Stūpa? It was because of the *kāṣāya*.
As for the matter of Saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses regarding sharing a seat, whether there was an explicit intent or not, the distinction between right and wrong is self-evident without further debate.
Alas! The greatest of all things is heaven and earth; the most profound of principles is yin and yang.
Yet the Sage welcomed the sun, calculated the movements of the stars, drew the Eight Trigrams, examined the River Chart, and measured the heavens with the armillary sphere.
By recording these in books of calendrical astronomy, one can then clearly perceive— as if pointing at them on the palm of one's hand— the movements and stillness of Heaven and Earth,

the courses and degrees of the sun and moon, the divisions of the stars and constellations, the cycles of Yin and Yang and the seasons of cold and heat, the variations of intercalary months, surplus days, and the waxing and waning of the phases,
as well as the hidden states of spirits and the netherworld. Viewed from this perspective, the wisdom and foresight of the Sage far surpass those of ordinary men.
If common men and women were to follow this and deliberate upon it, how could they not further increase their ignorance?
Confucianists employ numerical categories to manifest principles, asserting that principle (*li*) and number (*shu*) are inseparable. Yet, principle is the form and number is the shadow.
Now, number is substantial while principle is insubstantial; why then do you say that principle is the form and number is the shadow? It is because when principle is attained, number follows.

Thus, that which is indeterminate is in fact determinate, and that which is determinate is in fact indeterminate. Since numbers are indeterminate, one takes what is determinate according to principle to define "large" and "small.
Therefore, the analogy of form and shadow is employed. All of these, however, pertain to the peripheral matters of the Confucian school.
As for the Chan school, it first removes the obstruction of principle (*li-zhang*) and directly points to the essence of the mind (*xin-zong*). Even principle itself cannot be [grasped].
How much more so regarding their number! The "Māra-endurance" (mōrěn) refers to the *kāṣāya* robe, ranging from one stripe to twenty-five stripes, with each stripe consisting of five [sections].
Each section has four long and one short [panel], arranged in inverted and interlaced patterns, opening and closing through transformations.
This silently seals the vast, inherent mind-body of us humans; through its perfect fusion and sequential manifestation, it does not stagnate in any single partiality, only then exhausting this mind.
The profundity of this Dharma does not consist in some so-called "secret transmission" existing apart from the mind; such a claim is truly the teaching of Māra.
He has merely perused secular classics and seen that the number of Qian is twenty-five and the number of Kun is thirty. As for these thirty of Kun—
This is twenty-five, doubled by another five. Kun is governed by Qian; while Yang is substantial and Yin is void, Kun represents the number of the void.
Only the twenty-five of Qian constitutes the number of the substantial. Therefore, the number of Qian encompasses the number of all existing things.

Qian represents the process of constant generation. This constant generation is the heart-mind of Heaven and Earth. Although Heaven and Earth are without mind, humanity serves as the heart-mind of Heaven and Earth.
Thus, the number of these generative processes is twenty-five, and the number of the heart-mind is likewise twenty-five.
That the *kāṣāya* consists of twenty-five strips is a coincidental correspondence; it was therefore claimed that this symbolizes the vastness of the five men.
The essence of the mind has no connection whatsoever with the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Even according to the *I Ching*, as for what Confucius called the "Heavenly numbers" totaling twenty-five, how could he have foreseen that later generations would deduce this far?
It is simply that principle must correspond to number, and thus they naturally coincide. What is so extraordinary about this? As for...
Regarding what is called "directly pointing to the essence of mind": how could this be that very mind? Have you not seen the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* say, "This is not your mind"?
Furthermore, how does it relate to the *kāṣāya* robe? If one were to say, "This is precisely it," one would not realize that as soon as it is spoken, it is already not so;
even "is" cannot be established. Moreover, he certainly did not mean that "this is precisely it. He used this merely to entice and delude people.
Those scholar-officials who lack learning cause the multitude to proclaim "wondrous truths" and act as external protectors [of the Dharma].

Such mental conduct truly defiles the ancestral temple. Having claimed that the twenty-five strips of the *kāṣāya* silently seal the essence of the mind, they then realize their own argument is far-fetched and strange;
consequently, they further claim that the fundamental principle is not established upon the robe.
You have falsely cited public cases such as Lingyun’s peach blossoms as proof; in total, you have no place of arrival [in the truth].

To claim that when the World-Honored One held up the flower and Kāśyapa smiled, this was not yet the transmission of the Dharma, but that it must wait until before the Many Sons Stūpa for the kāṣāya to encircle him and the essential doctrine to be secretly entrusted—this is to live within a ghost cave, defiling the World-Honored One and forming a realm of demons. You ought to...

They follow [the path] to the Avīci Hell; their frantic barking remains unresolved. Suddenly, they turn back to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), claiming that among all things, heaven and earth are the greatest, and among all principles, yin and yang are the most profound.
They further claim that the Sage welcomed the sun and pushed the divining stalks, drawing the hexagrams and examining the diagrams to discover their secret mysteries.
Thus, they praise the Sage as one whose wisdom and deliberation surpass those of ordinary men, setting him apart as uniquely sublime.
Furthermore, he says, "If one were to let every man and woman judge this, how could their ignorance not increase?
By these words, he implicitly refers to his own teacher Fazang as a sage, while characterizing Miyun Tianyin as a mere common man and woman.
This secretly employs the meaning of Han Yu’s “Preface to the Departure of the Buddhist Monk Wenchang” to establish a connection with pedantic scholars and worldly gentlemen.
This is truly what is meant by "shouldering the burden and smiling sycophantically," those who suffer like laborers in the summer fields.

Where could such arguments find a place within the language of the Chan school? There is originally no need to debate this; however, I fear that ignorant persons of future generations might [misunderstand].
I say that within the principles of the Confucian school, there is still much to be taken; thus, I cannot help but add this as one more "snake's foot.

Now, heaven and earth are called the "Two Greats"—this is a term of supreme honor. Yet, although even the smallest of creatures, such as the *jiaoming* insect, its vital energy (*qi*) is entirely that of Heaven and its substance (*zhi*) is entirely that of Earth.
Thus, it may indeed be said that nothing is smaller than Heaven and Earth. How could one merely say [that they are the greatest]?
There is nothing greater than heaven and earth. As for the principle that is most profound, it lies in the discourse on yin and yang;
yet even this, one knows, he does not recognize. One can only say that nothing is more manifest than yin and yang. Now, yin and yang are spoken of in terms of correspondence:
the male is yang and the female is yin; the day is yang and the night is yin. Extending this to all things, it is the same throughout—dust mote by dust mote, world-system by world-system.
The *kṣetras* are fully present before one’s eyes; can they not be called "teeth"? Speaking in terms of mutual roots, the male organ is yang and the female organ is yin;
the day is yin and the night is yang. When extended to all things, there is nothing that is not likewise so. Thus, in every atom and in every *kṣetra*, everything is fully present before one’s eyes.
One might say it is "profound" (*you*). Yet even this single character "profound" still remains within the realm of yin and yang;
it must first be paired with "manifest" (*xian*) before one can discuss yin and yang.

If we discuss their manifestations, that which is manifest and external is yang, while that which is profound and internal is yin. If we discuss their root, that which is manifest and clearly evident on the outside...
That which has a form that can be pointed out is yin; it is obscure and presides over movement within. That which leaves no trace to be sought is yang.
How can you claim that principle (li) is more obscure than yin and yang? Furthermore, heaven and earth are not "things," and yin and yang are not "principles.
These two statements alone would be considered heterodox and demonic teachings even in the secular classics, let alone in the Buddhist scriptures.
The Chan School. That which makes a sage a sage is his clarity regarding human relations (*renlun*). Mencius said: "The sage is the perfection of human relations.
The *Great Learning* says: "As a ruler, one stops at benevolence; as a minister, one stops at respect;
as a son, one stops at filial piety; as a father, one stops at kindness. It is only by means of these three pervasive virtues that one [attains this].

Because he practices the five paths that lead to penetration, he is called a sage. As for such matters as calculating the movements of the sun by tracking its course, drawing trigrams, and examining diagrams to understand the cycles and patterns of heaven, earth, the sun, and the moon—these are merely the many skills of a sage.
Whether one is a sage or not has absolutely no bearing on these things. If one were to claim that it is precisely through such matters as these that a sage is what he is, then...
Those Westerners and Muslims who are capable in calendrical science are all sages.

Moreover, the calendars of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius are found in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, while the calendars of Yao and Shun are found in the *Book of Documents*. When examined through the lens of mathematical calculation, they are all equally crude and erroneous;
there are many points in which they fall far short of the contemporary *Shixian* calendar. If these [ancient calendars] were considered "sagely," then [the modern ones would not be].

This is like the blind man observing celestial phenomena and recklessly giving rise to arguments; it is no different from the current fashion of wearing the "scholar's cap" (dai jin xian), which surpasses that of Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius.
It is surely not the case that one should merely say that the World-Honored One was surrounded by his robe before the Many-Sons Stūpa, finding no other profound meaning therein.
Furthermore, to worry about practitioners entering their rooms at the third watch of the night—what kind of ground for gathering dust and defilement is this? Indeed.
This is superficial. If one were to follow what the "Māra-like patience" (mārakṣānti) proponents say, one would further belong to the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
Since students already possess right knowledge and right view, they must apply their utmost vigor and discernment to this matter.
Māra-ṛṣi said: "The adamantine śarīra is for the purpose of constructing stupas and establishing temples; these are fields where humans and devas plant merit.

That this lineage continues unbroken from generation to generation is the very task of one who truly transmits the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom.
Yet now, you dismiss the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the True Dharma Eye) of Linji as mere intellectual learning. Observing these words of yours, Reverend, how can you not be struck with alarm?
Regarding the adamantine śarīra, when building stupas and establishing temples, one must not merely hold assemblies for planting the seeds of merit for humans and devas.

If such an assembly is held, then that which is performed—the treasury of the true Dharma eye—is itself the adamantine śarīra; the building of stupas and establishment of temples [is thereby fulfilled].

If no such assembly is held, then the purpose of compiling the Dharma-eye and continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom does not even approach the cause of planting merit for humans and devas. It is far more than that which falls short.
This is precisely to extinguish the life of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*) and continue the life of Māra. How could this not be an evil fruit summoned by means of a virtuous cause?

Now, the *vajraśarīra* (diamond-relic) is itself the Dharma-eye. To take the *vajraśarīra* and erect a stupa or temple while treating the Dharma-eye and the life of wisdom as two separate entities is the mark of one whose heels do not touch the ground. How much more so, how could the Dharma-eye depend on...?
It was compiled [into a text]. If it were permissible to compile [it as such], how could it still be called "True Vajra" or "True Śarīra"?

My Way is likewise so. Discussing worldly dharmas: hearing with sagacity is called "acute," and seeing with sagacity is called "clear."

Now, you say that throughout ancient and modern times, there have been many who brought affairs to ruin through their clarity, intelligence, and penetrating wisdom.
This shows you do not understand what kind of demonic teaching this is. When Zhaozhou left the monastery, he encountered an old woman on the road who asked him, "Where is the Master going?"

Should it be the character for 'east and west,' or the character for 'to settle and lodge' (*xi*—as in *xipo*, 'lodging')? The monks replied, "It should be the character for 'east and west.

I shall provide you with a general understanding of literacy. If one observes this, then one sees that Miyun’s rejection of Ruiwang for the name "one who does not know how to read" cannot possibly be without foundation.
Furthermore, how can it be determined that those who do not know how to read are necessarily people who spend their whole day eating their fill without applying their minds?
Even a peddler or a common merchant who recognizes not a single character has a mind that is bustling and busy day and night; how could they ever find rest?
To say "stop" and "cease" is already a misunderstanding from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), let alone the words of Confucius:
"To eat one's fill all day long without applying the mind—how difficult this is! These were likely words intended to urge those at the level of lower learning.
As for the matter of the ultimate path (*paramārtha*), does he not further say: "I eat coarse rice and drink water; I rest my head on my bent arm, and yet joy is found therein"? It is just like this.

If one still possesses a mind that can be employed, how could one find joy within it? As for the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), one eats all day long yet never chews so much as a single grain of rice;
only then does one reach the state where one eats to satiety all day without having any mind to employ.
This is precisely the person of the Way who has severed study and is non-active. Moran then asked, "What auspicious name do you have?"
Thus, he falsely assumes such a persona. Not only has he never realized this ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), but he has not even heard its excellent name.
Furthermore, he ridiculed Míyún for claiming that the Dharma taught by Mózàng is unfathomable, thereby disparaging him as a heterodox offshoot;
yet he praised Ruìguāng as being similar to himself. Recently, having seen that Ruìguāng’s records were likewise unfathomable, his refutation arrived shortly thereafter.
The words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are indeed words as they are, true words, real words—words that are neither false nor deceptive.

A piece of wood is simply a piece of wood; a common brick is simply a common brick. Though these are stated with such clarity that they fall apart into fragments, the listener fails to awaken and instead clings to the whole.
Thus, the speaker does not rely on the mind, intellect, or consciousness, yet the listener...
Furthermore, one must not grope toward the boundaries of mind, intellect, or consciousness. What is there that can be measured or what cannot be measured?
The unfathomability of Māra’s treasury and Māra’s radiance is precisely what causes Mimiyun (Miyun) to feel such piercing anguish;
he could not bear to leave it unopened, yet he had no choice but to open it. Maren (Maren) then proceeded to flaunt the unfathomability of his own father and elder brother.
"Measurable. This refers precisely to what Zhuang Zhou said: "The owl and the rat delight in excrement; when the phoenix passes by, the owl and the rat look up and cry out 'He!

To employ these for the purpose of measurement is to cause the mind, intellect, and consciousness to fall away.
Once they have fallen away, it is like using ink to dye silk while seeking whiteness; the deeper the dye penetrates, the blacker the white becomes.

As for what these people call the "intermingling of the four dharmas," the "double-headed single knot," or the "binding into the unadorned secret seal," it is nothing more than forced interpretation and speculative transmission.
These four characters exhaust it. How could there be anything unfathomable? Reaching its ultimate subtlety, it all returns to the single circle (○).

Once it is this circle, then it is already fathomed. To the full extent of their cleverness, they are able to take up the old entanglements (*ge-teng*), matching branch to branch and pairing leaf to leaf. As for these entanglements, they should simply be set aside.
A torch. If it were reduced to a single burning brand, then one would have already fathomed it.

One might take the various schools of thought, the hundreds of masters, the four treasuries and ten thousand scrolls—all such nests of ignorance—to serve as the whetstone for their discursive blades and tongues.

I have already measured it. Yet, what more remains unmeasurable that you would dare to align yourself with the great masters such as Aśvaghoṣa, Mātrceṭa, and Nāgārjuna?
As the poem says: "Artful words are like reed pipes; how thick is the face of such a person!"

'The form of the signless samādhi is like the full moon. Indeed, at the time before the primal colors had yet manifested, and prior to the establishment of the distinction between the holy and the ordinary, how could it possibly..."
Is this being sought through such narrow and petty views? Yongjia said: "The great chiliocosm is but a bubble in the sea;

all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning. Prajñā said: "All Buddhas, as well as the dharmas of the Buddhas' *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, all emerge from this sutra. Thus, our former master spoke of the single circle (*o*) as the signless.
He is the progenitor of a thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas; this principle is certainly not contradictory.
He is not within, not without, and not in between. He has no beginning before, no end after, and no present now.
He is not the mind, not the Buddha, and not a thing. As for this [circle], it is merely a word.
At the point where thought is severed, one has no choice but to act.

However, this talk of "the point where thought is severed" and "having no choice but to act"—this is something that should simply be swept away with a single stroke by Yangshan. An ancient worthy said:

"The Westward Coming of Bodhidharma was solely because he wished to find a person who would not be deluded. If you see it at the point [of action], then it is already not that point; if you accord with it..."
○. ○ What further can be established? If one establishes a single ○, one is immediately deluded regarding the ○. If one is deluded regarding the ○, this is precisely slandering the ○.
Now, you take the ○ to be the progenitor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas. In that case, are the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas merely the descendants of the ○?
When a child holds up a mirror, are the mirror and the child the same or different? [The same applies to] the perfect wisdom of all Buddhas.
Regarding the mirror: is it the same as, or different from, [the mind]? How could it be used as an image to show people?
If that were so, why did Master Neng refuse the line, "The mind is like a bright mirror stand"?

Furthermore, since this mirror is said to be the image of the perfect wisdom (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*) of all Buddhas, yet it is also said that "this formless zero (0) is the ancestor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas"—then what of this zero?
If the elephant exists, how can you say there is no elephant? Damorin said:

This is especially true in the School of the Buddhas, where good and evil are equally discarded, fortune and misfortune are equally reached, and existence and non-existence are equally regarded.

Facing the wall for nine years to await the Second Patriarch—this was already perceived and exposed long ago by the nameless old master, who possessed the heart-mind of a demon or heretic.

Now, while disrupting the lineage is indeed a vulgar failing among the followers of the school, it is nonetheless fifty paces better than those who treat it as a substantial reality and falsely establish their own "founders' tenets.
For while the former is a hundred paces [behind], the latter is fifty. Thus, regarding the disruption...

The harm caused by [merely] unifying [the teachings] is easy to distinguish, like powder amidst snow; the harm caused by recklessly establishing a "founder's intent" (zongzhi) is difficult to discern, like soot within ink.

Now, what are called *dharmaprīti*, the joy of *dhyāna*, the Land of Bliss, the Pure Cause, the "leisurely Way-man," and the "man of no affairs"—these are precisely the mind and practice of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

On a day when Tiantong was in a state of intense rage, there were already those like me who dared to defy his countenance and struggle for the truth unto death.
What kind of words are these? What kind of mental conduct is this? I fear that future generations throughout the world will not know of the existence of a "demon-like" Ren (Mórní).

I fear people might say that his views are equal to his master’s, thereby diminishing the master’s virtue by half; they would surely desire to arrogantly claim the name of one who has surpassed his master. I fear...

He feared that people of later generations might instead take the Heavenly Boy as their model rather than himself, and he feared that the Heavenly Boy would precede him.

and in the end, will not attribute it to myself, but rather attribute the fault to Tiantong. They will cling to the principle of "grandfather and grandson" to mock one another,

When eaten in this manner, it is light and oily, capable of benefiting the *qi* and overcoming hunger. Nowadays, however, the people of Huizhou all boil it with the skin on, eat it cold, and find it hard and tough.

For the words "directly pointing to the human mind and seeing one's nature to become a Buddha" are like the pipes of a pan-pipe, while the "essential principles" (gangzong) are merely methods of wrapping fire in paper. These cause all those impoverished sons to wander about in search of food.
If one consumes it according to the Dharma, one will no longer suffer from hunger.

But as for those who obliterate the fundamental principle, mistaking the understanding of a raised eyebrow or a blink of an eye for true insight, and who—clinging to enlightenment while remaining deluded—manifest their madness through violent blows and abusive insults: is this not what is called "boiling the skin along with the meat"?
"Cease your recollections! When the pure wind pervades the earth, what limit can there be? Looking left and right, he said: 'Is there a patriarch here?

For this very thing does not fall within the confines of conceptual frameworks; it is not something that can be reached through formal cultivation or practice.
Therefore, it is said: "Pointing directly at the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha. This is the point where the ancient worthies held up [the teaching].
If you place this yam at the edge of someone’s mouth, that person cannot eat it. How could there ever be a "true method" to be described for wrapping it in paper and baking it over a fire?
This yam possesses a natural, extraordinary flavor; when eaten, it is neither lacking nor excessive.

It does not fall within the cycle of spring growth, summer maturation, autumn harvest, and winter storage. Why, then, would one need to wrap it in paper and bake it over a fire? Let the entire earth be made into [a single yam].
A single sheet of paper—it cannot even be wrapped. Pervading all of empty space, it is a mass of fire—it cannot even be roasted. It simply requires that a person be able to eat it;

then, it is the "Ninefold Great Reversion" (Jiuzhuan Dahuan), a direct leap into realization. What need is there for cooking, roasting, seasoning, or harmonizing? Is there anything of the "Dharma" or the "non-Dharma"?
Thus, he denounced Miyun as a "madman struck by the miasma of abusive, drunken insults," which was not even equal to Miyun’s own [teaching].
