The gate of Di (提) further sheds its skin like a cicada from amidst turbid defilement; yet this is but the daily descent of vulgar custom.
Whether one attains the fundamental principle or fails to attain it is like whether one attains wealth and honor or fails to attain them.

To harm others for one's own profit, to disgrace others for one's own glory—through myriad transformations and hundreds of subtle stratagems, Śākyamuni views these as truly identical to emanations from the Buddha-body.
It is blood. This is what Zhuangzi meant when he said, "The one who steals gold is executed; the one who steals a kingdom becomes a marquis.

When a sage governs a state through benevolence and righteousness, others simply appropriate that very benevolence and righteousness for themselves—is this not precisely what he meant? Compared to drinking wine and eating meat, [this is far more grievous].
Stealing wealth and committing sexual misconduct—these various karmas differ in their gravity as vastly as a single feather compared to a catty (jūn) of weight. *Imperial Composition:
Record for Distinguishing Heresies from Orthodoxy*, Scroll One.
*Imperial Composition: Record for Distinguishing Heresies from Orthodoxy*, Scroll Two.
Mofen said: "The Patriarch has a 'Inscription on Faith' of nearly a thousand words. Its essentials state: 'The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination.
Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and all will be transparently clear. A difference of a hair's breadth, and heaven and earth are set apart.
If you wish for it to manifest before you, do not maintain notions of favorability or adversity. To understand Linji and Deshan’s myriad wonders, it does not go beyond driving away..."

The scholar’s loss of his mental faculties accords precisely with these few words. Those followers of scholastic learning explain it thus: "The ultimate Way is fundamentally neither difficult nor easy;
it is simply a matter of not making distinctions. They liken it to painting a dragon: the head, horns, fangs, and eyes are all rendered exactly like the real thing, yet it cannot produce rain.
This is what is meant by the saying, "A hair's breadth of difference results in worlds apart. It is not so.
How is its essential purpose to be discerned?
Mokei (魔忍) states that the myriad wonders of Linji and Deshan do nothing more than drive students to exhaust their mental faculties;
this accords with the teachings of this school. Now, to exhaust one's mental faculties is still not yet to have known what it means to undergo a "great death."
"Is there great death and great life? By what means does this immediately accord with these few words?
Although there is indeed great death and great life, once the life of wisdom has been restored, Dongshan said, "Continuity is also very difficult.
Yongquan said, "I have been here for forty-nine years, yet I still occasionally stumble. You people must not open your mouths too wide; you who possess understanding—"
Among those who practice and understand, not one in ten thousand is found. The words of the ancient worthies are this truly earnest.
One who has personally tasted the flavor of the ambrosia speaks from a place that is naturally different; how could they be like those of the Mara-tolerance school who speak lightly of Prajñā?
Although it is said that within this there are no stages or gradual steps, yet within the absence of gradual steps, there are very great gradual steps—there is no climbing the ladder.

Regarding the levels of attainment, there are vast hierarchies; only through direct realization can they be known—how easy is it to speak of them? The treatises on "enduring demons" are like a scholar discussing war from behind a desk;
within a few lines of writing, one might claim to have personally experienced over a hundred battles, great and small, and to have reclaimed a hundred thousand *li* of territory.
But will such claims ever correspond to actual reality? Furthermore, as for Linji and Deshan, their pedagogical methods were...
In essence, these were merely means to guide beginners. Thus, the intent behind causing the student to "lose all mind and intellect" was to lead them to personally awaken to their own nature.

Even such instances as striking the student immediately upon entering the gate, or the simultaneous shouting of the two halls—where the truth is presented face-to-face and pointed out directly—are still matters belonging to the realm of shadows and light. When compared with the inscriptions and sayings of Master Huineng, they fall short.
Even this "place of falling" is like looking toward Chang'an while smiling westward; how much more so the entire string of knots such as the Three Essentials and Three Keys?
Furthermore, did the ancient worthies ever prattle with clever tongues merely to surpass others? They intended only for people to reach the point where words and thought are cut off.
A single thought of turning the light back upon itself is identical to one's original attainment.

As for what those who tolerate the demonic state say regarding the Three Essentials and Three Principles, it is nothing more than a desire to have future generations of the world recognize them as people who clarify the fundamental tenets, and to have others seek the very crux of the fundamental tenets from them so that they may appear to be true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Even if such a person were to speak...
To claim that one has obtained the *māndārava* flowers raining from heaven is itself a child prattling of wonders; how much less could it be that "a crow becomes a horse" (*wu yan cheng ma*)?
What end is there to such talk? It is merely a herd of blind donkeys huddling their heads together to solve riddles.

Furthermore, within these withered and rotten vines of discourse, what essential principle (*zongzhi*) can you possibly extract? And yet, you take this very principle to go about discriminating those same withered and rotten things.
Regarding the phrase "beating those who circle within the entanglements": is this a form of discernment (*viveka*) or non-discernment?
This is nothing more than a refutation of Mimi Yun’s “one blow to the end,” asserting that he merely resembles Master Linji Yixuan in his non-discernment, yet is not a true dragon.
Although its head, horns, tusks, and mane may resemble those of a dragon, it cannot bring down rain;
it is not like another who has attained the essential principle (zongzhi), being a true dragon capable of distinguishing between blue, yellow, black, and white.

If someone opens their mouth to such a person and their words accord with that person’s essential principle, then they are a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); if they do not accord with that person’s essential principle, they are merely a student using this to deceive others.
"Villagers, it is like this. Previously, you have never given rise to pure faith; how then can you speak of the 'Inscription on Faith'?
Master Can clearly stated, 'I only dislike discrimination,' yet you are solely occupied with discrimination.
He clearly stated, 'Only do not harbor hatred or love,' yet you are entirely full of hatred and love. You seek to understand [the truth] merely through words and letters."
To claim this is the work of Māra or externalists is already a clear and certain confession from yourself.
Mazu Ruzhen said: "When the Fifth Patriarch finished reading the verse of the Sixth Patriarch, he remarked, 'He has not yet seen his nature.

Yet, when [Huineng] entered the room at the third watch, the Patriarch questioned him until he reached the point of 'abiding nowhere,' and Huineng attained great enlightenment upon these words. Thus, the remark that he had not yet seen his nature..."

This is clear and self-evident. Later generations have glossed over it, claiming that [the Master] intentionally refused permission in order to quell disputes, and that he said the *kāṣāya* was used to surround him so as not to be seen by others, rather than for the sake of worldly dissemination. Is this not to slander the Patriarch?
Now, if one has already entered the room, closing the door is sufficient; why resort to such concealment and evasion, seeking to hide what becomes all the more exposed? This is without [foundation].

He merely wishes to provide an intellectual interpretation based on the notion that "originally there was not a single thing. Yet, where the *kāṣāya* robe encircles the body, his annotations fail to apply;
he has merely forced these words upon it, which will surely evoke the laughter of ten thousand ages.
Miyun Wu, relying on what is recorded in the *Platform Sūtra* within the Great Canon, stated:

One day the Fifth Patriarch suddenly saw the Sixth Patriarch and said, "I have considered that your insight is worthy of use, yet I fear there may be evil people who would harm you; therefore, I have not spoken with you.
Do you understand this? The Sixth Patriarch replied, "Your disciple also understands this intention; I did not dare go before the hall, lest someone should find out."
Upon awakening, the Fifth Patriarch saw that the assembly was entirely startled; there was no one who did not express amazement.

He then took the shoe, wiped it clean, and presented his verse, saying, "I have not yet seen my nature," and so forth, including the words, "The doubts of the multitude have been stilled. This was the subduing of Māra.

Later generations have glossed over this, claiming he intentionally refused permission in order to quell their disputes; this too is merely beating the air with an oar against a fixed post. Such accounts have been transmitted through antiquity and the present.

Those who can be trusted are very few. Even when historians take up their brushes, there are still many erroneous traditions; how much more so for a monk in an empty mountain receiving various hearsays from the past?
"Originally there is not a single thing; where could dust settle?"—this has never been seen as the realization of nature, but rather belongs to the category of an iron-clad legal case.
However, Mazu Ren followed the teaching of his master Mazang, asserting that this [verse] falls into emptiness.
"O you who have lost the Way! You must wait for the *kāṣāya* to surround and conceal you. There are five times five, making twenty-five.
Only after the subtle and esoteric purport has been transmitted and shown within the inner chamber can the Layman Lu obtain this essential principle at Huangmei.

To defile it in such a manner shows that you have not only failed to understand the meaning of Huangmei, but have not even seen the nature; in truth, [this principle] has been fundamentally non-existent at Caoxi."

I have never even dreamed of such a thing. Thus, although they claim to have attained the robe that provides protection and enclosure, their account of the circumstances at the Bahuputra Stūpa is not off by so much as a hair’s breadth; they too are merely those who parrot the words.

How much more so for what they call the "monastic robes," ranging from one to twenty-five strips, each strip consisting of five pieces, each of which is four lengths long and one length short—this is nothing but a confused jumble.
How mistaken! To open and close, to transform and change, silently seals the vast, inherent essence of the human mind.
How could these various demonic teachings—driving at the void with empty fabrications—be considered real dharmas?

Master Yi, who already rejected the phrase "originally there is not a single thing" as being the nihilistic path of externalists, now further rejects it for clinging to the side of purity. He fails to consider that when Caoqi first saw [the Sixth Patriarch],...
During the season of yellow plum blossoms, Huangmei ordered [Huiming] to perform manual labor with the assembly. Caoqi said, "My disciple’s own nature constantly gives rise to wisdom;
not departing from one's own nature is itself the field of merit. I do not know what task the Master instructs me to perform. Huangmei said:

This hunter’s innate capacity is too sharp. Send him to the stables for eight months. After those eight months have passed, there will be the matter of each person composing a verse on their own mind.
Before those eight months, Caoxi’s words remain fully intact; how could there already be talk of falling into emptiness or clinging to purity?
Are these not various forms of doubt? In general, they enter the room seeking to realize the three beats of the drum;

yet, separately, there are demonic teachings concerning the subtle essence and secret intent of the school, whereby they disregard the sin of slandering the patriarchs and act with utter recklessness.
Mofen said: "When the school of the Plucking of the Flower first entered China, it did not accord with you;
it was not greatly believed by either the clergy or the laity, nor was it renowned among the court or the common people.

For this reason, Bodhidharma suffered poison because of it, the Second Patriarch perished by execution, and Master Daman Zan hid his tracks at Mount Qian, remaining cautious and diligent while concealing himself from the Way."
Therefore, it is said: "Be careful not to say that [the Dharma] comes from what you have personally attained.
The four characters of the "Flower-Holding" school (*Huāzhǒng*) are themselves a demonic teaching.

One must truly fear that throughout the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, until the end of time, all sentient beings will mistake their heads for reflections, because of what Śākyamuni preached for forty-nine years.
With their minds, intellects, and consciousnesses, they attempt to fathom what was said, each clinging to their own views and establishing them as their own tenets.

Thereupon, [the Master] plucked up a flower and, amidst hundreds of thousands of humans and devas, directly and straightforwardly held it forth. Venerable Kāśyapa, unable to restrain his impatience, broke into a smile.
How could this be called "this is the very essence of our school"? To join together in deceiving and intimidating the common people is solely because—
This was a superfluous effort that left behind many complications, persisting to this day.

Those like the "demon-tolerant" (mo-ren) class, being people who do not understand the matter, continue to pick at the fringes of the flowers, becoming nothing more than unpleasant wooden buckets. As the Great Uncle Han said: "A single hare lies across the ancient road;
as soon as the blue falcon sees it, it seizes it. Later, the hunting dogs lack the necessary spirit; they [pursue] in vain..."
One seeks it at the site of the old withered stump. Thus, if one merely mentions the word "patriarchal school" (*zong*), Śākyamuni would have already knit his brows;
how much more so when speaking of "one" or "two"? How could there be anything else apart from this? Therefore, it is called "the Patriarchal School of the Plucking of the Flower.

Since Liuzi established this Patriarchal School of the Plucking of the Flower, his descendants multiplied. With separate branches becoming ancestors and the succession of those separate branches becoming patriarchs, there eventually came to be two.
From the three schools to the five schools—is it not the case that these have become even more unworthy than the six schools refuted by Bodhidharma?

Furthermore, you claim that when [the Dharma] first arrived in China, it did not accord with the ruler, was not believed by the clergy or the laity, and failed to gain renown among the court and the common people;
for this reason, Bodhidharma suffered poison, the Second Patriarch perished by execution, and Master Huìcǎn...
"Mingling my tracks among the mountains of Qian, I remain cautious and diligent, concealing myself within the Way.
Such phrases as these truly become the circulation of worldly conventions. Mo-ren was fond of using secular classics to harmonize with the Chan school;
yet, even judging by the Confucian tradition alone—as recorded in the "Biography of Confucius" in the *Shiji*, where it says of Yanzi: "The Way of the Master is great, therefore the world..."
It cannot be accommodated. Such words are simply untrustworthy; they do not resemble the speech of Yanzi.
Furthermore, the dialogue does not accord with the mental conduct of Confucius and Yanzi. Within the *Lunyu*, such a kind of discourse could not possibly exist.

The Way is that which all people share and that which has been possessed equally by all throughout ten thousand generations. How could it be that it belongs to one person alone as something uniquely great? And as for Heaven...
It is laughable enough that you would not admit this; how much more so regarding the Gate of the Patriarchs—it is all the more reason for a great burst of laughter!

If Dharma was not yet in China before Bodhidharma’s arrival, did China then have no Buddha-dharma at all? If that were the case, then Bodhidharma truly must have brought some kind of Buddha-dharma with him.
Furthermore, as for the flower held up by the World-Honored One: was it there before Bodhidharma came to China?
"Is it a flower? Or is it no flower? The flowers of China did not come into existence for the first time because of Bodhidharma;
how then could the Buddha-dharma have come into existence for the first time because of Bodhidharma's arrival?

If you conceive of the flower held up by the World-Honored One as something extraordinary, yet do not believe that it is simply the various kinds of flowers already existing in China, you have failed to see that when Nanquan was asked about Qingyuan."
"What is Chan? he asked. [Qingyuan] replied, "A brick. He asked again, "What is the Way? [Qingyuan] replied, "A piece of wood.
Was Qingyuan’s brick for Chan and his wood for the Way simply the same kind of Chan-brick and Way-wood that Bodhidharma brought from the Western Heaven?
If one were to say that the brick is not Chan and the wood is not the Way, then Qingyuan would be guilty of committing a great falsehood. Thus...
If you claim that Qingyuan was a speaker of truth, then the people of China have long lived in peace with common bricks and wooden stumps;
these bricks and stumps lack nothing and possess nothing in excess. Seeing no trace of anxiety or trepidation in them, where could there be any place for them to hide from the Way?
How can you, without cause, slander Bodhidharma and Huineng? And how can you slander Huineng?
What have these two great masters attained that they single out this "Flower-holding" school? They are restless in sleep and food, unsteady in sitting and standing;
unable to resolve their own calamity, they bring misfortune upon those who come after them.
Mowen said: "At the time of the Sixth Patriarch’s birth, auspicious light illuminated the heavens, and he was moved by a strange monk who bestowed a name upon him.

He recognized the consciousness of the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra’s ordination platform; hearing the *Vajracchedikā*, he attained awakening, and hearing the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, he was able to lecture upon it.

As for his outward manifestation, however, he could not recognize a single character 'dīng. Had he been made to engage even slightly in the realm of study, what need would there have been for ten thousand scrolls?"
Difficult indeed. Yet, considering that the times have come to this, those who lack even a basic knowledge of the classics in later generations will surely use Master Lu as a pretext.
I shall request to test them: Is their ability to expound upon what they hear like that of Master Lu? Is their realization triggered by hearing the sounds alone like that of Master Lu?
Is their preaching of the Dharma like clouds and rain like that of Master Lu? Are their verses and hymns perfectly refined and brilliantly penetrating like his?

O Master Lu! The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If the mind is directed toward clarity, one becomes sharp; if it dwells in the depths of emotion, one becomes dull. Now, those who do not even recognize the character "Ding" (the first letter of the alphabet) do so because their emotional defilements (*kleśa*) firmly obscure them.
When such people are spoken to regarding the mundane truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which are already shallow and minor, they remain deaf-mute; they stare with fixed eyes.
How much more so, then, would this be the case for the unsurpassed, wondrous Way?
When sentient beings come to sow seeds, the fruit arises from the ground. Within this realm of Jambudvīpa, whenever there is a great fruit, there must be a preceding omen.
It is like when small grass bears fruit within the soil; its sprouts and buds are identical [to others], yet people do not see them.
However, when a large bamboo produces a shoot, although it is still within the soil, several days prior, the surface of the earth already...

The ground has already split open extensively; those accustomed to digging for bamboo shoots would know this at a glance. This is what Zi Chan meant when he said that when the refinement of things is abundant, the *po* and *hun* souls become strong;
thus, possessing such refined spirit and clarity, one reaches the level of the divine and numinous. If it is so with death, why should it not be so with life?
Yet all of this pertains to the realm of arising and ceasing, like a dream: within the layered fragrance of brocade curtains, it is indeed...
This is one dream. Spreading one’s mat upon the earth and taking the heavens as one’s canopy is also a dream. Within that dream, what is its dwelling place?
To be surrounded by silken curtains and fragrant incense has no connection whatsoever with spreading one’s mat upon the earth and taking the heavens as one’s canopy.

If we consider the time of Caoxi’s initial birth, when auspicious light illuminated the heavens, a strange monk bestowed his name, and Guṇabhadra left a prophecy; he was awakened upon hearing the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Nirvāṇa*.

Yet they are able to lecture on various miraculous anomalies while searching for Caoxi at the periphery. They claim that Caoxi transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal because he was truly a reincarnation, and that this cannot be forced.
This is like seeking a good dream beside a golden duck in an embroidered curtain; they say a good dream is not obtained by closing one's eyes.
How could they know that everyone is fully endowed with it and that not a single person is excluded? One need only fear not [realizing it].

If you can close your eyes, do not worry about being unable to dream. Had Caoxi not possessed such manifold spiritual wonders, how could he have truly reached the state where "originally there is nothing at all," a realm where dust and grime find no foothold?
He was also able to turn a single grain of white rice into fragrant food. Without the power of Caoxi’s self-nature and self-deliverance, even if one possessed all manner of spiritual powers...
This is different. Even if one were to live out another lifetime, there have been various spiritual wonders in this world like those at Caoxi;
yet, those who do not transcend themselves through their own nature like Caoxi himself must surely number countless times throughout the kalpas.
Since they specifically failed to become a Caoxi, they likewise left no legacy for future generations. How, then, can they be said to have transmitted the Buddha-mind seal?
To claim that Xu was a "reincarnated one" who merely pressed the eyes of the people of the world to make them see flowers—is this not a delusion?

To go so far as to say that Caoxi did not recognize a single character (*dīng*) because the times required it, is even more preposterous and eccentric. Now, Cangjie created writing to replace knotted cords;
its utility is so great that it cannot be compared to any other implement. Yet, [to compare it] with the fashioning of the plow...
They plowed the fields; they constructed dwellings to live in; they fashioned furs and hempen garments to wear; they prepared roasted and grilled meats to eat.
In the end, these were all of the same path and same kind. Yet, before writing existed, were there no sages? Once writing came into being, do sages exist within the characters?
Sages employ characters; it is not that characters employ sages. Even taking the Confucian school as an example, it likewise depends on knowing and then putting into practice.
One must grasp the full meaning within the characters bequeathed by the Duke of Zhou and Confucius; it does not lie in merely identifying every character used by them to convey their intent.
How much more so in the School of the Gate (the Chan/Zen tradition)! Whether one recognizes the characters or not—what relevance does that have? Have you not seen Yongjia say:
"To diminish the Dharma-treasure and destroy merit—none of this arises except from this mind-consciousness"? I ask you: what does it matter whether one recognizes the characters or not?

"Consciousness. Is it possible to be separated from this consciousness of mind, intellect, and awareness? If you cannot separate yourself from it, you will lose the wealth of the Dharma and extinguish your merit.
This refers precisely to this very consciousness; how can you abandon the treasure trove of the Dragon Palace and instead stretch out your hand to beg a single coin from a pauper?

If people were truly like Caoxi [Huineng], who could expound upon the teachings upon merely hearing them recited, or truly like Caoxi, who could understand the meaning upon merely hearing the sound...
And thus you awaken. Indeed, the Dharma taught at Caoxi is like clouds and rain; indeed, the verses of Caoxi are perfect, wondrous, and luminously penetrating.

Yet, if one does not rely on Caoxi’s "self-nature and self-deliverance," it remains nothing more than a tethering stake for a donkey for ten thousand kalpas—a vast distance separating us as heaven and earth.
How then could you seek Caoxi in such places? There is no place for you to search or grasp. Moreover—

The solid obstruction of emotional defilements has nothing to do with whether one is literate or illiterate. Indeed, literacy may even more easily foster such solid obstructions of emotional defilements;
this sometimes occurs. If one were to attribute the solid obstruction of emotional defilements to the fault of illiteracy, [it would be a grave error].

This is truly what is meant by "Master Zhang drinks the wine, yet Master Li gets drunk. Furthermore, as for Caoxi (Huineng) not being able to read characters—was this because his emotional defilements were so firmly obstructing him?
It may well be that one who cannot read characters is deaf to the conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*), but as for the unsurpassed, wondrous Way, it does not reside within written characters;
it cannot be known through cognition. How could it have anything to do with whether one can read characters or not?
How ironic! It is no exaggeration to call Mowen a demon; he merely dismissed Miyun as illiterate and claimed that only those who can read characters are capable of awakening to the Way.
This was done solely to flatter the ignorant scholar-officials of his time, leading them to doubt Tiantong while favoring himself—he was nothing but a worldly person.
To call him a "demon" would still be an understatement. As for Yunmen’s preaching of the Dharma: [it was like...]
"Clouds and rain are cut off. This records how Yunmen refused to bind people with words and phrases;
thus, after a single utterance, he would not preserve or review it, nor did he permit disciples to record it.

Therefore, it is said that "clouds and rain are cut off," meaning that once rain has departed from the clouds, it never returns to them again—this is the same intent as the line in Li Bai’s poem: "The falling rain does not ascend to heaven."
How can it be said that his preaching of the Dharma was like clouds and rain? Furthermore, according to the *Nan shi* (History of the Southern Dynasties), Xie Lingyun criticized Meng Yi, saying:
"One who studies the Way must possess a karmic legacy of wisdom (*huiye*). Your Honor’s birth in the heavens occurred before mine, but your attainment of Buddhahood shall surely come after mine.

In the carved edition of the biography, a scribal error occurred: the character "丈" (*zhàng*) was mistaken for "文" (*wén*), thereby resulting in the erroneous reading: "One who studies the Way must possess a karmic legacy of wisdom-texts" (*xué dào dāng xū huì yè wén*).
This man, Mochizuki Ryōin, has dabbled in secular classics yet does not understand them deeply;
he has thus stolen the erroneous arguments of Xie Lingyun—which were themselves based on erroneous traditions—and produced this segment of demonic discourse that is truly laughable.
Even in terms of literacy alone, how could he have ever been considered literate?

Mofen said: "When the Marquis of Huaiyin defeated Zhao, he deployed a 'back-to-the-water' formation. He ordered his subordinate generals to pass around the meals, saying, 'Today we shall feast together after defeating Zhao.
None of the generals believed him, yet they feigned compliance by responding, 'Yes. Subsequently, he indeed achieved victory over Zhao.

The generals asked him, 'According to the art of war, one's right flank should rely on mountains and hills, while the front and left should face marshes and waters. Now, General, you have ordered us..."
"Facing the water in formation—your subjects find this unacceptable, yet in the end you were victorious. What artifice is this? Xun replied, "This lies within the Art of War;

it is simply that you gentlemen have failed to observe it. Does the Art of War not say: 'Only by being driven to a place of death can one survive; only by being placed in a position of ruin can one endure'?
Furthermore, I did not obtain soldiers who had been previously accustomed to me through constant attendance. This is what is meant by..."
"If you drive the market folk into battle, their momentum will not be such that they can be made to fight for themselves unless you place them in a position where death is certain.
Now, if you grant them a way to live, they will all flee; how then could you still expect to employ them? All the generals submitted, saying, "Excellent!

This is beyond our reach. Indeed, the essential principles of the Five Houses are fully contained within the teachings of the Seven, Two, and Three Patriarchs as they applied them according to the occasion."

In the midst of giving and taking, the blind master has no eyes; he cannot see for himself, yet he claims that after Caoxi, the paths branched out into various deviations, with strange names and diverse appearances.
Not only does he not know the Linji and other schools, but he has not even recognized Caoxi.
What kind of words are these? Alas!
This recalls the incident of Xiang Yu at Huaiyin’s "array against the water.
It is merely said that the lineages of the Five Patriarchs all involve leading one into a place of death before being born, and placing one in a state of ruin before being preserved.

Indeed, if one does not confront the silver mountains and iron walls until the thieving mind is utterly extinguished, one will certainly not achieve that single sound from the depths of the earth, nor the rending of the five banners and eight formations. However, regarding these [patriarchs]—the four sevens and two threes—who, when facing...
The principles of seizing and relinquishing are precisely the fundamental tenet. How is this different from mistaking a precious rat for a jade casket?

You turn your ridicule upon Mìyún, calling him a blind teacher without eyes; yet you yourself cannot see, and thus claim that since the time of Cáoxī, the path has branched into byways, resulting in strange names and divergent forms.
Not only do you fail to understand the various schools such as Línjì, but you have not even recognized what existed prior to Cáoxī.
Such are their false assertions. This is truly what is meant by taking one who is not insane to be insane. Now, as for those divergent paths and their strange names and differing appearances:
it is only by falling into the land of death that one subsequently finds life; it is only by being placed in the land of ruin that one subsequently survives.
These various skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) are it. "The Mara-tolerance of death lies beside its branches" (*māra-ksānti mṛtyuḥ pārśve tasya śākhe*).

Below the characters for "its branches" (*tasya śākhe*), which are its wondrous names and diverse characteristics, one does not know that these "branches beside it"—its wondrous names and diverse characteristics—are precisely what is spoken from within one's own mouth.
"To drive them into a place of death so that they may subsequently live; to place them in a place of ruin so that they may subsequently survive"—this is merely a commentary [on such a principle].
Thus, not only do you fail to recognize Caoxi, but you likewise fail to recognize Linji.

If that is the case, then even what is called "driving one into a place of death so that one subsequently lives" and "placing one in a place of ruin so that one subsequently survives" is merely the talk of those who cling to words; when has it ever been practiced from the beginning?

In the ancient times of the Sage’s dwelling, he obtained but half a ladle. It is like one who does not understand the art of war at Huaiyin; though the timing and seasonal conditions were right, he focused solely on a "back-to-the-water" formation.
When the general saw it, he drove them all into the water—this is merely following the precedents of King Cheng and Wang Yi at Kunyang.

Furthermore, to speak of this matter as a "principle" (zong) is already to depart from the fundamental; there is nothing that can be done about it. It is only through forced designation that it is called such.

The "School" (zong) has further given rise to the various schools of Linji and others; to call them "schools" is already enough to leave people stunned—how much less can one speak of "various schools"?
"The Bhagavāns of the ten directions share a single path to the gate of Nirvāṇa. How could this be defiled by the notion of "various schools"?
From the five organs and the hundred skeletal members down to the eighty-four thousand pores, there is but a single body; how could there be any branching off from its side?
As for these extraordinary names and diverse appearances, they are merely a single skillful means (*upāya*).

To claim that this body of eighty-four thousand pores is the true reality (*dharmatā*) is impossible. Furthermore, can it be right to claim that these various branches, these extraordinary names, and these diverse appearances—which are themselves skillful means—are themselves the ultimate reality?
Mozhen said: "Six generations after Bodhidharma’s arrival in the East, there was Caoxi. Following Caoxi, the lineage split into two branches. One was Qingyuan Xingsi;
from Xingsi came Shitou, who became the patriarch of the Caodong school. The other was Nanyue Huairang;
from Huairang came Mazu, who became the progenitor of the four schools—Linji, Weiyang, Yunmen, and Fayan."
The *Li* (Book of Rites) states: "A collateral son becomes the progenitor (*zu*). One who succeeds the collateral son becomes the patriarch (*zong*).

That which does not change for a hundred generations is the lineage of the collateral son. Now, in the Way of Bodhidharma, Nanyue is the collateral son, and Linji is further a collateral son of Nanyue’s lineage.
Once the five schools are established, each should revere its own original collateral progenitor; thus, the source and transmission begin with [the respective collateral founders].
Linji is, in principle, settled. I do not know upon what basis Guangtong could claim to "pull back the patriarchs' wind" and "directly inherit from Dajian (Huineng).
If one says this is to trace the current back to its source, then in India it begins with Kāśyapa, and in this land it begins with Bodhidharma.
Guangtong thus abandons the primal ancestors Kāśyapa and Bodhidharma above, while forgetting that Linji was the first to branch off below.
This is the fundamental tenet [of our school], yet the lineage was subsequently transmitted through the Sixth Patriarch; what, then, would he have done?
Furthermore, his words state that from Mazu onwards, [the masters] acted with unrestrained freedom, employing strange names and eccentric appearances to ensnare scholars throughout the land.

Thus, the crime of eradicating the fundamental tenets is all too evident. Sanfeng strove to defend against this, which provoked their resentment and led to a series of accusations spanning many pages.
I have written repeatedly, and even today I do not cease; this is because [others] fail to examine Sanfeng’s true intentions. The *Book of Documents* says:
"When a person possesses skill, treat it as your own; when a person is eminent and sage, let your heart delight in that.

If those who transmit the Buddha-mind lineage in recent times could truly delight in Sanfeng’s Way to assist themselves, they would cause him to examine and finalize the teachings of their ancestors and patriarchs.
Regarding the Dharma and its ranks, the Cao-Dong and Gui-Yang schools may be praised as equals. Alas, it is already too late.

In the Gate of the Patriarchs, spiritual heirs are called "father and son. While the meaning of father and son refers to that from which one's physical body originates, the meaning of a Dharma heir does not originate from a physical body.
This is certainly not a case of having only a provisional name without actual substance; one must understand what this actual substance is.

This is merely a provisional designation (*prajñapti*). Nevertheless, it must be understood entirely according to worldly conventions, such as those concerning ancestors—high, great, or paternal—and descendants—sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further generations.

To discuss these matters minutely, one must not speak of dreams before a fool. As for the statements in the *Liji* (Book of Rites) regarding "the separate son becoming the progenitor" and "the successor to the separate son becoming the clan head," these were formulated because of the differences between the Central Kingdoms of antiquity and the tribal confederations of the present-day frontier.
The distance between them was not great, yet they could not help but each rule their own state and govern their own people.

Once they had each ruled their own state and governed their own people, they could not avoid establishing the system of ancestral clans (*zongfa*) to distinguish between the Great Clan (*dazong*) and the Lesser Clans (*xiaozong*).
This ensured that the Great Clan would perpetuate its rank and territory to nurture the Lesser Clans, while the Lesser Clans would maintain their titles and principles to serve the Great Clan.

Therefore it is said: "Zong" (clan) means "honored. Although the feudal system of later generations changed into the system of commanderies and counties, the Confucian school still attempts to manage the present-day kinship of its followers using the ancient clan laws; this is like trying to tell a dream to a madman.
Now, Magu Ren claims that Nanyue was a collateral branch, and Linji was a further collateral branch of Nanyue. Once the five schools are thus established, each [should be treated as such].
To take the founder of that lineage as its progenitor is nothing more than a deluded dream speaking of another deluded dream.
Now, a "separate son" (biezi) is a branch son, a son of secondary rank; the designations "branch" and "secondary" arise only because there is a legitimate son (zhidi).
Because he is distinguished from the legitimate son, he is called a "separate son. Among the forty-three Dharma heirs of Caoxi, in the end, which one among those forty-three...
How can one say that Renren was not the legitimate heir? Is it then permissible to treat both Qingyuan and Nanyue as collateral branches?
Furthermore, you disparage the teaching that Guangtong received the direct lineage from Caoxi, branding it a "destruction of the fundamental tenets.
Moreover, you condemn him for abandoning the primordial ancestors, Kāśyapa and Bodhidharma, above, while forgetting the original school that first branched out with Linji below.
Now, when discussing self-nature and self-deliverance, it is not obtained from another person; nor can it be said that one has obtained it oneself.
Furthermore, Śākyamuni and oneself are both equally "without attainment. It cannot be said that it was obtained from Śākyamuni, nor can it be said that it was not obtained from Śākyamuni.
Yet, in attaining this non-attainment, there is none who does not rejoice, praise, and feel profound gratitude—though there is nothing by which it can be named.
To speak thus, one calls Śākyamuni Buddha the Great Compassionate Father.

If, according to the treatise of Māra-Endurance (Māradharṣa), one were to designate Śākyamuni as the Great Compassionate Father, this would mean that one has utterly extinguished the ancient virtuous masters of antiquity and arrogantly claimed those from the Third Patriarch of India onwards as one's own descendants. As for the fundamental tenets, not even a single one can be cited.
If one speaks of the "gate and courtyard" (the pedagogical expedients), then its wondrous names and diverse forms can accommodate anything.

How much more so when what is called the "fundamental tenet" is itself a wondrous name and a diverse form, and is likewise a gate and courtyard expedient? To interpret these as substantial dharmas is to misunderstand both the fundamental tenet and the gate and courtyard expedients.
This is because one wishes for the followers of later generations throughout the world to all cherish their master’s teachings, rather than merely examining [the literal words].
He has fixed his ancestral laws and titles, and dragged them all down into a single pit to be buried.
Not recognizing these ancestral laws and titles of his, what kind of demonic outsider would he be? An ancient said:
"Even Linji’s little lad possesses a single eye. Although they sought to drag him into a fire pit, Linji was as steadfast as water.
It cannot be entered; it is like fire that cannot be approached, like the earth that cannot be discarded, and like the wind that cannot be grasped.
The School of the Lineage (Zongmen) does not involve itself with written words, so it certainly cannot be debated by means of texts.

Yet, when Mazu and his son [Baizhang] were active, they frequently cited secular classics to arrange and force connections between ideas. Therefore, one cannot help but use those very secular classics to clarify their errors.
This is erroneous; it is intended to resolve the delusions of those who have not yet attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Now, the "patriarchal lineage" (*zongfa*) of the ancestral laws and the "patriarchal school" (*zongmen*) of the Chan gate share the same character "patriarch" (*zong*), yet their realities are as different as a square base and a round lid. In the patriarchal lineage of the ancestral laws, "patriarch" (*zong*) means "venerable.
For example, the Son of Heaven of Zhou was the Great Patriarch (*dazong*), revered by all under heaven; whereas the states of Lu and Wei were merely collateral branches (*biezong*).

The son becomes a minor lord (*xiǎozōng*), revered by his own state. As for those of a different surname, such as Taigong Wang, who founded the state of Qi, they become great lords (*dàzōng*) and are revered by their state. Those such as Ding or Huan, however, become separate branches (*biézi*).

It constitutes a minor school and is revered by a single lineage. As for the character *zōng* (宗) in the term "Chan School" (*Chanzōng*), what connection does it have with the concept of a "lineage" (*zōng*) in the secular sense?
"Lineage" (*zōng*) refers to that which holds everything together (*sōji*). Reaching this point, the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases;
it is a singular totality-holding (*sōji*). It is non-dual with *nirvāṇa*. Not knowing its name, we forcibly designate it as "lineage. Therefore, the teaching says: "To speak is [the teaching]."
"Penetration. As for "Principle" (zong), it means "the penetration of the principle. The term "principle" signifies "it is thus, it is thus.

Bodhidharma shattered the six schools to establish the one school of the "special transmission outside the teachings. Dajian Huineng and Daotong Huairang divided this into the Southern and Northern Schools.
Subsequently, the Southern School further divided into the five houses: Caodong, Linji, Guiyang, Yunmen, and Fayan. All of these were proponents of the teaching.
At one time, people merely revered and exalted them as the founder of a particular school; what connection did this have to the principle of spiritual succession?

How could they so arbitrarily join and force together these concepts? Throughout the ages, ignorant and witless sheep have rashly sought to claim famous masters of antiquity as their ancestors for the sake of worldly glory, mistakenly conflating the character *zong* (宗) used in the Chan school with the character *zong* (宗) used in the context of clan lineage and ancestral rites.
The meanings were identical, yet debates arose like swarms of bees, and the clamor of litigation never ceased. Consequently, five schools emerged, each with its own tenets;

each transmitted them to their descendants, standardizing the phrasing of the texts and dividing the words into distinct sects. Passed down orally from ear to ear, they were understood through conceptual thought and mental discrimination.
Thus, the single flavor of Caoxi’s nectar was transformed into five kinds of poison—how lamentable this is! It is truly not so...

When considering the principles of ancestral lineages (*zong*), one must necessarily discuss them in relation to both the father and the mother; thus, one distinguishes between the *zhengzi* (legitimate son) and the *biezi* (branch son).
How could the Chan school forcibly conflate these? Even the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* contains the designation of "collateral dharma-heirs," which likewise belongs to a mistaken view.
The Buddha taught that the Bhagavans of the ten directions share a single path to the gate of *nirvāṇa*, and further said: "This alone is the reality; all else is..."
That would not be true. To deviate even slightly toward a bypath is to belong to the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika).

How could there be the principle of being a byproduct and yet still being called a Dharma heir? This matter is boundless and not centered; can it be called a bypath? It neither emerges nor enters; can it be called an emergence?
For Míyún Wù to transmit the Dharma-treasury and leave it as a branch that emerged as a bypath would belong to mere intellectual speculation.
Their vision is clouded. Muzang and his son sought instead to adjudicate the ancestral dharma and establish themselves as the orthodox lineage of Linji.
Their various manifestations of greed, anger, and delusion were nothing more than an attempt to conceal the two characters "side-lineage" (pángchū).

Yet they remained unaware that their own doctrine had reached such an extreme of fallacy and contradiction. Whenever Muzang and his ilk rebuked Miyun for being illiterate, they did not realize they were merely exposing their own ignorance.

They do not realize that the harm of knowing this [name] can, at its greatest, sever one's life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*), and even at its smallest, cause others to laugh until their teeth turn cold.
Magu Ren said: "The six people together testify to a single essence, like the skin, flesh, bone, and marrow of the First Patriarch; this is used to distinguish the Way."
The meaning of "partial" and "complete" certainly does not lie therein; your critique merely follows the words and gives rise to interpretations based on them.
Long ago, when Master Xuedou Xian was serving as the guest prefect at Taiyang, a visitor discussed the fundamental principle of Zhaozhou with him, saying:
"In the past, Chan Master Fayan encountered Jue Tiezui at Jinling and asked him: 'Do you still remember the karmic connection regarding Zhaozhou’s white oak tree?'"
Jue said, "The former master did not say such words. Do not slander the former master. Fayan clapped his hands and said, "Truly he has come from the lion’s den.
Jue Gong said there were no such words, yet Fayan approved him; where does the meaning of this lie?
Xian replied, "In the Gate of the Patriarchs, there is the art of suppression and exaltation; how could there be fixed rules? There was a man of ascetic practice named Han Dabo, whose appearance...

While Xian was sleeping in the cold, [Dongshan] would stand by his side and then depart with a hidden smile. Xian said angrily, "I am speaking to a guest; how dare you laugh at me with such insolence?
He replied, "I laughed because I knew that your eye of wisdom was not yet upright and your discernment of the Dharma was unclear.
Xian asked, "Is there a verse for this? He answered with a gāthā: "A single rabbit lies across the ancient road; As soon as the blue hawk sees it, he seizes it."
Later, the hunting dog lost its spirit and continued to search for the old spot where the withered stump had stood.

Xianyin found this strange and took the dog as a companion. Alas! Han Daobe was indeed extraordinary; yet Master Xian received his kindness and transformed his faults—such a person is truly a peerless figure of antiquity and today alike.

There is no good; there is no fault. Even the non-existence of both good and fault is itself non-existent. When even this "non-existence" is gone, that is precisely what is called the first stage of the Bodhisattva path, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*).
Regarding the Tripiṭaka, the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and the seventeen hundred koans: if one says they are good, they are all good.

This goodness does not depend on their being completed as scrolls, nor on their being formed into chapters, phrases, or characters. From the moment the brush is raised and ink is applied—*ping bi qin mo*.
It is sufficient that the brush falls upon the paper to form a dot; it is sufficient that the mouth opens and the throat turns to emit breath and produce sound.
To claim that these are errors is to say that all such acts are errors—even before a scroll is completed, a rule established, a sentence formed, or a character written.

From the moment the pen is raised and ink is infused until the dot is formed on the paper, the error has already been committed; from the moment the mouth opens and the throat turns to emit breath and produce sound, the error has already occurred.
This results in a great error. If one has not yet even grasped this, yet wishes to discuss the essence and expound the ultimate meaning, it all becomes mere worldly discourse.
How could there be anything of our school? This is why Fayen praised Jue’s critique of Tiezi’s discussion of Zhaozhou’s "cypress tree" koan.
Jue said to his late teacher, "The Master did not say such things; do not slander the late teacher. Fayen clapped his hands and exclaimed in admiration.

He praised [Xuedou] as truly coming from the lion’s den itself; yet Han Dabo refused to accept Xuedou’s words regarding the lack of fixed tracks in the exaltation and disparagement of the Chan school.
Thus, there arose the analogy of the "fierce hawk seizing the rabbit" versus the "stubborn dog seeking the post.
Magu Ren then claimed that Xuedou had improved his character and reformed his errors. But what was good about Han Dabo, and what was wrong with Xuedou?
Indeed. His intention was nothing more than to secretly disparage Tiantong’s opening of the book as a way of glossing over his errors and refusing counsel;

he did not realize that he was burying Xuedou, burying Han Daipo, burying Jue Tiezui, burying Fayan, burying Zhaozhou, burying Bodhidharma, burying the "Pine Tree," the hawk, the rabbit, and the dog, and burying Moran himself.

Regarding one’s own original life-source (*mūlāyana*), [Mazu] specifically instructed Miyun Yuanwu in the "one-piece head-hard Chan," allowing him to display his wit and exercise his authority, striking with a single blow straight through to the bottom.
Now, while that single blow could become a habitual trap for evasion, is it not also the case that a single blow penetrates directly through the three barriers?
If, because of being struck by that single blow, one perceives the physical body within the physical body—this is where the matter lies.
This is not seeing. It is a good view that sees through false views; it is to burn away and confess them.
To then harbor doubts about them, to slander them, to misrepresent them, and to ensnare them—unaware that the staff-bearer has long since leaped up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven!
If you continue to search for him in his old place, you are truly acting like the hunting dog of Great Uncle Han, which lacks any spiritual nature.
Mozhi said, "When Master Ma was propagating the Dharma in Jiangxi, Nanyue asked the assembly, 'Is Daoyi preaching the Dharma for the community?
The assembly replied, 'He has already been preaching the Dharma for the community. The Master said, 'I have not yet heard anyone bring back any news of it.
The assembly had no reply. Thereupon, he sent a monk away, instructing him: 'Wait until he ascends the hall; simply ask him, "What is it?""'"
Sheng said, "I will record these words for you. When the monk departed, he followed the Master's instructions exactly.
Upon his return, he told the Master, "Master Ma said, 'Since the time of confusion, for thirty years I have never lacked salt and sauce. The Master approved of this.
This single phrase is an iron bolt that blocks the path of conceptualizing the nature and mind, and a sharp sword that destroys the demon army of birth and death. It is direct...
This is the guiding chariot for pointing to the human mind and seeing one's nature to achieve Buddhahood.
It was from this point that the "Vajra thorns and brambles" began to pierce through people's nostrils; it simply cannot be explained as a dream to those who are deluded.
The path of the meaning of the mind-nature is precisely the true exposition of *vijñapti-mātra*. Birth-and-death and the demonic armies are themselves the nirvana and the fruit of Buddhahood.

An ancient worthy said: "If you grasp at even one dharma, you do not realize the Dharma-body; if you abandon even one dharma, you do not realize the Dharma-body; if you lack even one dharma, you do not realize the Dharma-body;
if you have even one dharma in excess, you do not realize the Dharma-body. How could one then give rise to a mind of weary detachment?
The path of the meaning of nature is thus rendered solid and obstructed by shackles. To obstruct it oneself is to fear one’s own head; to obstruct it for others is to administer a delusive drug.
Moreover, while the Buddhas dwell within the ocean of birth-and-death of sentient beings, sentient beings dwell within the Buddhas’ gate of no-birth-and-death.
If the perception of "Buddha" arises, that itself is Māra; if the snare of Māra is seen as empty, that itself is the Buddha. One who desires to sever [this]—
Birth and death—this is precisely the failure to understand birth and death. Once birth and death are understood, they are fundamentally non-existent;

how, then, could there be any need for a sharp sword to destroy the demonic army of birth and death? Moreover, the path of conceptual meaning is the very root of the consciousness-spirit’s birth and death.
If one only thoroughly realizes the nature of the mind, then the path of meaning is itself nirvana. Now, you have conflated the nature of the mind and the path of meaning into one;
yet, since you speak of the "nature of the mind," why do you call it the "path of meaning"? And since you speak of the "path of meaning," why do you call it the "nature of the mind"?
Birth and death are merely what sentient beings perceive; they do not understand birth and death while yet wishing to sever them—this is to be regarded as the vision of Māra.

Now, taking birth and death themselves as the army of Māra, one can see that they have not yet understood birth and death. Indeed, heaven, earth, and all things exist within the ocean of birth and death;
how could one dismiss them by calling them "Māra"? It is clear enough that such a person belongs to the retinue of Māra. Directly...
Pointing to the human mind to see one's nature and attain Buddhahood: horizontally it encompasses all places throughout the ten directions;
vertically it penetrates all times throughout the three periods. All are mind; all are Buddha. Therefore it is said: like a *maṇi* jewel, its substance is not of a single color;

like a net of precious threads, the layers reflect one another in continuous connection. This is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*). Since there is no exiting and no entering, how could there be a need for a guide?
Regarding the analogy of the chariot: if one uses the south-pointing chariot as an analogy, then this Perfect Teaching (yuanzong) is a fixed location.
Yet this phrase by Mazu possesses the power of direct pointing; when both subject and object are simultaneously detached, the Perfect Teaching is suddenly obliterated.
This very thing can only be known through realization; it cannot be transmitted through language or writing.
Even with unimpeded eloquence, one cannot cause those who have not yet realized it to do so by means of my words and writings.

If they were to realize it because of them, it would still be their own mind realizing itself. Otherwise, even if the speaker explains it thoroughly and the listener relies [upon it], [realization will not occur].
However, this [approach] remains muddled and, conversely, obstructs one's right view. Therefore, the ancients had the saying: "The mouth born of one's parents shall never speak for you.

This causes people to realize it within their own minds through direct verification. As for skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they employ words devoid of conventional meaning and place them within the field of the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*), like a vajra-ring or a thorny acorn—neither able to swallow it nor able to spit it out.
If one attains true inquiry and genuine realization, there will be a share in repaying the debt of gratitude.

This is precisely the great compassion without conditions and the great pity of shared essence of the ancient worthies. How could they wish to use this to pierce through people's nostrils and exercise control at will?
What kind of mental activity is that? Furthermore, these few phrases are identical to Mazu’s ascent to the hall: "Since the time of chaos, for thirty years..."
"How does having used too little salt and sauce have anything to do with it?
When Mazu was propagating the Dharma in Jiangxi, Nanyue, because no one had brought back any news of him, sent a monk to visit him. He suddenly asked, "What is it like? Mazu then spoke these words.

This was because his state and wisdom were interfused and principle and phenomena were non-obstructive; not even a hair’s breadth departed from his fundamental nature, so he immediately [responded] with his fundamental nature.
When engaging with people, one responds according to conditions and adapts to their capacities; this is merely answering the monk who asks, "How is it?
What has ever been meant by saying that these few words can block off the path of meaning, sever the cycle of birth and death, or possess the power to point out a person’s attainment of Buddhahood?
It may serve as an instrument for piercing the nostrils of men; it has been transmitted for several thousand years. Is it not from this that the fundamental principle first became established?
As for those who claim it is like a "demon's patience," they are truly deluded people talking in their sleep.

To then say that one must not speak of dreams before deluded people—how utterly absurd! Yuanwu said: "If one were to provide detailed guidance and support, one would strike the meditation seat or raise the whisk."
A blink of an eye, a raising of an eyebrow; sometimes speaking, sometimes silent; saying there is, saying there is not.
If one is lifted up toward the ultimate, it is like the spark struck from flint, like a flash of lightning. At times he strikes with the staff, at times he utters the shout;
at times their arrowheads meet point-to-point, at times even the Buddha-eye cannot see him. Although this is so, there is still "upward" and "downward. Suddenly, one encounters that which is within.
People, however, do not have so many various affairs; it is simply as it is. Therefore it is said:
"The mountains are mountains, the waters are waters, heaven is heaven, and earth is earth—not shifting by even a hair’s breadth. At this very moment, do you truly understand?
When the myriad realms follow the Way and return to the imperial transformation, weapons are laid aside and all rejoice in great peace. Thus did Yuanwu comment on this passage.

If a student can verify this phrase, they will know for themselves where Mazu Daishi has arrived; it is truly manifest and complete. Whether it be the "Devil" (Māra) or the "Patience" (Kṣānti), or the discourse on the "Wondrous" and the "Ultimate," all are the True Dharma.
Mofen said: "The Great Master is the one recognized by Prajñātāra as the foremost Dharma King of China.
Observing his arrangements, they are like those of Shi Jilun when hosting guests: even in places such as kitchens and latrines—grounds of filth and impurity—he displayed a variety of precious gems."
A guest may happen upon this by chance; often they will bow to a maidservant as if she were a lady, only to be startled and withdraw, imagining they have entered the chamber of the Duke of Chong.

Yet when they ascend the grand banquet hall, where they are made to drink from massive goblets, illuminated by bright moon pearls, with Lu Zhu singing before them, and a ten-foot coral tree shattered to pieces at a single blow—they suddenly realize their error and feel a profound sense of disillusionment. This is the Great [Dream].
Wisdom was attained by twisting the nose, yet lost at the final shout. This is what Linji meant when he said, "When you have used a blade sharp enough to shave a hair, you must immediately grind it.
Indeed, the majesty of tigers and leopards is truly fierce, yet they cannot always avoid the spear and halberd;
the fish that swallow ships are truly vast, yet they find it difficult to escape the great flood. The qíjì (steed of the sun)...
A fine horse gallops a thousand *li* in the blink of an eye, yet a person can capture and tether it because its tracks remain behind.
It is not so with the dragon. Whether in the vastness of the ocean or within a small cup, it rolls up and unfurls itself with ease;
it displaces mountains and stirs clouds and rain, passing through without lingering, its transformations beyond measure. One who attains this Way is called a dragon.

The Samādhi of Vigorous Exertion—is this not the Great Master Mazu? He transformed the methods and regulations of the thirty-four patriarchs, dissolving their defects and sweeping away their tracks, like a sudden peal of thunder shattering a mountain.

He caused the "thieving mind" that seeks a path through the nature and mind to die upon hearing him, just as the King of Golden-Winged Birds directly seizes and swallows a dragon, thereafter soaring through the nine heavens without dwelling even in the void.
Emptiness. It is not separate from emptiness, nor is it obstructed by the nature of emptiness. I am the Dharma King; I possess sovereign mastery over the Dharma.
It is not merely a matter of dragon-transformations. Later, Linji, Yunmen, Yangshan-Huiqiu, and Fayan each erected their own jeweled banners.
They did nothing more than bring forth [the truth]—how could there be any other school-seal beyond the "three days of deafness"? Nevertheless...

Thus, those of today who have not penetrated the heavy gates and who mistake delusion within enlightenment for a substantial dharma are no different from the guest who found treasure while on the toilet.
It matters not that Mazu never altered the methods and regulations of the thirty-fourth patriarch; do not slander Mazu. Furthermore, three...
The Fourteenth Patriarch—how could he have ever possessed any fixed formal rules? Do not slander the Thirty-Fourth Patriarch.
To claim that the Thirty-Fourth Patriarch has tracks to be swept away or defects to be melted away is to slander the Thirty-Fourth Patriarch;
yet to claim that the Thirty-Fourth Patriarch has no tracks to be swept away and no defects to be melted away is likewise to slander the Thirty-Fourth Patriarch. Why is this so? It is because...

To say that Mazu dropped the word "wu" (no) was to dissolve the legacy of the thirty-fourth patriarch and sweep away his tracks, making him the first Dharma King of China; this is no less than to denounce Mazu as the greatest demon in China.
From antiquity, all the virtuous masters have ascended the gate of singular liberation and have fully received equal enlightenment.

This is recorded in the *Dharmatrāta-śāstra*. As for allowing one's nature to expand or contract at will and responding to things according to conditions, the specific times and causes for each instance are not the same.
Therefore, the various modes of speech and silence, or action and stillness, do not overlap or interfere with one another.

It is like the four directions—east, west, south, and north—one cannot say that this direction is superior to that; it is like earth, water, fire, and wind—one cannot say that this element is higher than that.
"Great! All of this concerns only matters of the gate and courtyard; it has nothing to do with the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*.
If the eighty-four spiritual friends under Mazu’s guidance were each capable of serving as a guide for the ten directions, it was certainly because Mazu’s forge was extraordinary.
Yet, fundamentally, it was also due to the circumstances of that particular Dharma assembly, where the stars of virtue gathered together. Each of these individuals..."
Self-nature saves itself; one attains that which is non-attainable.
How could it be that Mazu ever taught each person the "Secret Seal of No-Text," the "Double-Knot of the Single Head," or various fabricated dharmas?

Indeed, this very thing turns its back when you face it, departs when you approach it, is lost when you grasp it, and becomes slow when you hurry it. The thousand sages fold their hands in helplessness, having no plan.
To penetrate deeply into a single gate and forget all sensory perception, realizing it within oneself—this is not something obtained from others;
