Statements such as "the five schools" and so forth all belong to erroneous discourse. When the World-Honored One [taught] at the seven locations and nine assemblies, was that not a model for a hundred generations?

Yet, in the end, he said, "I have never spoken a single word. Thus, it is clear that the World-Honored One did not intend for the seven locations and nine assemblies to serve as a model for a hundred generations.
Whatever constitutes the provisional arrangements of a school's gate is not the true model. This is the business of the Confucian school.
Matters are real dharmas; therefore, there are teachings concerning "canons" (*dianxing*). A "canon" (*dian*) refers to that which may be recorded in books and scrolls.
A "model" (*xing*) is a metaphor for a mold made of clay or cast metal, signifying that which can serve as a fixed standard.
Since the Chan school possesses no words or phrases, nor does it bestow a single dharma upon others, what then constitutes its canon? What serves as its model?
To speak of the five houses (wǔzōng), they are all merely matters of the gateways and courtyards.

To speak of the fundamental division (běnfèn), it is the Dharma that came from the West, its light illuminating a thousand lamps—a lamp of inexhaustibility reaching to the end of the future. All are equally one in their illumination of heaven and earth;
one cannot even say that Bodhidharma is the archetype for ten hundred generations or the crown jewel of the five houses, let alone [when facing] the present.
Ji: "If there are crowns and caps, there must be robes and garments; since there are crowns and robes, there must be ranks and grades. Can such distinctions as these not exist?

Furthermore, Māranirghātana, in this chapter, again employs words intended to resolve the confusion and protect the Celestial Youth (Devaputra), claiming that both Māra’s inverted weapons and the Celestial Youth’s attacks are not worldly dharmas."
This is precisely a clever defense of Māra’s treasury; this is precisely a worldly method. How could it possibly escape being seen through by those with clear eyes?
Furthermore, you say that while one person sings and the other clears away, you yourself follow along and join in;

only then does Linji’s eye of wisdom fail to fall, and he emerges as an extraordinary and lofty stream, such that where there is not much of the Buddha-Dharma, ten thousand doors are all pierced through. This is...
To encounter such [views] morning and evening is all the more laughable. Indeed, when auspicious grain and noxious weeds are submerged by the earth’s yin and yang, neither can grow;
likewise, within the pure and vast ocean, both living and dead things cannot remain. Thus they advocate one thing while refuting another.
If these were merely matters circulating within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), then they would both vanish upon the ground of yin and yang, with neither remaining attached.

However, if we are discussing the fundamental vehicle (*mūla-yāna*) through rigorous analysis, then even the *Tripiṭaka* and the *Kṣānti* [Sūtra] belong to the discourse of Māra; even Tiantong has already cast his entire body into the weeds.
Carrying water and dragging mud—though there may be a distinction between life and death, in the end, neither can dwell within the pure great ocean.
How could one possibly attain the Buddha-dharma or have "many children" to realize therein? Furthermore, let alone discussing the gateways of the school.
First, one dissolves the distinction between person and phenomena; with both the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena, what is there that can be "is" and what can be "is not"?

Departing from "is not" within the hundred negations, it is that which cannot be negated. Transcending "is" within the myriad affirmations, it is that which cannot be affirmed. It is that which cannot be negated.
Then there would be no "non-being. If that which is taken to be "being" cannot actually be affirmed as being, then there is no "being" at all.
Even if one reaches the realm where there is neither being nor non-being, one has still not taken a single step beyond the hundred-foot pole.
To now seek the Buddha-dharma within this heap of right and wrong is not much different from seeking a single drop of water in a great mass of fire.
The verse on Mazu’s three blows of the staff at Huangbo says: A multi-storied tower, high and lofty—climb it in a single step. At the very end, having been struck, one soars away with speed.
From the tip of the horn, the essential core of the primordial source bursts forth; This is what the true masters of ten thousand ages have valued and transmitted.
If we take the journey as a metaphor, then even a hundred-foot tower, though far from the ground, ultimately arises because of the earth.
The first step and the topmost level are equal and non-dual; to tread firmly at every step is precisely to ascend into the void at every step.
To ascend into the void at every step—how could that not be to tread firmly at every step? If one wishes to soar aloft, that is to be one whose heels do not touch the ground. If...
This is an analogy for awakening: the single mind is the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm is the single mind. It encompasses the ten directions without leaving even a hair’s breadth exposed.

Now, since there is this tower, and there is this person ascending the tower, and one speaks of its layered heights and the swiftness of a single step, reaching the very tip and soaring to the absolute summit—is this not the union of person and dharma?
They cling simultaneously to both subject and object, like pressing one's eyes and seeing flowers, or being deluded by mistaking a head for its reflection.

It is no wonder they take a dead rat as a precious jade or point to a mountain fowl as a phoenix. Taking Linji’s moments of defeat and exposing his flaws, they enshrine them as the Unsurpassed True Doctrine;
yet, from within this, a sharp horn protrudes, and there is a verse of essential import from the Primordial Source, the true master of all ages, which honors what has been received.
Yongming said: "When people hear that the Buddha transmitted the Dharma of the mind, they assume there is a separate dharma apart from the mind that can be realized or grasped.
Consequently, they seek the dharma with the mind, unaware that the mind is itself the dharma and the dharma is itself the mind. One cannot use the mind to further seek the mind;
even after passing through a thousand kalpas, one will never reach the day of attainment. Now, the Three Essentials and Three Points are taken as the ultimate."
In that case, there would be a separate dharma apart from the mind that could be realized or grasped.
If one takes this to be awakening, then what is thus awakened to—how would it differ from, or be distinct from, what is studied and awakened to by the nine schools and the hundred masters?

How could there be entry [into reality] without employing the discernment of consciousness? Even if one were to push this analysis to the great totality of the infinite and encompass it down to the subtlest...
To enter the Avīci Hell is like entering the ocean to count its sands; what connection has this with our own numinous awakening?
Although the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, he finally showed people at the end, saying: "I have never spoken a single word.

Thus one may know that throughout the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, there is not a single word that can serve as a true teacher, nor a single word that can be taken up and transmitted. Linji—
Who is it that can say: "Within a single phrase, the three gates are complete; within a single gate, the three essentials are complete"?

Only such a person may be called a true master of all ages. Only such a person may take these two phrases and, from generation to generation and from successor to successor, transmit them so they do not fall into ruin.
Only such a person may gather the immeasurable and boundless, vast gates of the Buddha within this very space.

If a student has not yet been able to truly investigate and attain genuine awakening, nor gain sufficient confidence in their own realization, they should for the time being compare the World-Honored One with Linji,
and the Three Pitakas and Twelve Divisions of the Canon with the Three Essentials and Three Keys; by doing so, they will naturally no longer be deluded by demonic teachings.

Mōjin said: "When Linji was at Huangbo’s place and received blows from him, he could only cause all the grasses and trees throughout the great earth to simultaneously radiate a great light, such that even Śakra and Brahmā could not fully praise it.
It is a pity that he was suddenly struck across the face by the old woman Dayu, causing him to inevitably fall flat on his face on level ground. Now, the venerable masters of all quarters say—"
Linji realized the principle of what is struck by the staff and touched by the whisk. But tell me, does Linji himself approve of this?

O virtuous ones, suppose the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives; when the light of the eyes has fallen to the ground, one will not know the pain of being sawn apart or hewn with axes, nor will one know the joy of being anointed with gold dust and incense. At such a time as this, this very staff and whisk— [The text ends here.]
"To what place do you apply it? Do you understand? What I have said here is merely like trying to cure a dead horse with medicine.
Linji said, "Twenty years ago, when I was at Huangbo’s place, I received the staff three times; it was like being brushed by a bundle of mugwort.
This statement has two meanings: first, it describes how his "lacquer bucket" (his mind) was not yet clear back then, and thus he received those three blows.
The painful blow is like being brushed by a stalk of mugwort; one knows neither pain nor pleasure. Second:

if a student is truly able to undertake the causal conditions for the Great Matter, practicing authentically and attaining genuine realization, then even though they receive three painful blows, it will be as if they were brushed by a stalk of mugwort.

Thus, subject and object are forgotten, self and other are extinguished, right and wrong are cut off, and delusion and awakening are stilled. Spontaneously, the silver mountains and iron walls collapse with a single strike.
A hundred fragments scattered. This is why, upon a single word from Dayu, one suddenly awakens.
If one does not reach this stage, one will ultimately never attain even a small measure of resonance with the truth. Now, Mazu died under the staff and whisk of Miyun;
yet, the old masters of various quarters nowadays claim that Linji attained enlightenment through the principle of being struck by the staff and whisked by the whisk.
This is the principle. But tell me, would Linji have approved? O virtuous ones, suppose the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives;
when the light of the eyes falls to the ground, one will not know the pain of being sawn apart or hewn with axes, nor will one know the joy of being anointed with gold and incense.
At such a time as this, where would that staff—upon which you have been struck—be placed? This...
Such words are merely an attempt to fabricate a false narrative, like dense clouds; they fail to recognize that one is already bearing the weight of one's own transgressions.
For instance, as long as the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month has not yet arrived, and before the light of the eyes has fallen to the ground, one’s two pupils remain bright and clear.
At such a time, speaking of being sawn apart or hewn with axes brings fear of pain, while speaking of gold powder or fragrant ointments gives rise to joy. It is precisely at this moment.
Where, then, can one place this staff that brushes against [the mind]?
Furthermore, Linji’s receiving blows from Huangbo was nothing more than a failure to understand; it was only upon being awakened by Dayu’s seal that he finally let out a roar of realization.
There is a most extraordinary and strange person here. This son of Māra intends to elevate Linji, using him to boast that he himself is a descendant of Linji’s lineage.
How lamentable it is that after a thousand or ten thousand generations since Linji, he must suffer such defilement and neglect at the hands of this unworthy demonic grandson.
Moshi said: "In the 'Three Exhortations' dialogue from Luzhou, Huangbo struck him three times; since he did not awaken, he was further directed to consult Dayu.
This precisely reveals the subtle and profound skill of these three elders’ forging tools, and the entire foundation upon which Linji established his school rests therein."
People today know only that Huangbo asked three times and struck three times; they thus rely on the single staff as the ultimate principle.
Without the hand of a master carver from Ying, even ten thousand blows could not bring people to life.
After the robe was transmitted at Caoxi, Huangmei saw him off at the Jiuyang Post Station. Caoxi said, "One should simply deliver oneself by means of one's own nature.
Huangmei replied, "So it is, so it is. This "delivering oneself by means of one's own nature" is the single path to nirvana for the Bhagavāns of the ten directions.
Although the World-Honored One possesses great majestic power, he can only deliver others through their other-nature.
"No. For while the nature of returning to the source is non-dual, the expedient means have many gates. Since ancient times, the virtuous ones of old have established various devices:
sometimes they employ the staff or the shout; sometimes they blink an eye or raise an eyebrow; at other times they set an arrow to a drawn bow;

and at others they brandish a blade or point a finger. Although the timing and conditions differ, and the partial, the complete, the sudden, and the gradual vary, when all is brought to its ultimate conclusion, it returns to the same point."
Come! This is for the student to personally realize their own mind. When has it ever raised so much as a single hair’s breadth to give to others?
Outside of self-nature and self-deliverance, what extraordinary or secret thing is there?

As for those who stubbornly fail to realize their own nature and refuse to deliver themselves—just like the *luo* insect transforming the *mingling* caterpillar—it is entirely not under its own control; it relies entirely upon the power of another.
If such a thing existed, it would be a demonic heterodox teaching; if one says it exists, that is to slander the Great Dharma Wheel.
Now, Mōjin claims that the three elders—Muzhou, Huangbo, and Dayu—possessed a subtle and profound skill with their "tongs and hammers," and were thus able to forge Linji out of them.
He further claims that Linji established his school’s tenets because of this, and that had it not been for [the precision of] Ying...
The hands of a craftsman, though they strike ten thousand times, how could they bring a person back to life? It is just like Muzhou, Huangbo, Dayu, and Linji;
they truly possessed a wondrous and secret Dharma capable of delivering people, yet they brought no small amount of trouble upon these four elders.

Now, Miyun has never taken a single blow of the staff as the ultimate standard; rather, he simply asked a thousand times and struck a thousand times, asked ten thousand times and [struck ten thousand times].
Ten thousand strikes. How could these not save people? Consider the single finger of Jūchi, the single arrow of Sekkō, and the single staff-blow of Mitsuun—are they the same or different?
If you say they are different, how is it that the eyes were not exchanged for the sake of the finger and the arrow?
If you say they are the same, how can you grant them to Jūchi and Sekkō while refusing to grant them to Mitsuun? Furthermore...

Not permitting [the transmission to] Mìyún was still merely a secondary matter. By forcibly establishing a "founder's intent" (zongzhǔ), you cause those who are like unpainted wooden buckets to falsely claim that the Chan school possesses a truly extraordinary and secret dharma. This has no relation to one’s own genuine inquiry or authentic realization;
it seeks only the oral transmission and face-to-face instruction of masterful teachers. If this current continues unchecked in this manner, will it not sever the transmission of the lamp?
The Venerable Māra-jñānin said: "Zhao Jianzi wished to test the worthiness of his sons. One day he said to them, 'I have hidden a precious tally on Mount Chang;
whoever finds it first shall be rewarded. The sons galloped to Mount Chang and searched, but found nothing. A short time later...
Zi Mu Xu said, "I have already obtained the auspicious signs. Jianzi said, "Report them. Zi Mu Xu said, "From Mount Chang, one can look down upon Dai; Dai can be taken.
Jianzi esteemed him for this, and consequently deposed the crown prince Bolu and established Zi Mu Xu as the crown prince.
Alas! That which Huangbo and Linji demonstrated is a hundred times more profound than the words of Jianzi. It is near.
The scholars of this world possess instruments that are not refined; their departure from the Mother and their lack of compassion exceed [the former] a hundredfold.
They have consequently taken "striking straight through to the end" as a banner for future generations. How could their errors be limited merely to seeking a tally with Changshan?
Dai was the state to which the daughter of Zhao Jianzi had been married. The Lady of Dai was her mother’s paternal aunt. Zhao Jianzi coveted its territory;
he disregarded the people of Dai, he disregarded the ancestral sacrifices of Dai, and he disregarded both his son-in-law and his daughter.
With a heart set upon it and through long-continued deliberation, he resolved on murder, and thus [sent] a precious token in secret.
He tested his sons to see who was most loyal; only Zhongzi showed compassion for his mother and could manage her wickedness, whereas the others did not care for their elder sister.
Upon reaching Changshan, he immediately recognized the strategic advantage of taking over the state and, without the slightest hesitation, resolved upon his ambition to seize it.
As the saying goes, "A tiger's cub must be loved by the tiger"; Jianzi subsequently regarded him as worthy and established him as his successor. Subsequently, indeed...
He supplanted the legitimate successor and seized his territory; he slaughtered people until they filled the city, and his own elder sister, Magandikā, committed suicide.
Such evil deeds as these are regarded by the world with inverted views, such that they are instead considered virtuous. This is something Śākya could not bear to hear.

The realm of Jambudvīpa is indeed an age of the five turbidities and evil worlds; having acknowledged this, let alone the school of Nature (Xingzong), could one possibly attach such filth to the midst of the six perfections and myriad practices?

Now, if there were someone who took the Buddha’s scriptures to wipe knives in a slaughterhouse or to cover jars in a tavern, then regardless of whether they were a monastic or a layperson, none would fail to feel compassion and say: "This is a sin!"
[This is] an error. Now, regarding the incident of Zhao Jianzi’s mother’s *muxu* (the "mother's sorrow"), its filthiness exceeds that of a slaughterhouse or a wine shop ten thousandfold.
Yet you, Mohen, cite this as an analogy for the matters of the Buddhas and Patriarchs beyond the ordinary—how could you not fall into the Avīci Hell?
Furthermore, you claim that Miyun’s capacity was not sharp, being a hundred times worse than that of *muxu*. How can your perversity reach such an extreme? Even if one...

An ordinary person of the marketplace who, though perhaps foolish, has shaved their head and left the household life—even if they remain dull-witted throughout their entire life and know nothing at all—if they are simply able to refrain from conceiving any evil thoughts, exercise a modicum of caution, and leave no manifest traces of killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct; [they may still attain liberation].
This person has already surpassed the grief of Jiaofu by a hundredfold; how much more so, then, for Miyun?
Furthermore, it is said that what Huangbo and Linji taught was a hundred times deeper than the words of Zhao Jianzi.

If this were true, then the artifice and guile of Huangbo and Linji would be a hundred times deeper than those of Zhao Jianzi—not only would they be inadmissible within the Buddha-dharma, but even in [the secular world]...
The Discourse on Worldly Dharmas is likewise something for which execution is warranted even without instruction.
How could you have gone so far as to defile Huangbo and Linji to such an extreme? In short, Ma Zongyi and his son did not recognize what Chan school truly is;

they entirely used mind, intellect, and consciousness to speculate upon the matters that transcend the Buddhas and Patriarchs, thereby becoming great demons within the Buddha-realm. How much more so, then, regarding Guanyin...
The human mind and the course of the world are not superficial matters; this concerns not only the study and practice of the Zen school, so how could one cease from engaging in debate?
Mazu Daoyi said: "It turns out that Linji did not establish his own unique doctrine, nor was it merely the Huangbo lineage."

The essential point: if one traces back against the current, the fundamental tenet of the lineage of the seven Buddhas from Kāśyapa to Śākyamuni and beyond the Sound-Voice (Vighuṣṭa) has fortunately been established here, so that it is not ruined by the "severing and threading" Chan. Is there anyone present now who can wipe it out?
Bring them all here bound, and I shall give each of them thirty blows of the staff, so as to ensure peace throughout the world. He then offered this verse: Three days...
Three days before and three days after, Puhua and Kefu both slipped away; now that Linji has arrived at Sanfeng, he shall pierce him with a single arrow through the Three Gates.
Linji said to Kefu and Puhua, "I wish to establish the fundamental tenets here; you two should first test me.
The two took their leave respectfully and departed. Three days later, Puhua came back up and asked, "What did the Master say three days ago?
Linji struck him. Three days later, Kefu came up and asked, "Master, what [did you say] before..."
Linji struck Puhua. "What are you doing? he asked. The Master (Puhua) also struck him.

If one were to say that Linji indeed established his school's fundamental tenets when he struck Puhua and struck Kefu, then Miyun’s single blow—which does not function as a single blow—would likewise be the fundamental tenet. Furthermore, what various distinctions would there be?
This is a discourse on the various points of contention. If you claim that there is something distinct [between them], then where is the point of Linji’s striking Ke-fu and Pu-hua?
And where is the point of Ke-fu and Pu-hua’s single instance of “the chick pecks and the hen pries open”? How could these three ancient masters have ever been obstructed by even a hair’s breadth?
Why then do you falsely misrepresent them? Mo-zang then said: "From Linji, tracing back to Kāśyapa and Śākyamuni..."
The fundamental tenets of the Seven Buddhas’ lineage of Wei-yin were fortunately established from this very source, so that they would not be ruined by the "cutting-and-piercing" Chan.
My intention was to exalt Linji; it is not that I have failed him in the slightest. This matter covers heaven and earth.
Past and present, it horizontally encompasses all places throughout the ten directions; vertically, it penetrates all times throughout the three periods.
It is like the ocean having no self-nature while its entire substance is water, or like water having no self-nature while its entire substance is the ocean.
To take a single drop of water on the tip of a needle, the entire ocean is not diminished; to pour the great ocean into the great ocean, the original water remains as it was.
There is no remainder; there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither action nor cessation, neither before nor after. How, then, could there be formation or destruction?
This holds true not only for one Huangbo or one Linji, but even if there were a thousand Śākyamunis and a thousand Kāśyapas, they could not bring it into being, nor could they ever destroy it.
There must first be a time of formation before there can be a time of destruction; there must necessarily be something that is destroyed.

Only after there is something established can there be one who can destroy it. Since fundamentally nothing is established, how can there be destruction? Since fundamentally there is nothing to be destroyed, who could possibly destroy it?
As for the claim that "it cannot be destroyed by the 'cutting through the hanging cord' Chan," this sufficiently shows that he died under the words of an ancient;

he has not yet attained true understanding at all. He falsely establishes his own school of thought precisely because he has not awakened to the "cutting through the hanging cord" Chan. If he had understood...
One attains the Chan that severs the binding cord; naturally, one does not falsely establish a sectarian tenet.

If one is willing to directly take responsibility for severing the binding cord, the task of a lifetime of study is finished. How could one give rise to the delusion that can bind, thereby creating the illusion that is bound?

From this point on, there arise a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions, with strange names and anomalous forms, even extending to the defilement of Huangbo and Linji. And so it continues...
Regarding the lineage of the Seven Buddhas—Śākyamuni, Kāśyapa, and Vimalacitra—you have committed a great falsehood.
If you were even slightly in accord with this [truth], you would surely have seen your position crumble like ice melting or pearls rolling away.

Even the "leakage" of Linji, Ke-fu, and Puhua still belongs merely to the periphery of the gate; how much more so, then, are these various erroneous doctrines that purport to establish the fundamental tenets?
Moshen said: "When Master Fengxue spoke to Nan-yuan, he said: 'If ordinary speech does not linger in ordinary sentiment, it immediately falls into the view of the sages;
this is a great malady of the student. The former sages took pity on them and provided skillful means, like using one wedge to extract another.

Cao Shan has four prohibitions, which say: Do not travel the path of the mind; do not don the garment of the original source; what need is there to insist on 'just so'? One must strictly avoid [these pitfalls].'"

When [the illness] has not yet arisen, the four ailments are all perceived by the sages. The ancients prepared various medicinal remedies for them, treating and restraining each according to its specific malady.
It is appropriate to wait until the illness has departed before removing the medicine. Now, while the medicine may be removed, the physician must not be removed.
The physician is one whom the sages established in advance to await the ailments of all people throughout future generations. If you must necessarily...
To destroy the fundamental tenets is to act like a physician who has abandoned his patients; how much more so now, when the malady of disorderly lineages is raging throughout the monastic groves?
Teachers suffer broken heads and split foreheads yet cannot restrain it; they face blows and counter-punches yet cannot discern the truth;
peddlers of falsehood fill the roads yet cannot be stopped—yet they instead busily occupy themselves with the task of eradicating the fundamental tenets. This is like a disease...
To suffer from a malady that fills one's entire being and yet to scold the physician and reject the medicine—how could this possibly be the intent of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' entrustment?
Furthermore, Master Deshan Xuanjian was one who most vehemently reviled "real dharmas," yet he possessed the "First Phrase. This is true not only for him;

as for Yunmen, Yangshan, Caodong, and Fayan, it goes without saying. If the fundamental principle (zongzhi) were itself a real dharma, then these venerable masters would have established it themselves.
Thus, one should reproach oneself for being deranged and having lost one's mind, lest one fall into such a state. An ancient worthy said:

"One need only clearly grasp the fundamental principle (*mūla-gotra*); fundamentally, there are no real dharmas. Now, this fundamental principle is the forge for smelting real dharmas; so why should one have any doubt?

Where there is a body, there is illness. Since the body and its constituent parts are empty, where can illness adhere? Where there is consciousness, there is illness. Consciousness is itself True Suchness (Tathatā); where can illness abide?
The illness of the physical body arises from the body itself; it is treated with medicines produced from the great earth.
These medicines are not the body, and that which is not the body is the Great Body. Therefore, it is appropriate to say that the body treats the body.
The illness of the Dharma-body arises because consciousness remains present. It is treated with the medicine inherent within its own fundamental nature.
This medicine is "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*); since consciousness-only is itself consciousness, it may be said that consciousness cures consciousness.

Since ancient times, the virtuous ones have untied the adhesions and removed the bonds for others, causing them to attain liberation in that very place and achieve great peace and security; they did this by taking the person's own [nature].
There exists the True Mind of Consciousness-only, which is neither adhering nor bound. By removing its adherence and bondage, it is said that "poisonous medicine is transformed into clarified butter.
If, apart from this fundamental nature, there were separately some divine formula or marvelous remedy pre-arranged to await the illnesses of the world, [it would be superfluous].
Even if it were personally prepared by the hands of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, it would still be nothing but poison.
Thus, medicine is inherently not separate from what the student originally possesses; how can one forcibly establish a "school" (zongzhi) as a means of healing?
While the corruption of the lineage is indeed a vulgar custom within the monastic community, its failure stems fundamentally from the initial resolve (cittotpāda).
It is not necessary to have attained true realization; one need only clearly understand this Great Matter.

Yet there are those who merely harbor idle thoughts of joining the ranks of the Dharma assembly, donning the name of a monk as their starting point. How can such deluded and false individuals be counted? They do not even maintain the five precepts.
How could there be any occasion to inquire about the One Vehicle? If one stands before a person of clear vision, it is like five metals entering the furnace;
not even a hair’s breadth of them can be confused. How could there be any principle for mixing copper and tin with gold and silver?

If one’s own eye is not clear, yet one wishes to rely on oral transmissions and manual instructions as an authentic dharma to test and verify [the truth], then one belongs first and foremost among those who must be excluded.
How can you presume to discriminate against others? To engage in such discrimination is precisely like a jackal discriminating against a wild fox;
if it were to encounter a true lion cub, how could it ever recognize it? Thus he said: "The malady of chaotic leadership is currently rampant within the monastic forests;
even when masters suffer broken heads and split foreheads, they cannot restrain themselves, and though they receive blows and counter-punches, they lack the discernment to respond."
While peddlers of superficialities fill the roads and cannot be restrained, they instead busily strive to obliterate the fundamental tenets.
This is like having a house full of the sick while shouting at the physician and rejecting the medicine; how could this possibly be the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs’ entrustment?
To speak thus is to sweep the Gate of the School clean away. How can such people be counted among those who study the Way? Even these types must be weighed and measured.

If one were to weigh and examine this, then by extending the principle further, one would find that the five turbidities and evil practices within the realm of Jambudvīpa are so vast they could not be fully recorded even upon bamboo tablets.
How, then, can merely establishing a "foundational tenet" (zongzhi) possibly cause such conduct to cease?

Furthermore, it is said that Master Deshan Xuanjian was one who most vehemently reviled the existence of "real dharmas," yet he nonetheless spoke of "the first phrase. This is also true of Yunmen, Miaoyan, and Daowei.

That the Dharma-eye of Caodong does not require further explanation is self-evident. If their school’s fundamental tenets were indeed a substantial reality, then the various masters would have established them for themselves and then criticized them;

they would not have reached such a state of madness and loss of mind. This particular line of argument—Mogarim directly characterizes as madness and loss of mind—is a slander against the Buddhas and the Patriarchs that leads one to fall into the Avīci Hell. That sentient beings are thus inverted is precisely...
They are called "those who are to be pitied. This is as Deshan Jian said: "Riding the tiger's head and grasping the tiger's tail;
the primary phrase clarifies the fundamental principle. What kind of phrase is this primary phrase? If there is a phrase, one has already fallen into the secondary.
The various "falling into the weeds" discourses of Yunmen, Miaoyan, Caodong, and Fayan are entirely for the sake of compassion.
Out of pity for them, how could one merely nail down a stake and shake the oars, falsely claiming that [the patriarchs] established a "school doctrine"?

Furthermore, although the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, at the end he said, "I have not spoken a single word. He often said, "Do you think I ever turned the wheel of the Dharma?
Having clearly expounded the Three Baskets and the Twelve Divisions of the Teaching, he made such a statement; is this not [an example of] self-contradiction?
Do you stand there and scold yourself? Māra’s endurance of the root of illness lies entirely in this single word, "self.
For as long as there is a "self" in the past, future, or present, one fails to see that the ten directions and the three realms are nothing but mind.
Consequently, one mistakenly regards those who are not deranged as deranged, and those who have realized the mind as having lost their minds; all such various inversions are due to this.
I do not know from ancient times where the virtuous ones established themselves and then rebuked themselves; it all stems from clinging to a single "self.
Once one has clung to this single self, then from the very beginning of their study, they have never undergone a great death and a great life;

there is simply no place from which to speak of an awakening. It is like trying to apply the rites, music, punishments, and governance of the imperial court within a butcher’s stall while wielding a cleaver.

People deliberate upon this. Furthermore, they cite the words of the ancient masters, stating only that one must clearly grasp the fundamental tenets (*gangzong*), for there are originally no real dharmas (*dharmasatya*).

They claim that these fundamental tenets are the furnace and bellows for smelting real dharmas. Now, the intention of the ancient masters was that the fundamental tenets themselves are not real dharmas;
yet Māra and those who tolerate his views now wish to take these fundamental tenets as the furnace and bellows for smelting real dharmas. How strange!

This is a grave error. Substantial dharmas (*dravyadharma*) are like poisonous weeds; even if they are processed with medicinal decoctions, how could they ever restore life? Substantial dharmas are like gravel and pebbles;

even if they are melted and cast, how could they ever become functional vessels? If one does not interpret the oral lineages of the Five Houses as substantial dharmas, [then they will truly serve as medicine].

Thus, all [these views] can benefit those who study. However, if one were to establish a "convention of real dharmas" (shifa hui), one would have already lost the fundamental intent of the Five Houses;
it would become entirely like poisonous weeds or gravel. How could this be another kind of "real dharma" that one wishes to refine through the "headings and principles" (gangzong)?
What, then, are real dharmas? What are the headings and principles? Space originally has no flowers; they are merely the cataracts of the eye.
Yet it exists. To enter the great ocean to search for a clay ox—when will there ever be an end to this?
Mazang said: "Striking through the turbulent flow with a single palm; the Zen board of the former master was most clear.
Had we met face-to-face at that time, we would not be sighing over injustice as we do today."
This is the verse on the Zen meditation board and desk composed by Mochizuki Sōkō for the transmission to Rinzai at Huangbo.
It is said that he personally understood the essential principles of Linji and was worthy of receiving Baizhang’s entrustment.
Had he lived during that time and received Linji’s direct transmission himself, there would not have been various claims of injustice from those such as Miyun Yuanwu. This is truly great!
Arrogance and overweening pride are fully present; this is merely the circulation of conventional truth. What Zen school is there?

Furthermore, Linji clearly said, "Attendant, bring me some fire. Having already known that after thousands and hundreds of generations someone like Mazu’s disciple Magu would appear, he preemptively blocked and sifted him at the very moment Huangbo’s voice fell silent. How can one still remain so negligent?
To scrutinize and reflect: do you still die upon your meditation board and desk, flickering and deluded, giving rise to so much lack of freedom?
If this is the case, what distinction is there between you and those who steal names and pilfer profits, or who covet rank and yearn for emolument?

What was the purpose of your initial resolve to leave the household life and become a monk? Regarding the Buddha’s mirror-like wisdom, how can speech and silence involve both transcendence and subtlety? How can they be?
This is universally non-offensive. The verse says: Within the shadows of variegated clouds, a celestial immortal appears; In hand he holds a red silk fan to shield his face.
One must urgently fix one’s gaze upon the immortal; Do not look at the fan in the immortal’s hand. If it is a "Māra-concealer," is it not the person who looks at the fan?
Tiantong’s *Bishu* says: "Ciming’s verse states: 'A single shout distinguishes guest and host; illumination and function act simultaneously.

Since a single shout already distinguishes guest and host, how could a single blow not be the 'seal of the three essentials'—the narrow red dot that allows no room for conjecture or recognition, wherein the distinction between host and guest is revealed?
Mogarěn says: These words seem right but are actually wrong. This is the seventh refutation and the third opening.

Most of the cited proofs are of this nature. Now, as for the hundred skeletal members, the nine apertures, the five viscera, and the six repositories—these reside within a single body and can be understood even by a child.

Yet, when one asks about the principles of their mutual production and overcoming (*sheng ke*), or the manner in which the channels and vessels circulate, even Lu Shan and Bian Que would have had to pause in deep reflection;
how much more so regarding the Linji school’s fundamental tenets, which are as secure as a thousand locks and a hundred bolts, exactly as stated in the *Pibushu*.
Furthermore, why must one study the teachings to seek awakening, and having attained awakening, seek a "great awakening"? Those who harbor a profound resolve for this Way should reflect upon this.

Indeed, students of the Way must avoid swallowing dates whole or grasping at a vague, superficial Buddha-nature. However, if those such as Zangren and Renjun were to equate this with the fixed literalism of the scriptures...

The essential meaning is this: to divide the single realm of the eternally quiescent light-land (sahaja-prabhāsvara) into separate boundaries and territories, and then, atop the crown of Vairocana, to reject what is "not" and grasp what is "is"—to claim that such an act constitutes freedom from superficiality—is merely a point of contention.

How can the arts of Qibo and Huang Di serve as a metaphor for the Vehicle of the Dharma-treasury? A square base and a round lid—how could they ever be forcibly joined? As for the hundred bones and nine apertures...

The five viscera and six腑 (fu) organs, the principles of their mutual generation and overcoming as mother and child, the manner in which the channels and vessels circulate, the cyclical flow of the five movements and six pneumas therein,
the waning and waxing of qi, blood, yin, and yang, the differing natures of south, north, east, and west, and the distinct conditions of the old and young, male and female—
these myriad variations and differences are so subtle and intricate as to be difficult to distinguish. The Bhagavāns of the ten directions [are one]...

Within the gateway to Nirvana, how could there be such entanglements? When the subtlety and density of the fundamental principle are difficult to distinguish, and the fruit is merely similar [to the cause], how can that which is thus established as a fundamental principle not be called a heterodox teaching of demons and outsiders?

The fundamental principle of Linji is truly "a hundredfold fragmentation. To speak of "a hundredfold fragmentation" already constitutes a superfluous addition, like adding legs to a snake. Now, however, you call it...
"Thousandfold secure and hundredfold firm. One does not know how they were woven so secretly and stitched so finely to achieve such thousandfold security and hundredfold firmness;
is this not entirely a product of contrived effort? When has one ever dreamed of the fence of "absolute learning and non-action"?
Since the Master has used his intellectual power to manufacture this entire school of thought—making its principles thousandfold secure and hundredfold firm—the student must necessarily...
It functions entirely through the mind, intellect, and consciousness; only then can one investigate and fathom it. This is just like the arts of Qi Bo and Huang Di:
if one does not receive oral transmission and manual instruction, yet wishes to realize and seek it for oneself, by what path can one enter?

As for this matter, if it can indeed be compared to the arts of Qi Bo and Huang Di, then it must certainly not depend on investigation and awakening (*canwu*) at all. Is this not the same as the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity?
Are these words not utterly contradictory? On one hand, you claim that the essential tenets of Linji are "a thousandfold secure and hundredfold firm";

yet on the other, you say one must "investigate to seek awakening, and having awakened, seek great awakening. I do not understand how this "thousandfold secure and hundredfold firm" tenet can be entirely achieved through artificial fabrication.
How is one to investigate? How is one to awaken? And how is one to awaken and then seek great awakening? This is like planting...
These various erroneous doctrines are a great harm to practitioners who have not yet attained realization;
compared to those who "swallow dates whole" and take a vague, superficial view of Buddha-nature, the gravity of this harm is vastly different.

For while those who hold a vague view may indeed rouse their fundamental ignorance and engage in genuine inquiry and true awakening—thereby reaching a day when they are no longer vague—if these erroneous doctrines enter [the mind], [the damage is far greater].

Within the eight consciousnesses of human beings, the more diligently one studies, the further one moves from the Way; it is like traveling toward Yue while heading for Yan, or adding firewood to extinguish a blaze.
Tiantong uses a single blow as the seal of the Three Essentials, opening the vermilion dot so narrow that there is no room for deliberation, thereby distinguishing host and guest.
Demons and those who tolerate delusion find this too blunt and superficial, hence they say it is "resembling but not being. They do not realize that Tiantong—
This treatise states: "There is no such place [for this]. How could it not be so? Tian Tong’s single blow is half coarse and half not coarse;
Linji’s single phrase is likewise half coarse and half not coarse. That which is coarse is itself coarse;
that which is not coarse is itself not coarse. This is no different from Tian Tong’s blow and Linji’s phrase.

What connection is there? Now, taking a single staff as "resembling but not being" and a single phrase as "a thousand locks and a hundred bolts"—this is like the story of the monkeys who were angry when given three in the morning and four at night, yet delighted when it was changed to four in the morning and three at night.
Is this not the inverted nature of sentient beings?
Mofen said: "The 'Opening of the Book' refers to the Three Essentials and Three Principles; these are nothing more than the words from a single occasion when Linji ascended the hall.
That those who, after Linji’s passing, have repeatedly picked up and pointed to them are all like mad dogs chasing clods of earth. Alas! Did they not fail to realize the excess of their own words?
Furthermore, it was because a monk asked about the true Buddha, the true Dharma, and the true Way that Linji revealed the three phrases."

To state that "the three phrases are contained within a single phrase" and so forth implies that the Three Essentials and the Three Essentials of the Pivot are not merely incidental remarks made at one time.

Since the *Pibushu* (Refutation of the Book) already treats the Three Essentials and the Three Essentials of the Pivot as incidental, it further drags in the lines: "The seal of the Three Essentials is opened;
the vermilion dot is narrow, leaving no room for deliberation; host and guest are distinguished," and pairs this with a single blow as being entirely guest or entirely host.

Master, when it comes to accepting or rejecting [doctrines], how can one ever be certain? Lacking any settled view of my own, you have used merely private opinions to cast aside the methods of the ancient sages and the formal systems handed down from above;
this is nearly like sweeping everything off the ground. Master Chan Master Hong Juefan said:
"In the past, I was dwelling in a hermitage beneath Jiufeng in Gaoyang. A monk asked me: 'In the assembly of Linji, two monks once met one day and simultaneously [acted]...'"
He gave a shout from below. Hearing this, Linji ascended the seat and said, "If you, great assembly, wish to understand the Linji phrase of guest and host, go ask the two Zen monks in the hall.
A monk then asked, "Which one is the guest? Which one is the host? Linji replied, "Guest and host are distinct and clear.
Just as I was about to offer a response, I suddenly perceived the essential meaning of the Three Essentials and the Three Keys. Thereupon, I prostrated twice.
He said: "How magnificent is the banner of light of non-action and tranquil extinction! Even in a hundred thousand lifetimes, one who hears of it will have all thieving thoughts utterly extinguished;
how much more so for me, who lived two hundred years after the Great Master? I shall compose a verse: "A single phrase contains the three gates;
Within a single gate lie the three essential paths. Look closely, and it is a trap for tigers; Suddenly, it roars!"
A single sound of the poison-smeared drum; the thieving mind dies out and the eyes grow dazed. The hair of the stone woman stands erect in her dream.
Pibo then cited the two characters "Trapping the Tiger" (*xiàn hǔ*) as proof of the "Three Essentials of the Three Principles.

He claimed that these words were established as a provisional device (*quán*) merely to trap those who study the teachings. Was Juefan’s intention truly such? Yangshan said: "One need only clearly grasp the ancients..."

Once one has grasped the essential meaning of the human mind, the clarity of one’s own mind will emerge; furthermore, one will attain mastery in transformation and experience an inexhaustible enjoyment.
This is called the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (Body of Self-Enjoyment). It is most evident that what is termed the *svasaṃbhogakāya* is certainly not a provisional device.

For if the tiger does not fall into the trap, the thieving mind will not die; if the mind does not die, the hair on the woman’s body will not stand on end. Only through direct realization can this be known. If...

Because of the two characters "entrapped by a tiger," it was consequently claimed that [the teaching] was merely a provisional device. If that were so, how would one account for the "poisoned drum" or the "woman with hair"? An ancient worthy said:

"To interpret the meaning based on the literal text is an offense against the Buddhas of the three ages. If even the teachings of the scriptures (*śāsana*) cannot be understood through mere intellectual interpretation, how much less so the principle of the separate transmission outside the teachings?

Tiantong’s *Pishu* (Excerpts from the Books) asserts that the "Three Essentials" and "Three Principles" are nothing more than the words Tiantong spoke on a single occasion during Linji’s formal assembly.
This was Tiantong’s way of repaying Linji’s kindness, exceeding even the "Three Phrases" of Baoling; yet Mazu Ren claimed this was an error of expression.
Not only do they not recognize this very point, but they also fail to recognize the Three Essentials and the Three Keys.
When a monk asked Linji about the true Buddha, the true Dharma, and the true Way, he replied: "The Buddha is the purity of mind; the Dharma is the luminosity of mind."
The Way is that which is unimpeded and pure radiance everywhere. To bifurcate the Buddha-dharma and the Way into three is already beyond remedy;
to then further differentiate between the true and the false within them in an attempt to seek the "true" one—can such a monk even be spoken with?
Linji, while bestowing his teachings according to conditions, uttered these three statements and then, following his own impulse, set them aside, saying: "Three."
"It is all one. All are merely empty names and lack substantial reality. This has already been clearly and explicitly revealed. Furthermore, it says:
"As for a true practitioner of the Way, their mindfulness is uninterrupted from moment to moment. Since Bodhidharma came from the West, he sought only a person who would not be deluded.
Later, meeting the Second Patriarch, he was enlightened by a single word; only then did he realize that all his previous efforts had been in vain. Mount [Shan].
"This monk’s realization today is no different from that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Having spoken thus with complete thoroughness—just like taking a night-light worth a thousand chariots and pouring out its full measure—the monk’s eyes flickered; he was as if entering one dream within another.
Thereupon, [the Master] gave him another ladleful of "evil water," saying: "If you can realize it in the first phrase, you are fit to be a peer to the Buddhas and Patriarchs."

The Master said: "If you attain realization within the second phrase, you are fit to serve as a teacher for devas and humans. If you attain realization within the third phrase, you will not even be able to save yourself.
[The Master] struck this monk to dispel his ignorance, intending to wait until he attained realization in the first phrase so that he might serve as a teacher for the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
He then asked, "What is the first phrase? Linji said: "The seal of the three essentials opens; the vermilion dot is narrow."
Before there is even room for deliberation, the distinction between host and guest is established; yet this monk failed to offer a response and instead asked about the second phrase.
Nanquan said, "How could one of wondrous understanding fail to respond to Wuzhuo’s question? How could Subhūti fail to match the power of the one who cuts off the flow?

Though he explained it thus, those who do not understand still do not understand. When he was asked about the third phrase, he was truly like a puppet, entirely controlled by the mind, intellect, and consciousness.

"It is the pulling and tugging [of the strings]. Therefore it is said: 'Just look at the puppeteer on the stage manipulating the marionettes; the pulling and tugging depends entirely upon the person inside.
To inquire in such a manner—when will there ever be an end? Thus he himself provides the footnote: 'In general, when chanting and performing the Lineage Vehicle (Zongcheng),'"
Within a single phrase, one must possess the three mysteries; within a single mystery, one must possess the three essentials. There is the provisional and the real;
there is illumination and function. How do you all understand this? Thus, these three mysteries and three essentials are truly matters of mere coincidence;
yet, throughout the generations, they have been taken up and emphasized without ceasing, regarded as the "Upward Direction. Even so, this is merely recognizing the "Limit" (Lin).
Regarding "whether saved or not," Tiantong judged this to be an incidental remark; he may indeed possess the single eye. Yet Moran considers it not to be a mere incidental occurrence at that time;
truly, this is like the difference between incense and rotten weeds, which cannot coexist in the same vessel.

Furthermore, the two characters "incidental" (ou ran) within a single phrase embody the three gates of the One Vehicle, and within one gate they embody the three essentials. Therein lie both the provisional and the real, as well as both illumination and function. Moran—
How do you all understand this? Since it is coincidental, it is not coincidental; since it is not coincidental, it is indeed coincidental.
What is coincidental? Why is it not coincidental? To say it is coincidental is already not coincidental; that which is not coincidental is truly coincidental.
Coincidence is its being so; why would being so not be coincidence? Is it coincidence? Is it non-coincidence? It is neither.
"Coincidental? Indeed it is so. Not coincidental? Indeed it is not so. Now, as you distinguish between these two words, "coincidental" and "not coincidental"—is it coincidental?
Is it not coincidental? If you can realize this here and now, there will be no room for deliberation or for the distinction between host and guest; yet even this has not yet been clarified.

This is nothing more than a puppet show on a stage. Tiantong uses a single blow to represent both the complete guest and the complete host, matching it to the "Three Essentials" (sanyao) with the phrase:
"The seal opens; the vermilion dot is narrow; there is no room for deliberation; host and guest are distinguished.

Magun, however, argues that since the Three Elements and Three Essentials are already considered coincidental, how can one force them into such a synthesis? He thus rejects Magun’s selection and interpretation.
It is indeterminate. This means that it sweeps away the formal methods of one’s ancestors. Now, being without taking and without abandoning is called the Perfect School (Yuanzong).
How can one speak of "taking" or "leaving," or of being "determinate" or "indeterminate"? The Three Essentials and Three Points cannot be called the formal method of Linji;
likewise, Yunmen’s single blow cannot be called the formal method of Yunmen. If one were to treat these as formal methods...

I understand. Both schools are merely puppets. If you can attain realization in a place where there is no fixed method, then it may be said that within a single phrase the three gates are complete, and within a single gate the three essentials are complete. It may also be said that a single blow does not function as a single blow.
Ultimately, how much distance lies between a single phrase and a single blow? A single phrase is permitted to contain the three.
The three essential points (san-yuan-san-yao) must necessarily be present within a single blow; how could one blow fail to possess these three essential points?
Furthermore, how could one insist that the words are not the blow, or that the blow is not the words? If so, what do you mean by saying that the ancestral methods have been swept away?
In short, the Buddha-dharma is not a matter of such logic. It is just like judging this monk right now.
Question: Regarding Linji’s statement that [the monk] was like a "dumb sheep," this was simply Linji using it to scrutinize the monk.
Yet, since the monk did not utter a single word in response, how can one know he was not a man of extraordinary capacity?
If one were to scrutinize Linji based on this monk, Linji would be found entirely at fault; having already exposed his own failings to the monk, what further standards of propriety could there be?
There was a monk who asked, "What is the true Buddha, the true Dharma, and the true Way? [The Master] knew what kind of mental activity he possessed.
Linji said, "The Buddha is the purity of mind; the Dharma is the luminosity of mind; the Way is the unobstructed pure light everywhere.
Is this not like driving a wedge into the crown of Vairocana’s head? I see many who do not know their own measure.
He then realized for himself his shame and remorse. He immediately uttered: "Three is one. All are empty names and lack substantial existence.
Setting aside the "three" for a moment, how can this "one" be brought forth? Can you say that it too is an empty name and lacks substantial existence?
Can this very thing still be described as empty or as existent? Your entire body is covered in mud and water, yet you say that Bodhidharma sought only one who would not be deluded;
you also say that the mountain monk’s realization today is no different from that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
If this is merely a matter of one's own fundamental practice, then how does this monk differ from the Buddhas and Patriarchs? How could he dare to compete with the Dragon King in terms of wealth?
If you speak of the point of realization, then even before a word is uttered, there are already a thousand miles and ten thousand leagues of white clouds.
Furthermore, he distinguishes three phrases, calling them the first and second, which are fit to serve as teachers for Buddhas, Patriarchs, humans, and devas; yet if one falls into the third...
Three. This is precisely failing to save oneself; that is to say, one’s own views become untenable. As this monk listened and questioned in turn, observing his performance, [the Master] uttered:
"The Seal of the Three Essentials opens the narrow crimson dot; there is no room for hesitation, and host and guest are distinguished.
This is called the First Phrase. "How could subtle understanding allow for Wuzhuo’s questioning? How could the *upāya* fail to match the momentum of cutting through the stream? This is called...
The second phrase: "Just look at the puppeteer on the stage; the pulling and tugging entirely depend on the person inside. This is called the third phrase.
[The master] considers that the monk’s nostrils are in his own hands, yet he does not realize that his own nostrils are [not under his control].
Yet it remains in the hands of this monk. If you can realize it through the first phrase, you truly cannot even save yourself.
As soon as a single phrase is established, you are seeking your own Dharma from another, taking their eye to make it your own universal penetration;
how could you not be unable to save yourself? If you can realize it through the third phrase, you are precisely fit to serve as a teacher for the Buddhas and Patriarchs. The Buddhas and Patriarchs...
"Who is the teacher? The one whom the Buddhas and Patriarchs take as their teacher is none other than sentient beings themselves.
When this monk heard these three statements, it was like the song of a nightingale passing by his ear; how could he have known that he had not truly reached the ground of non-doubt?
Let others do as they please, clamoring outside the gate. At the end of his life, Linji spoke forth the Three Essentials and the Three Keys, grasping the perfect *i* with its three dots.
The Grand Unity (Taiyi) contains the three; it is all but a set of ordinary household furnishings. To bring them all out and perform them with full intent—this monk never uttered a single word.
Seeing nothing and hearing nothing, there is inexhaustibility. Only then did Linji’s thread snap and everything come to rest.
Is this not his greatest defeat of his entire life? Judging it thus, I do not know how those followers of Māra will react upon hearing it—they should surely seize [the opportunity].
"Should one take the former discourse as the standard? Or should one take the latter discourse as the standard?
It may be that both are correct, or both are incorrect; it may be that they are both correct and incorrect, or neither incorrect nor correct.

Only when you can definitively resolve this shall you be permitted to examine the words and phrases of the ancients, and only then shall you be permitted to examine the words and phrases of Linji. This is precisely what Linji himself said."
How do you all understand this? The "Three Essentials" and "Three Primary Essentials" are originally but inconclusive talk.
As for Juefan’s verse, what is there worth taking up? Yet Juefan’s intent is also fundamentally not something that those of the "patience of demons" can comprehend.
Observe it closely: it is a mechanism for trapping a tiger; suddenly, with one thunderous beat of the "poisoned drum," the thieving mind [is destroyed].
"Death exhausts the eyes and leaves them clouded; the stone woman’s hair stands on end in her dream. The footnote below states:
"If the tiger does not sink [into the pit], the thieving mind will not die. If the mind does not die, the woman's hair will not stand on end. This is truly laughable. Such statements as these—
It is as if you have yourself convened a meeting on "real dharmas. Not only has the very spirit of our school been swept away from the ground, but how can even words and letters be made to pass?
That your body hairs did not stand on end—what kind of language is that?

You thus dismiss Tian Tong’s provisional establishment of the three principles and three essentials as being a theory intended to ensnare students. While Tian Tong’s statement certainly contains leaks, yet...
The error of Ma Rin is, moreover, the most egregious of errors.
Ma Rin said: "The establishment of the fundamental principle was originally intended as a prohibition against those who shout 'hu' and wield wild clubs.
If one were to say, 'All of you must learn my shouting,' and then later say, 'Henceforth you must not learn the old monk’s shouting,' this could be called a clear and manifest contradiction."
This is indeed a grave error. Now, to open up this book and employ such inverted arguments to suppress the fundamental tenets—is this not utterly improper?

I have once ventured a private critique of it, saying: It is like a man with many sons who, when he is ill and on the verge of death, hands over his promissory notes to his children, saying: [text continues]
"I have many young sons who have been away for a long time; this alone can serve as proof. Whoever's name matches the contract shall be my true son.
Upon receiving these instructions, the sons passed the word along to one another, but they were mistakenly sheltered by a neighbor.
That neighbor took possession of the house and burned the contract. Consequently, whenever any of the sons returned from afar, he was all refused entry and cast out.

Among one's own clan, one does not act as a monster; among friends, one does not act as an eccentric. Why is this? If one borrows for a long time and does not return it, that which was borrowed becomes one's own.
Now, the fundamental principle of the ferry is the contract; the source and flow of the ancestral lineage is the dwelling.
From Xinghua to Xueyan and Gao Feng, spanning more than twenty generations, these are all true sons who have successively verified the transmission. As for the late Master Sanfeng...
The Master is truly like a son who has traveled afar and subsequently returned. Alas! As for those neighbors, I cannot bear to speak of them.

Using the analogy of the son and the bond to identify the true son, the evidence of the demonic endurance and the state of the offering was fully prepared; the iron case was settled. This is indeed the [conclusion] of the Perfect Teaching (Enzo).
The true Dharma cannot be transmitted [merely] through written documents; this is just as the bond between father and son does not rely solely on legal contracts.

Indeed, the significance of being a Dharma heir truly concerns the continuity or cessation of the life of wisdom (prajñā-jīva). Therefore, it is said that those born from the Buddha’s own mouth are the Buddha’s true children.

Nevertheless, although one might search throughout the ten directions and the three realms for someone who is not a Buddha and find no such person, one likewise cannot find anyone who is not a true son.
Since ancient times, this has been transmitted through the generations by employing the worldly principle of the relationship between father and son.
To repay one's origins and return to the source, not forgetting that from which one was born, there arises the doctrine of dharma-heirs.
In this, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); thus, there is nothing improper about it.

However, if one were like those of the Jin and Tang dynasties, who vied with one another over the ranking of their lineages and gave rise to disputes, considering it a glory to have received the Dharma themselves while [denigrating] others...
To take the attainment of the Dharma as a cause for resentment, claiming oneself to be true while disparaging others as false, is to sweep the ancestral style (zongfeng) from the ground;
it has no connection whatsoever with the essence of the Buddha-dharma. Since it has no connection with the essence of the Buddha-dharma, where could one escape beyond the laws of the world?
How can one allow someone to not regard their own father as father, but instead regard another as father? Such claims of truth and falsehood [are mere fabrications].
Deceiving the common folk and arrogantly exalting themselves, they claim to be descendants of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; are they not those whom the ways of the world cannot tolerate?

From the ancient Buddhas and Patriarchs down to the present day, there has never been a lack of individuals who have engaged in true inquiry and attained genuine realization—those who have undergone "great death and great life" and share the same nostrils as the Buddhas and Patriarchs, solely for their own original nature.
The primal spirit (*yuanchen*) has always been thus. It is no different for Buddhas and Patriarchs; it is likewise for me.
How could there be another dharma that can be proclaimed or kept secret, received or transmitted?

Mōrin merely wishes to disparage Tiāntóng as not being a descendant of Línjì, like a neighbor who occupies a house and burns the deed—claiming he has already obtained the true essence of the Māra-treasury.
It is transmitted that those who follow after the true sons of the Far-Traveling One cause the blind, the mute sheep,
and the followers who bark at mere sounds to mutually revere and pay homage to them, regardless of the defilement of the wise life of humans and devas; thus, their great false speech is accomplished,
and they fall into the Avīci Hell.
Mogarim said: "Linji has four guest-host relationships; there are phrases of guest and host where there is distinction within identity, yet identity within distinction—they must not be confused.
Therefore, our former teacher said: 'The simultaneous shouting in the two halls is the mother of the four guest-host relationships.'"
When it comes to the moment of critical decision and exhortation, the palaces of Māra and the lands of Buddhas appear simultaneously before one.

This is like the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, whose hundreds of thousands of hands and eyes—whether manifesting compassion or majesty, meditative concentration or wisdom—arise according to the specific station established by the practitioner.
Giving and taking are like a pearl rolling upon a platter; it turns in circles, moves sideways, and slants, manifesting a thousand manners and ten thousand forms.
What is called the "four" refers merely to the condition in which the pearl does not leave the platter.

In the past, the youth Sudhana visited fifty-three great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and at each friend’s place, he attained immeasurable Dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as beheld...

Facing the cruelty of King Anala, the blazing intensity of the Brahmin Jvalanaprabha, and the seductive charms of the woman Vasumitrā, as well as the various distinctions among the followers of external paths, one cannot help but recoil in fear. Why is this?

Because the distinction between defilement and purity has not yet been forgotten, and the measure of one's samādhi has not yet been dissolved. Thus it is said: "One may enter the Buddha, but one cannot enter Māra. Directly...
Upon arriving within the Great Pavilion, he arose from samādhi; suddenly, he lost his cloth bag and cast out everything he had previously attained—his fundamental subtlety—to its very bottom.
He cut off the ten directions and left not a single dharma remaining; only then did he realize the original face of Sudhana.
Yet, this could not have been achieved were it not for the fifty-three elders who drove the plow and seized the food, employing their mastery over capture and release through transformative means.
This is merely an ear-opening. Opening the books, I recall that in years past the Master forbade [such talk], saying: "The terms 'host' and 'guest' refer to 'you' and 'I.
Recently, he has again explained it, saying: 'You shout, I shout; shouting at the ox, shouting at the horse—this too is the clear manifestation of host and guest.

This is because at first he was complacent in his ignorance, but recently he has forcibly taken what he does not know to be knowledge. From beginning to end, his arguments are contradictory; he disregards future generations. Alas!
"Alas, how painful! I did not expect the Way of Linji to have reached such a state.
Linji’s 'Four Guests and Hosts' has no connection whatsoever with one's fundamental share [of the Dharma]. This is why, at that time, after he had finished expounding the Four Guests and Hosts,"

He immediately summoned the Venerable One and wrote a commentary and refutation, saying: "What this mountain monk has cited is entirely for the purpose of discerning demons and distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox, so that one may know their deviations and correctness.
This is because one must not recognize these matters as being within one's own personal domain.

Indeed, prior to Caoxi, the complete and sudden Mind School had not yet been widely transmitted throughout China; therefore, some [teachings] were direct, consisting of perhaps only a single phrase or half-phrase."

He was thoroughly penetrating, and thus he granted his seal of approval. By the time of Linji, although the light had shone forth like a thousand lamps, the later stream had already become turbid at its source.

Thinking of those who rely on words, they are found everywhere; if one does not meet people by changing one's countenance, but relies solely on a single phrase or half-phrase, how can one know what their mental conduct is? Therefore, the various arrangements of the school’s gateways are nothing more than this.

If one wishes to discern demons from the authentic, to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox, and to know their respective natures, how could one ever take this as the fundamental practice beneath one's own feet?
Furthermore, how could one ever claim that if a person can learn such a display of skillful means, they will thereby be able to resolve the matter of birth and death?
The father and son, Māgandika and his kin, have not yet attained the "eyebrow-mark" or the "single eye" regarding these matters;
they have consistently mistaken a servant for a master, coming instead to deceive and intimidate the common people. How could they avoid being of no benefit to themselves and harmful to others?

This is because their own minds are fundamentally unrighteous, and ultimately they remain in a state of total delusion. Now, when both halls shout in unison, the roles of guest and host are clearly distinguished: as for the guest, he is entirely...
The guest is entirely guest; the host is entirely host. One host, one guest; one guest, one host—is this not perfectly clear?
Tiantong said: "Guest and host" refers to you and me. He further said: "You shout, I shout; shouting at oxen, shouting at horses—this too is guest and host, perfectly clear.
These two explanations are neither identical nor different, yet Mazu Ren criticized them for being contradictory from beginning to end. This is as follows:
Following their master Mazu Daoyi, the two halls (the Abbot’s Hall and the Sangha Hall) chant in unison as the "mother" of the four guests and hosts; this serves as a guiding manual.

Truly, those who mistake the scales of a precious fish for bright pearls are like this: the chanting of the four guests and hosts together with the two halls is entirely without connection [to the truth].
Why then do they repeatedly pick it up and play with it? Furthermore, they claim that within it there is a relationship between mother and child.

Is the meaning of "arising" not merely the delirious chatter of a dream? Furthermore, to say that before Sudhana entered Maitreya’s pavilion, he could only enter the Buddha-realm and could not enter the Mara-realm, is even more of a fallacious argument.
Although Mara and the Buddha are as incompatible as fire and water, they are nonetheless as closely related as the front and back of a face. The Buddha-realm is like the realm of sentient beings.
The realm of sentient beings is like the realm of Māra; the realm of Māra is also like the realm of the Buddha.
To realize this is to have neither Māra nor Buddha; not to realize it is to have only Māra and no Buddha. When there is neither Māra nor Buddha, that is the true Buddha.
When there is only Māra and no Buddha, the Buddha has never lacked even a single iota; it is simply that perceiving a Buddha as existing is itself to have entered the realm of Māra.
How could there possibly be a traveler on the path who can only enter the Buddha-dharma and cannot enter the realm of Māra?

If it were truly the case that one can only enter the Buddha-dharma and cannot enter the realm of Māra, then such a person would have already realized the stage of Buddhahood; what further level of realization could there be beyond that?
If there were yet another level with a distinct realm of experience, then the claim that one "can only enter the Buddha-dharma" would be untenable.

This is precisely entering the realm of Māra. When one has not yet distinguished between Māra and Buddha and the eye of wisdom has not yet opened, how can one even concern oneself with whether or not one’s heels touch the ground?
By inferring from this, are Śāriputra, Sudhana, and Maitreya not merely people of the bean trellises and wheat fields?

Regarding the matters discussed within the Zhongshu Hall: since Moran has already spoken so as to "strike and lose the cloth bag," he has completely cast away all that he previously attained—the fundamental and the subtle.

With his ten directions cut off and not a single dharma remaining, how could there be such things as the "Unwritten Secret Seal," the "Double-Headed Single-Knot," or the "Interlocking Four Dharmas"? All these various strange names and anomalous forms can be understood by him.
The ancient masters’ single heart of compassionate concern has cast its entire body into the weeds;
their urgent discourse for the sake of others has all been reduced to mere words for reading and recitation.

Whether it be demons or those who surpass them by a hundredfold, if one does not personally grasp one’s own nostrils, turn over one’s skin, and sever the life-root, one will never attain even a fraction of correspondence with this matter.

Even if one can speak it, understand it, and even pass judgment on public cases (gong’an) with precision, it is all termed "vague karmic consciousness" (*ye-shi mang-mang*) with no fundamental basis to rely upon.
How much more so for those of the demonic-tolerance school (*mo-ren*), whose entire being is filled with what they call "primordial subtlety" (*yuan-miao*).
Yet they merely imitate the speech of the ancients, claiming that whatever primordial subtlety they have attained must be fully proclaimed; this is truly a mere counting of... [the void].
The treasures of others do not relieve one's own poverty; these are people who starve to death while clutching their rice baskets, simply because they have never truly sought to eat the rice.
Therefore, they do not realize that there is rice within the basket. A student’s study must be a true study, and their awakening must be a real awakening.

If it is not so, then even if one possesses as much learning as Ānanda, what can it possibly accomplish? It is nothing more than— [Note: The original text ends abruptly with "不過" (not merely / no more than).]
To merely remember the texts of many palm-leaf *nāga* treasuries (*nāgārjuna-piṭaka*)—what difference is there between this and a library?
It is far better to have no trace of mind, consciousness, or awareness, for that is truly an ancient Buddha.
Even if one can speak with a semblance of the melody, one is still but a craftsman of Chan; what distinction is there between such a person and a worldly scholar of vast learning?

Furthermore, what distinction is there between this and a talking parrot? Though you lift your feet and set them down day after day within the *dōjō*, you have yet to take a single step upon the *dōjō*. You must realize that Zen is not a matter of words, tongues, paper, or brush.
Students, be careful not to turn this great matter of importance into a livelihood based on mere talk, paper, and brush.
To do so is to slander the Great Prajñāpāramitā, resulting in inexhaustible karmic retribution. The case of Māra-Endurance (Māradharṣaṇa) serves as a warning from those who went before.
