Mogarěn said: The former master said, "To await the death of the mind so that it may be suppressed and executed, one must urgently employ the illumination mentioned previously to first capture it."
Cast it down and sever the bonds. To briefly select and employ the "lamp of the later [teachings]" is like using a true tiger for illumination;

it is like a divine physician who, when scraping the bone to treat an ailment, must first see the disease before applying the blade. If one were to fixate on a single method and recklessly apply needles or incisions, this would merely add another layer of illness.
As the ancient masters said: "The moment there is attachment, one has already fallen into a habitual trap. For those who study, this is the case.
The specific methods vary, yet as for the master’s illumination and function applied according to the occasion, no sage of antiquity has ever failed to act thus.
This is like Jia-shan’s reception of Yuepu or Da-jue’s reception of Xing-hua, wherein it is said that the mind must die so that it may be executed.
This refers to those who are captured and taken away in bonds. The illness of these two masters lay in their having a single, rigid "peg" of Zen as their governing principle;
thus, as soon as they were questioned, they would shout, believing that the Way of Zen was nothing more than this.
Fortunately, the two great elders confronted them with the mirror of the Dharma, leaving them no place to hide or evade. Only then did they beg for their lives from me; hence, with a single word—
This arouses his chronic ailment. What he calls "briefly picking out and using the later lamp" is precisely this. He has written a letter on this matter, repeatedly forbidding it;
yet now he again offers his own justification for it. His intention seems to be that it is not that he does not know [the truth], but that he knows it and yet does not act upon it.
Alas! One may perhaps deceive the world, but can one deceive the successive patriarchs of old? Can one deceive one’s own mind? I—
This means that the Venerable Master Tiandong would certainly not have used his mind in such a way. It is likely that some who seek to cause trouble have borrowed his name to defile the Dharma-gate.
As he explains the "Four Illuminations and Functions" in the *Piboshu*: "If the person does not accord with the Dharma, the Dharma cannot be established;

if the Dharma does not accord with the person, it lacks a standard. If the Dharma lacks a standard, then its application has no fixed point; if the person does not establish itself, then the illumination has no fixed pattern."
It is called "illumination" because one person illuminates another; it is called "function" because one uses the Dharma to guide a person.
This [interpretation] follows Linji’s words, yet people take the Dharma as being superior and generate their own interpretations based on the phrasing.

They fabricate this explanation by observing its intent, taking the person facing them as the "person" and defining a single, fixed blow as the "Dharma. Is this not a grave error? Linji said: "First, illumination..."
The person who exists after [the action] is not what is meant by "person. The dharma that exists before and illuminates after is also not what is meant by "dharma.

If one takes the person who stands in opposition as the "person," and the single, definitive blow of the staff as the "dharma," then how would one explain the statement that "both person and dharma are stripped away"? The former sage said: "It is valued not..."
I shall speak plainly. Having no choice, I have briefly opened a single thread of understanding. That which constitutes the ultimate reach of Linji certainly does not lie here.
As for the man who is a "do-nothing idler of the Way beyond study," there is not even a needle-point’s gap between him and his own fundamental nature. Such is the person he is.
Yet it unfurls and rolls up according to its own nature, appearing and disappearing in accordance with conditions. It is like the moon’s reflection on water—empty yet visible;
like an image in a mindless mirror—illuminating yet eternally void. Abiding in the immovable site of enlightenment, one performs great functions through great capacities.
As Mazu Daoyi said: "Wait for the mind to die so that it may be executed. One must urgently employ the aforementioned illumination to first capture it below.
Yet it goes on to bind. To briefly employ the lamp that follows [the initial illumination] is a mechanism for filling the belly;
it completely constitutes the self and others. Once the illumination has ceased, what use is there in employing it? Māra tolerates this and calls it the "true tiger" of illumination and function.

While it is indeed a tiger, how can it be anything other than a beast of prey that devours people? For the very arising of a thought is itself attachment; if the mind does not arise, [there is no binding].

All phenomena are unborn. Should there be even a hair’s breadth of a place where they arise, they all fall into the realm of seeing and hearing; they are born of discrimination and are in no way real.
Now, to say that one must wait for the mind to die in order to be executed is already to lose the flavor of the path of the mindless man, let alone to say: [as follows].
If you insist on using the previous illumination, you will simply fail to let go for even a single moment, causing the mind to dwell upon that illumination;
furthermore, by dwelling at every moment upon the person being illuminated, everything falls into the conceptual marks of seeing and hearing.
If one must act in this way to be considered a human being, would this not result in self-benefit and benefiting others becoming two separate, disjointed poles? As for...
The ancient worthies unloosed entanglements and severed bonds, fearing only that [the student] might not be able to respond with total purity at every turn;

thus they did not hesitate to explain and clarify again and again, cutting directly through to the depths. Though it be but a single word or a single phrase, it is not concise, for the entire person is fully contained within it.
Though it be a thousand words or ten thousand phrases, it is not prolix, for not a single thread deviates from the center. It is only that the student must truly be able to follow...
If one accords with the essential meaning and the fundamental principle, then even if no Dharma is being preached, one constantly hears the wondrous sound upon encountering any object.

If this is not yet the case, it is because one's obstacles are deep and one’s conditions are adverse; thus, even if one dwells within the assembly of Buddhas, one will not hear a single word when the Dharma is being expounded.

It is the listener who distinguishes [the teaching], for the speaker never fails to overturn everything to its very bottom. How could there ever be an intention to leave behind even a hair’s breadth of obstruction for the sake of creating hindrances for students?

Get out! Yuelu said, "I have come from afar to pay my respects; I beg the Master to receive me. Jia Shan said, "Before my eyes there is no *śāli* (disciple);
here there is no old monk. Yuelu then gave a shout. Jia Shan said, "Wait, wait! For now, *śāli*, [let us consider this]."
"Do not be so hasty and hurried. Clouds and moon are the same; streams and mountains are each different. It would be enough for you, Ācārya, to sit and silence the tongues of all people in the world.
But how can you make a tongueless person speak? Le Pu had no reply. Jia Shan struck him, and from then on he took his teachings to heart.
This was the manner in which Da Jue received Xing Hua. When Xing Hua was serving as the abbot of a monastery, one day—
The questioner asked, "I have often heard you say that as you traveled once toward the south, the tip of your staff never once brushed against a person who understood the Buddha-dharma.
On what principle do you base this statement? Xinghua then gave a shout; Da Jue struck him. Xinghua shouted again;
Da Jue struck him again. The following day, as Xinghua was passing by the Dharma Hall, Da Jue—
He summoned him, saying, "Head of the Monastery, I have a direct doubt regarding you for your shouting yesterday; explain it to me.
Xinghua said, "All that Cunjiang has learned from Sansheng throughout his life has been completely overturned by the Master."
He wished for Cunjiang to be granted the Dharma-gate of peace and happiness. Da Jue said, "You blind donkey! Cast off your patched robe and receive a severe beating!
At these words, Xinghua attained awakening to the principle behind Linji’s receiving blows from Huangbo.

Those who seek to gain understanding through intellectual study are all brought low; they come to their teacher for a dharma-gate of peace and ease, yet how could they know it might be a trap for tigers?

Having attained the principle behind Huangbo’s three blows of the staff, how could one know that what he had previously suspected regarding those three blows was not something else entirely subtle and profound?
Only upon reaching this point does one realize it was nothing more than this. If one were to say that one has awakened to the three blows of the staff...
Thus, with a single arrow he pierced through the three barriers; then, even at a distance of thousands of miles, he was already present.
The Buddha-dharma is vast, immeasurable, and boundless. How could this place be a point of rest?

Nevertheless, regarding Xinghua’s relationship to Dajue, how could one see it as his mind having died, thereby submitting to execution, being captured and led away, and bound in shackles? One day, Xinghua ascended the hall and took up [the staff].
Xiang said: "If you wish to make him one of the Three Sages, the Three Sages are too few. If you wish to make him the Great Awakened One (Dajue), the Great Awakened One is too remote.
It would be better to continue calling him Linji. If he had indeed attained sudden perfection based on a single word from Dajue, how could Xinghua not have succeeded Dajue?
The father and son, Mazu and Baizhang, constantly used their 'hard Zen' of a single wooden peg to denounce Mipan."
To further characterize Xinghua and Lepu as being merely "vain and deceitful" is truly a false and arrogant claim.
These four ancient worthies all operated through the "knocking, singing, picking up, and holding up" from the standpoint where not even a hair’s breadth is established.

Yet Muzhe and his son [Fayan] claimed that the Chan of Xinghua and Leputuo was merely "one peg"; it was only after receiving the instructions of Jianshan and Da'ue that their Chan could become "many pegs."
Not only did he defile Xinghua and Le Pu; how could he not have defiled Jia Shan and Da Jue?
This is truly what is meant by saying that summer insects cannot be discussed with regarding ice.
As for his denunciation of Mi Yun, he further claimed that the *Pibushu* was not written by Mi Yun at all, but was a forgery, using this to delude sightless scholars and thereby exonerate himself.

To specifically denounce the faults of his ancestors becomes even more intolerable. As for the interpretation of the "four illuminations and functions" in the *Pibushu* (Refutation Treatise), it certainly cannot be considered a discourse on the ultimate principle.
However, to claim that Miyun took "a single blow of the staff" as his dharma is truly a false and baseless accusation.
Since you speak of "a single blow," how can you also speak of "ascertainment"? A single blow is the Three Essentials and the Three Keys.
Regarding the four aspects of guest and host, and the four modes of illumination and function—whether fully raised or fully withdrawn—one might say they are definitively established.

Yet, as for the statement, "When illumination comes first and function follows, there is a person present; this is not what is meant by 'person. When function comes first and illumination follows, there is a dharma present;

this is not what is meant by 'dharma,'" this merely belongs to the realm of vague and shadowy discourse.密云悟 (Miyun Wu) said: "This is what is meant by 'person'... [and so on]. This "is" and "is not"... [the text continues].
"This is what is called a person; this is what is called the Dharma. How far apart are that which is not this and what is called the Dharma?
Speak quickly! Speak quickly! If you cannot speak, then [the spirit] who urinates on beds shall kill you! These words are quite penetrating.

In short, this refers to Linji’s four ways of "shining light. He has already clearly stated that if one is a person of transcendent capacity, they should "lift up and go" even before the words are raised;
such a person is still somewhat superior. How can you fail to realize the truth in this very place, instead fixating on the mere arrangements of his gate?
This is merely a case of blurred vision and dizziness—what is called being "turned by external objects."
[This refers to] what is called "sentient beings.
In the *Bishu Buo Wuzong Yuan* (The Book Refuting the Origins of the Five Houses), it says: "The treasury of the true Dharma-eye has already been extinguished by the blind donkey;
how much more so could names such as 'the one-circle,' 'host and guest,' or 'Śiva's eye' remain to harm future generations? Moran said: "According to [this] refutation..."

I have written this treatise. If these three sages had not conformed to the intent of Linji and extinguished the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, why would Fengxue have praised the Sage as a true "son who has entered the room," and why would Nanyuan have nodded his approval?
If he praised him when it was not worth praising, then Fengxue lacked eyes; if he nodded when it was not appropriate to nod, then Nanyuan also lacked eyes. Yet...
From that time until now, more than twenty generations have passed; are they not the descendants of the "blind elder"?

This is what is discussed in the *Pibishu* (Book of Refutation). As the saying goes: "If one loses their footing once, there is nowhere to place their feet; if one loses their words once, there is nowhere to place their mouth.
Is this not precisely what the *Pibishu* asserts?
Linji said, "After my passing, you must not let my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye be extinguished.
Sansheng stepped forward and said, "How would we dare let the Master’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye be extinguished? Linji asked, "If someone asks you this in the future, what will you say to him?
Sansheng gave a shout. Linji said, "Who knew that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye would be extinguished by such a blind donkey?"
[The text] was set aside. Later, Fengxue stated that Sansheng was a true disciple who had personally entered the inner chamber, unlike a mere visitor outside the gate;
Nan-yuan nodded in agreement. Since Mazu Ren had already established this through the judgments of Fengxue and Nan-yuan, it is said that Linji deeply approved of Sansheng’s words.
Furthermore, [the text] refutes what Tian Tong said regarding the "Treasury of the True Dharma Eye" (Zhengfayan zang), which is still directed toward...

The phrase "extinguish it at the side of the blind donkey" is intended to judge that the Three Sages did not accord with the intent of Linji. This is truly what is meant by those who interpret the meaning based on the literal text.
Now, the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is nothing other than a dry piece of dung. To the traveler outside the gate, one might ask, "What is the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye?
If one has already personally received the transmission upon entering the room, the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye must certainly be extinguished. However...
Subsequently, it extends horizontally throughout the ten directions and penetrates vertically through the three periods of time; it is, in its entirety, this very Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
Although Linji has passed away, how could the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye ever perish? Moreover, even now Linji does not perish.
Thus, as for those who say, "After my passing, you must not let my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye perish," how could such words be understood as referring to a substantial, concrete dharma?
The Three Sages said: "How would we dare to extinguish it? This does not mean they dared to extinguish it; rather, how could one extinguish it?
Since there is no extinguishing, that is true extinguishing. Fengxue used the phrase "extinguishing" as a word of affirmation, yet he still only managed to express half of it.
How much less so for Mazu and Huineng, who truly did not know Fengxue’s point of arrival, and who recklessly presumed that Mimi Yun was the same as Fengxue?
This was a contradiction. Consequently, [the critics] leaned on the gates and peered through the windows, relying on the prestige of Fengxue and Nanyuan to vehemently denounce Miphan (Miyun).

They did not realize that Fengxue, Nanyuan, and Miphan were, in fact, members of one family. Miphan stated that even the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the True Dharma Eye) had been extinguished within the mouth of a blind donkey;
how much more so would names such as "The One Circle," "Host and Guest," and "Śiva’s Eye" leave behind harm?
In later generations, these words struck precisely at the core of the illness of Zang and Ren, father and son.
Furthermore, names such as "One Zero," "Host and Guest," and "Śiva’s Eye" were the very instruments used by the demonic Ren and his followers to bewitch the men and women of households;
they were what he had cherished most throughout his life. Therefore, in his denunciation of Mìyún, he likewise spared no effort.

Mokei said: "Linji was the legitimate heir of Huangbo. If Linji’s fundamental tenets were not already present in Huangbo, why did Huangbo refuse to go among the various quarters [of the monastic community] while considering Linji worthy? Furthermore, during Linji’s era, the Buddha-dharma was at its zenith.
If his establishment [of the lineage] had truly been impossible, how could the veteran masters and long-established elders have remained silent?"—Zhaozhou Daoyi, Weishan Lingyou, and so forth.

Master [Linji] was of the same generation as [Huangbo] Ji’s father; thus, Linji privately addressed Huangbo as "Venerable Elder" (zunsu). Puhua, on the other hand, was of the same generation as Huangbo, yet he turned northward to serve him as his teacher.
[Puhua] was a man of the stage of fruition known as "Little Śākyamuni. At that time, it was Linji who made a vow to continue the severed lineage;
indeed, at such a juncture, none surpassed Deshan in his censure of those who merely rely on intellectual understanding. When Linji passed away, Deshan was still...
"I am well. You have never uttered a single word to correct the errors of [Zhao] Ji. Is it because you fear Ji that you remain silent? But Ji has already passed away;
do you not wish to avoid provoking a source of contention? Furthermore, Deshan was truly the foremost of those who reviled the Buddhas and scolded the Patriarchs."
Examining it in light of antiquity, verifying it against the consensus of one’s peers, and tracing its origins within the lineage of masters, none considered Linji (Ji) to be in error;
yet today you alone condemn him. Why is this? Furthermore, the "staff and shout" were what Linji constantly employed, and the "fundamental principles" (*gangzong*) were likewise what he established.
If you truly deem Linji to be wrong, then you ought not to emulate his staff and shouts.
Since you employ the staff and the shout, how could you not know the essential principles of the staff and the shout? Furthermore, how could you forbid others from saving those essential principles?

As a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one must discern the errors and confusions of antiquity and the present as clearly as looking at fruit in the palm of one's hand, penetrating them with certainty so as to distinguish who is right and who is wrong.
Only then may one distinguish between dragons and snakes, mete out rewards and punishments, and settle cases based on the facts. To act otherwise would be—
This is a model that shall not be effaced for a thousand ages. It causes the disciples of Sanfeng to clench their mouths and tie their tongues;

even with world-surpassing eloquence, they cannot proffer a defense. Is this not the deed of a heroic and fierce man? Now, regarding the critique of the "Opening the Book" (Bishu) concerning the fundamental tenet (zongzhi):
it is like the eye receiving sound or the ear perceiving form—vague and superficial, failing to penetrate one another, merely a state of muddled confusion.
Ultimately, if one speaks only of "real dharmas" and "real dharmas," what standard will there be for the world and future generations?
Linji said: "I have not a single dharma to give to people; I merely treat illnesses and untie bonds.
It would be better for you to take my words and simply rest in non-action. Thus, the principles of the staff and the shout are nothing more than the same thing.
The means for untying adhesions and removing fetters are like food used to relieve hunger; yet it is the person who is hungry or satiated, not the gruel or rice.
They are like sleep used to relieve exhaustion; yet it is the person who sleeps or awakens, not the quilt or pillow.
To doubt the gruel and trust the rice, or to doubt the rice and trust the gruel, is in both cases delusion. Both gruel and rice can satisfy a person; it is simply that one does not eat them.

In that case, one could not be satiated; yet, if one does not hunger, it is likewise impossible to eat. To discard the quilt and take the pillow, or to discard the pillow and take the quilt—both are delusions.
There is nothing about the quilt or the pillow that is not a requisite for sleep; it is simply that without sleep, one cannot slumber.

If one is not exhausted, then there is likewise no need for sleep. When Huangbo, Baizhang, Yangshan, Puhua, Deshan, and other venerable patriarchs revered Linji, was it because they valued his establishment of the fundamental principles (gangzong)? Furthermore, how could fundamental principles be related to matters of weight?
And as for Miyun’s non-adherence to fundamental principles, how has he ever ceased to be Linji? Moreover, how could fundamental principles even be relevant [to this]?
This is not it. This matter is beyond right and wrong; both subject and object have vanished. It is like a mosquito on an iron ox—it has no place to bite.
As soon as there is right and wrong, one becomes distracted and loses the mind. Can you understand this current debate as being a matter of right and wrong?
How could the ancestral style ever involve contention? Contention extinguishes the ancestral style. Throughout his life, Deshan’s wild views ran rampant.
He scolds the Buddhas and reviles the patriarchs; his words and phrases are utterly devoid of merit.

Yet, the flavor of him dwelling in a thatched hut atop a solitary peak cannot be compared to those like Ma Rin, who cling to signs, pursue the mundane, and chase after fame and profit—how could they be spoken of in the same breath?
Thus, judging others by one's own heart, he claims that [the Master] has violated the Linji tradition.
Zong was deeply moved and submitted his heart in full accord; thus, throughout his life, he never uttered a single word of disparagement.
Otherwise, while Linji was still in the world, perhaps out of fear of him he remained silent. But after Linji passed away, what would he have feared that prevented him from opening his mouth?
He would have used his own filthy inner organs to suddenly smear over Deshan, who was one who reviled the Buddhas and scolded the Patriarchs.

As for the karmic retribution: it is further said that one who acts as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) must discern the errors and confusions of antiquity and the present as clearly as looking at fruit in the palm of one's hand, penetrating them with certainty so as to know who is right and who is wrong.
Only then may one distinguish between dragons and snakes, administer rewards and punishments, and settle cases based on the facts to establish a precedent that shall not fade for a thousand ages.
This is precisely like a beggar hoping for sudden wealth, yet eating his fill of sour yellow pickled vegetables. All...
To take what is right as right and what is wrong as wrong is entirely a matter of the Confucian school; how does it concern the School of the Patriarchs?
Since you are a great *kalyāṇamitra*, there should be no gap even as small as a needle or thread in your fundamental practice. If you depart from this fundamental practice, everything is discarded;

when you do not even attend to yourself, how can you be concerned with others? At such times, one should take up and bring forth the words of the ancient worthies regarding the ultimate standard of fundamental practice.
Among humans, there are indeed those who, taking the various fox spittle and wildcat saliva of over a thousand years, do not disdain their stench and filth, yet taste their sourness and saltiness.

Is there any such great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra)? Māra-ren (Mori) delighted in his own self-satisfaction, claiming a slight proficiency in literature and history, and further relying on his eloquence, he wished to overwhelm Miyun—who was illiterate—saying that Miyun’s...
Regarding this "Refutation of the Book": how could it possibly cause the followers of Sanfeng to clench their jaws and remain tongue-tied?
It merely speaks in a muddled fashion, saying "real dharma, real dharma" to the end; yet it fails to realize that Mipan does not even recognize a single character.
Thus, it truly cannot cause the followers of Sanfeng to remain silent, and as for Mipan’s own status as Mipan, there is no connection whatsoever, nor is there any increase or decrease.
Yet Māra desires to rely on his worldly eloquence to dispute the perfect teaching of non-action and non-effort;

that he is possessed by demonic influence is already self-evident without further inquiry. Furthermore, it is said: "If one considers 'rescue' (ji) to be wrong, then one should not emulate his use of staff and shout.
Since he does employ the staff and shout, how could he not know the fundamental principles of the staff and shout? This is even more [evidence of] demonic possession."
Treatise: Before Linji, were there not already the methods of the staff and the shout? Yet, can it be said that Mipan merely imitated the staff and shout of Linji?
If one could say he did, then one might as well say that Linji merely imitated the staff and shout of Huangbo.
Even with the very same hands and mouth, eating today is not an imitation of eating yesterday; speaking today is not an imitation [of speaking yesterday].
As for the discourse of yesterday, how much less could one emulate the staff and shouts of others? How could such things be imitated? Each person possesses their own hands and mouth;
who would emulate whom? Only those of the Mara-tolerance school focus their minds and apply themselves with single-minded devotion to emulate the fundamental principles of Linji.
For this reason, he became a demon and defiled Linji’s ears. Modan said:
"The Master is brilliant and gifted by Heaven; like a tiger born on the third day, its breath is already enough to devour an ox.
He and Yuepu were both attendants of Linji, yet both remained fixed upon their single awakening and viewed the rest of the world as being of no account. Cheda said, "Jue! (Great Awakening).
Jiashan would then have fallen into the ranks of those who lack a tail.

When a student enters this Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), they realize the Truth in every thought-moment and merge with the essence in every dust mote. They attain enlightenment simultaneously with the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
their notions of past and future vanish, and they enter Nirvana on the same day as the ten classes of sentient beings. With all views of beginning and end severed, their perspective is as follows:
Among all people in the world, there is not a single one who is not a Buddha, yet there is no perception of "Buddha. There is not a single one who is not oneself, yet there is no perception of "self.
Meeting face-to-face, how could there still be the perception of "person" remaining within the field of the eight consciousnesses?
Now, Mazu Ren says that when Xinghua was a servant to Linji, he sat viewing the heavens from the perspective of a single awakening.
There is no one below [him]. Although Xinghua had not yet attained complete penetration, he did not reach such an extreme;

this is sufficient to know that he had not even dreamed of the matters of light and shadow at the gates and thresholds of the enlightened ones. How could it be that after having awakened, one considers oneself capable of awakening, and moreover, considers oneself to have actually attained something to awaken to, clinging to that awakening and boasting of one's own ability to awaken, saying: [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be an excerpt from a Zen discourse (likely from the *Wumenguan* or similar collection), and the final sentence is incomplete.*
Among all people in the world, none have realized the principle that transcends self and others, the capable and the incapable, right and wrong, or delusion and enlightenment.

Such various false views and perverse thoughts arise and cease in a state of chaotic confusion. If this is the case, it is entirely the conceptualizing activity of the *vijñāna* (consciousness), a mere reflection of mental fabrication.

When the karmic consciousness is vast and indistinct, there is no fundamental basis upon which to rely. How, then, can this be called "awakening"? If even this were called awakening, then those who merely skim the surface [of the teachings] would also be awakened.
Regarding the books of the Zen school, those who merely gather the drool and saliva of foxes and wildcats are all immediately called "enlightened.
It is said in the world that Miaoxi attained great enlightenment eighteen times and minor enlightenments beyond counting; such talk is a sign of incomplete understanding.

Among the various forms of demonic patience, this is its most profound poison. Thus, they falsely establish the names and characteristics of "Great Enlightenment" and "Small Enlightenment," as well as "Small Dharma" and "Great Dharma," deceiving and deluding the common people.
How could such persons have ever truly reached the stage of non-doubt? As the Sūtra says:

"When one person gives rise to the true realization and returns to the source, then the empty space of the ten directions will all vanish away. Yet these people, being petty and calculating, are preoccupied with their own self-satisfaction, claiming—
There is something to be awakened to. I am one who is capable of awakening. Yet, wearing such a "hat of dripping fat," you are a legal document destined to receive iron staffs before King Yama;
you have brought the staff yourself to the court of judgment. I ask you: what is this awakening?
Is it not the realization that brings an end to birth and death? Once birth and death are ended, there is no more birth and death. If even birth and death...

There is none. What could I, as a person, be attached to? Yet there still remains the realization that "others are not my equal," and there still remains the realization that "all people in the world are not my equal.
Is this not a single slab of clear ice that extinguishes a raging, fierce fire?
Mozhen said, "Linji said: 'Sometimes my one shout is like the Vajra King’s sword; sometimes my one shout is like a crouching lion;
sometimes my one shout is like a probing pole or a blade of grass; sometimes my one shout does not function as a shout.
One who possesses this eye is like a bright mirror set upon its stand. Although those of the family of the Dharma may have attained thorough realization,"
When the Great Dharma has not yet been clarified, as soon as one opens the mouth and moves the tongue, various images and forms manifest therein.
This can be seen roughly through such examples as the several cases of Master Xinghua’s examination of monks.

Because later generations do not investigate the meaning of the "four times" (sishou) phrase, they imitate it by saying, "A single blow does not function as a single blow," and when asked about its essential purport, they further [respond] accordingly.
The commentary says: This specifically refers to the moment when [the breath] enters and exits through the gateway of the human face. Someone might further challenge this by asking:
"When the light of the eyes falls to the ground, where does this thing that enters and exits the gateway of the face go?
He then offers another explanation: "The entire great earth is none other than this very point. If this were truly so, then why did Min De bow immediately after the two shouts? Where [is the answer]?
Have you attained the principle of entering and exiting through the face?
Among Linji’s four shouts, each shout possesses the function of not being used as a single shout. If they do not possess this, then even three shouts will not suffice to save oneself.
Yet, this one shout, which does not function as a single shout, has already been mired in mud and water.
Why is this? Above it, there is not a single shout that does not function as a shout; what connection could it have with our own spiritual awakening?

An ancient worthy said: "Even if you were to shout all the way up to the Thirty-three Heavens, when the force of the wind ceases and you reach the ground and regain consciousness, I would still say to you:
'Not yet. Now, Magu Ren is dying under the phrase "the four times. (Selected from Miyun).
To realize that "one blow does not function as one blow" truly defiles Linji. How could the entirety of Linji’s lifelong practice of benefiting himself and others reside merely in his four shouts?
If one were to judge by those four shouts alone, they would not even compare to Miyun’s “one blow that does not function as one blow,” which is direct and decisive.
When the student’s bottom of the bucket falls away, there is not a single dharma left to be grasped.
This is what constitutes a response; this is what constitutes awakening. How could there be a place where awakening reaches its ultimate limit and yet the Great Dharma remains unclarified?

If that were so, then that which is called the "Great Dharma" would exist apart from awakening, not being clarified through awakening, but necessarily obtained through oral transmission and secret instruction.
Would this not be to slander the Great Prajñāpāramitā? "The Dharma is originally without dharma; the absence of dharma is itself dharma. Now it is entrusted.

When there is no dharma, how has any dharma ever been a dharma? If you claim there is a separate "Great Dharma" that exists outside of awakening, does this not clearly contradict the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs?
Furthermore, for what purpose is it so prized to reach the ultimate point of awakening?
Is it merely to desire to open one's mouth and move one's tongue, to gnash teeth and snap jaws with the wild fox spirits of the mountains, vying with them over who is dull and who is clever?

Jieye: What is the use of clarifying such a great Dharma? Furthermore, as soon as a single dharma arises, all infinite myriad dharmas are simultaneously and perfectly interfused. Thus, outside of a single dharma, there are no further dharmas;
and within those no-further-dharmas, not even a single dharma is established. Precisely because not a single dharma is established, it is therefore complete and boundless.
All phenomena are thus. However, when one attains thorough awakening, does one still fall into the realm of views regarding phenomena?

A sovereign of the nine palaces will certainly not plow the fields alongside the common people. Now, you say that although you have reached the point of thorough awakening, the Great Dharma is not yet clear;
that as soon as you open your mouth and move your tongue, various images manifest within. From this, it can be known that you have not even dreamed of what it is.

This is an awakening. To insist on interpreting it as a mere intellectual understanding is like an old pedant from a village of three households suddenly claiming that the palaces of the Weiyang Palace were not magnificent;
such a person is either delirious or insane. When Linji ascended the hall, he said:
"Upon this ball of red flesh, there is a true person of no station who constantly enters and exits through the gate of your face. Those of you who have not yet attained verification, look! Look!"
At that time, a monk came forward and asked, "What is the true person of no station? The Master descended from his meditation seat, seized him, and said, "Speak!
Speak! As the monk hesitated, the Master pushed him away and said, "The true person of no station—what is he? A dried piece of dung. He then returned to his quarters.
Later, Miyun used this single blow not as a mere blow, calling it "the direct pointing to the person."
Regarding the timing of the breath entering and exiting the mouth, using this to guide beginners is not inherently flawed.
However, Linji’s most urgent concern for others did not lie in the phrase about the "true person of no rank" entering and exiting the mouth;
rather, it lay in the phrase, "What is this dry dung-squatter? People simply refuse to accept this "dry dung-squatter" directly, instead seeking it within the "person of no rank."

At the gateway from which the True Person enters and exits, one conceives extraordinary thoughts. Thereupon, the notions of "I" and "mine," along with the mind and mental factors, blaze forth in turbulent conflict.
One gives rise to conceptualization and casts oneself into the city of the five aggregates; one grasps at signs and sinks into the sea of the six sense bases.

If you can awaken to Linji’s phrase regarding the "dry piece of dung"—that it is true speech, that it is speech in accordance with reality—then you will naturally possess a small measure [of realization].

Regarding the section on "Applying the Correspondence": Throughout his life, Mìyún took up and raised [the teaching] by using the single staff not as a staff, but to point directly at the gateway of every person’s face, where it enters and exits.
He did not provide commentary or analysis upon this matter, leaving it for practitioners to realize for themselves.
Thereupon, Magu Ren repeatedly pointed out and refuted this, saying: "When the light of the eyes falls to the ground, where does this face that enters and exits go?

Now, if it is said that when the light of the eyes falls to the ground there is nowhere for this face that enters and exits to go, then it must be that while the light of the eyes has not yet fallen to the ground, there was a place for this face that enters and exits to go. But if that is so, then [it is] non-existent."
The "Unranked True Person" truly possesses the capacity for entering and exiting; yet the face-gate of every person is indeed the place where this Unranked True Person enters and exits.

Is this not like mistaking a wooden stump for a ghost? Having established the "Devil Endurance" as a means of interrogation, [the Master] further divined the intention of Mìyún and offered this response:
"The entire great earth is none other than this single point. To grasp at it in the void is to fabricate.
[The author] selects [this passage]. What kind of mental activity is this? Therefore, on that day, Miyun composed the "Refuting Delusions to Rescue [the Truth]" (*Bikwang jiuyun*), stating:
"If the eye-light has a further time of falling to the ground, or if at the moment the eye-light falls to the ground there were yet another face entering and exiting, where would you place it?
How could one say it is always entering and exiting the face? Before the deceased monk, this is the bodhi before one's eyes."
It is said that throughout the entire great earth, there is nothing that is not this very point. If there were yet another "this very point," it would already be thousands of miles away;
how, then, could it be said to constantly enter and exit the gate of the face? This sufficiently proves that Miyun never made such a statement.
An ancient worthy said: "The one mind is the Dharma-realm; the Dharma-realm is the one mind. It encompasses and covers the ten directions. It does not...
The dew is on the hair. How could it be that only the mind possesses it? The body, too, contains it everywhere. Thus it is said: "The entire earth is a single eye. Cuiyan ascended the hall and said:
"For an entire summer, I have chatted with my brothers here and there; look—do Cuiyan’s eyebrows still remain?
If a student truly finds an entry point here, they will naturally not give rise to the delusions of sentient and insentient beings.
Contemplate this: do not give rise to erroneous thoughts concerning the internal or external mind.

If you have not yet done so, it is not only those who feign patience with demons who speak falsely and pass judgment, thereby easily falling victim to their poison; even that which Mìyún has shown contains grit within the rice.
Mokuren said: "The Master was grieving because he felt that the prophecy concerning Mount Ōyama rested upon his own person; thus he wept all day long.
It was not that he lacked enlightenment. Rather, he feared that those who were enlightened would fail to penetrate the essential tenets, thereby bringing harm to the world and future generations.
He was like a divine physician revered by the people for saving their lives, who, having grown old, examined the talents of his sons and found not one of them to be worthy."
"It may be so. If I were to keep it secret, then this art of saving the people of the world and future generations would be cut off by me.
If I were to transmit it, I fear I could not fully convey its subtlety, which would only further mislead the world and future generations. This, perhaps, was Fengxue’s intention.

Some say that when Fengxue replied to Master Nian, he said, "Those who are clever and intelligent are many; those who realize their nature are few. Observing his meaning, one sees what his concern truly was.
"Is it because they are intelligent? He replied, "No. It means that although those who are intelligent are many, those who have realized their nature (jianxing) are not easily found.
