it is the true gain and loss within the absence of gain and loss. Is this not a blind participation and a blind realization? It is the same nostril as that monk.'"
Kong. As for this public case of Fenyang, it has not yet been fully grasped at the point where it is taken up.
The words cease; the text below says: "It is no ordinary matter. He then offers a verse for the assembly, saying: "The Three Essentials and the Three Keys are difficult to distinguish;
When the meaning is attained, the Way is easy to approach. A single phrase clearly encompasses the myriad phenomena; On the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh. Return.
Do you understand? If you understand it in such a way, you are not a monk of fiery temperament.
How should one understand it? Mowu Ren did not attend to the latter half of this kōan at all; he took only the first half and interpreted it as a fully realized dead word or a substantial dharma.
Although this was not the ultimate teaching from Fenyang, it was further diminished by Mowu Ren’s editing. Thus, it becomes even more...

This is a shortcoming. Now, as for the statement that "the Three Origins and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish," it is clear that the three phrases do not individually possess the Three Origins.

Regarding the statement that "when one attains the meaning and forgets the words, the Way is easy to approach," it is further clarified that this refers to one phrase possessing the gate of the Three Origins, and within one Origin, possessing one of the three essential phrases;
it is by no means a matter of fixating on specific words or phrases as being the "phrase. Furthermore, from [this point] onward...
The commentary states: "A single phrase clearly encompasses all phenomena: on the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh.
If you understand it in this way, you will still regret that there is this one phrase remaining; therefore, you are not a monk of impetuous nature.

Now, Mōjin has died for the sake of the first half of this statement, asserting it to be the true gradual process within the absence of gradual stages, and [the truth] within the absence of gain or loss.
As for the "genuine gain and loss," had Fengyang seen this, what kind of monk would he have rated him as?

Furthermore, he cites the words of the Dong lineage, saying, "Scholars, commoners, dukes, and marquises look at it as one and the same Way; nobility and meanness, high and low, clarify their respective positions.

He claims that only by knowing this can one speak of the fundamental tenet (*zongzhi*). This is even more intolerable. These two phrases belong to a separate tune and are not worth discussing. It may be so.
Know that the error lies in what has not yet been raised. For instance, as for Jia Prefecture, Shan Prefecture, and the West River—who is noble and who is base?

Regarding the Great Image, the Iron Ox, and the Lion—who is honored and who is lowly? If you insist on forced interpretation and contrived association so that future generations throughout the world might know the transmission of the fundamental principle, it belongs to the realm of Māra and Duṣprasaha;
such acts of fabrication result in wearying the mind and increasing one's own deceptiveness day by day.
Mofen said:
"Fengxue’s instruction regarding the fundamental tenets of Linji is like the bright sun in a clear blue sky;
there is not a hair’s breadth of obscuration, yet the blind simply cannot see it. Guanyin said: "Those who do not know the Way yet recklessly attempt to divine its meaning are like..."
Shooting at objects covered by a bowl: those placed high contain gold or jade; those placed in the middle contain horn or feathers; those placed in the bottom contain tile or stone.
Is it so? Or is it not so? Only the one who placed the object knows. This is what Píshū [discusses] regarding the fundamental principles on the banks of the Jì River.
The reality is indeed like this. One opens [the box] but finds nothing; one tries again to unravel it, yet it remains impenetrable, so one opens it once more.
Seven times opening and three times unraveling—it was truly laborious to guess what was concealed beneath the lid.
Yangshan ascended the hall and said: "All of you, turn the light inward and reflect upon yourselves; do not merely memorize my words.
Since beginningless kalpas, you have turned your backs on the light and cast yourselves into darkness; your roots of deluded thought are so deep that they cannot be uprooted all at once.

Therefore, I provisionally employ skillful means to seize your coarse consciousness—what value is there in this? It is like using yellow leaves to stop a child's crying; what efficacy does it have? It is also like a person..."
He takes a hundred kinds of goods and displays them together with gold and jewels in a single shop for sale, intending merely to gauge the capacity of those who come, weighing their worth.
Thus it is said: "Stonehead is a shop of pure gold; here, I am a shop of miscellaneous wares.
If someone comes seeking mouse droppings, I likewise pick some up and give it to him; if they come seeking pure gold, I likewise pick some up and give it to him. Let the student observe Yangshan.
This is merely a matter of words; it is a statement cited by Mowu Ren from the *Guanyinzi* that mocks Miyun for not knowing the fundamental principle.

His delusions and errors are so manifest that there is no need for further explanation. If a student of the Way can truly pick up a bit of mouse-dung and find even a slight point of resonance, then [his delusions] will naturally melt away like ice and crumble like a fortress. He will see the true dullness of his own essence, and it will turn as smoothly as jade.

The pearl turns; its radiance is full and perfect. Yet, because from time immemorial we have been obstructed by shells and mired in ignorance, we desire only gold while feeling ashamed to acknowledge mouse droppings.
We do not realize that the entire great earth is but a single mass of mouse droppings, and that there is no gold at all.

Thus, throughout kalpas, we have drifted in samsara, emerging and submerging again and again. When a Master acts for the sake of others, he looks for the hole and drives in the wedge, or perhaps picks up [the object].
Gold, or perhaps picking up mouse droppings—all these are skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). They are indeterminate gateways: if you realize it is gold, it is gold;
if you do not realize it, it is dung. It is dung and it is gold; it is gold and it is dung. It is neither gold nor dung; it is dung and it is gold.
How can this be compared to shooting at an overturned bowl? Within it, gold may be found, jade may be found, horn may be found, feather may be found, tile may be found, or stone may be found;

it is simply a matter of which object happens to be placed there. It is precisely those like the Mara-tolerant who pick up the spittle of foxes and the drool of wildcats, treasuring them as gold and concealing them beneath an overturned bowl. They gather male and female Māras together, further deceiving and deluding one another.

He conjectures, claiming that he alone recognizes the foremost extraordinary treasure beneath the bowl; those who recognize it are true patriarchs, while those who do not are merely common fellows like "Old Man Meng.
He thinks this will not lead him astray, and that he intends to lead all fellow practitioners of Chan throughout the world and for future generations.
Everyone was swept along by the prevailing wind, all drinking the same poisoned milk; this is why I could not help but decline and refute it.
Thus, you turn around and mock those who refute it, saying they do not know what is beneath the bowl.
As for the thing placed beneath the bowl by the demonic folk—what use would a student of the Way have for knowing it? This very thing is gold, it is jade, it is horn, and it is feather.
It is both tile and stone, manifest before the eyes of the myriad people, yet looking at it, one does not see it;
resonant within the ears of the myriad people, yet listening for it, one does not hear it. It cannot be divined or pointed out; there is neither "is" nor "is not.
Vertically, it exhausts the three periods of time; horizontally, it spans the ten directions. Nothing is higher than heaven, yet it cannot cover it; nothing is greater than earth, yet it cannot...
When it is placed in a basin, it is simply a basin; yet the basin does not conceal the basin. When objects are placed therein, they are simply objects; yet the objects cannot conceal the objects.

How could those who endure as demons recognize this? If things were fixed and unchangeable like gold, jade, horn, feather, tile, or stone—then where gold exists, it must be called gold and cannot be called jade; where tile exists, it must be called tile and cannot be called gold.
To say that such is the essential tenet (zongzhi) would mean that the essential tenet is itself a substantial dharma.
If this were so, then the demonic patience of self-exertion would be a hundredfold more effective than the art of divining hidden objects; how utterly erroneous and deluded this is!
Imperial Composition: *Record for Discerning the Heterodox and Eliminating Demons*, Scroll Four;
Imperial Composition: *Record for Discerning the Heterodox and Eliminating Demons*, Scroll Five.
Mōnin said: "Foguo said, 'Not doubting the words and phrases is a great illness. Yantou said: "The Great General Principle."
Regarding the matters within our school, one must first understand the phrases; yet Fengxue further taught that students should personally investigate these words and phrases.
Lately, however, senior masters have uniformly rejected and dismissed such phrases. Are they intending to make the scholars of the world take walls and tiles as their teachers?
Now, walls and tiles are indeed worthy of being taken as teachers; it is simply that students do not know this—how can you reject them?
"These are words and phrases. Mañjuśrī said: "The true essence of the teaching in this land lies in the purity of hearing sounds.
This Great Being would not disagree with people of the present day.
The study of the Zen school consists in directly realizing the one mind. To directly realize the one mind, one must utterly sever emotional attachments and intellectual views.
For this reason, [the masters] constantly place words devoid of conventional meaning within the field of the eight consciousnesses of others—words that can neither be swallowed nor spat out.

When the time and conditions finally arrive, with a single "keng" sound from the ground, the five gates and eight windows shatter open, and one naturally realizes that which the World-Honored One did not speak.
It is said: "Kāśyapa has not heard that which is to be heard. If one becomes entangled in subtle details at this point, one has ultimately never attained thorough penetration.
One must simply continue to investigate the words and phrases. Nevertheless, regardless of whether one understands them or not, they are entirely unrelated to the words and phrases themselves.
If you understand them as mere words and phrases, then even if you were to resolve all seventeen hundred koans, [you would still be lost].

One may be able to deliver words [in ordinary circumstances], yet before King Yama, regardless of whether you can answer or not, the thirty-day period of judgment arrives, and as before, your karmic consciousness remains vast and茫然 (mángmáng), with no foundation to rely upon.
Yuanwu’s statement that "not doubting the words" is a great illness is because such non-doubt arises from a lack of faith; if there is no faith, how can it be attained?
One enters [the Way] through faith, and only after faith does doubt arise. Only after doubt does one truly reach the ground where there is no doubt.

If one were already free from doubt from the very beginning, then one would be fully possessed of the arrogance of superiority and great conceit; even if one possesses the fundamental tongs and hammer, from where could one begin to apply them?
Yantou said that regarding matters within the Great Universal Framework of the School’s Principles, one must first recognize the "phrase" (*ju*). Now, as for what is called a "phrase":
"What is a phrase? "In our school, there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma given to others; this is what is called a phrase.

If you truly recognize this "phrase of no-phrase," you will naturally transcend the four propositions and sever the hundred negations, while simultaneously dissolving the hundred affirmations within those very four propositions. If it is so, then Yantou must first recognize the phrase, as instructed by Fengxue.

To investigate the words and phrases of the human body is precisely to employ words and phrases that negate and exclude them; yet the words and phrases of Mìyún that negate and exclude are, in fact, precisely words and phrases that establish them.

If one were to say that Mòrěn died beneath these words while claiming they are all uniformly negations and exclusions, then would this cause the scholars of the world to take walls, tiles, and rubble as their teachers? How could such a person know that walls, tiles, and rubble are precisely...?

These are words and phrases. If one were to claim that walls, tiles, and rubble are not words and phrases, then it can be known that among the seventeen hundred public cases (gong'an), there is not a single word they have been able to realize.
Furthermore, it is said that although walls, tiles, and rubble are indeed true teachers, students do not recognize them;
how can one then sever words and phrases? If one can realize [the truth] at the very point where words and phrases are severed, one will naturally be able to...
If you investigate the words and phrases to their essence, you will naturally be able to realize that walls, tiles, and pebbles are the true Buddha, the true Dharma, and the true Sangha.
If you do not realize this, yet wish to measure and speculate beneath the words and phrases, then as soon as there is right and wrong, you will fall into confusion and lose your mind;
you will follow after the dust while turning your back on the source, like waves rising that darken the water. Even if you were to lecture and recite the Tripitaka ten thousand times...
To divide it into two parts is merely to become an enemy of the Buddhas of the three periods; how much more so for the drool of various wild foxes?
Mazu Ren further cited Mañjuśrī’s words: “The true essence of the teaching in this land is pure in hearing sounds.
He said that this Great Being should not be at odds with people of the present day. Mañjuśrī’s these words are like the World-Honored One’s “not speaking is speaking,” and Kāśyapa’s...
"Listening and listening—this is one, or is it two? This Great Being should not contradict the World-Honored One Kāśyapa.
Indeed, this very thing encompasses the three periods of time vertically and spans the ten directions horizontally; it is immeasurable, boundless, radiant, and pure.
One cannot use 'this' to clarify 'that,' so how much less can one use 'this' to distinguish 'that'? For those who have awakened, to bring forth even one..."
A single drop already penetrates to the source of the ocean; yet the deluded person, amidst surging waves, fails to realize that they are entirely of the nature of water.
When studying the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one investigates their words and phrases, yet remains unaware that one has never actually attained those words and phrases oneself.

If you truly understand this, how could you ever die clinging to the side of words and phrases? Students need not concern themselves with "how" or "what"; you must simply engage in genuine inquiry and achieve true awakening.
If one has truly investigated and attained realization, then it is appropriate both to reject and sever words and phrases, and it is also appropriate to investigate and examine them.
However, as with those who are like demons or heretics, neither investigating and examining words and phrases nor rejecting and severing them will lead to attainment.
Mōrin said: "Juefan replied to the Layman Wujin, 'The ten wisdoms are identical with reality;

they share the same mechanism as the three mysteries. He then composed a verse, saying: 'The ten wisdoms are identical with reality—their true face is complete. Among them, one wisdom is the root source.'"
"If one wishes to see the Old Man of Fenyang, he splits the Three Essentials into two parts. As for the meaning of "splitting," it is like painting the eyes on a dragon;

it cannot be communicated through words or discourse. To claim, as the *Pibushu* does, that since they have been split, there should no longer be "Three Essentials" in later generations—what kind of statement is that?
I have observed that the old masters of recent times open their mouths only to scold.
Understanding this, one should gauge the point of realization like a lion king: with a single roar, standing firm and upright for ten thousand fathoms.
Now, I truly believe that the Three Essentials can be split asunder. Is this taking a lump of clay or a mud drum to be the Three Essentials?
Upon reaching these words, I cannot help but burst into laughter. The Master also has a verse which says: "The Three Essentials and the Three Points..."
Difficult to divide. When one attains the meaning, one forgets the words; the Way is easy to approach. A single phrase clearly encompasses the myriad phenomena.
On the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh. Another verse says: The primary source is the Dharma-realm, vast and boundless. The forested peaks, the myriad phenomena, and all things therein.
All are perfectly complete within the mirror. Second Yuan asked: "World-Honored One, when Ānanda was questioned, he answered according to the matter;
he responded according to the capacity of the vessel, whether square or round. Third Yuan stepped directly before the Ancient Sovereign.
Beyond the four propositions and the hundred negations, Lüshi asked Fenggan: "This is the verse of the Three Yuans. What is the essential meaning of the Three Yuans? Straightforwardly—
The instructions must be clearly determined; do not merely look toward the void and form false understandings, saying, "I have personally attended upon the Master and he has explained this for me.
Such empty fabrications and deceptive words will one day result in you being struck by an iron staff. He wrote in his rebuttal:

"The Three Essentials and Three Mysteries are nothing more than the words from Linji’s single occasion of ascending the hall. At that time, there were those who took them to be the fundamental tenets."
Therefore, Fenyang composed a verse as a warning, saying: "The Three Essentials and the Three Points are difficult to distinguish," and so forth.

I do not know upon what textual authority this [critic] relied to make such a claim. If the verse were itself the warning, then it would be improper to divide them and separately praise the Three Essentials.
To prohibit something oneself and yet violate it oneself—could it be that Fenyang was so ignorant and perverse as to reach such a state?
For the most part, when these critics encounter even a single or two phrases from the ancients that seem similar, they rely upon them as if they were Mount Tai;
yet when they encounter what they cannot understand, they attack it as if it were an enemy. Those things that seem similar are few, while those that they find inexplicable are many.

Thus, one cannot avoid the contradiction between what precedes and what follows. For instance, in the *Rendianrenmu* (The Eye and Mind of Human and Heaven), Master [Zhaozhou]’s "Eighteen Questions" states:
"Whenever a student employs clever phrases to cover things over, the master’s eye tests them all and beats them down. Why? It is simply because they recognize it for what it is.
The *Bishu* (Book of Eradication) cites this as evidence for "a single blow of the staff," yet it fails to realize that "recognizing it for what it is" is not [the point].
One who possesses a talisman tucked behind the elbow cannot do so. Furthermore, as for one Fenyang alone: when he recited the "Hymn to the Three Essentials," he was dismissed as a mad dog;
yet when he composed the "Eighteen Questions," he was relied upon as a support. How could the ancients have known how to position themselves?
If the "Hymn to the Three Essentials" were wrong, then Fenyang’s own realization was certainly mistaken, and his "Eighteen Questions" would likewise be insufficient.
Observe this! If the eighteen questions were correct, then Fengyang’s state of realization was fundamentally right, and Yuan’s verse would likewise be so.
Why then is there such confusion and instability, with one praising while the other scorns?
I have often remarked that, among the lifetime sayings of Fenyang Shanzhao, there is nothing worth taking up other than the "Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality" (Shi zhi tong zhen).

From this, one knows that even the "Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality" belongs to the path of intellectual understanding. How much more so when they are elaborated and expanded in such a manner—what end could there be to it?
It is just like entering the sea to count its sands; it fails to resolve the doubts of a beginner and instead merely leads them astray from the outset.
They enter into the ranks of those who rely on intellectual understanding, which offers no benefit to those who have resolved to train and investigate the Way.

For throughout their lives, the only things upon which they have relied for mastery are the "Three Essentials" and "Three Points"—mere incidental furnishings; they have not yet set foot upon the supreme step.

Now, observing their general and specific verses on the Three Essentials and Three Points, one sees that these too belong to the realm of seeking standards within words and searching for meaning beneath the surface of thought.
It would suffice to clarify the Three Essentials and Three Points; yet this has no connection with that.
Mochizuki Ryōnin relied upon them as a Mount Tai, dismissing Miyun’s Three Essentials and Three Points as merely the non-essential words from a single occasion of Linji’s formal discourse.

He debated back and forth to extol the Three Essentials and Three Points as the ultimate pinnacle of the matter. From this, one can clearly see his [Mochizuki’s] attitude toward the Three Essentials and Three Points.

This is essential. Yet, it has not even been glimpsed in a dream. As for the "Three Essentials" and the "Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality," how could one possibly be attached to them or engage in contention?
When Miguang reached the realization of the "Dense Clouds," he declared that since the Three Essentials have already been split asunder, there should henceforth be no further "Three Essentials."

This is indeed my clumsy speech. Yet, Mazu laughed at me for identifying the Three Essentials as the "mud ball" and the "earthen drum," thereby passing over the meaning of Fengyang’s "splitting them apart" with a vague generality.
He said it was like adding the eyes to a painted dragon, which only makes one more of a lacquer barrel.
Now, how could the mud ball and the earthen drum not be the Three Essentials and the Three Keys? Not only within the mud ball and the earthen drum, but they are inherently present therein.

Regarding the Three Origins and Three Essentials: if you can directly take responsibility for the "clay skull" and the "earthen drum," you will be perfectly able to split asunder the Three Origins and Three Essentials and dissolve the Ten Knowledges into the True. Thus, utterly naked and radiantly pure, you will reach the Precious Abode directly.

Perfectly penetrating and unimpeded, how could one who is willing to face the Three Essentials and Three Keys, where the Ten Wisdoms are identical with Reality, treat these as mere idle words or redundant speech, merely to perform circumambulations before the gate?
Furthermore, Magu Ren used Yangshan’s general verse on the Three Essentials not to negate the Three Essentials;
if the general verse were meant to negate them, would the individual verses not then constitute both self-prohibition and self-transgression? Yangshan was deluded.
How perverse! It does not come to this. Not knowing that this is the Dharma-gate of neither being nor non-being, how can one attempt to conjecture it through emotional views?

When Fenyang summarized the Three Principles in a single verse, he could not be said to have prohibited them; later, when they were divided into separate verses for the Three Principles, [the same applied].
Furthermore, how can it be said that he has committed an offense? Moreover, Fenyang clearly stated that "the Three Essentials and Three Mysteries are difficult to distinguish.
He then divided them into the First Essential, the Second Essential, and the Third Essential, composing a verse for each. I ask you: did he divide them or not?
For those who do not understand, to call this "confused and perverse" would be the height of confusion and perversity. How could Mazu have tolerated such a thing?
Furthermore, out of fear and apprehension, you dare not point your finger at him directly, yet you single-mindedly direct your criticism solely toward Mìyún.

As for Mìyún’s citation of Fényáng’s eighteen questions—wherein every one was "struck down"—as the basis for his "single blow," how could Mòrěn have recognized this as a fraud had he not possessed the talisman behind his elbow?
Since he did not recognize it as such, how could he possibly strike it down? It is sufficient.

He knew that [Zhaozhou] was taking this single staff and treating it as a substantial dharma; not only would he have no end to his receiving blows, but he would also have no share at all in receiving the staff.
As for what Fenyang meant by "recognizing it through penetration," how could it mean recognizing it within the realm of meaning, words, signs, or numbers?
If one were necessarily to recognize it through meaning, words, signs, and numbers, then even the dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—how could they possibly be grasped?
These eight questions encompass all that can be asked. Even with Ānanda’s vast learning, how could he have known them all?
If there were not a single thing he did not remember, and not a single thing he did not understand, then his eight consciousnesses would be filled to overflowing with such a mass of complications;
his emotional views would blaze forth, and with whom could one possibly speak? If there were something apart from mental discourse and conceptual signs...
This refers to the principle that one who has already mastered the eighteen questions has completely resolved their essential meaning.
Once this has been mastered, the "talisman behind the elbow" is already possessed; what other talisman could one seek to bind to the elbow?
A single blow is both punishment and reward, both construction and destruction; fundamentally, it possesses no substantial meaning, nor does it possess any substantial dharma. How can one—
This is a groundless fabrication. Is it like seeing flowers by pressing one's eyes?

Furthermore, regarding the claim that Miyun was critiquing Fenyang’s position—if the "Three Yuan" verses were incorrect, then Fenyang’s own realization would certainly be wrong, and his "Eighteen Questions" would likewise be unworthy of regard.
If it were as the eighteen questions suggest, then Master Fenyang’s realization would already be correct, and the "Verses on the Three Essentials" would likewise be so;
why then is there such confusion and inconsistency, with one praising him while another reviling him?

Examining Mìyún’s relationship to Fenyang, it is clear that he had not yet fully opened the single eye of the forehead, nor did he distinguish clearly between the monastic and the lay; thus, his profound reverence for Fenyang was carried to an extreme.
How could he ever have dared to point out and condemn [his teacher]? Furthermore, Mageren was not unaware that Miyun had never actually condemned Fenyang;

his specific intent was merely to fabricate a false accusation against Miyun. Thus, the matter was made out of thin air, so that if anyone in future generations were to criticize his own ancestor Miyun for having reviled Fenyang, they would say:
"Miyun’s treatment of his own ancestor Fenyang was likewise like this."
This is so. It is not merely that those who doubt Míyún are made to believe in him; it is also that those who already believe in Míyún are made not to doubt him.
His methods are indeed clever. Yet, his dogmatic and erroneous arguments are truly sufficient to mislead students; they must be examined and distinguished.
Now, as for this Perfect Teaching (Yuánzōng), its principle of "neither being nor non-being" is not like the reckless ravings of the heterodox paths.

Such a view allows one to act with unrestrained freedom, claiming there is neither right nor wrong. This is because when analyzed through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), everything is found to have no place of abiding and no point of attachment;
thus, it transcends all dualistic relativity. Once one transcends relativity, one leaves behind the four propositions;

once one leaves behind the four propositions, one cuts off the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*). If one can realize this, then the seventeen hundred public cases (*gong’an*) will not be entirely [mere words].

There is nothing that is not entirely so; there is nothing that is entirely so or entirely not so; there is nothing that is neither not-so nor so. This holds true for whichever single principle one may bring forth.
Only then can one distinguish between heaven and earth within the absence of gradations, and discern the Sheng and Zhi rivers amidst the absence of discrimination.
Otherwise, there will inevitably be right and wrong; one will become distracted and lose one's mind, unable even to save oneself. How then can such a person act for others?
Now, if this is the case regarding even a single koan, how could it be otherwise when considering the entire life’s record of a single person?

If the *Three Verses on the Essence* were correct, then the *Eighteen Questions* would necessarily be incorrect; if the *Eighteen Questions* were incorrect, then the *Three Verses on the Essence* would necessarily not be correct.
It is so. From the perspective of its being so, the *Threefold Verse on the Essentials* is so, and the *Eighteen Questions* are also so.
From the perspective of its not being so, the *Threefold Verse on the Essentials* is not so, and the *Eighteen Questions* are also not so.

From the perspective of its having both "so" and "not so," the *Threefold Verse on the Essentials* has both "so" and "not so," and the *Eighteen Questions* also have both "so" and "not so. From its...
I speak of neither wrong nor right. The *Threefold Praise* (Sanyuan song) is likewise neither wrong nor right; the *Eighteen Questions* (Shiba wen) is also neither wrong nor right.
One might rely on the *Eighteen Questions* to refute the *Threefold Praise*, or rely on the *Threefold Praise* to refute the *Eighteen Questions*.
Or one might rely on the *Threefold Praise* to affirm the *Eighteen Questions*, or rely on the *Eighteen Questions* [to affirm the Threefold Praise].

This may be called the "Three Essentials" verse. If you can realize it here, then though there is no fixed point for shifting or changing, the distinction between the monastic and the lay will become clear.

If you do not realize it here, then the very clarity of the distinction between the monastic and the lay is precisely the dualistic clinging to person and dharma—it is the view of one who endures the demonic.
Let alone whether you have fully understood where the eighteen questions of the Three Essentials verse of Fenyang fall; even if you were to...
Though one may attain clarity through discernment, it remains that the karmic consciousness is vast and indistinct, with no fundamental basis upon which to rely.
Mo Ren said: "Guan Ying, Lord Teng, Fan Kui, and others rose from the region of Feng and Pei under Emperor Gao of Han.

They besieged cities and plundered lands, advancing gradually according to their merit until the House of Han possessed the empire; yet the rank of these several men did not exceed that of enfeoffed marquis. To this point...
If one were like Han Xin, then upon a single meeting, he was granted the authority of a supreme general; this is the case where rank precedes merit.
As for those who occupy a position of high status yet fail to establish any meritorious achievements, there are few who do not meet with extermination.

Even if meritorious achievements are established, if one becomes slightly self-conceited and boastful, there are likewise few who do not meet with extermination. The *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* says: "The principle must be sudden..."

"Awakening is realized through the gradual cultivation of practice. Changsha said: "If one's merit has not yet equaled that of the various sages, then the three vehicles and ten stages are comparable to the likes of Guan Ying and Lord Teng.
If awakening surpasses merit, it is like a great-minded ordinary person who transcends all categories and precedents—comparable to Han Xin.
If merit surpasses awakening, it is the 'merit of no-merit. Observing this, I see the realization and conduct of Fenyang."
Is this not precisely the direct transmission to the supreme general, one who does not boast of merit or claim victory?
As for the Tathāgata, there is nowhere from which he comes, nor anywhere to which he goes. He departs to respond to the capacities of sentient beings yet does not go;

he constantly returns to quiescent extinction yet does not come. Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. Upon entering this Perfect Teaching, it is said: "In a single leap, one enters directly into Thusness."
Coming to this ground, as the universal retention (*dhāraṇī*) of all phenomena, he bears the title of Dharma King;
acting as the eyes for humans and devas, he is thus called a Teacher. Yet these names and characteristics are ultimately empty space; though praise may be abundant, empty space does not receive it.
How can this compare to the worldly system of ranks and emoluments, which distinguishes between dukes, marquises, counts, viscounts, and barons, and establishes governance?

In governing the state, there are the positions of sovereign, minister, people, and things. Yet Māra and his followers take refuge within the gates of the Buddhist school, while their minds gallop through the ocean of worldly dust.
Beneath their three-strip kashaya robes, they wrap themselves in this illusory body that seeks wealth and honor but never attains it;

atop the hundred-foot pole, they indulge in the foolish dream of leaving a name for a thousand ages. Furthermore, having perused the classics and briefly observed the records of past and present, I have noted these matters in history.
The idle remarks of this gentleman are not worthy of admiration. He suspects that the mental conduct of the ancient sages was merely worldly toil;
he thus equates the ten stages of a Bodhisattva with the likes of Jiang Kang and Guan Ying, and compares the true cause of the Tathāgata to the general Huaiyin.
To treat it like a belt or a whetstone, and transform it into a "red script" for inheriting the ancestral seal; or to take it as a precious mirror for the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*,
yet remain neither self-effacing nor conceited— this is nothing more than a source of ridicule, not even enough to be called a heterodox path or a demonic influence.
Moshi said, "When jade is in the mountains, it is exquisite; when pearls are in the river, they are lovely.
How could it be otherwise for the Way within a person? I have observed Master Hui; he has deeply attained the Way of Ciming and served him with great diligence for a very long time.

Yet, upon his emergence into the world, his fellow practitioners did not recognize his practical cultivation or his realization of the truth. He concealed himself so profoundly and remained so deeply obscure that he is now worlds apart from those of today."

Master Fushan Yuan, the Abbot, said to the Head Seat: "The means by which one governs the mind must seek wondrous awakening. When there is awakening, the spirit is harmonious and the breath is tranquil;
the countenance becomes reverent and the expression dignified. Delusive thoughts and emotional anxieties all melt away into the true mind.

By governing the mind in this way, the mind naturally becomes numinous and wondrous. Only then can one guide others; who would not follow such transformation? Master Yuan was the legitimate grandson of Shoushan.
Such is what you have shown. Yet those who are called "enlightened" in recent times behave like butchers or executioners;
their speech and actions are worse than those of birds and beasts, yet the world honors them, assuming they must possess some realization.
I wish that those with good intentions who protect the Dharma, but whose insight into the Way is not yet clear, might use the words of Master Huiyuan to discern this.
This refers to those so-called "enlightened ones" of recent times who appear like butchers or executioners;

their speech and actions are worse than those of birds and beasts, yet the world venerates them, believing they have attained enlightenment. I do not know what these few words are intended to indicate:

are they referring to figures such as Guangtong among one's fellow practitioners, or are they specifically pointing to the patriarch Miyun? In any case, it is nothing more than an attempt to [justify oneself].
At that time, you gentlemen should not merely respect others out of social formality, but rather respect this man himself.
As for his speech and demeanor, does he not embody what Yangqi called "the spirit is harmonious and the breath is still, with a reverent countenance and dignified appearance"?

Has he not dissolved all delusive thoughts and emotional anxieties into the realization of true mind? Yet he floats in a pool of dregs while admonishing others against drinking; he wields a knife in a butcher’s stall [while preaching non-violence].
Yet they urge others not to kill living beings, causing people to feel revulsion and ridicule them. How much more so regarding realization and practice, which are like water and rice:
when cooked into a meal, they cannot be separated, nor can they be joined back together once formed. For those who have not yet realized, [the two are likewise inseparable].
Even if one practices through successive kalpas, as long as there is the notion of "self" and "what belongs to self," it merely increases the fruits of human and celestial merit.

It is like having water but no rice: the meal cannot be prepared. Furthermore, if one has attained realization but practice has not yet reached its fullness, its power is insufficient and its merit is not equal to that of the sages.
This is like having too much water and too little rice: the meal is unfit for consumption. Indeed, that which is called "cultivation" (xiūxíng) is...
From this point on, the six perfections and myriad practices are merely peripheral matters—what are called "Buddha-works within a dream" or "adornments within a mirror.

They are nothing but dreams and mirrors; they are both illusion and reality. Only after one no longer regards dreams and mirrors as illusory phenomena can one fulfill the ocean of Samantabhadra’s vows and perceive dreams and mirrors as identical. As for when a Master acts for the sake of others, he applies the hammer with great force.

As long as one establishes oneself in self-realization, there is no need to concern oneself with whether these words of mine are right or wrong, or whether this conduct of mine is like that of a butcher or an executioner.
Since ancient times, has there ever been a true master who focused solely on language and outward appearance? As the ancients said:
"Whether it be right or wrong, people do not recognize it; how could one take such [superficial] means—which are intended to untie the knots and remove the bonds for others—to teach people?"
To be stuck in attachment to comparison is like the story of Yunmen, who knocked on Muzhou’s door three times;
each time Muzhou opened the door, he immediately closed it, leaving Yunmen with a broken leg. Was this not like a butcher or an executioner?
When Linji struck Huangbo three times in the ribs at Dayu, and again slapped his teacher twice, he even went so far as to strike the ground with his hoe while addressing his master.
He said: "In other regions they practice cremation, but here we bury people alive. Is this not the work of a butcher or an executioner?
Take, for example, when a nun asked Zhaozhou, 'What is the meaning of the profound mystery? and Zhaozhou pinched her with his hand;
or how Juzhi, because a boy raised his finger, took up a blade and cut off that finger. Instances such as these are beyond counting. How can one endure such demonic acts?"

In such places, will you not also give rise to slanderous criticism? If you dare not give rise to slanderous criticism, how can you falsely distinguish between black and white to deceive the common people?
Take, for example, what Guishan said: "I shall go down the mountain to become a water buffalo.
On one side he wrote "Guishan Monk," and on the other side he wrote "Water Buffalo. He said that he was both a Guishan monk and a water buffalo.

The Way is a water buffalo; it is also a monk of Mount Gui. One who does not know the deeds of Māra and Ren, yet claims to be a well-intentioned protector of the Dharma—how should such a person distinguish between those to whom one should pay respect and those to whom one should not?

Would they dare to regard the Master of Mount Gui as a mere beast? By citing the ritual laws of the Confucian school to misrepresent the karmic conditions of the Chan school, they naturally [reveal their own ignorance].

A square base with a round lid—this is the intent of the Mara-like patience. It was simply because Mìyún struck him as soon as he asked a question that [Zhaozhou] immediately labeled him a butcher or an executioner, and consequently reviled him as a beast.

This was done to bewitch those among the scholar-officials who lack discernment, and to entice the monastics of the four quarters so that they all would delight in such sycophancy. Such mental conduct, however, is...
These are the very ones designated within the Confucian school as being worse than birds and beasts.

Yangqi’s words of warning to the Head Seat were intended as a prescription specifically tailored to a particular ailment; yet, Magu Renruo arbitrarily added his own commentary, thereby causing no small amount of stagnation and confusion.
Mogarěn said: "In the past, after Miaoxi had attained great enlightenment, he encountered several Zen practitioners who harbored doubts.
He took their questions to Zhaojue, who said: 'My Zen is like the great ocean; you must empty yourself like that great ocean before you can receive it.
If you try to hold even a little in a bowl, it is because your capacity is such as that. What can I do? Alas! Today..."
As for those who have filled their alms bowls with what they obtained—if it were truly seawater—it would still be something conspicuous and worth observing even in this degenerate age.

Yet, what they have filled their bowls with are entirely filthy and unfit things; they wish to cast aside the Teacher’s Dharma, acting with such madness, transgression, and perversity that they cannot be turned back.
Re-reading the words of Baiyun three times, I shed tears from my eyes and nose.
"You must bring the great ocean here; you must empty the great ocean away. If you are deluded, you will die of thirst within the heart of the ocean.

If you awaken, it is inexhaustible and boundless. For this Great Perfect Enlightenment Ocean is neither shared nor divided; it neither goes out nor comes in. It cannot be known by wisdom, nor can it be cognized by consciousness.
It is without distinctions of large or small, defilement or purity. Thus have the ancient virtuous ones of old [declared].

It is traditionally said: "Not otherwise, it is thus; I am also thus. If this is so, then a single drop of water lifted by the tip of a needle is no different from the moist nature of the great ocean.

Were it not so, even the River God (Hebo) would gaze out at the vast sea and sigh that he is being laughed at by those of great capacity—how much more so for one who takes up water with a bowl? Thus says Māra-ṛṣi: "Now..."
As for those who daily fill their alms bowls with what they have obtained—if it were truly seawater—it would still be something remarkable and worthy of observation in this degenerate age.

Yet, what they place therein are all filthy and loathsome things; they wish to cast aside the teachings of their masters, acting with such madness, perversity, and obstinacy that they cannot be opened to reason.
Re-reading the words of Baiyun three times, I shed tears from my eyes, not knowing what to do with the alms bowl.
"It is filled, yet it is not seawater; and this very bowl is also within the sea—how could it have been filled?
From the heavens above to the earth below, from antiquity to the present, [the mind] is like a fish in water, its entire body being water.
If it were stranded on sand or mud and one were to gulp up a spoonful of water, the fish would cease to be a fish; it would become anxious and preoccupied, calculating what the bowl has taken."
To say "this is seawater" or "this is not seawater," or that it is "impure" or "pure," is entirely because he has not yet seen the great ocean.
If one truly reaches the great ocean, such thoughts of right and wrong, or impurity and purity, will naturally not arise.

One will naturally know that when it is poured into a bowl, it becomes the bowl and is no longer the great ocean; the principle of something distinct and observable is completely severed. Furthermore, since...
Once it enters the bowl, it becomes stagnant water. Scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind, covered in dust and fouled by soil, it immediately becomes defiled and unfit for use.
Although it was originally divided from the hands of the Dragon King, it has ultimately turned its back on the true ocean water.
If one wishes to obtain the true ocean water, one must go directly to the sea oneself; there is no teacher’s dharma to be grasped. If there were a teacher’s dharma, [it would not be the true ocean].
This is precisely the stagnant water within the alms bowl, passed down from the blind to the blind, believed and guarded as such. For a lifetime, there has been no discernment of the ocean;

the malady of "endurance of Mara" lies precisely in one’s own confidence that the true seawater exists within the alms bowl, while doubting that the water in Mìyún’s alms bowl is filthy and unfit for use.
One does not realize that Mìyún’s alms bowl has long since been smashed to pieces. Although...

Not having reached the other shore, there has never been a time when one was not personally within the sea. It would be better to die while practicing the patience of a Māra, guarding a single bowl of poisoned milk, than to become a man who dies of thirst in the midst of the ocean.
Mokuren said: "I have already presented a verse that struck the essential point, and Baizhang has already granted his approval. Yet you have once again produced this profuse sweat of words;
people today cannot help but harbor doubts. How difficult it is! Zen must be realized, and it must be realized through a great awakening."
One must not fail to understand the Great Dharma. What is called the "Great Dharma" does not consist merely of limited conjecture regarding names and characteristics.
Guifeng Zongmi said: "Chan is a term from India; its full form is dhyāna, which is translated as 'cultivation through contemplation. It is also...
"Cloud," [it is said,] "is a general designation for both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*").

Nowadays, there are those who refer to true nature alone as *chán* (dhyāna), failing to distinguish between the phonetic transcriptions of the Chinese and Indian languages. However, it is not that there is a separate essence of *chán* apart from true nature;

rather, when sentient beings are deluded regarding true nature and unite with sensory dust (*rajas*), they are termed "distracted. When they turn their backs on sensory dust and unite with true nature, it is termed "meditative concentration" (*dhyāna-samādhi*). If one discusses the fundamental source directly..."
The nature is neither true nor false; it neither opposes nor accords, neither fixed nor distracted. Who would speak of "dhyāna" here? The innate, celestial nature is neither defiled nor pure;
there is no distinction between ordinary beings and sages. Dhyāna, however, has its degrees of shallowness and depth, with distinct stages and levels.
That which is practiced while harboring heterodox views, with longing for the higher realms and aversion toward the lower, is the meditation of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

That which is practiced with the correct cause of faith in the fruit, likewise through longing and aversion, is the meditation of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). That which is practiced by awakening to the principle of the pervasive truth of self-emptiness is...
That which is practiced by awakening to what is revealed by the emptiness of both self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*) is the meditation of the Hīnayāna.

If one suddenly awakens to the fact that one’s own mind is originally pure, fundamentally free from afflictions, and that the nature of untainted wisdom is inherently complete—realizing that this mind is itself the Buddha and ultimately no different from it—and practices in reliance upon this, this is the meditation of the Mahāyāna; it is also called the Tathāgata-meditation.

Pure meditation is also called the Samādhi of Single Practice and the Samādhi of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This is the root of all samādhis. If one can practice it moment by moment, one will naturally and gradually attain hundreds of thousands of samādhis. That which has been transmitted from master to disciple within the lineage of Bodhidharma is this very meditation. As for the interpretations of various schools prior to Bodhidharma’s arrival: [The text continues with a critique of these earlier views. ...and so forth. All such explanations are merely intellectual understandings; they do not constitute the true essence of meditation. Why? Because they are based on conceptualization and discrimination. If one relies on such views, one will never be able to enter the gate of the Tathāgata’s true dharma. Therefore, you should abandon all such views and simply maintain the mind in its original state, without seeking anything else. This is what is meant by "the mind-ground.
