All of these are the four dhyānas and eight samādhis practiced by eminent monks of old, all of whom attained their respective spiritual powers.

Although the teachings of Nanyue and Tiantai—based on the principle of the three truths and the practice of the three types of cessation and three types of contemplation—are most perfect and subtle in their doctrinal meaning, the sequence of their entry points and gateways is likewise nothing other than the characteristics of the various meditative practices mentioned above. It is only that which was transmitted by Bodhidharma [which differs].
It is suddenly identical to the Buddha-body and stands far apart from all other approaches; therefore, those who practice this school find its essential meaning difficult to grasp.
To attain it is to become a sage and swiftly realize Bodhi; to lose it is to fall into error and quickly enter the mire of suffering.

The Patriarchs, to transform ignorance and prevent such loss, transmitted it one-to-one for a time. Later generations now have something to rely upon, so let a thousand lamps shine with a thousand lights. Guifeng examined and rectified [the transmission].

Such are the name and meaning of *dhyāna*. Now, regarding what the Māra-tolerance [treatise] discusses—that one must awaken to *dhyāna*, that one must have a great awakening, and that one must know the Great Dharma—is this the *dhyāna* of the four *dhyānas* and eight *samādhis*, and the three *śamathas* and three *vipaśyanās*?
Or is it the *dhyāna* of the Dharma that came from the West, which does not rely on words and letters, directly points to the human mind, and realizes Buddhahood by seeing one's nature?
...of Chan? As for what is called "the Chan transmitted by Bodhidharma," did not Guifeng say: "If one attains it, one becomes a sage and swiftly realizes bodhi;
how could there be stages such as 'small enlightenment' and 'great enlightenment'? Furthermore, he stated that after great enlightenment, one must still clarify the Great Dharma.
Moreover, the Great Meaning of the West—pointing directly to the human mind—is precisely what Guifeng [upheld].
It is said: "Neither true nor false, neither opposed nor conjoined, neither fixed nor distracted—in this state, even 'meditation' (dhyāna) cannot be apprehended.
How much less could there be a separate 'Great Dharma' to be clarified that serves as a condition or a counterpart to the primordially self-existent, natural, and celestial Buddha?
Thus, that which is called the 'Great Dharma' is certainly not the Three Stills and Three Contemplations of Tiantai."
The teaching of Nanyue is precisely what Guifeng described as the "dhyāna of non-Buddhists who harbor heterodox views, delighting in higher realms while loathing the lower.
How could there be any doubt about this? Furthermore, you claim that what is called the "Great Dharma" is not merely a matter of limited speculation regarding names and characteristics.
Yet, is the Great Dharma not itself a name? That which you have fabricated—the single circle (○) representing the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas—is it not likewise a conceptual construct?

"Characteristics! Are not the various great dharmas themselves characteristics? Yet, when one sees the ancient worthies denouncing and rejecting names and characteristics, one must learn that this is not merely a matter of calculating and speculating about names and characteristics.
To do so is truly like a man who covers his ears while stealing a bell."
Mowen said: "When the Fifth Patriarch remarked that his predecessor’s words were clumsy, he did not thereby show disrespect to his honored teacher.
When Dahui wished to destroy the woodblocks for the *Biyán jí*, he did not thereby seek to appear superior or assert himself.

When Huangbo and Shishuang refused to acknowledge the various venerable masters under Mazu, they did not thereby engage in personal egoism or disputes over right and wrong. One who understands this is a true gentleman of the Way."
Now, among the monastics and laypeople within the realm, even those who are most virtuous and wise say:

"While it is true that the Three Peaks' dispute over the school's tenets was justified, their failure to observe proper titles and distinctions is unacceptable. Alas! This suggests that the Way is held in lower esteem than mere formal titles.
Furthermore, the two elders were not significantly different in age or virtue; they merely humbled themselves and yielded to one another out of respect for the Way of Linji. If indeed...

If one abandons the Way, from what source could its constituent parts possibly arise? Alas! That such a person, though supremely intelligent and virtuous, should make such a claim is simply because they have not yet understood the Way.
The "Māra-tolerance" (魔忍) refers to those among the clergy and laity within the realm who, though most virtuous and discerning, still say:

"While the dispute over the 'Three Peaks' regarding the core tenets is indeed correct, the matter of nomenclature and status cannot be permitted. Now, since Bodhidharma came from the West, he transmitted the direct pointing;

the milk-dripping stream of Caoxi has flowed and spread throughout China. Although students fill carriages and measure out bushels, those who truly attain it are as rare as phoenix feathers and qilin horns. Yet this—
The single lamp of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) has shone through both past and present, with no lack of worthy successors throughout the ages.

Yet the father and son Mazu and Baizhang, by means of their "double-headed" and "single-knotted" [teachings], and the intermingling of the four dharmas, created various strange names and anomalous appearances that misled and confused practitioners.
Thus, they cast filth upon a field that is a single expanse of pure, vast emptiness—a ground as radiant and bright as the sun and moon—arbitrarily styling themselves "Linji."
Regarding the Essential Teaching: Since the poison of heterodoxy has already entered one's own heart, it causes others to repeatedly sink head over heels into the pit of evil waters.

For this reason, the late master Miyun feared that future generations would successively deceive one another by falsely claiming their own doctrines to be the Essential Teaching, failing to awaken on their own, thereby destroying the Buddhas and Patriarchs and extinguishing the life-force of human wisdom, leaving behind inexhaustible harm as the Dharma-torch was about to grow dim. Zen...

As the river was about to run dry, he therefore composed the *Qibai* (Seven Expositions) to open up the treasury of Māra, and the *Baiwangjiu* (Exposition on Dispelling Delusions and Saving) to open up the patience of Māra.

Within these, the treasuries and patiences turned their weapons against one another, bitterly denouncing each other like dense clouds. At that time, those lacking the eye of wisdom consequently gave rise to a proliferation of disputes.
Although Mimi Yun may still have points that have not yet been fully realized, he essentially possesses correct knowledge and correct view.
As for the crime of Mi and Ren, father and son, in falsely establishing their own school of thought, this is an iron-clad case for all eternity.

If the monastics and laypeople within the realm are truly wise and discerning, how could they fail to recognize the various actions of these men as being substantial dharmas—actions that are ultimately false and utterly erroneous?
In principle, if those who still take what was contested between the father and son as being correct are all considered blind men,
then can one who does not see the sun and moon as they adorn the sky be called supremely wise and enlightened? Furthermore,

since those whom you call supremely wise and enlightened all consider the contest over the fundamental tenet to be correct, yet you also claim that such persons have not yet realized the Way— is this not a contradiction?
If the Way lies outside of the fundamental tenets, does it follow that the fundamental tenets lie outside of the Way? What, then, are the fundamental tenets he espouses?
And what, indeed, is the Way he advocates? It is nothing more than an attempt to fabricate a false image of Mimiyun and to incite delusion among the literati of his time.
Although those literati were all as headstrong as the "Eighth-Son Man" (Meng Balang Han), they failed to discern who was right and who was wrong.
This is not so. Yet, disciples cannot extinguish their masters, nor can descendants extinguish their fathers and ancestors; this is understood by all, so how could there be no discussion?
Thus, they formulate this doctrine to exonerate themselves. First, they honor it with the reputation of being most virtuous and wise;
then, they delude others with doctrines that do not yet understand the Way, speaking of it themselves without realizing it.
This is contradictory. If so, what kind of mental activity constitutes "Māra-patience"?

Although they are father and son within the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), having inherited the Dharma-milk from one another, they nonetheless share the conventional designations of the worldly realm.

Yet, if Mimiyun were to falsely establish his own school while Zangren offered admonitions and remonstrances, it could be compared to a father having a contentious son. Now, these [monks] take the Buddha’s... transmitted from the masters above.
Such is the general purport of the Dharma: it has been stained and extinguished in this manner.

When dark clouds arise, one attempts to rectify them, yet instead willfully slanders and defames them, even seeking to eradicate its very name and status. Such a person is a traitor to the family; truly, not even one in ten thousand could be tolerated.
Mofen said: "One must first penetrate the Dharma and subsequently forget the Dharma; this is true even for worldly arts and crafts, let alone the unsurpassed path of Awakening.
Those who nowadays dismiss the fundamental tenets are like those who burn their boat before they have crossed the river. Those who are mired in names and forms [are likewise lost]."
If one forgets the crossing yet clings to the raft, both are errors.
One must penetrate the Dharma and subsequently forget the Dharma; this is true even for worldly arts and crafts, let alone the unsurpassed path of awakening.
By these words, it can be understood that even the patience of Māra has not yet realized that the Way and worldly arts cannot be spoken of as being on the same level. Indeed.
In the arts and crafts, one comes to know through knowing, acquires through learning, refines through practice, and attains mastery through proficiency.

Whether great or small, there must be rules and standards. Once one has attained spiritual clarity within these rules and standards, yet undergoes transformation beyond them, then one reaches the state where the feet are forgotten because the shoes fit perfectly, and the waist is forgotten because the girdle fits perfectly. This is what is meant by...
It is one who penetrates the Dharma and subsequently forgets the Dharma. As for the path of unsurpassed enlightenment, it cannot be known through cognition, nor can it be attained through study.
It is not something that can be perfected through practice, nor can its spiritual power be mastered through habituation.

Not lacking a single dharma, not exceeding a single dharma, not grasping a single dharma, and not abandoning a single dharma—even if one were to raise up a single dharma from among the dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there would be none.
The supreme path of awakening cannot be attained; what dharma, then, could be penetrated?
To raise even one [point] is not to say that the supreme path of awakening cannot be attained; what dharma, then, could be forgotten? Māra-ṛṣi perused external classics;
having heard the discourse of Zhuang Zhou, he merely gathered up the remnants of his spittle. Zhuang Zhou’s parable says: "Zhongni traveled to Chu."

He came out from the forest and saw a hunchback catching cicadas with a pole, as easily as if he were plucking them up. Zhongni asked, "Are you skilled, or do you have a way? He replied, "I have a way.
For five or six months, I stack two pellets on the end of my pole without letting them fall; then my misses are but a fraction of an ounce.
When I can stack three without letting them fall, my misses are one-tenth. When I can stack five without letting them fall, it is as easy as plucking them up."
"Furthermore, in my posture I am like a fixed stump; in my holding of the arm I am like a branch of withered wood.

Though the heavens and earth are vast and the myriad things are numerous, I perceive nothing but the wings of the cicada. I do not turn back nor lean to one side; I would not exchange the myriad things for the wings of the cicada.
What could possibly prevent me from succeeding? Confucius looked back and said to his disciples, "This is the power of focused intent."

He made no distinction between them; he was one who questioned the divine—this is what is meant by the "hunchbacked old man. Now, to balance five pellets on a stick without dropping them is a profound method.
At such a time, he forgets his own person within and forgets all things without, knowing only the pellets. He does not exchange the pellets for all things;
only then can he transfer this skill to catch cicadas with a pole, as if plucking them from the ground. Truly, he has forgotten.
Furthermore, Mowen’s arbitrary interpretation of the Five Houses’ essential tenets is like stacking pellets on a pole.

When his skill reaches maturity and he realizes the path of supreme enlightenment, it is still like stacking pellets until they are firm, then catching cicadas as if picking them up with one's fingers. This is an extreme error.
For when the will is undivided, one attains a state that borders on the divine; how could this be used to illustrate the supramundane Dharma? Within the royal treasury, there is [the true jewel].
There is no such knife. Since there is the will to employ it, and furthermore the object upon which that will is employed, this is the shadow-work of the discerning consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Since there is the skill of the active spirit, and furthermore the capacity of that spiritual skill, this is the artificial mechanism of karmic power.
By means of the shadow-work of the discerning consciousness, one constructs the artificial mechanism of karmic power. Through these...
"This is a raft or a boat for crossing the ocean of pure awakening; it is like mounting a wheel of fire to enter a house of fire.
One is still unable to reach the shore, let alone inquire about the other bank. At this point, Heyang ascended the hall, raised his whisk, and said:
Look! It is simply this. In Linji, illumination and function proceed together; in Yunmen, principle and phenomenon are both complete;
in Caodong, the partial and the correct harmonize and penetrate; in Guishan, the hidden mechanism is perfectly integrated; and in Fayan, how could it be limited to the mind?
Nevertheless, while the various establishments and pedagogical devices of these five houses are not lacking, even if one were to discern them...

To attain a state of boldness and clarity is still merely an affair on the periphery of light and shadow. If one wishes to resist and overcome birth and death, there is a world of difference between the two.
When a student contemplates the words of Master Heshan Fang, they are like the statement by Māra that the fundamental tenets are negated;
they are like the words of one who has not yet crossed over but burns his boat, or one who is mired in names and forms and clings to the raft after having forgotten how to cross.

One may thus be free from delusion. Even if one is bold and clear in the arrangements of the gate and courtyard, and has penetrated the Dharma while forgetting the Dharma, what connection does this have to the Unsurpassed Path of Enlightenment?
This is not like boarding a raft to cross the sea; it is merely like ascending to heaven by means of a staircase. Someone might say:
"The five houses and lineages change their countenances to receive people; the ancient worthies acted thus to liberate others."

To strip away attachments and sever bonds through the skillful means of compassion—can this not be called ascending to heaven by way of a staircase? One might ask: "Is there no error in this? I reply: There is no error.
The empty space before one's face is itself the Great Heaven; there is nowhere that is not Heaven. For one who knows Heaven, it requires not even a single step.
Yet among those within Heaven, there are those who do not know Heaven and wish to ascend by treading upon a ladder; though they may labor for hundreds of years, they shall never reach it.
One may climb up a hundred fathoms, yet that azure-green color can ultimately never be grasped by touch.
Therefore, for the enlightened, whichever of the five houses of Chan they invoke, it is all the unsurpassed path of awakening.

If one is a follower of Māra, then even if they understand the five houses with great clarity and distinction, it is like climbing a ladder of a hundred fathoms; they will ultimately never be able to grasp that azure-green sky.
As for the matter of form (rūpa), it is because they do not know that the body resides within the heavens that they falsely imagine a ladder can be used to ascend to them.
Since there is certainly no ladder for ascending to heaven in this world, how could there possibly be a dharma for realizing the Way?
Mogarun said: "The late Master Sanfeng sought to find a successor among the ancients;
whenever he saw that a student’s character and capacity were not upright, he would immediately dismiss them, hoping they would wash their hearts and cleanse their stomachs.

Yet, time and again, these students became resentful, even going so far as to fabricate various similar phrases and falsely claim them to have been transmitted by Sanfeng. That people can lose their hearts to such an extent is truly lamentable."
Furthermore, it is known to all under heaven that Sanfeng regarded those who destroy the Dharma as his enemies, and those who destroy the Dharma likewise regarded Sanfeng as their enemy.
Even if there were words and phrases transmitted by you, would he have been willing to expel you merely to provide resources for his adversaries?

This is something that anyone with even a slight understanding of the nature of affairs would not do. Now, words and phrases exist to carry the Way; yet the Way itself certainly does not reside within words and phrases.
If the Way were contained within words and phrases, then those who obtain such words and phrases would certainly have obtained the Way of Sanfeng.
Yet Sanfeng sought disciples with the intensity of one’s hunger and thirst; how could he have been willing to perform such an unfeeling act as to expel you, his true son who had attained the Way?

I observe that when Foguo was about to attain enlightenment, there were instances where the Patriarchs did not grant their approval despite his having exhausted all his skillful means; how much less would they approve of mere rote memorization and retention!

Regarding these words and phrases, you falsely claim to have attained the Way; it was indeed appropriate that they be expunged. Yet, you still fail to recognize your transgression, thereby undermining the teachings and violating their principles.
To cause others to extol Sanfeng while simultaneously bringing such mutual disgrace upon yourselves—is this not exceedingly grave?
Does space have an enemy? It does not. One may push it or seize it, yet space remains unaware.
Does the great earth have an enemy? It does not. One may tread upon it or trample it, yet the great earth remains unaware.
It is not that space is unaware; rather, those who push it or seize it are themselves space. Furthermore, within this very space, there is no duality of space.
Space. Know that it resides on the side of space that is capable of displacing or grasping, not on the side of space that is displaced or grasped.
The great earth is likewise. Those who tread upon it and walk across it are themselves the great earth; moreover, this very great earth is non-dual with the great earth.
Know that it resides on the side of the great earth that is capable of treading and walking, not on the side that is trodden or walked upon.
It treads upon the very edge of the great earth. Its substance is its own substance; its knowing is its own knowing.

When it does not stand in opposition to the myriad things, it harbors no enmity toward even a single thing. When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, empty space and the great earth both vanish and perish.
Pure and naked, bare and clear, there is nothing to grasp. Vertically, it exhausts the three periods of time; horizontally, it spans the ten directions. How [could it be otherwise]?
With cessation, what arises? What is loathed and what is loved? What is grasped and what is discarded? What is right and what is wrong? What is that and what is this?

What is turned away from and what is headed toward? Sharing the same root as heaven and earth, sharing the same substance as the myriad things, one does not yet perceive a "self"—how then can there be another person?
One does not yet perceive another person—how then can there be an enemy? In the *Book of Rites*, Zizhang asked Confucius:
"How should one dwell when harboring a grievance against one's parents? How should one dwell when harboring a grievance against one's brothers?
How should one dwell when harboring a grievance against one's paternal uncles? Confucius answered each of these questions one by one;

yet we do not hear that Zizhang asked how one should dwell when harboring a grievance against oneself, nor do we hear Confucius speak of how one should dwell when harboring a grievance against oneself.
Why is this? One can know that the learning of the Confucianists is certainly not antagonistic. To be "antagonistic" (chóu) means to be a match or an adversary;
thus, a resentful union is called an "antagonist," while an auspicious union is also called a "good antagonist. The Perfect Man has no self, yet there is nowhere he does not manifest his self.
Since he manifests his self everywhere, he transcends all relativity. Having transcended all relativity, what is there to be antagonistic toward? Thus, through the Confucian...
Even when discussing worldly laws with those of the same gate, one remains without enmity; how much more so regarding the supramundane Dharma?
I have heard of those who harbor enmity toward others, but I have never heard of anyone harboring enmity toward themselves.

Since there is nothing that does not belong to oneself, yet one still harbors the enmity of jealousy—is this not indeed harboring enmity toward oneself? For one who has nothing that does not belong to oneself, it is simply impossible to possess such [jealousy].

One’s own views already persist; how much more so when one further establishes a distinct self, and outside that self, further establishes a distinct dharma, and outside both self and dharma, further establishes a person who destroys the dharma, whom one then envies and hates?

To give rise to such views regarding the Dharma is truly and utterly foolish and deluded. To envy others for destroying the Dharma, while remaining unaware that one has long since destroyed it oneself.

As for Magerin’s description of his master, saying, "My late teacher regarded those who destroy the Dharma as enemies, and those who destroy the Dharma likewise viewed my late teacher as an enemy"—regarding these two statements, both Mazu and Baizhang have not yet broken through their fundamental doubt.

Since they have already clarified this for themselves, there is absolutely nothing left to suspect. Indeed, to give rise to views of Buddha or views of Dharma is still like being caught between the two Iron Ring Mountains.
Shan: "If one gives rise to jealousy and views [others] as enemies, is this not the dark hell manifest before one?
Nevertheless, the claims made by Māra-garbha and his son—that those who strive to extinguish the Dharma through jealousy are like enemies—is but a falsehood.

In reality, it is merely that they harbor resentment toward those whose fame surpasses their own, regarding them as enemies. As for what they call 'Master Yi' and 'Māra-garbha,' there are no words or phrases [attributable to them]."
Those who transmit [the Dharma] do nothing more than attempt to cover over the errors of demonic storehouses and verbal phrases;

they recognize these as the blood of demons and the saliva of foxes, wishing to wash them away once and for all. Furthermore, they cast aside their fellow practitioners in order to manifest themselves as the legitimate successor.
He deceived the scholars and officials of his time; his base character was truly not worth mentioning.
Moran said: "The Diamond King Sword is something that neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs can retain. This reached Huqiu Ying’an, the twelfth in the lineage.
It is like pouring from one vessel into another. At that time, there were those who appeared in the world either before or after Linji;

for instance, at Shishuang, where the assembly was mostly "withered trees," they took sublime states of meditative experience as the ultimate goal. When the Head Seat passed away, the fundamental principle of the school was no longer understood.
Had it not been for Jiufeng, who else could have corrected this? Subsequently, this degenerated into the heterodox Chan of "silent illumination. Yet, it was Zhenjing Wuzu who...
The venerable elders of Miaoxi severely rebuked this error. By the time of the succeeding dynasty, this malady had grown rampant;

even those of vast capacity could not avoid entering through the narrow paths of foxes and rats. Fortunately, these two elders were forged from cast iron, and thus they ultimately attained correct awakening.
Although after their awakening they bitterly lamented their past mistakes and the errors of their former ways, students remained addicted [to their old habits].
They remained in a state of tranquil stillness, ultimately unable to abandon it. How profound indeed is the penetration of false teachings into people!
From the beginning of our dynasty until now, the practice of "sitting in silence" (mozhao chan) has been widespread throughout the North and South, so firmly established that it cannot be broken.
Yet, within the span of some ten years, Tiantong and Sanfeng emerged side by side, completely uprooting the dark lairs of the demonic army; they did so through wild beating and unrestrained scolding.
The fault of recording names and leaving traces arises before one has even turned a heel. The difficulty of preaching the Dharma in the final age is thus.
One must, however, fan the pure breeze, move others with utmost sincerity, verify through the essential tenets, and select among those of true human capacity.
Only then can one restore the primal energy and fundamental source—the total functioning and great utility—of Mazu, Baizhang, Linji, and Xinghua. This is not merely...

To be "proudly boastful" is to engage in verbal contention. As for Xueyan and his father [Wuzu], their handling and raising of the essential principles of the Jishi lineage—where they applied the blade and administered the medicine—truly possessed an interval of distinction from the ancients.
Even were they to apply these methods today, could they not be called an excellent remedy? Therefore it is said: "The Way is the year; the Sage is the season."
Zhuzhu resided at Shishuang Mountain for twenty years. Among his disciples, there were those who practiced long-sitting meditation without lying down, standing as motionless as tree stumps;
thus, the world called them the "Dried Wood Assembly. Jiufeng Qian served as his attendant. When Zhuzhu passed away, the assembly requested the Head Seat to succeed him as abbot.
Qian addressed the assembly, saying, "One must first comprehend the meaning of the former master before one may do so. The Head Seat replied:
"What was the meaning of the former master? Qian said, "The former master said: 'Rest! Cease! Be cold and still!
A single thought for ten thousand years! Like cold ashes and withered wood! Like an incense burner in an ancient temple! Like a single length of white silk!'"
He did not inquire about anything else. [Zhao] Qian asked, "How is it that one goes forth as a single strand of white silk?

The Head Seat said, "This merely clarifies matters on the side of 'one color' (monochromatic). Qian said, "I see now that I have not yet understood the meaning of our former teacher. The Head Seat said, "Just bring some incense.
When the smoke of the incense is severed, if you cannot go forth, then you have not understood the meaning of our former teacher. Thereupon, he burned incense. When the incense...
Before the smoke had even dissipated, the Head Seat had already passed away. Qian patted his back and said, "To sit and pass away, or to stand and die—this is certainly not lacking;

yet you have not even dreamed of the late master’s intent. Under Shishuang’s guidance, the assembly applied themselves with such diligence in their studies that they were praised by all at the time, earning the name "the assembly of withered trees.
Later, when the Head Seat likewise passed away while seated, Jiufeng Ming [inherited the lineage] and pointed toward the path above.

It does not involve any meritorious achievement. Since he was already able to demonstrate to others how to "slip away while sitting" or "pass away while standing," it means that there was still "this" remaining.
How could this be what is called the principle that "life is non-arising"? This is merely two kinds of conventional precedents within the assembly of Shishuang.
This has no connection with the "dead tree assembly. Originally, this head seat did not exist because of the dead tree assembly;
nor have we seen that the head seat must necessarily be one among the members of the dead tree assembly. Furthermore, even within this very dead tree assembly...

Furthermore, while the myriad phenomena are not uniform, there are certainly those who sit steadfastly and practice diligently, yet do not realize the Way for many years; they nonetheless cultivate the fruits of merit for the future.

How could one know that among them there might not be those who develop the true nature and return to the source, attaining a vast and penetrating clarity, and thus perform the Buddha-work within their dreams through the four dhyānas and eight samādhis?
It is merely the demonically-tolerant who fabricate connections and false associations, claiming these to be the assembly of "withered trees."
To take a superior and wondrous realm as the ultimate goal—would Jiufeng not have rightly rectified this failing? Would Jiufeng have instead willingly accepted it?

Furthermore, you claim that later it flowed into the heterodox Chan of "silent illumination" (*mozhao*). If that were so, was Bodhidharma’s nine years of facing the wall also the heterodox Chan of silent illumination?
Even speaking only of silent illumination, one is merely a fellow who dabbles with the spirit; yet you still do not refrain from slandering him.

This is a grave offense against the Great Prajñāpāramitā. How could it be anything less than claiming to have attained what one has not attained and claiming to have realized what one has not realized?

To fabricate names and signs, to blind the eyes of people, to falsely profess the essential tenets, and to defile the life-force of wisdom—how can such a person be permitted to further engage in diligent inquiry and vigorous investigation?
Seeking their own realization and entry, they refuse to follow the path of vermilion and ink, utterly dismissing it as the dark army of Māra or the narrow alleys of foxes and rats.

As for Magu Ren’s own admission that his three blows with the staff and three shakes of the door panels correspond to the Three Essentials and Three Principles, this cannot escape the glance of those with clear eyes. Thus, by means of Tiantong’s—

The fault lies in wild beating and abusive scolding; the fault of Sanfeng lies in recording names and clinging to traces. If one says, "Sanfeng originally had no extraordinary name or strange appearance;
this is merely the fault of his disciples for recording names and clinging to traces," and uses this as a defense, the stratagem is indeed clever.
Yet how could he know that in the end it is difficult to escape the single glance of those with clear eyes? Furthermore, Tiantong used a single staff—
Pointing to the place where a person stands is still the fodder of one’s own fundamental allotment; how could it ever not be the skillful means (upāya) of the ancient worthies?
Yet, you instead criticize it with wild blows and drunken insults, causing those of future generations throughout the world to mistake the staff for mere striking and the shout for mere cursing.
Thus fixing their eyes and views, this very act constitutes a dark army of demons that plunders the gift of the Dharma.

As for what they call "fanning with a pure wind," "moving through utmost sincerity," "verifying through the fundamental tenets," and "selecting according to human types"—these merely restore the primal energy and root of Mazu, Baizhang, Linji, and Xinghua, and their discourse on the total functioning of the Great Utility.
One truly does not know what kind of delirium this is. To enter this Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) is like cutting through a handful [of hair].
A single cut severs them all at once. What need is there to speak of "pure customs" versus "corrupt customs," or "ultimate sincerity" versus "extreme hypocrisy"?

Since we speak of the fundamental principle (zongzhi), then the pure water jar is itself an ancient Buddha; how much more so for those who share these same eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—who among them is not Śākyamuni appearing in the world or Maitreya returning?
Yet you wish to select based on human categories; I fear that in seeking to choose people, you will find none at all.

As for "kindred" (lei), they have never been of the human kind from the outset. From the Buddhas and Patriarchs above, they were originally unborn in the past and are fundamentally unextinguished now.

Within the alms bowl and at the tip of the staff, they constantly turn the wheel of the Dharma, without interruption and without end. Among the descendants of later generations, who could ever obscure them?
That which can be obscured is merely false dharma; what use would it be to obscure them? If you cannot do so, then why [bother]?
It must be said again: throughout past and present, above and below, east and west, south and north—the inexhaustible ocean of all dharma-gates—converges within the single site of the Way.
Regarding the "Four Sevens" of the Western Heaven and the "Two Threes" of this Eastern Land, even to say they are the same here is impossible;
how much more so to say they are different? How could it be that Mazu, Baizhang, and Linji [arose]?
Transformation. What other "original vitality" or "fundamental root" could there be? It is the total functioning of the great utility.

If you claim that it was only after the Gate of the Patriarchs reached Mazu, Baizhang, Linji, and Xinghua that the original vitality became complete, the fundamental root became firm, and the total functioning of the great utility was manifested, would this not utterly slander Mazu, Baizhang, Linji, and Xinghua? Moreover, as for Mazu, Baizhang, and Linji...
Xinghua: It is just like large pearls and small beads; jade is precious while glass is base. How can they be mentioned together as being of the same class?
This is sufficient to know that he has eyes but is blind as a bat. Why must one laboriously pretend to understand things?
*Jianmo Bianyilu*, Volume Five. *Yuzhi Jianmo Bianyilu*, Volume Six.
Mogujin said: "Regarding the Great Dharma of Linji, there have been those in later generations who attained its 'self-enjoyment,' though such instances were rare.

As for 'driving the plow and seizing the food' and 'untying the sticky and removing the bonds,' from Yinyuan, Huizhao, and those below them, those who could speak it did not necessarily master its application;
those who could apply it did not necessarily employ it fully. Some were exhausted by it without reaching its core, while others toyed with it without refining their mastery."
Therefore, the various masters of the past, such as Tianqi, no longer brought [the teachings] forth. In recent times, the core tenets have consequently come to be regarded as strange and absurd;
this has truly evolved from gradual beginnings to a manifest state. I have composed the *Wuzong jiu* (Rescue of the Five Schools), in which I must record both gains and losses.

It is not that I am flaunting what I have heard to criticize the former virtuous ones; rather, the flourishing or decline of the Dharma depends upon this. If you know this and yet find fault with me, what regret could there be?
The man of the Way who has severed learning and is non-active simply receives that which is for his own personal use.
Now, receiving that which is for one’s own personal use does not mean seeking to obtain it before receiving it.

To seek to obtain that which is for one’s own personal use before receiving it would be like starting in Yue and heading toward Yan. Nevertheless, this is not a matter of actually having realized the "attainment of non-attainment."
The original intent is that one can never attain self-enjoyment [of the Dharma]. Once self-enjoyment is attained, the task of a lifetime of study is complete.
Even "driving the plow and seizing the food" or "untying the sticky and removing the bonds" are merely instances of self-enjoyment.
If you give rise to the view of a person, then you have already ceased to enjoy yourself. Students only fear not becoming Buddhas; they do not fear...

The Buddha did not preach the Dharma using such methods as driving away oxen and seizing food. The ancient worthies called this "confiscating the family estate all at once," followed by demanding the payment of a fine.

It was because he could not do otherwise that he caused people to forget both subject and object, exhaust their emotional consciousness, obliterate right and wrong, and merge the holy and the mundane.
He severed the life-root so that there might be great death and great life; truly, he had no other choice.

This is not for the sake of boasting of one's own verbal fluency. Once a person has truly attained self-enjoyment, they will naturally be able to kill or bring life to others with a single blade of grass held in their hand. This kind of skill—how could it be obtained from another?
Have you not seen the Buddha say that even the empty Way is itself an enemy? If it were something obtained from another, what would it be worth?
Mao Ren-dong claims that this is the Great Dharma of Linji; yet when one examines the source and lineage of its fundamental tenets, he is nothing more than a hired hand.
Within the Gate of Non-duality, where could such a person find a place? Truly, acting as a guide for others is no small matter;

it is like piercing the eye with a golden needle—if the point deviates by even a hair’s breadth, the eye is blinded. Nevertheless, to pass judgment on the relative merits of the ancient worthies is a perilous task indeed.
To judge whether one can truly untie the knots and remove the bonds for others, or whether one possesses the skill to "drive the plow and seize the food," is the ultimate test.

Yet, even so, how could this be settled? Driving the plow and seizing the food, as well as untying the knots and removing the bonds—how could these ever reside merely within the realm of various provisional marks such as words, phrases, or karmic encounters?
Even if one understands them as expedient and skillful arrangements, it remains like floating upon a single leaf.
A light boat upon the great ocean. When Bodhidharma came from the West, he sat facing the wall for nine years without speaking a single word.
Yet tell me, was Bodhidharma a person or not a person? Because of this, Magu Ren disparaged Ying’an, Huazang, and those below them, using particularly subtle and critical words regarding Tianqi.
Furthermore, as for the character of Ying’an, Huazang, and Tianqi, Magu Ren...
How could one possibly know this? It is because Ying’an Huazang and Tianqi—father and son of Mazu’s lineage—share a single nostril.
All the various grandiose names and strange appearances of the "Great Dharma" and "Small Dharma" fabricated by this father and son are nothing more than such things.
How could Ying’an Huazang and Tianqi, from several hundred years ago, have so mysteriously coincided and silently harmonized?
He used this to mock his own ancestors, yet further compared himself to Confucius’s composition of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, sighing that "the world will know me and the world will condemn me.
How utterly狂妄 (mad) and 悖逆 (rebellious)!

Mozang said: "Since Xinghua had already awakened to these two shouts and further stated that he had studied the 'Guest and Host' phrase, why would he have waited for a great awakening within the context of soft words?
Zhongfeng said: "Dajue and Xinghua’s staffs and shouts flew back and forth; how could they be contained by thought?
Since these two elders shared the same nostrils, why would Xinghua have waited for a subsequent word? Regarding those of today—
Those who understand the fundamental purport often rely on Zhongfeng’s remarks regarding "sweeping away the fundamental purport" and "medicine and disease" as if they were definitive teachings.
They cling to their initial realization and refuse to believe in such matters as the thoroughgoing guest and host.
If one can reach a resolution here, one will no longer harbor doubts concerning the subtlety with which the five houses each expounded the patriarchs’ mind-seal. He further offers this verse:
Since the shout has already been clarified, how could one not understand the blow? Meeting twice, why would one who has awakened return to intoxication?

When the patched robe is stripped away and the mallet is struck again, even Huangbo would surely be shattered into a hundred pieces. It is laughable that the descendants pursue the crowd in such numbers;
they instead find it regrettable that Linji was not deemed noble enough.
Zhongfeng’s learning was profound and vast, and his literary elegance surpassed that of the practitioners of the Way.

Later, upon attaining personal realization, he deeply lamented the harm caused by following the traces of words and becoming mired in names and forms. Therefore, in guiding his fellow practitioners of Chan, he constantly exhorted them:

"One must practice true practice; one must attain true awakening. Realize it within your own mind and verify it for yourself; do not seek it from others. He instructed them with earnest and repeated admonitions.
He swept away the tenets of the Five Houses. As it is said: "When Bodhidharma came from the West, he transmitted the direct pointing alone; originally there was no complexity.

Later, as the Dharma became long-established, it grew corrupt, giving rise to heterodox views. Some established the 'Five Ranks of Ruler and Subject,' others the 'Four Kinds of Critical Examination,' the 'Three Essentials and Nine Belts,' or the 'Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality.
Each set up their own school and proclaimed their doctrines to one another. Although these were all provisional establishments for a particular occasion," [he swept them away.]
Yet they do not consider how they will deceive their descendants in future generations. Each one falls entirely into towering thorns;
climbing branch upon branch, trailing vine upon vine, they see nothing but tangled creepers covering the ground, with no time of escape in sight.

When they reach the point where their hair is white and teeth are yellow, and their life-root is on the verge of being severed yet remains unsevered, they look back and reflect upon their former intellectual understandings.
Not a single hair’s breadth of spiritual efficacy exists; they would rather willingly rush toward the gates of death. What use is regret once it is too late?

In the monastic communities of recent times, those who study in such a manner are as numerous as nine out of ten, drifting and collapsing like grass in the wind. Master Zhongfeng’s life was replete with such words and phrases.
As for his *niangu* (picking up ancient cases) and *songgu* (eulogizing ancient cases), they did nothing more than overturn and revitalize old koans, desiring that students understand this.

This person does not fall into right or wrong. One must not give rise to thoughts of superiority or inferiority regarding words and phrases, thereby causing oneself to descend into the realm of emotional consciousness.

This would turn the ancient masters’ opportunities for teaching—intended to loosen attachments and untie bonds—into occasions that increase those very attachments and tighten those bonds, leading one to bob up and down within the sea of birth and death.
If you recognize this intent, then you will understand his twenty-six "Citations of the Ancients" (Niangu) and thirty-one "Verses on the Ancients" (Songgu).
They originally follow the same rule. Regarding the public case of Dajue’s two strikes on Xinghua, it is said:
"Beneath two tigers, no beast can find a hoof-print; between two blades, no man can find a foothold.
At the moment when Dajue and Xinghua’s staffs and shouts were exchanged, how could there have been any room for the mind to deliberate or conceive? Nevertheless, as for Dajue saying, "Take off..."
"Give this patched-robed monk a thorough beating! Upon these words, Xinghua attained great enlightenment. But what did he realize?
If you can see it here, I grant you the status of being half a true descendant of Linji. Zhongfeng’s statement precisely refers to the ultimate guest and host.
This is merely a provisional arrangement at the gate; yet Māra’s treasury seeks to draw them together and use them as evidence for the tenets he has fabricated.
He claims that since the two elders share the same nostrils, why wait for subsequent words to realize it?
His intention is to claim that what Xinghua realized was precisely this tenet, thereby constructing this dark demonic den to lead others astray.
When a person falls into a pit, both Xinghua and Zhongfeng, though neither had yet reached ultimate realization, nonetheless arrived at this very extremity.
Now, if one seeks the thorough mastery of host and guest within names and forms, one remains far from initial awakening.
Once initial awakening is attained, one no longer walks where the Tathāgatas walk; how could one possibly believe in these "crimson and purple hues that confuse the vermilion"?
He speaks thus, yet he becomes even more deluded and frantic, running outside [the truth].
If one truly realizes the meaning that the ancient worthies were guests from beginning to end and the host from beginning to end, then where else could his fabricated tenets possibly be placed?
Yet it is said that if one reaches a definitive understanding here, one will no longer harbor doubts regarding the subtlety with which the five houses each expounded the patriarchs’ seal of the mind;
one will no longer be a "lacquer bucket" of dullness. It is thus, it is thus. Now, as for the place where the patriarchs transmitted the direct pointing alone:

using mind to seal mind and using mind to expound mind—is this not entirely a matter of the boundaries of mind, intellect, and consciousness?
The karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, with no fundamental basis upon which to rely.
Now, what "mind-seal" did the Patriarchs possess? It was entirely for the purpose of pointing out the matter within each person’s own immediate experience.

Although the five houses differ in their outward appearance when receiving students, they do nothing other than guide people toward self-realization and self-awakening; how could they ever have bestowed a single substantial dharma upon anyone?
To speak of a "Patriarchal mind-seal" already constitutes the phenomenon of seeing flowers in the sky due to pressing on one's eyes. Furthermore, as for the five houses each...
To expound upon the Seal of the Mind (cixin) is truly what the ancient worthies meant when they said: "To mistake the bridge of a donkey’s saddle for one’s father’s chin.

Therefore, I have earnestly exhorted you to diligently cultivate yourself, to maintain the lineage of the Buddhas and patriarchs, and to ensure that the Way of the Great Master does not decline. Now, having received your letter, I have felt compelled to speak my mind once more. I pray that you will take heed of these words and act accordingly. I am sending this letter with haste. To rouse the Dharma in this final age—how could such a person be easily found? Our late Master Sanfeng stood alone in accordance with the mandate, directly administering a surgical strike against the chronic malady of the Way.
His cultivation of merit and virtue, his conduct, and his literary works are not merely matters of conventional praise.

"This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. For this reason, the Buddhas and Patriarchs said: "Do not deliberate upon good or evil at all;

Because of this, followers of the school merely adopt the sudden and perfect [teachings] while failing to honor the practice of precepts. They do not realize that the provisional is the reality of the real, nor that the true is the reality of the illusory.

The Real is the power (upāya) of the True; the illusory is the manifestation of the True. If one rigidly establishes a position of "true reality," then appearances will block the path before one, and one will remain on this shore.
If one does not cultivate the practices of provisional illusion, one will sit idly in ignorant emptiness, which is itself worldly affliction.
Regarding the essence of the single flavor, do not err by even a hair’s breadth; regarding the gateway of myriad virtues, do not abandon even one.
The Dharma: By taking non-attainment as his skillful means, the Bodhisattva traverses the realm of existence without contradicting emptiness;

relying upon the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), he gives rise to gates of transformation; treading the truth, he is not obstructed by the conventional. He constantly kindles the torch of wisdom and does not obscure the light of the mind;

he spreads the cloud-like gates of compassion and surges with the ocean of practice. Thus, he attains unimpeded engagement with the mundane dust, acting with sovereign freedom according to conditions; all his deeds are thus accomplished.
There is nothing that is not a Buddha-activity. This is because one employs a mind like space to accord with the principle of space, yet remains without the limited measure of space.

If a student wishes to resolve birth and death and sever the cycle of saṃsāra, they must ply the wise oars of the pāramitās and board the compassionate vessel of the Great Prajñā, crossing the treacherous strait of the three realms of existence to enter the ocean of Samantabhadra’s vows.

How could one possibly achieve the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena, or the identity of body and mind? How can one loathe the illusory and rejoice in the real, or reject the provisional to recognize the ultimate?
To employ the very root of birth and death to fathom the nature-school of the Perfect and Sudden is merely to produce empty flowers; in the end, there will be no wondrous fruit.
Māra-Endurance (Mōjin) claims that the path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs’ single transmission does not speak of merit, virtue, or conduct; this is what is called a parrot learning [to speak].
People say: "To rely on words and lose the meaning. But how could the single-transmission path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs ever be like that?
Have you not heard the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* state: "To abandon great compassion while contemplating non-arising is the work of Māra;

I fear that by falling into partiality regarding merit, fortune, and conduct, one’s entry into the Way will lack refinement, thereby further succumbing to the teachings of Māra.

Now, as for what is called the "Way," both the sentient and the insentient are entirely contained within it; those who awaken do not enter it, while those who are deluded do not exit it. Until one has attained full realization, [this remains so].

Now, this Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) is free from the four propositions and transcends the hundred negations;

however, according to Māra’s view, if one does not partially fall into merit and conduct, then one must partially fall into the Way (*mārga*). Now, where there is left and right, there are two partialities;

If the Way is taken as the center and merit, virtue, and conduct as one partiality, then as for those other three partialities...

True son: once one possesses right knowledge and right view, then both the harmer and the harmed are simultaneously extinguished;

They seek only to make their households warm and prosperous; they claim to have attained what they have not attained, and claim to have realized what they have not realized.

As for the rest—the dregs and the offshoots of the current—there is nothing they will not do.

To have no place for receiving acupuncture yet to claim one can practice it oneself—is this not a vain expenditure of effort and a hollow fabrication of wonders?
Thus, you say that Qianyan was unable to fully penetrate Linji’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, citing Song Lian of Jinhua’s raised eyebrows and smile as proof.
Now, regarding Song Lian’s raised eyebrows and Qianyan’s smile—do you know what kind of mental activity Qianyan possessed?

How much more so regarding the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye (*saddharmadharmacakṣu-kośa*), which extensively pervades the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). There is not a single dharma outside of this upon which one may rely;
rather, it dwells securely within all dharmas, encompassing all sensory objects and completely enveloping the three periods of time.

How, then, can the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye be exclusively attributed to Linji? And how can it be said that "this is the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye of Linji"? This reaches even to the present day... [text truncated]

If they understand them as entirely dead words, then what need is there even to mention Linji and Sansheng? They would simply be fit for praise throughout all quarters.

Not knowing the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye—how could Qianyan have prepared it? And how could he have used it?

"It is real. White clouds stretch for thousands upon thousands of miles. Thereupon, he used the lineage whisk as a token of faith, saying:

To one who has awakened, the gate is the courtyard, the courtyard is the hall, and the hall is the inner sanctum. To one who has not awakened, they cannot say that the Way is the hall and the inner sanctum, nor can they say it is the gate and the courtyard;
the entire earth is none other than this very point. If one awakens to this very point, then...

To speak of these as gates, courtyards, halls, and inner sanctums, yet to claim there is no one who enters these gates, walks through these courtyards, or ascends to these halls and inner sanctums—if one does not awaken to this, to say that the Way possesses such gates, courtyards, halls, and inner sanctums is the demon of illusion;

To walk through the courtyard, ascend the hall, and enter the inner sanctum is the characteristic of the person (*pudgala-lakṣaṇa*). If one were to take up the characteristic of the Dharma (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), one would be unable to enter the gate, walk through the courtyard, ascend the hall, or enter the inner sanctum.

If one takes up the characteristic of the person, one is already within the gate, courtyard, hall, and inner sanctum, yet one cannot grasp or apprehend these gates, courtyards, halls, and inner sanctums.
Furthermore, the person is identical to the Dharma, and the Dharma is identical to the person; the person itself is the gate.
The courtyard, the hall, and the inner sanctum—how can these be spoken of? Entering the gate, walking through the courtyard, ascending the hall, and entering the inner sanctum:

this is neither person nor dharma, yet neither non-person nor non-dharma. Since the characteristics of persons and the characteristics of dharmas are both unobtainable, how could there further be the various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of gates, courtyards, halls, and inner sanctums?
Only when the great earth sinks into stillness and empty space vanishes can one truly return to the ultimate point.

It is merely that one does not fall to the ground; yet, is it not the case that one alone avoids touching upon what is taboo? Confucius once composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
As for the phrases "eternal bliss, self, and purity" and "the Land of Ultimate Bliss," many ancient masters have spoken of such bliss within the Dharma-gate of Non-duality.
Although this is bliss, it remains a matter within the realm of emotional consciousness (*saṃjñā*); in reality, there is no bliss that can be named.

However, when one reaches the point where the grease-stained cap is cast off and the coarse cotton shirt is stripped away, there is pure clarity and vast emptiness, with a brilliance as bright as the sun and moon.
How could this not be named? It is impossible not to name it "Bliss. Within this state, how could there be any weeping or shedding of tears out of grief?
The Master said: "Arouse the compassion that has no object; give rise to the realization of the same substance..."
How tragic! For one who practices the vows of a Bodhisattva, even the Buddha-work performed within a dream is still there;

how then could they harbor a dispute over their own correctness or disparage the compassion of others, claiming that "no one in the world understands me"? This is the principle by which one looks up and down and gives rise to compassion. Mazu Daoyi said:
"To bring up one thing, to bring up two things—these are the words of a close relative. After three such turns, Nanquan appeared. For seven hundred years since then...
Linji arose, beat his breast, switched hands, and wailed to the blue heavens. Chanruo (Mo-ren) recounted his master’s intent, saying:
"It is truly a lament for those who uphold the ancestral Way, who allow the students of the house to pass through the three turns [of the staff] without realizing it.
Is this not what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refers to as 'the demon of grief entering one's heart and viscera'? Thus, he relied upon the meaning of the *Xiaobian* and the *Li Sao*."
This is merely self-aggrandizement. Now, as for the *Xiǎobàn* and the *Liáoāo*, even within the mundane laws of the world, they already do not represent the path of centrality and rectitude.
If the Duke of Zhou or Confucius had encountered such circumstances, they certainly would not have acted in this way; how much less could these works be used to discuss the supramundane Dharma?
The supramundane Dharma is fundamentally free from contention. Why, then, do you so insistently debate the length of a tortoise’s hair or discuss the sharpness or dullness of a rabbit’s horn?

Your heart pounds with agitation and resentment, even to the point of wishing to raise Linji from his grave at Jiuyuan to question him—how can one be so foolish as this? If Linji were truly such a man, then in the past he was originally...

Unborn, it is likewise unextinguished now. While he grasps his pen and stirs his tongue to speak and write this—which bewitches the men and women of households and defiles the words of the life of wisdom—he has long since, in every dust mote and every world-system, given rise to the great compassionate heart of Avalokiteśvara, crying out:
"Alas, Buddha! You cannot save him! Were it not so, Linji would simply be...
What use is it to question this bed-wetting ghost? Have you not seen Dharma Master Zhao say: "Ordinary people seek the ancient within the present, claiming that it does not abide;
I, however, seek the present within the ancient, knowing that it does not depart. If the present were to reach the ancient, the ancient would have to possess the present;
if the ancient were to come to the present, the present would have to possess the ancient. Since the present lacks the ancient, one knows it does not come from the ancient."

Yet there is no "now," because one knows that [the past] does not go away. If the ancient did not come to the present, and the present likewise does not go to the ancient, then each phenomenon abides in its own nature;
what thing could possibly come or go? Thus, it is precisely within the demon’s treasury that the single word of Linji arose seven hundred years ago.
This can be understood through the meaning of the "Treatise on Non-Transmigration. Since the meaning of the "Treatise on Non-Transmigration" has not yet been clarified, it may be...
If you do not yet understand even the two characters "Tathāgata," you cannot yet be reckoned among those disciples who possess intellectual understanding of the school's principles;
how then can you, a student, be so loquacious as to speak of "raising one" or "raising two"? To truly realize the One, all matters are concluded.

On the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a single speck of dust is established. There is not so much as a speck of dust’s worth of difference between the dharmas of a sage and [ordinary phenomena]. Furthermore—
There is not even a speck of dust’s worth of difference between the dharmas of ordinary beings and [the state of awakening].
If you let one point slip and fall into the second, then at the gateway of the myriad practices, you will not abandon a single dharma; how then could you fail to uphold the five precepts?

To let forth the karmic consciousness and ignorance to argue with the teacher over who is right and who is wrong—even to the point of beating your breast, changing hands, and wailing to the heavens—is truly lamentable.

"O Heaven! You can weep for me, but you cannot laugh with me. This "The Old Woman Weeps for the Blue Sky" koan has been cited by him in such a manner that, although dead Zen monks are as numerous as hemp and millet, the Old Woman herself did not anticipate being defiled by this demonic cache to such an extent.
As for the transmission of the lineage, he cites the affairs of Confucius and Mencius regarding the rulers of Liang and Lu.

To consider this as an interpretation is to contradict the Way and injure righteousness; it is not merely that which Buddhism cannot tolerate, but is also that which the royal law must surely execute.
For the duty between ruler and subject is like that between father and son; it is ordained by Heaven.
When Confucius served as a minister of Lu, was it for Confucius to choose [whether to accept or decline]? If Confucius did not serve Lu, how could he have...?
He replied: "It was not a minister of Lu. How could Confucius dare to discuss the ruler of Lu as being wrong?
Furthermore, he was not a minister of Yao or Shun. Moreover, that which makes Yao and Shun what they were lies solely in the righteousness of ruler and subject, father and son;

from Yao and Shun onward, this became increasingly clear, and for ten thousand generations they have enjoyed its blessings. Thus, when Confucius and Mencius spoke, they invariably cited Yao and Shun. How could there be..."
While harboring a base and contemptuous heart toward his sovereign and father, he verbally expounds the Way of Yao and Shun to scrutinize them.
Such a person is precisely one whom Yao, Shun, and Confucius would have surely executed;
yet this Māra-like tyrant uses this very thing to defame Confucius and to defame Yao and Shun—how perverse this is! As for the era of the Warring States, the world was divided into fragments.

The righteousness between ruler and subject had fallen to such a state that it was like a single thread. When Mencius was born into that era, the circumstances were even more transformed than they had been during the time of Confucius.
Nevertheless, when he served the rulers of Liang and Qi, he never dared to employ the Way of Yao and Shun as a standard to scrutinize Hui and Xuan.
This was not merely because of Mencius’s own virtue; it was because of the Way of Yao and Shun itself.
When the Way is presented before a ruler, it is because one feels ashamed that one has not been able to cause that ruler to become a Yao or a Shun; this is not for the sake of self-examination.
If [the ruler] were to believe that the Way of Yao and Shun is entirely within himself and proceeded to examine King Xuan and Lord Hui of Liang, how could he still be considered Mengzi?
The loyalty of Mengzi is not something a shallow person can understand; as for the filial piety of Mengzi, however—
This is one of the twenty-four examples of filial piety transmitted by the children of Sanchi Village. Loyalty and filiality are of one mind;
ruler and father are of one principle. Have you not heard that Mencius used the Way of Yao and Shun to examine the conduct of Mengzi’s mother?
Now, Master Canger and his son have betrayed their teacher, Miyun Wu, comparing themselves to Confucius and Mencius when they did not find favor with their rulers.
The rulers of Liang and Lu claim to have attained something of the Way of Linji;
they wield it to scrutinize Miyun, comparing themselves to Confucius in his composition of the Spring and Autumn Annals.

Their absurdity and delusion reach such an extreme that, regarding the books of Confucius and Mencius, they have never even touched their shores, yet they plunder the common knowledge of village schoolmasters who lack true understanding.

At that time, Wen’s exegesis was a fabrication that misrepresented the sages and saints and defiled the Buddhas and patriarchs, used to delude the contemporary scholar-officials who lacked learning and discernment. How did this differ from heterodox paths and demonic speech?
He truly did not know what the Way of Yao and Shun was, nor did he know what the Way of the Buddhas and patriarchs was. Not so.

Miyun mistakenly regarded himself as the successor to Huanchou in the Linji lineage, seeking to obtain its seal of transmission and whisk to open a hall and gather a following for the sake of reputation and fame;
thus, Miyun’s wisdom-eye remained unclarified, and he was deluded by him.
At one time, he entrusted him with the lineage; yet when it came time for repentance, it was too late, and there was no way to save him.
Consequently, Zangren went so far as to indulge in reckless rhetoric, openly becoming an enemy of Mìyún, claiming that although Mìyún was indeed a descendant of Línjì, [he was not the true heir].
Yet he did not attain the Way of Linji; nevertheless, he claimed that the entirety of the Linji Way resided within himself.

In this way, he deluded the world and deceived the people, causing those throughout the land to say that Miyun was inferior to his own disciples, while he himself was the one who had truly attained the direct lineage of Linji.
Furthermore, he feared that scholars and officials lacking learning and discernment would not understand the [true nature of] Linji’s...

"What is this 'Way'? he asked. Thereupon, he went to where [the other] was in the village schoolhouse and, regarding what he had heard there—namely, the "Way of Yao and Shun" and the matters of Confucius serving in Lu and Mencius serving in Liang—he spoke of them with vague semblances and obscure allusions, using them as a means of bewitching him.
He then compared that which the other called the "Way of Linji" to the "Way of Yao and Shun."

To compare Mimi Yun to the rulers of Liang and Lu, and for Yi [Hui] and his son to compare themselves to Confucius and Mencius, is truly to commit the sin of envying those above and the arrogance of great pride;

it constitutes a great falsehood that leads one to fall into the Avīci Hell. Since the transmission from the Four Sevens of the Western Heaven to the Two Threes of this Eastern Land, we have heard of the source and its stream being described as "father and son," but we have never heard of them being described as "ruler and subject."

This is a matter of analogy. For example, if one takes the relationship between ruler and subject as an analogy, yet regards the failure to encounter a sovereign like Yao or Shun as an obstacle to liberation, why not consider the time of the "dense clouds" [of the Dharma-rain]?

Furthermore, how could it be that only after all ministers were exactly like Gao Yao, Kui, Ji, and Xie could they be employed? When Miyun succeeded Hanyou in the transmission of the lineage, the Chan school was in a state of decline.
It is so. Among the students, those such as Māgandika and his like may have sought understanding through their own paths of reasoning, which cannot be said to be entirely without insight;

or they may have possessed firm faith and a sincere earnestness in seeking the Dharma. At that time, I offered them praise and encouragement, awaiting a later day when I might gradually instruct them.
Subsequently, however, some were abandoned because they remained forever obstructed by heavy barriers, while others fell away midway.

The "Transformed City" (Gandharva-nagara) is further upheld by Chan Master Mocheng; this is also a common practice among teachers. This was precisely where Chan Master Mo Ren had spent his life organizing the Dharma-treasury.
[Mocheng] then rebuked him, asking why he first affirmed something and later denied it. He further remarked that it is not only the case with the "Māra-treasury";
the same applies to several of those who received the transmission of the Dharma. Where, then, is the pure Dharma-eye? According to Master Ren’s own intent:

If a master of the lineage must, upon receiving the Dharma-transmission, never again dare to point out the faults of his disciples for the rest of his life, only then can he protect his own pure Dharma-eye. Is there such a thing as a pure Dharma-eye within the Buddha-dharma?
Since it was the case with all those to whom Mìyún transmitted the Dharma, it is clearly evident that Mìyún did not transmit blindly.
This was a "blind transmission. Among all those people, each must have possessed some degree of excellence that was worthy of being adopted;

furthermore, it is not heard that any other person possessed such a "demon-treasury" (mōzàng) as he did. From this, one can know that while Míyún had never once lost his pure Dharma-eye regarding others, regarding Mōzàng alone, he opened it seven times—once, twice, and up to seven times—and yet still managed to save half of his pure Dharma-eye.

Now, if Māra’s forbearance is instead turned into what is deemed wrong, then it would mean that once the Gao, Kui, Ji, and Xie among the gateways of the Dharma can no longer be found, one must not execute the Hunchun, Qiongqi, Taowu, and Taotie;

rather, one should approve and employ them all, never daring to point out their faults for the rest of their lives—is this truly acceptable? Furthermore, the source and its stream are like father and son.
What you have said uses the provisional names and forms of the mundane world to manifest the true transmission of the supramundane.

In reality, although father and son are most intimately related, they appear as two distinct bodies; yet when one is born from the Buddha’s own mouth as a true son of the Buddha, then following the source to produce the stream, they are truly one body—just like water.
The source is this very water, and the stream is also this very water. Once [this is understood]...
Once the source and the stream are in accord, then the waters of ten thousand miles and a thousand leagues are all one and the same. If there were any difference, how could there be a source?

How could there be a stream? Now, although Mazu’s lineage has already transmitted the source and stream of Miyun Yuanwu, you nevertheless claim that Yuanwu’s Way is not the Way. If so, what kind of source and stream is this? Since it possesses none...
As for its source and tradition, what then could it mean to speak of "the Way" (dào)?
To give it the forced name "the Way" is merely to borrow the terminology of worldly conventions within the vehicle of the teachings (*śāsana*) as a means of expression.

In reality, how could it be discussed as being the same as that which is called "the Way" in worldly teachings? Those who speak of the Way in worldly teachings often say: "Yao transmitted it to Shun; Shun [transmitted it to Yu]..."
"This was transmitted to Yu; Yu transmitted it to Tang; Tang transmitted it to Wen, Wu, and the Duke of Zhou;
Wen, Wu, and the Duke of Zhou transmitted it to Confucius. Although such a theory exists, in reality, no such thing ever occurred.
How could these several sages have ever gathered in one hall to hand down a record, saying, "I am thus, and you are also thus"? It is merely a fabrication of later generations.
These individuals, because the virtuous marks of several sages were similar and their minds were identical, calculated them according to their respective eras:

the senior was called the "giver" (*shou*) and the junior was called the "receiver" (*shou*); the former was called the "giver" and the latter the "receiver. This is what is meant by saying that "so-and-so transmitted it to so-and-so.
As for the Gate of the Patriarchs (*zongmen*), in a single hall they "crack and peck" together, like ice melting in water; when one reaches this state, words...
The Way is cut off; the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. It is thus, and so it is with me.
Having entered this stage, there is truly nothing that can be expressed in words or names. Out of necessity, one uses worldly dharmas to name supramundane dharmas, calling it "transmitting the Way.
In reality, even to speak of "the Way" is impossible; to speak of "transmitting" is even more impossible. How could it be otherwise than Yao?
This is what is meant by the saying that Shun transmitted it to Yu. If one wishes to use this as a comparison, it would simply mean that a Buddha transmits it to a Buddha;
though it passes through several hundred transmissions, it remains but a single Buddha. Only in this way can it be called a source and its stream.
Now, regarding Muzhang and his son’s relationship to Miyun: what is their source? What is their stream? And furthermore, what is their path?

At first, they took Miyun to be the direct successor of Linji and sought to obtain his staff and whisk. Once they had obtained the staff and whisk, they further claimed that the essential principles of a hundred generations were not something Miyun knew.

Thus, as for what is called "source and stream": *(Note: This passage critiques the lineage claims of the Muzhang family, questioning the legitimacy of their transmission from Miyun and their subsequent assertions regarding the Dharma-lineage.)*
To equate this with worldly rank and title is, at its very source and flow, nothing but a false rank and false title.

Since one regards it as a false rank and false title, yet claims that the ancestral teachings received through a hundred generations must rely upon such false rank and false title to be propagated, then not only will the supramundane Dharma be lost, but...
It is a principle that such things have never existed; it is a worldly matter, a principle that has never, ever existed.

Furthermore, as for the lineage of the staff and whisk—what purpose do they serve? Since the World-Honored One entrusted the golden-threaded *kāṣāya* to Mahākāśyapa, who transmitted it to his successor until Maitreya’s descent, and continuing down through Huangmei and Caoxi, the robe was no longer passed on.
The Transmission: The robe is not transmitted, yet the whisk is used to signify faith.
Why is it that the robe and the whisk are neither two nor different? Furthermore, what is this "faith"? And why can the whisk alone signify faith?
If one remains vague and muddled regarding this, would not that which has been transmitted without interruption since the time of the Buddhas and Patriarchs be rendered meaningless?

Is this merely idle chatter? Shushan Ren played with a wooden snake. When someone asked about it, he said, "A daughter of the Cao family. [The questioner asked: "How can a wooden snake be a woman? And how can this woman belong to the Cao family? Is this wooden snake the same as or different from a staff or a whisk? If you have not yet clarified this, it is only right that you should equate the staff and whisk with worldly ranks and titles. Thus it was said of old: [The text continues with the verse: "An ancient worthy once said: 'If you do not see the staff and whisk, How can you see the Buddha-dharma? If you see the staff and whisk, You will see the Buddha-dharma. This is why it is said: "The staff and whisk are the Buddha-dharma; the Buddha-dharma is the staff and whisk. If you understand this, you will know that the staff and whisk are not separate from the Buddha-dharma, and the Buddha-dharma is not separate from the staff and whisk. If you do not understand this, you will surely fall into the trap of regarding them as mere worldly objects. Therefore, the ancients used the staff and whisk to point directly at people's faces; they did not use them to deceive or entertain others. If you can grasp this meaning, you will realize that the staff and whisk are the very lifeblood of the Buddhas and patriarchs. If you cannot, you will continue to mistake them for ordinary tools.
