In the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the Tathāgata distinguishes five types of individuals who are not suitable vessels for those whom this teaching is intended to reach. First, he excludes those who contradict the truth. What is meant by "contradicting the truth"?
It refers to those who do not resolve to attain bodhicitta, who do not seek liberation, and who rely upon this sūtra to seek fame and profit, thereby adorning their notions of self and personhood.
For such people, the sūtra is not a conducive condition; thus, they are not suitable vessels. As the sūtra says: "To preach the Dharma for the sake of fame and profit—this is [the first]."
This is the work of Māra. Now, as for the seeking of the source and stream of the *Mozang* (Cang), it originated with Miyun.
Since the Buddhas and Patriarchs had already exposed this long ago over a thousand years prior, can it still be claimed not to be the work of Māra?
Once Cang had humbled himself before Miyun to entice and obtain that source and stream, and having obtained it, he regarded Miyun as a discarded straw dog and trampled him underfoot. This—
What kind of mental conduct is this? To possess such mental conduct is to engage in what kind of false speech;

it brings harm to the Buddha-dharma, it brings harm to humanity and the way of the world, and it incurs the offense of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. It incurs the offense of Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius.
In the Buddha-dharma, such a person is called a "demon-follower"; in the secular law, they are called a "wicked person. How can they not be executed?
Mozhen said: One day the Sixth Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying, "I have an object that has no head and no tail, no name and no character, no back and no face.
Do you all recognize it? Shenhui stepped forward and said, "It is the original source of all Buddhas, the Buddha-nature of Shenhui.
The Patriarch said, "I told you it has no name and no character; yet you immediately call it 'the source'."
"Regarding 'the source of Buddha-nature': if you go forward with a thatch roof over your head, you will still only become a follower of the school of intellectual understanding.

This is the original statement of Caoxi (Huineng). I observe that since the sect of the Plucking of the Flower flowed to China, from the First Patriarch to the Sixth Patriarch, there have been various offshoots.
Master Hui would calculate the source of Buddha-nature upon the basis of namelessness and wordlessness, and he rejected [all conceptualization].
It is indeed appropriate that they seek understanding; for this reason, each of the five houses established its own school tenet specifically to treat the malady of such intellectual understanding.
This was not out of a distaste for the old or a desire to pursue the new. For example, when a monk asked Yunmen, "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge?
he replied, "Water flows uphill on the Eastern Mountain. When a monk asked Dongshan, "What is the Buddha? he replied, "Three pounds of flax. Linji...
Ji said: "Within a single phrase are contained three principles; within one principle are contained three essentials.

If this is so, how could the conceptual understanding of the original source, the Buddha-nature, ever arise? Now, to open up a written treatise and establish a school’s tenets as a form of conceptual understanding is to act in direct opposition to the words of the Sixth Patriarch."
This matter, directly and immediately, has no peer and no companion; it is neither identical nor different; it has no beginning and no end; it has no interior and no exterior.
Therefore, it cannot be known by cognition, nor can it be recognized by consciousness. It is so, and thus it is; it is not so, and thus it is not.
If it is so, then there is not even a hair’s breadth of what is not right; if it is not so, then there is not even a hair’s breadth of what is right.
Now, regarding the tradition of the Flower-Picking [Anecdote], which flowed to Zhendan (China): from the First Patriarch to the Sixth Patriarch, each had collateral lineages.
One may recognize him as a follower of the school of memorization, but he cannot yet be called a follower of the school of understanding.

The ancient worthies said that to know through thinking and to understand through deliberation is the "livelihood of ghosts"—a solitary lamp beneath the sun. Today’s followers of Magu and Ren can merely memorize;
they have not yet attained understanding. They fall one step further below those who possess understanding. How, then, can they rely on the literal text?

Mazu Daoyi, and about to describe the origins and conclusion of his doctrinal debates with Miyun,
he first cites the incident of Confucius being in distress at Chen and Cai, comparing himself to Yan Hui and his teacher to Confucius.
As for those among the disciples of Mìyún who do not align themselves with him, they may indeed be compared to the rulers and ministers of Chén and Cǎi;

truly, they are not enough to provoke even a single laugh. Now, although this Perfect Teaching (Yuánzōng) is said to be a doctrine difficult for the world to believe, once one has entered this gate of non-action, it is truly like looking up at the heavens and observing the earth below: naturally, all who possess eyes will see it together. It is not otherwise.

It is particularly difficult to believe because, for the time being, one must say that "belief is not possible. It can only be realized through direct correspondence; it does not reside in words and speech. Thus Yongming said:

"To speak of causes and conditions or spontaneity belongs entirely to worldly language; to discuss existence and non-existence, or the ultimate and conventional truths, is all merely the functioning of the discriminating consciousness.
At the moment of seeing one's nature, how could there be any lingering observation or hearing? This applies to the act of speaking.
At the limit of clarity, one transcends words and thought. If this is so, what connection can there be between a person’s faith and lack of faith?

If a person has indeed realized it for themselves, it is most difficult to force them to disbelieve; if a person has not realized it for themselves, it is likewise most difficult to force them to believe.
Even if they were to give rise to faith, it would not be pure faith or perfect faith. How, then, could one claim to be among the ranks of the Buddhas?
The Dharma transmitted by the Patriarch is a teaching difficult for the world to believe, yet it truly resides within oneself.
To desire to compel all under heaven to share in this belief—do you not observe heaven and earth? Those with eyes see heaven and see earth, yet heaven and earth do not question them;
those without eyes see neither heaven nor earth, yet heaven and earth likewise do not question them. Why, then, must one fixate so intently on such matters?

How much more so regarding the tenets fabricated by the patriarchs Zang and Ren, and their various methods for deluding the world and deceiving the people—how could these ever be made to be believed by all under heaven? To hope that others will believe is nothing but greed.
The resentment that others do not believe one is *dveṣa* (hatred). To harbor such resentment and expectations is all *moha* (delusion).
When greed, hatred, and delusion have not yet been eliminated, this single word "I" is like oil mixed into flour, lacquer poured into glue, a fly sunk in wine, or maggots in filth.
There will surely be no day when you emerge from this [karmic state]. How could you find the leisure to raise the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*?

You cite the *Shiji*, drawing parallels and making circuitous references to extend your arguments, seeking fame and using your own views to distort those of others. Your karmic consciousness is vast and murky, with no fundamental basis to rely upon.
When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, even before the Old Man Yama, you may still speak with crafty words like a reed pipe.
To say that a "rare rhinoceros" appears at an improper time and endures suffering to propagate the sutras—is this not a variety of erroneous arguments?
You lacquer buckets who have not yet emerged from the shell—prudently reduce your reading of texts. A single extra character constitutes an extra obstruction.

Even if it were Māra’s forbearance, he would still be merely a pitiable wretch. As for his praising his own teacher Māragarbha, saying: "Riding a winged tiger, drawing a ten-thousand-jun bow," and speaking of the Way...
At this great time of uncertainty, the mind is weary and the will is obstructed. When stationed at a critical pass, one should not shrink from practicing benevolence;

when occupying a position of honor, even the imperial meal may be spat out. To pursue the ancients in order to find a teacher, and to restore the Five Lamps to continue the Patriarchs—these few words are indeed a demonic confession, an iron-clad case.
In Yang Xiong’s *Fayan* (Discourse on Law), he censured cruel officials, saying: "Tigers! Tigers! Their horns..."
It is said that those who "provide wings" refer to cruel officials who, like tigers with wings, fly about to devour the flesh of others.
Ma Rin had perused worldly texts but did not fully comprehend them; he nevertheless honored his teacher with such a title.

Nevertheless, it is said that the Māra-garbha vehicle possesses the "winged tiger. Truly, truly, it is so! That school fabricated its own tenets and struck at the vital organs of those of mediocre capacity.
For those companions who later resolved to study and practice, yet lacked right knowledge and right view, they were deluded by reading his books and being captivated by his doctrines;
even if a Buddha were to appear in the world, he could not save them. Thus, this [teaching] severs the life-force of wisdom in others—it is no small matter.
It is like a tiger with wings! This Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) is the center within the periphery; therefore, there is no dharma with which it can be compared.
It is the truth within the delusion; therefore, there is no dharma upon which it must depend. How could the Buddha-dharma further depend upon the Buddha-dharma?
It is the sole, non-dependent Dharma-realm of the Tathāgata. Beyond the Dharma-realm, there is no further dharma; there is nothing upon which to depend and nothing to be transcended. Thus...
As the ancient masters have said: "When a single leaf falls, autumn comes to the world; when a single speck of dust rises, the great earth is gathered up.
When a single flower blooms, spring comes to the world; when one thing is stilled, the myriad dharmas are true. For one who has seen their nature, this is suddenly realized without doubt.
It is like attempting to lift a jujube leaf with the point of a needle—it would not even suffice to describe how easy it is, for the needle's point still possesses the capacity to lift.
Even a jujube leaf still has something that can be lifted. Why then exert the strength required to draw a ten-thousand-jin crossbow?
If we speak in terms of strength, even with the power of an asura, it is easy to lift Mount Sumeru, but difficult to lift this.
That which is to be lifted is precisely this very thing. Furthermore, by what power could one lift this? Great Nirvana.

The Sūtra speaks of one hundred phrases of liberation, repeatedly and earnestly teaching people that liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and that the Tathāgata and liberation are non-dual and without distinction;
for all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane realms are entirely non-existent.

All arise from the perception of written characters. If there were no perception of written characters, then names and essences would be fundamentally empty. Within the wondrously luminous mind, what further thing could there be?

Therefore, that which exists is the existence of non-existence; and as for that which is non-existent— (Note: The final phrase "and as for that which is non-existent" is left untranslated here as it appears to be a fragmentary conclusion or transition.)
It is the non-existence of that which is not non-existent; it is the non-existence of that which is not non-existent. It does not abide in non-existence.

It is the existence of that which is not existent; it does not abide in existence. Abiding neither in existence nor in non-existence, all dharmas are entirely liberated. How could there be anything to be done?

When the Way is great, the doubting mind fatigues the will and creates obstacles through various distortions and monstrosities. Such is their "Way"—the way of the heterodox; such is their mind—the multitude.
With a mind of birth-and-death, they dwell upon the marks of sentient beings; with these marks of sentient beings, they practice the ways of external paths.
Regarding this inconceivable Dharma-door of liberation, it is truly as if they were bypassing the state of Yan to travel to Yan, or embracing ice while seeking fire.
Yet they wish to lead all under heaven to follow them—this is the doubt of the age and the obstruction of their own resolve. This is the True Dharma.
It would not end in total extinction. The intention of Māra and his followers is that everyone in the world must remain without doubt, so as to satisfy their demonic will;
is this not the creation of infinite karmic obstacles? How could one rely upon such "heavy gates"?

As soon as there is something to rely upon, one has already lost the First Ground (Prathamabhūmi). Where, then, are there any heavy gates? Neither Bodhidharma nor his son Huike ever trod upon the First Ground.
Therefore, the mind, intellect, and consciousness burn fiercely, giving rise to deluded perceptions of various strange names and diverse forms.
Having heard the ancient masters speak of the "Double Barrier" (Chongguan), I truly did not know what this Double Barrier was. Thus, I applied the character *ju* (to rest upon).
If there were indeed such a critical pass or narrow gorge, it would be laughable. Upon reaching the Double Barrier, mountains are simply mountains.
Water is water. The master abides in the position of the master; the disciple abides in the position of the disciple.
It is for this reason that when the King ascends the jeweled throne, the village elders sing songs of joy. Awakening is unconditioned yet active; the myriad practices are unpracticed yet cultivated.

Furthermore, how could there be any "doing" such as to not yield to one's teacher when it comes to practicing what is right? Caoshan’s verse on the Dharma-body says: "Not eating the stipend of the Empty King, yet again..."

The commentary states: If you encounter "imperial rice," you must immediately spit it out. This is to clarify that matters pertaining to the Dharma-body transcend [dualistic categories]; there is neither Buddha nor sentient being.
If you give rise to a view of holiness and conceive the thought of being the foremost person, you will thereby damage the wealth of the Dharma and destroy your merit.
Therefore it is said: "One must simply spit it out. Now, Mazu Ruzhen says that when one occupies a position of honor, even imperial rice is spat out.
What a fine example of a man who covers his ears while stealing a bell! Since he already harbors the notion of being honored, he has long since swallowed the imperial rice;
how can he now say that even imperial rice is spat out? Furthermore, once one forms the notion of occupying a position of honor, one has already been consuming dregs and swallowing chaff. Why?
Upon seeing the imperial rice, Māra’s mind was filled with resentment; he thought that his teacher had already realized the Dharma-body, which is most supreme and most noble.
As for Caoshan’s remark about "spitting out the imperial rice," he took it as a direct slight against the sovereign and his ministers, failing to understand it as a refusal to partake of such food.
Thus, were these two, father and son, not indeed rebellious subjects? Since it was imperial rice—

To do so would be to slight sentient beings and fail to honor the Buddhas; one would be acting as a person of sudden enlightenment while completely failing to accord with the true countenance of the Dharma.
Why, then, do you say that you have sought a teacher throughout the ages? Where is the meaning of "spitting out the imperial rice"?
It is merely because your demonic storehouse of pride and arrogance makes you ashamed to be a disciple of Mìyún, and you long for heaven.

Those of inferior caliber consider Mi Yun to be superior to themselves; they immediately seek means to disparage him, recklessly aspiring to the high peaks [of realization] to claim Mi Yuan as their master for the sealing of mind (*yinxin*) and Juefan as their master for the sealing of Dharma (*yinfa*).
This is a single stream of demonic speech, demonic words, demonic mind, and demonic conduct.
Yet Māra tolerated and deluded him; he praised him with great enthusiasm, unaware of his own ugliness.
This is truly pitiable. Now, as for the distinction between teacher and disciple: if there is no true awakening, it remains merely a worldly convention and a system of names;
one cannot be called father and son in the sense of having given birth to the body of non-arising. Thus, Fazang’s relationship with Miyun could not fundamentally be termed [that of father and son].

To claim that father and son [Zhaozhou and Dongshan] reached the point where the former was the master who sealed the mind (*yinxin*) and the latter was the master who sealed the Dharma (*yinfa*) is truly empty talk and idle chatter.
How could there be a Dharma separate from the mind? And how could there be a mind separate from the Dharma?
If one has already sealed the mind, why must one also seal the Dharma? One person seals the mind and another seals the Dharma—this is incomprehensible; what will they do with this?
What is meant by "mind"? What is meant by "dharmas"? Yongjia said: "The mind is the root; dharmas are the dust. These two are like blemishes upon a mirror.
When the stains of these blemishes are completely removed, the light finally appears. When both mind and dharmas are forgotten, the nature is itself the truth.
Thus, what Mazu refers to as "sealing the mind" and "sealing the dharmas" is truly different from Yongjia’s discourse. Yongjia teaches people...
When both mind and dharmas are forgotten, Magang then took the two seals of mind and dharma. Although Gao Feng Juefan was extremely mediocre, he would not accept such an unworthy son.

Furthermore, the grace of the Dharma-milk must have its source; if one claims that wherever one has gained strength throughout one's life constitutes the grace of the Dharma-milk, then all the words and phrases bequeathed by the sages and worthies for the benefit of future generations...
All people can obtain this power. Why does Mōzang not have everyone inherit it from afar?
Although the master-disciple relationship in the Chan school differs from that of worldly fathers and sons, how could there ever be a principle of selecting only one or two "excellent fathers"?

Furthermore, among the ancient worthies and superior sages, those who were peerless and outstanding appeared in every generation; yet the blind do not recognize them. Peakong was truly [one such person].
It is settled. Juefan’s selection of these two most inferior individuals to serve as his "fathers" is truly enough to provoke a great laugh.
In the room of Vimalakīrti, there was the saying that from one lamp, an inexhaustible succession of lamps is transmitted;

later generations consequently designated those whose dharma-teachings flourished most vibrantly as the "Five Houses," calling them the "Five Lamps. This is nothing more than a provisional name coined by later people.

If you argue that beyond the Five Lamps there cannot be a Sixth Lamp, and that because the lamps of these five each have distinct lights that shine and transmit separately, they cannot constitute a single lamp—then those so-called Five Lamps are all but demonic fires that ought to be extinguished immediately;
why then do you restore them once they have been extinguished? Furthermore, regarding the Dharma lineages of the Five Lamps, although some have been interrupted...

Furthermore, the light of the five lamps pervades the trichiliocosm; even after passing through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is no principle by which they could ever be extinguished.

Why, then, labor to restore them from the *māra-garbha*? Moreover, these lamps cannot be extinguished by human power, nor can they be rekindled by human power. What, then, does it mean to "restore the five lamps and continue [the lineage]"?

Master, you can truly be said to be devoid of shame. Judging by these several eulogistic words, that Fazang was a subject of Māra is surely like a formal indictment established and an iron-clad case settled.
Yet, how is it that this wretched demon of a man, Māraripu, first says "as if revealing the sun and moon," and then again says "majestic as the sun and moon adorning the sky"?
What kind of petty fiend is this, who does not cease his audacity toward Confucius?
They have even so rudely encroached upon the sun and moon, acting with such utter recklessness as to reach this extreme.
Furthermore, it is said that Mazang (Māra-garbha) raised up the sun and moon to illuminate the faults of others, thereby inciting the world’s jealousy; who would say this is not appropriate?
Now, this Dharma-gate is neither right nor wrong; what constitutes a fault, and what does not constitute a fault? For the moment, let us not discuss whether Miyun was at fault or not.

Mogong concealed [the matter] within a dense cloud of secrecy; yet, after only one day had passed since the formal rites between teacher and disciple were completed, he made it his lifelong vow to expose the transgression to the whole world.
If this was indeed his ambition, then could Mogong still be tolerated within the Buddha-dharma?
Could he still be tolerated in the world? Although Morin exerted every effort to shield and conceal Mogong, how could he have known that—?
Having concluded the case, he instead exhausts every effort to expose their depravity without leaving anything behind. *Imperial Composition:
Record for Discerning Heresies and Distinguishing the Authentic*, Volume Six;
*Imperial Composition: Record for Discerning Heresies and Distinguishing the Authentic*, Volume Seven.

In the *Mōnin Shū* (Collection on the Patience of Mara), it is recorded that the thirty-first generation successor of Linji, Zen Master Yumitsu Hōzō of Mount Dengwu in Suzhou, was a dharma heir of Tiantong Wu.

Born into the Su clan of Liangxi, he received the tonsure at Deqing Hermitage in Wumu at the age of fifteen. Shortly thereafter, he came to despise his studies and began wandering among the mountains and rivers.
In his leisure time, he once said to his peers, "I shall realize the Way at forty; I will die at sixty. Those who heard this marveled at him.
At twenty-nine, he encountered the *Recorded Sayings of Peak* (*Gao Feng yu lu*) and was able to memorize it with a certain clarity. He then resolved to practice Chan.
That year, he received the precepts from Master Yunqi Hong. Ten years later, he received full ordination from Master Guxin at Linggu Monastery.
Furthermore, the following year, he resided at the Three Peaks of Haechu. For over ten years, he exhausted his mind and strength;
with thatched roofs and broken walls, grass huts and ivy fences, eating bean dregs and wearing patched clothes, he did not consider this to be suffering.

He once investigated the koan, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? Without closing his eyes for a wink and without his side touching the mat, he practiced through the night. For—
Enveloped by lethargy, the Master hung a large wooden board beside his seat and ordered his disciples to distribute incense and strike it, the sound of the Buddha’s name resonating to the heavens.
He sighed each time, saying, "I once said that I would realize the Way at forty.
If there is any truth to that, I am now thirty-eight years old, yet my efforts have been thus in vain. Could I ever truly fail this word? Thereupon, he was filled with dread and wept.
He imposed a strict retreat upon himself. By the *Renzi* year of the Wanli era, when the Master was forty years old, his investigation became even more intense;

he resolved that he would not rest until he had attained awakening. It happened that an elder residing at Fengzhong Monastery named Langquan was in retreat; seizing this opportunity, the Master requested to enter.

Just as he was prostrating before the elder, he suddenly felt dizzy and vomited nearly a peck of phlegm. He then collapsed and fell into a deep sleep for five days, remaining unconscious of all affairs.
Outside the window, two monks were leaning against a fence, breaking a large bamboo stalk; the sound was like a sudden clap of thunder.

The Master leapt up from his pillow and immediately attained the realization of the emptiness of mind. He then thought to himself: "What the ancients have done involves severing the continuity of past and future; one must not remain settled therein.
He then applied himself with all his might to investigation, until suddenly he lost his nostrils while looking at a Lin-yi cotton robe from Qingzhou. This is what the Patriarchs have said.
The words were exhausted all at once. From this point on, he attained awakening wherever he encountered anything; his realization grew ever deeper.

He found particular great utility in the "message of the pillow falling from the high peak. He then composed a verse, saying: A single coffin with three nails, Each stroke of the axe sends off a lifetime.
Since the mournful song of the *xièlù* has ceased, I have won the verdant cypress for my grave every morning.
Furthermore, a verse says: Cutting through the surging waves, he comes and goes of his own accord; The new moon and autumnal moon-seal hang cold upon the fishing line.
The aged fisherman, holding his small carp, returns home; How could he ever behold the dragon’s pearl in the palm of his hand?
When a monk asked Longya Dun, "What did the ancients attain that they simply ceased [their seeking]?
Dun replied, "It is like a thief entering an empty room. This phrase most skillfully depicts the state of a guest’s realization after awakening.

However, before the thief has even entered the empty room, he naturally engages in false conceptualizations, imagining there are gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, and amber within the room.
Because there are treasures such as pearls and lapis lazuli, one would exert every effort to steal them.
How could one have foreknowledge of it and announce to others in advance, saying, "On such a month and day, I shall see this room empty and devoid of even a single object"?
Furthermore, having known it, one would say, "You must dig through the wall and bore through the fence early to go and steal. [This is impossible.]
Is there any道理 (principle) in this? Māgaxiang fabricated a narrative of his enlightenment to deceive those of his time;
yet Māgeren recounted it, claiming that at the age of fifteen, he knew for himself that he would attain enlightenment at forty, and spoke of this to others.

When he reached thirty-eight and had not attained enlightenment, he wept and wailed in grief, fearing that what he had said was untrue. He further claimed that if [the prediction] were not to come true...
I fear that I may ultimately fail to live up to these words. Just as I reached the age of forty, I slept for five days;

upon hearing the sound of a bamboo breaking, I suddenly attained great enlightenment. This was exactly as he had said when I was fifteen years old. Thus, that which I have realized— [The text provided ends here.]
Did you ever awaken to this? When Master Lianchi Zhenke was about to pass away, he instructed his disciples, saying: "Recite the Buddha’s name with sincerity;

do not fabricate strange wonders. This was because he had a profound insight into how those within the Chan school at that time—such as Maming and Fenzhou Fazang—had defiled themselves and defiled the Buddhas and Patriarchs to such an extreme, yet remained unaware of it. His words were thus both painful and urgent.
The root cause is that they have not realized that [the object] truly exists; they falsely imagine that after awakening there is something truly attained.
Once they think they have attained it, their reputation rises above the world and their benefit lies in themselves alone. Yet, whether they have attained it or not, there is no evidence whatsoever.

Nevertheless, they do not hesitate to claim for themselves that they have already attained it, and no one knows otherwise—just like a thief who, before entering the room, does not know it is empty, yet wishes to steal from it.

Boasting of his extraordinary treasures to his companions, he said, "At the age of fifteen, I already knew that by my fortieth year I would have stolen a great quantity of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, tridacna shell, agate, coral, amber, pearl, and other such gems.
When the time arrived, it was indeed so. Having spoken thus, he further brought out countless bricks, rubble, excrement, and soil to deceive them.
The companions each claimed that they had obtained extraordinary treasures;
yet, in truth, they did not know what was actually inside the room, nor had they seen the shapes of the jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, tridacna shell, agate, coral, amber, or pearls.
Thus, they deceived one another in turn, and none of them ever left.
Furthermore, one may feel pity for him. Moreover, Mocaang (Mogujŏn) and his son delighted most in comparing themselves to Confucius and Mencius.
Confucius said, "At fifteen, I set my will upon learning," and Mencius said, "At forty, my mind was unshakable.
Thereupon, they falsely claimed that at fifteen they already knew [the truth] and would realize the Way at forty; thus, the statement that they realized it at forty was used as a veiled allusion.
He deluded the scholars and gentlemen of his time, who were neither learned nor wise. With such mental conduct, was he not possessed by a demon?
The demon concealed its slander against its master, Miguang Yunwu. On the summit of Mount Tongguan, the sentient and the insentient suddenly and brilliantly manifested.
This was merely a case of his eyes deceiving him. He claimed that his enlightenment arose from this, thereby deluding his disciples.

He said that as soon as he prostrated himself before Langquan, he suddenly felt dizzy and vomited about a pint of phlegm; he slept for five days. Then, outside the window, two monks were breaking a large bamboo stalk against a fence, the sound like a sudden clap of thunder.
Startled by this, he leapt up from his pillow and suddenly attained the realization of the emptiness of mind. He thought to himself: "The ancients..."
What people call the "severance of the past and future limits" cannot be settled by mere sitting; one must investigate it with all one's strength.
Suddenly, while looking at his own Linquan cloth robe, he lost his nostrils. To speak such a falsehood—how could this be merely a single instance of blurred vision?
It is truly that five days later, his dream has still not awakened. He certainly did not yet know the true meaning of the "severance of the past and future limits," yet he spoke falsely.
He says, "I am having a 'borderland' experience; it must be because there is a stone of phlegm in my chest. I have only vomited about one *dou*, yet eight or nine *dou* still remain unvomited.
How does this relate to whether one is sitting or not sitting, which cuts off the past and future?

Does he mean that the five days before falling asleep constitute the "past limit" (*pūrvānta*) and the five days after falling asleep constitute the "future limit" (*aparānta*)? From this, one can clearly see that he has never [practiced].
To take up three limits as one limit—that one limit is no-limit—and for that no-limit to abide as the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi):
if you have not yet realized this, how can you speak of the "Qingzhou cotton robe"? Furthermore, the Qingzhou cotton robe is precisely the nostrils of the monk;
how could they be lost? Moreover, the Qingzhou cotton robe is simply the Qingzhou cotton robe. For those who have awakened, what need is there to push it away?

If one does not awaken, how can it be attained merely by exerting all one's strength in investigation? One might boast that awakening becomes deeper with each turn, yet remain unaware that as it deepens, it becomes increasingly erroneous.

Having exhausted the mind and its powers of thought, one takes the direct words and true words of the ancestral masters from of old and interprets them all as idle furniture regarding the "Three Essentials" and "Three Essentials. One explains every item as being "one" or "three," taking this to be...
Is it not the case that the fundamental tenet of Linji is: "When consciousness is vast and boundless, one has no foundation to rely upon; how could one ever attain great utility?
Yet you instead take the appearances of the ancients' enlightenment and, with a semblance of artifice, fashion them into your own achievements to deceive the world and future generations.
How can you know that this matter absolutely cannot be fabricated? You merely cause those with clear eyes to deride it as a fabrication.
With a false mind, one labors daily in increasing deviousness. Demon-Ren (Mo-ren) composed a verse on this: "Cutting off the vast waves, he comes and goes by himself;
The new autumn moon and its reflection make the fishing line cold. The old fisherman holds his small carp and returns home; How could he ever hold a dragon’s pearl in the palm of his hand?
As for the Tathāgata, he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is named "Thus-Come One" (Tathāgata). Thus, the past mind—
It cannot be apprehended. The future mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended.

If one thoroughly understands this mind, then one knows that birth-and-death, coming and going, are ultimately without intrinsic nature. This is called the severance of the prior and posterior limits.

When the prior and posterior limits are severed, then the three limits become a single limit. The prior limit has already passed; the posterior limit has not yet sprouted; and the present limit, moreover, does not abide.
Since there is neither before nor after, there is no middle; thus, the single limit is the limitlessness.

To clearly realize limitlessness while vividly discerning the three periods of time, and to vividly discern the three periods of time while clearly realizing limitlessness—then this "non-existence that is not non-existent" is precisely the "existence that is not existent," which is the actual reality of the limitless. Thus, how could there be what is called a "severing of the great flow"?

Is it that the flow itself involves coming and going? Since there is both coming and going, it has never been severed. Since there is this inherent coming and going, one has already fallen into the great torrent.
Furthermore, this great torrent, which does not cease day or night, is precisely the Immovable Site of Enlightenment (*acalabodhimaṇḍa*).
To say that it is severed is to be a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*), for there is simply no principle by which the great torrent could ever be severed. And...
If one does not cut through [delusion], there is no stream that is not severed; yet this remains unclarified. Furthermore, what then would constitute the moon, and what would constitute the seal?

The father and son of the Tsang lineage (Tsongkhapa and his disciples) falsely identified the ancient sayings regarding the severance of the anterior and posterior limits, as well as "great death" and "great life," as being actual dharmas.
Consequently, they took five days of sleep to be "great death," and were startled awake by the sound of breaking bamboo.

To take five days as the limit for life and death, defining them as the boundaries of the past and future—how could one know that upon awakening from this single dream, one is still merely a spirit within a bamboo leaf?

Even if, upon awakening, one were to master all manner of supernatural powers—shifting stars and changing constellations, riding on clouds and spewing mist—it would still be nothing more than a spirit within a bamboo leaf; it has not yet been...
The past and future limits are severed. This is like the state where, amidst the dense clouds atop Mount Tongguan, the sentient and the insentient suddenly manifest with brilliant clarity;

it is similar to this realm. Yet, you mock Miyun for remaining fixed in this realm and seeking no further progress, claiming he is not as good as Magong, who after attaining this, went on to study the Three Essentials and Three Points, and so forth.
This is a Dharma-gate. Thus it is said: "The old fish, holding its carp, simply returns home; how could one obtain the dragon’s pearl to gaze upon in the palm of the hand?
Such demonic teachings are truly capable of severing the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*).

If one can indeed sever the continuity of the past and future limits, then even if Śākyamuni Buddha were to appear in the world and personally transmit the Buddha-dharma from his own mouth, one would not deign to desire it—let alone speak of a dragon’s pearl. Only such a person [is fit].
The two aspects of phenomena are empty; therefore, the limits of the past and future are severed.
How could there be a principle of separately going to study a most profound and essential dharma-gate after the limits of the past and future have been severed?

Old Fisherman Mìyún already knew that within the True Truth not a single dharma can be obtained—this is "returning home with a full boat, carrying only the bright moon," and furthermore, he has never once carried away a small fish in his gourd.
Ren’i, father and son, constructed boundless dragon-palaces and mirage-towers, boasting of their skill as masters of playing with pearls;
this was precisely what made them demons.
Ren’i’s record further states: later, while attending to the essentials of the Three Honored Ones, at the moment when the two head seats (shuzuo) simultaneously shouted, he suddenly—

Though more than four hundred years had passed, he felt as though no time had elapsed at all, as if he were receiving the seal of transmission personally within the very room. He was thus delighted to accept Gao Feng as his "Seal of Mind" and Juefan as his "Seal of Dharma.
Furthermore, lamenting that Master Jue had no dharma heirs, he intended to succeed him from afar. Thereupon, he closed his door and lay in high repose, focusing solely on...
He took what he had acquired and presented it to the ancients, who thoroughly investigated the subtleties of the Five Schools. He then composed the *Wuzongyuan* (The Source of the Five Schools).
Although the masters Zang and Ren had once memorized various scriptures of both the inner and outer teachings, [Zhi] merely plagiarized and imitated them, like a parrot that can mimic human speech;
though its words may be heard clearly, one does not realize they are ultimately bird cries. Such a person has not yet attained a human body. This is what is meant by...
Whether four hundred years pass or not, they are neither extended nor abbreviated. Is this not what is meant by "untimely"?

To act as if one were in the same hall personally receiving the seal of transmission—is this not what is meant by "unlawful"? As a verse in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "The abiding of time cannot be apprehended;

the passing of time likewise cannot be apprehended. If time cannot be apprehended, how can one speak of the characteristics of time? Time exists because of things; apart from things, there is no time."

"If time itself does not exist, how much less could there be a 'time' when things do not even exist? Yongming said: 'Since there is no phenomenon of coming or going, there is likewise no time of abiding or stopping.
One clarifies time by means of phenomena, and distinguishes phenomena by means of time. Since phenomena themselves do not exist, how could time possibly be established?
Worldly people take external objects to be themselves; they turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of sensory objects, taking movement to be the self."

When movement becomes the object, one acts with inversion; the nature of the mind loses its truth. While the objective realm does not actually shift, it is only the mind that moves delusively—like clouds racing and the moon appearing to move, or the shore seeming to slide as a boat travels.
If one attains direct realization of nirvana, then every dharma abides in its own station of True Suchness (tathatā);
there is not a single thing that comes or goes, nor has anything ever dwelt for even a single thought-moment, for all things exist without depending upon one another.
How could there be any shifting? Thus, if one is indeed able to realize and enter the Way of the non-shifting, eternally abiding single mind, then one does not race through past and present;

each nature dwells within a single lifetime. How then can one partition and segment it, such that it applies only to the four hundred years of the Awakened Model (Bodhidharma), while failing to distinguish between extension and brevity elsewhere?
Having clarified this principle of the non-distinction between extension and brevity, [the text continues: still...
How could there be any dharma to be attained? It is as if one were in a single hall, personally receiving the seal of certification.
Thus, that which has been done for over four hundred years—whether long or short—is exactly like a dream; it is still something created by the mind, intellect, and consciousness.
When has there ever been a severance between the past and future limits? And yet, that which was done—as if in a single hall, personally receiving the seal of certification—is precisely this.

It is like a hungry person who suddenly dreams that the rice steamer overflows; though he has not yet attained true fulfillment, he merely fancies himself at Mount Tiantai and studies the treatises of Sengzhao, composing these vague and indistinct arguments.
It is just like a parrot learning human speech—it cannot truly convey the meaning intended by people.
As for having already declared that the "prior and posterior limits are severed," yet still dwelling idly within the Three Essentials and Three Points; this is a contradiction.
[It is] complete. To say that one is "hotly deceived" by Linji implies that the continuity of the past and future has not been severed.

If one were to say that Gaofeng [Zhaojue] was certified in the mind and Juefan [Huihong] was certified in the Dharma, this would be to bifurcate the mind and the Dharma, which is all the more delusory and erroneous.

This is something even Ge Lu could not have known; it is not merely the talk of parrots among students of the Way. Furthermore, it is said: "Shutting the door and lying high in bed, he relied solely on what he had attained..."
"Let us consult the ancients. But where are those ancients? They are none other than the people of today.

To distinguish between the present and the past is itself clear evidence that the continuity between the preceding and succeeding limits has never been severed. If you wish to consult the ancients, why do you shut your door and lie in high bed?
To observe your closing the door and lying in high bed, it is evident that you have never once met an ancient. Moreover, since you yourself claim—
If there is anything to be gained, then the lacquer bucket has not yet been broken; nor is it necessary to further consult the ancients on this matter.
That one’s spirit is plundered and toyed with, revolving within the consciousness of karma, is already evident the moment one hears these words. Furthermore, he says:

"To exhaustively study the subtleties of the Five Houses and compose the *Wuzongyuan* (The Source of the Five Houses)—the single word 'subtle' alone suffices to humble the Five Houses. As for the *Mocong*, that which was composed by him—

Zongyuan presented [his understanding] to Miyun, but Miyun would not look at it. He informed him with a letter, saying: "Regarding the single character 'original' (yuan) you presented, I fear you have already become a follower of the school of intellectual understanding (*jiejie*).
If even the character 'original' has already become an object of intellectual understanding—how much more so when each of the five houses is like a great mass of fire?

Moshi further recorded: Later, hearing that Master Tiantong Wu had appeared in the world at Jinsu, the Master took up his staff and followed him.

"From the beginning, it has not been easy to find one who can settle the position of Chief Seat (Anshouzuo). Now, we entrust this responsibility to you, Master Han. That very day, he invited the Master to serve as the First Seat.

In matters of human affairs, there are those that complement one another so as to become more manifest, and there are also those that obstruct one another so as to bring mutual detriment. Take, for example, the father and son of Miu and Yang:
in a single hall, they "cracked the egg" and "pecked the shell" together to reveal the primordial sound. Is this not what is meant by "each enhancing the other's excellence"?
As for the words recorded by Mo-ren regarding Mi-yun’s address to the assembly, they merely buried Mi-yun; how could they have ever rescued Fa-zang?

Miyun composed a defense against false accusations; this is recorded in detail in the differing accounts of Yimo, Han-yue, Tan-ji, and the others, which serves to demonstrate the falsity and absurdity of what he said.

To boastfully display the Dharma-treasury would mean that Miyun was not a descendant of Linji, and his lineage would likewise not be the lineage of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
This would be more than just a tortoise bearing a divine chart only to meet its own doom;

it is hardly worth mentioning in the case of Miyun himself, let alone regarding the Dharma-treasury he received as an entrustment. If this were not so, then [his claims] would be nothing but a fabrication.

Regarding the words of Miyun shown to the assembly, and the claim that Miyun’s Way was made even more venerable by Fazang serving as his head seat—this may indeed be considered both deceitful and foolish.
While [Fazang] was bobbing his head in and out of the pit of excrement, he dragged Miyun along with him and buried them both in the same pit.
Is this not a case of one’s actions causing obstruction and bringing ruin upon another? Furthermore, as for Miyun...
If Yungu’s statement— that Master Han had realized the truth, was truly a great scholar, and that his fame preceded his appearance in the world— were to be accepted,
then before Miphan reached the Dharma-treasury of Jinasāgara, he would have already presented his entire life’s record of transgressions.
A single word has judged it all. Furthermore, he has already exerted every effort to uphold the Dharma-treasury and cause others to overturn their habitual thoughts;
yet, alas, they fail to awaken, and the calamity extends to their descendants, who instead take this very thing as a source of pride.
He repeatedly used pretexts to interrogate Mìyún, and in turn, Mìyún sat with him using double-tongued speech.

This truly is what Sīmà Qiān meant when he said that such matters "cannot be recounted one by one to people of the world. he presumed his own state of awakening to be authentic, believing he had recognized several words and had read through [the scriptures].

Those who study the secular classics boast of their great learning, yet they are but blind scholars of their time; those who practice Chan are like sheep with no tongue, passing on what they have heard.

If, after hearing these words from Miphan, you feel a sense of shame and dissatisfaction, take this seed and plant it in your heart.
Vomit forth all the toxic heat of passions. Generate a fierce and powerful resolve to seek that which accords with your own fundamental nature;

then you shall not fall into the power of Māra or the external paths from beginning to end. Alas, before even reaching the Golden Grain, one is already drenched head-to-foot by a ladle of foul water from the dense clouds, yet remains entirely unaware.

Yun: One can be certain and free from doubt. Although Miyun’s realization had not yet reached the ultimate ground, observing his words throughout his life, they never fell into the realms of demons or externalists.

Since you do not recognize the esoteric point of "a single blow," how can you possibly recognize that establishing the intent through the phrasing and dividing the schools according to the words is not esoteric?

To have such leisurely domestic affairs as these is not even comparable to the transmission of the various crafts and skills of the hundred artisans, which provide practical utility for the world;

"The Tathāgata’s wisdom of knowledge and vision refines it with such secrecy that how could one ever exhaust it? This remark by Huanglong is a muddled account.

Furthermore, he said: "The ancient masters established their fundamental tenets with such thousandfold security and hundredfold firmness, yet there are still those who ride upon empty air and catch echoes, muddying our true school.

The flowers are yellow; they have long been mixed up. Crows cawing and magpies chirping—bamboo is green, flowers are yellow. Turning toward this, one realizes its perfect fusion and inexhaustibility.
Even the current Master Zang and his son, who treat demons, spirits, and heterodox paths as such, are themselves creating demons, spirits, and heterodox paths.
How could the True Dharma ever have been mixed up by them? Furthermore, regarding what...

Your conception of a self is as secure as a thousand locks and a hundred bolts, yet you fear others might seize upon empty echoes to confuse it.
It is like using filthy water to wash sandalwood while hoping to remove its dust and grime, unaware that the filthy water itself will stain it.
