Compassion based on shared essence is brought forth for the sake of others to untangle their predicaments and release them from their attachments. Yet, when various Dharma gates are used as such, they all become poisonous drugs;
to use them to harm oneself is nothing more than a lifetime of delusion, and to use them to harm others is to enter the Avīci Hell immediately.
Now, one who captures birds uses a net; a single eye of the net cannot function as a net. Fundamentally, it requires both guest and host.

Your Majesty and your ministers all believe that this is for people to "untie the glue and remove the bonds. If one can indeed untie and remove them, it is precisely what is meant by "catching a bird with a single mesh in the net.
If those like Zangren were to cling to this as a substantial dharma, they would be treating a single mesh as the entire net.
If it is as you say—that one has realized the "message of Peak Master dropping his pillow"—then you should go on to study Linji.
Originally, there was only the host and the guest; furthermore, you have gone off to join the four peripheral schools.
To investigate in such a manner is like having already tied one mesh of a net, only to tie another mesh of a net.
Even if you were to tie as many meshes of single-eyed nets as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, how could there ever be a day when you catch a bird? As for this—

Furthermore, searching for the terminology of the *He* and *Luo* diagrams can provoke a great laugh. If one awakens to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), even the *He* and *Luo* are contained within it.

If one seeks the Perfect Teaching through the *He* and *Luo*, it is like seeking ice from fire. As for the *He* and *Luo*: during the time of Fuxi, a dragon-horse bore a diagram out from the Yellow River.
Upon its body were markings: one and six in the north, two and seven in the south, three and eight in the east, four and nine in the west, and five in the center.
Eight is in the east; four and nine are in the west; five is in the center. This is it. During the time of the divine Yu, a divine tortoise emerged from the Luo River carrying a book.

The markings on the tortoise’s back were such that it wore nine upon its head and stepped upon one; three was on its left and seven on its right; two and four formed its shoulders, while six and eight were its feet.

The five [elements] abide in the center; this is so. Confucian scholars of the secular tradition do not understand this and suspect that there lies within it some mysterious and unfathomable mechanism.
They fail to realize that Fuxi evolved the *Yi* (Changes) based on the River Chart, and the divine Yu evolved the *Fan* (Patterns) based on the Luo Book.

These were the divine wisdom of the sages, by which they could penetrate the patterns of Heaven and Earth and exhaust the transformations of the myriad things—[wisdom] comparable to that of the dragon-horse and the divine tortoise.
How so? If the dragon-horse and the divine tortoise had not encountered Fuxi and Shennong, they would have been nothing more than mere hairy insects and shell-dwelling insects.

Among the moving and stationary creatures of heaven and earth, there are many whose patterns, veins, and numerical structures correspond with those of heaven and earth—not only the dragon-horse and the divine tortoise, but even the human body itself, with its five viscera, six bowels, nine apertures, and hundred skeletal members.

How could it ever fail to encompass the numerical principles of Heaven and Earth? Since Fuxi evolved the *Yi* based on the River Chart (*Hétú*), its significance was already fully contained within the *Yi*.
Since the Divine Yu evolved the *Fàn* based on the Luo Book (*Luóshū*), its significance was already fully contained within the *Fàn*.

Yet the Confucianists set aside the *Yi* and *Fàn* without expounding upon them, while regarding [the numbers] one-six in the north, two-seven in the south, three-eight in the east, four-nine in the west, and five—

Regarding the diagram among these ten: it bears nine on its head and wears one on its feet; three is on the left and seven on the right; two and four form the shoulders, while six and eight form the feet;

five occupies the center. As for the script [of this diagram], to laboriously investigate and research it in search of its numerical significance is like planting rice to harvest grain, yet refusing to cook it into rice to eat, instead chewing upon the straw and husks—how could one possibly fill one’s belly? This is the "Demon’s Storehouse."
Having dabbled in non-Buddhist classics, he encountered the texts of the *Hetu* and *Luoshu*.
Delighted that these were such dark and obscure nests, he then dragged the Perfect and Constant [Dharmakāya] into the *Hetu* and *Luoshu* to flatter the ignorant scholar-officials of his time;
he dragged the *Hetu* and *Luoshu* into the Perfect School to deceive the illiterate Chan monks of that day. There is originally no need for deep refutation, yet now I fear that Chan...
My fellow students do not yet understand the grand purport of the Great Changes (*Yījīng*) and the Great Plan (*Hònfàn*).

Some may still claim that the patterns of the Yellow River and Luo River provide supplementary benefit to the Perfect Teaching (*Yuánzōng*). I cannot help but add this "foot to a snake. Now, regarding how the *Hétú* evolved into the *Yījīng*:
Heaven produces by means of the numbers one, three, five, seven, and nine, while Earth completes by means of the numbers two, four, six, eight, and ten. Thus, there is production and completion.
They combine to form the six children: mountain, marsh, thunder, wind, water, and fire. These eight interact and complete one another, and therein all things are contained.
The nature of Heaven is strength; the nature of Earth is compliance; the nature of the Mountain is stillness; and the nature of the Marsh is joy.

The essence of thunder is movement; the essence of wind is penetration; the essence of water is sinking; the essence of fire is clinging. These eight elements intermingle and intersect, encompassing the nature of all things.

Within this realm, man possesses a transient body that communicates with the qi of the two great powers and the six children, and interpenetrates the bodies of the two great powers and the six children. This body, along with the family and the state—

Heaven and earth join, and thus the myriad affairs arise and the myriad emotions emerge. Now, the governance of affairs depends upon principle (*li*); yet if the emotions are not in harmony, principle cannot be realized.

The Sage, wishing to demonstrate the true nature of the myriad affairs to people so that each may accord with its proper principle, found that while emotions are manifold and cannot be fully enumerated, he therefore returned to them by means of these eight [categories], interweaving and synthesizing them through the methods of threefold and fivefold combination.
It is shown to them: from eight up to sixty-four, and from sixty-four up to four thousand nine hundred and sixty.

This causes people to contemplate the images and understand their underlying sentiments; to master those sentiments and clarify the principles; and to apply those principles to regulate their affairs.
In this way, they commit few errors. This is the general outline of the *Yi*. As for the *Luoshu*, it evolved into—
This is the pattern. Although its categories are nine, its net consists of only three: first, revering Heaven; second, cultivating the person;
and third, diligently serving the people. Among the nine categories, the numbers one, four, and seven represent the way of revering Heaven; the numbers two, five, and eight...
The way to cultivate oneself consists of three, six, and nine. The way to diligently govern the people consists of one, four, and seven.
First, regarding the five elements (*pañca-bhūta*): water, fire, wood, metal, and earth. Their substance resides in the earth, while their essence resides in heaven;

these constitute the body of Heaven and Earth. Fourth, regarding the five cycles (*pañca-yuga*): the year, the month, the day, the stars and constellations, and the calendrical calculations; these constitute the movement of the body of Heaven and Earth.

This is the locus. Seventh is the examination of doubts. There are five types of tortoise-shell divination: yu (rain), ji (clearing), meng (obscuration), yi (movement), and ke (success). There are two types of stalk divination: zhen (the primary hexagram) and hui (the secondary hexagram).
In all matters concerning the movements of the body of Heaven and Earth, there must be a mind. The mind of Heaven and Earth cannot be seen;
one dares not attempt to fathom it with the consciousness of an emotional being that possesses attachment and stagnation. And...
By examining the patterns and numerical calculations of insentient things, one seeks the ultimate fruit of the mind of Heaven and Earth.
When one acts in accordance with what is determined to be correct, the Way of revering Heaven is fully realized. As for the "two, five, and eight": [these refer to the hexagrams and trigrams].

The second is the five matters: appearance, speech, vision, hearing, and thought. These consist of an appearance that is reverent, speech that is compliant, vision that is clear, hearing that is acute, and thought that is sagacious.

Fifth, when each person accords with the ultimate standard, they are said to possess "Serenity," "Orderly Governance," "Wisdom," "Counsel," and "Sagacity. Outwardly, these govern the person; inwardly, they govern the mind. Regarding the Five Imperial Standards:

the Son of Heaven manifests Serenity through a reverent countenance; he manifests Orderly Governance through compliant speech; he manifests Wisdom through clear vision; he manifests Counsel through acute hearing;
and he manifests Sagacity through profound reflection. Thus, the Emperor establishes the Imperial Standard. From the high ministers down to the common people...
The people all take this as their refuge, following the instructions of the Son of Heaven and receiving his blessings;
thus, what is called in the Great Learning—that from the Son of Heaven down to the common people, all must take the cultivation of the self as the foundation—is established here.
Eighth is the "Manifestations of Fortune" (*shuzheng*): rain, sunshine, warmth, cold, and wind. From the Son of Heaven down to the common people, their person...
Whether one cultivates these virtues or fails to do so, all resonate with the qi and numerical cycles of Heaven and Earth, just as a form has its shadow and an echo follows its sound.

Whether rain, sunshine, heat, cold, and wind accord with what is appropriate or not, all are brought about by the appearance, speech, sight, hearing, and thoughts of humanity—just as a person is satiated when they eat and hungry when they do not; there is no other cause.
Because of these distinctions between them, there must be no failure for rain, sun, warmth, cold, or wind to accord with what is appropriate.

Only then will one know that the people of the world each cultivate their own persons. When the people of the world each cultivate their own persons, the Way of cultivating the person by a single individual is perfected.
As for the "threes, sixes, and nines," the three are the Eight Administrations (*aṣṭa-karma*): food, wealth, sacrifices, the Ministry of Works (*sīkōng*), and the Ministry of Justice (*sī*).

The Tu (Ministers), the Sikou (Minister of Justice), the Bin (Guests), and the Shi (Teachers)—these eight constitute the means by which the affairs of the people throughout the world are governed and regulated.
The sixth is the Three Virtues: Rectitude and Integrity, the Power of Firmness, and the Power of Gentleness; these three can encompass the customs of the people and the local traditions of the world.
The ninth is the Five Blessings and the Six Extremities: the good are encouraged toward them by means of the Five Blessings, while the evil are [discouraged] by means of the Six...
The second [section] is "The Great Plan" (Hǒngfàn), by which the inequalities of the world are leveled to reach ultimate equilibrium, and the way of diligent governance for the people is perfected.

This is the general outline of the Great Plan. Now, although the *Great Changes* (*Dàyì*) and the *Great Plan* emerged from the River Chart and the Luo Book, even though the markings were complete upon the body of the dragon-horse and the numbers were arrayed upon the back of the divine tortoise, yet...

As for its meaning, it was elucidated by Fuxi and the divine Yu; now that this meaning is fully contained within the *Great Changes* (*Dàyì*) and the *Great Plan* (*Hóngfàn*), why seek it separately from their texts and numerical systems?

When the meaning of these *Great Changes* and *Great Plan* enters this Perfect Teaching (*Yuánzōng*), it is precisely "seeing mountains as mountains and seeing waters as waters," which can serve as the six perfections and myriad practices.

The wondrous flowers in the sky, the auspicious events within the dreams of the four modes of birth and the three realms of existence—when compared with the supramundane Dharma, they are indeed close to the Vinaya.
If one seeks the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) therein, it is just like boiling sand in hopes of making rice.
To make a mirror by polishing a tile—how could sand be the cause of rice? A tile is not the substance of a mirror;

how much less so can that which was produced by the "Demon Treasury" regarding the Yellow River and Luo River be anything more than the empty talk and fragmented words of worldly scholars who seek out texts and calculate figures, abandoning the fundamental for the peripheral?
To claim that one can realize the Perfect Teaching within this [system] is not merely mistaking one's head for a reflection;
it is to take the shadow of a Han-lu hound and consider it one’s own true head. This is truly something that cannot be met with even a single laugh.

Furthermore, you boast shamelessly in grand words, claiming not only to carry the burden of the Hetao (Linji) lineage, but also to cause the four houses—Yunmen, Guiyang, Caodong, and Fayan—to look on from afar.

I am deeply grateful for your recent favor, which has caused the five schools to shine once more. May we be the seeds that reconnect the severed lineage in every life and birth—how can such words even be uttered?
It is simply because you have taken all the skillful means (upāya) of the five houses used to untangle attachments and loosen bonds, and arranged them exhaustively as the *Hetu* diagram:
one and six in the north, two and seven in the south, three and eight in the east, four and nine in the west, and five and ten in the center.
In the Luo Shu, nine is worn on the head and one is trodden underfoot; three is on the left and seven on the right;
two and four form the shoulders, while six and eight form the feet; five occupies the center. This is the actual number and the actual method of assembly.
For this reason, although the Five Patriarchs were already divided into five, he further divided Linji into two: assigning the Mind to Gao Feng and the Dharma to Jue Fan, and thus comparing them.
These two lineages of the Dharma may be merged to establish the true orthodoxy of Linji; let this be taken as the fundamental tenet.
Those who do not accord with one's own views are treated as enemies; first one seeks to deceive others, and eventually, one deceives oneself.

It is like drinking a delirious drug: one takes what one has fabricated oneself and, in turn, believes it with deep conviction and without doubt, regarding it as the seed for reconnecting a severed vein.
Little do they know that this is actually severing the very root of the life-force of wisdom.
In the end, those who had previously studied at Beiquan Temple in Wumen—both old and new practitioners—gathered together all at once; hundreds and thousands assembled without number.
A consciousness like an ignorant, mute sheep, it incites a host of powerful and influential external protectors;
acting as cranes and geese, they form ranks and lines, establishing a military array for a sectarian doctrine.

They vow to engage in a fierce battle with Mìyún and seek to seize him, swearing that they will not rest until they force him to adopt their doctrine. How demonic! How demonic! This is no mere Vairocana.
Above our heads, within the Constant Quiescent Light (Dharmadhātu), there exists this demonic saliva and calamitous water.
Nevertheless, if such a kalpa must thus run riot, then as for the fundamental tenets [of our school], whether they are right or wrong, there is truly no need for deep deliberation.
In his final moments, he felt a sense of shame and remorse, realizing that he could not ultimately escape the definitive judgment of the two characters "Real Dharma" (shí-fǎ).
Consequently, with his deluded views and attachments, he sought to incinerate in a single furnace the High Peak Juefan whom he had taken as his heart-approved successor,
the Mìyún who had fraudulently passed on the staff and whisk, as well as the patriarchs of the four, seven, two, and three generations, down to the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the Vairocana Era.
"However," he said, "I wish to avoid causing harm to those who come after me. I do this as a way to repay the kindness of the Dharma-milk;

I wish to shield myself, yet I do not realize that in the end it is impossible to shield oneself. To act with such a heart and conduct is merely to be a *chao* or a *jing*—a creature that reveals everything it harbors within.
Is it not the case that whatever exists within must inevitably manifest on the outside? Magu Ren then remarked, "Miyun follows [the path]..."
This is the principle of the Xingzong (School of Practice). Yet, from this point on, the case of the "source and stream" (yuanliu) was settled.

If it is already a fundamental principle, how can one seek its ultimate resolution within the mouths of others? Instead, this merely washes away the shame of Mimi Yun for recklessly entrusting the Dharma-treasury regarding the source and stream.
How could you then claim that the case of the source and stream was settled from this point forward?
Moksin said: "I served my late master for the longest time, yet I have often harbored doubts regarding the moment of transmission.

It seems that while the initial relationship between father and son was not handled with sufficient care, it underwent alteration later on. Was it perhaps because his great vows were so vast that his conduct became careless?

Why is there such profusion of words? Upon searching through his written inquiries, however, I see that he yielded and declined the succession two or three times before finally granting permission for its practice."

Only after [the Emperor] had accepted the fundamental purpose did he receive the letter. King Kimsul (Suvarṇa-śāli) personally replied to the correspondence, praising every single character as brilliantly as the stars and the sun;
this may still be seen today at Mount Muryeong in the Yuanzang Canon. If this is so, from where could the current rift have arisen? Alas!
To be arrogant in a high position is not without its defense of shortcomings; to be overly direct in loyal speech often resembles self-importance. For this reason, slander—
Within their mouths they concoct schemes, while onlookers watch them stir up turmoil from without. They weave together patterns of artifice and set traps for calamity;

they degrade the Way and its righteousness to mere human sentiment and impose legalistic categories upon the Buddha-dharma. This is simply because those who propagate the Way have failed to perceive it clearly.
To seize such treacherous men and cast them before the wolves and tigers—those who utter such talk, how could they avoid the blade or the carving block?

After Mo Ren had recounted in detail the beginning and end of the dispute between his master and Mìyún regarding their respective tenets, he stated that Mìyún had personally replied to the letter, praising every single word.

He further claimed that in his later years, Mìyún had listened to slander and subsequently engaged in difficulties with Fǎzàng, citing a verse from the "Village Official" chapter of the *Xiaoya* (Minor Odes) to express his desire to cast that wicked man to the wolves and tigers. Furthermore—
To wish to sacrifice one's life for this, not shying away from the blade or the chopping block, is truly laughable and ridiculous; it is pitiable and moves one to tears.

When the Perfect Teaching reaches such a state, it is utterly swept away and destroyed. Now, the Dharma of the Buddha is free from contention; to engage in contention is to fail to uphold the five precepts, and if that is so, how can there be a "school" (zong)?
Setting aside the question of whether the books of Mip’an preserved at Dengwu are authentic or forged, even [if they were genuine...]

Suppose there were such a thing. How would you understand it? When the three Buddhas followed the Fifth Patriarch on his night journey, each uttered a phrase, and the Patriarch alone granted his approval to Yuanwu, saying, "The one who will extinguish my school is Keqin.
When Linji was about to pass away, he said to Sansheng, "What a pity! My treasury of the true Dharma-eye is about to be extinguished by this blind donkey. If Miphan had answered...
I write: If one were to interpret [the teachings] as praising each single word, then the words of the Fifth Patriarch and Linji would have to be interpreted as mere insults.

Furthermore, why should one not take his staff for what it is—a staff—and his shout for what it is—a shout? Yet, picking up the drool and saliva of foxes and wildcats, you interpret them as the "Essential Principle" (zongzhi).
Clinging to what you have grasped, you claim that others do not understand; you take advantage of their lack of understanding to boast of your own ability to understand. This is self-delusion.
They fall into saṃsāra, with no time of emergence in sight. When Master Fazang and his son received this "first ladle of foul water" from Míyún directly upon their heads, they still did not awaken;
instead, they cherished this ladle of foul water as a precious treasure, passing it down from son to grandson and recording it in vermilion writs and iron bonds.
How bitter! As the *Śata-śāstra-vibhāṣā* states: "If one follows one's own deluded awareness and clings to a self, how could that not [lead to suffering]?"
It is merely by taking the impermanent body and so forth as objects that one engages in false discrimination and clings to them as having a self. Why is this?

We see in the world that it is only with respect to the body and so forth—across their preceding and succeeding states—that, according to the distinctions of various conditions and positions, one falsely calculates:

"I am fat," "I am thin," "I am bright," "I am dark," "I am suffering," or "I am happy. Such things may occur in relation to the impermanent body and its like; however, [they could not occur] in relation to something permanent.

In reality, there is no such distinction between self and non-self. Thus, these various demonic patiences and sticky arguments are like the shadows of snakes seen in a cup by those who cling to the view of an impermanent body;
they arbitrarily give rise to right and wrong, falsely conceptualize a personal self, and recklessly intrude upon the matter that lies beyond the Buddhas and Patriarchs—is this not a sinful karma?
As for his disparagement of Mìyún, it goes without saying that he did not understand Mìyún’s mind at all.

[This is] the practice. In truth, Mìyún was not like this. If one were to say that Mìyún truly was like this—that Mìyún was merely a dull-witted worldly fellow—then what trace of even a hair’s breadth of Buddha-dharma could possibly be spoken of?

If so, then as for what Mócháng and his son obtained from the source and stream of Mìyún, what would that source be, and what would that stream be? And yet, they remain in a state of ceaseless indignation and resentment. It is essential...
To take the essential tenets [of our school] and argue with others over "you are wrong" and "I am right" is exactly like a drunken elephant entering a pond;
the more it leaps and bounds, the deeper it sinks. When will the clouds of delusion ever part? When will the fires of anger ever be extinguished?

To say that those who engage in such talk do not fear the blade or the chopping block is to misunderstand; for as for the right or wrong of these tenets, they are matters not discussed within the worldly dharma (*saṃvṛti-dharma*). Who would...
"The blade and the cutting board are already upon us; however, as for the sin of slandering the Buddha, one cannot escape the mountains of knives and trees of swords in the realm of King Yama.
Moran said: "When Chan Master Xinghua Jiang was initially the attendant to Linji, he had already attained realization.

Later, at Sansheng and Dajue, he thoroughly penetrated the source of the Dharma. Having entered the world [as an abbot], he offered incense and said: 'This single stick of incense was originally intended for...'"
"Three Holy Elders, my elder brothers! To me, the Three Holy Ones are too remote; to me, Great Enlightenment (Dajue), my elder brother, is too distant.
It would be better to make offerings to the late Master Linji. I remarked that Xinghua’s incense offering thus brought forth, in its entirety, the ancestral style of the Ji North lineage.
Among those of recent times, my late master alone was one who understood this ritual form. However—
From this, polemical writings were produced; from this, rifts and dissensions arose. How difficult it truly is to speak! On my part, I say:
"The fundamental tenets are that which the life of wisdom depends upon. My teacher is one who continues the Buddha’s life of wisdom.
If I do not contend for them, who would dare to contend? On their part, they say: "Three Peaks is my disciple. For a disciple to surpass his teacher is an ancient [principle]."
It has not yet happened. If I do not suppress it, who can? Furthermore, those who place their faith in Sanfeng distort the truth to obtain a semblance of it;

those who favor Tiantong delight in the easy path to achieve fame. They scrutinize others with harsh intent while tolerating flatterers to attach themselves to their own person, each claiming to be propagating and protecting the Dharma in the Final Age.
This is like being on the same boat, sailing together toward a common destination.
Amidst such perilous and treacherous waves, they brandish spears and fight one another;
even a passerby would feel chilled with fear at the sight, yet those who do not cease their fighting—can they truly be called wise?
When Xinghua held up incense, he clearly identified Dajue, Sansheng, and finally Linji as those to whom he made offerings.
This was spoken by Xinghua solely from the perspective of what he himself had realized within his own mind; how could it ever have been intended as a model for ten thousand generations?

Yet, like a demon hiding behind a mask or Dong Si mimicking the frown of a beauty, and like learning to walk at Handan, Mingchu followed the example of Gaofeng and Juefan, finally making offerings to Muzhou.
Yun: "Mōrin thus claimed that, among those who know these ritual methods in recent times, his own master was the only one.
By doing so, he deluded the world and deceived the people. One does not realize that before those with clear eyes, this would not even merit a laugh. Let alone the significance of Xinghua’s action."
This [case] is inherently insufficient to serve as a model for others. How could it have any connection with the family style of the Ji-Bei (Jinbei) lineage?
Let us discuss this by comparing the two matters of Xinghua and Fazang. The mental activities of these two men were as far apart as heaven and earth.
Although Xinghua studied under Dajue and Sansheng, what he claimed was that "he learned the 'Guest and Host' phrase from Sansheng, while at Dajue..."
As for those who fall into error, how can they seek the "great bird's tracks" in the snow and claim that Xinghua attained the Dharma from Dayue?
If this were the way to attain the Dharma, it would mean attaining some substantial dharma—and that would be to betray the Three Sages and Dayue.
As for the point where he grasped the tip of the nose, it was because he had personally approached Linji; thus, [Dayue] brought forth Linji’s [teaching].

Ji: This is precisely where Xinghua’s direct mind and direct action lie. If Magang claimed to have attained his mind from Gao Feng and received the Dharma from Juefan, only to seek further certification from Miyun—and yet Miyun did not accord with him—then it would mean that Miyun owed him not even a trace of the grace of the milk of the Dharma.
His receiving Miyun’s staff and whisk was merely like the "costume of Youmeng."
As for Guan’s extensive offerings made to Mìyún, what can they possibly signify?

Since he owes Mìyún no debt of gratitude as a "Dharma-milk" (spiritual progenitor), his claim that he attained the mind from Gāopíng and received the Dharma from Juéfàn is precisely what is meant by an "unlearned externalist.
Now, while the fundamental tenets of our school are indeed tied to the life-force of wisdom, [the transmission must remain authentic].
The master is indeed one who continues the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom.
Yet, when discussing the very tenets that constitute this life-force of wisdom with another who likewise continues it, he says, "I do not dispute. Who then would dare to dispute him?
Is this not the very essence of the teaching: that there is the dharma of contention? It is precisely because of the existence of a self (*ātman*) that there is contention;

if there were no self, who could contend? It is precisely because of the existence of dharmas that there is contention; if not even a single dharma could be apprehended, what would there be to contend over?
As long as craving for dharmas is not exhausted, one is a person who has fallen from the summit. Even the perfect realization of *nirvāṇa* is still a view of self.

For those who [practice this], attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is difficult to forget; it is the most subtle, establishing the root-source of birth and death, serving as the foundation for all suffering, obstructing the great path to Bodhi, and severing the primary cause of liberation. Even if one diligently cultivates the fruits of sainthood...
Throughout many lifetimes across kalpas, [those who follow such paths] are merely termed "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) and do not realize the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment].

How much less so for the likes of Māgandika and his son, who cling to fabricated tenets such as the "double-headed" or the "single-knot"; what strange names and bizarre forms these are! They are but non-Buddhists and demonic influences.
Thus, father and son have succeeded one another in engaging in contentious debate with their own grandfather, severing the life-force of wisdom in others and defiling the Dharma-gate.

For all sentient beings who wish to repay the Buddha’s kindness and who are unwilling to allow the life-force of wisdom to be severed, they must certainly distance themselves from and refute such views.
How much more so, given that Mimi Yun has personally received a prophecy regarding these disciples of Māra and externalists—how could this be permitted?

He did not merely repeat himself, but explained the profound meaning with clarity, opening the way once and again, hoping that others would turn their heads toward the further shore and block the cross-currents of heterodox teachings.
This ensures that future generations will not perpetuate errors indefinitely and serves as a means for him to save half of his own soul.
As for Mogen’s claim that Miyun suppressed [his disciples] because he resented their superiority over his own followers, this is truly an act of measuring the great by the mind of a petty man.

The belly of a gentleman is like oil mixed into flour; there is no end to it. A cup of water cannot extinguish the fire of a wagonload of firewood, nor can animal glue stop the turbidity of the Yellow River.
This must also be something that even Mimiun could not remedy, as there was nothing he could do about it.
Now, regarding this wondrous mind of nirvana, the ocean of pure awakening, an ancient master once asked: "What kind of place is this? May it be contained therein.
You speak of the coarse and the subtle; you speak of the coarse and the subtle, yet even this is not permitted.
You then liken it to being on the same boat crossing treacherous waves, only to take up spears and fight among yourselves—how can your defilement reach such a state?
Since you are already amidst these treacherous waves, you have not yet escaped the ten thousand sufferings of saṃsāra and birth-and-death.

Various bitter karmic seeds remain. What is meant by "the fundamental tenet" (zongzhi)? Those who take up weapons and fight one another over a fundamental tenet—are they disciples of Māra or disciples of the Buddha?
Is it the fundamental tenet or not the fundamental tenet? Surely it need not necessarily be the enlightened who can discern this.
In the *Mōnin-ki* (Record of Mōnin), the Small Sermon on the Dharma-Treasury states: "The state prior to the stimulus is where you all establish yourselves;
the first stroke prior to the stimulus is where you all establish your life-force. Within this interval, moving left or right, extending or contracting," so it is said.
"This is the place where you all tread with your feet. This final phrase is the place where you all emerge your heads.

These four phrases alone—if you can penetrate each one through them, it is like transforming a single path of pure wind that passes through a thicket of thorns, entirely free from even a single point of obstruction.
If there is even the slightest thing you cannot penetrate, it is like wearing a tattered cotton robe while passing through [the same thicket].
Within a forest of thorns, there are eastern pagodas and western stupas; one has no freedom of movement. Is there anyone who can penetrate through?
Come forth and sing a verse in response! After a long silence, [the Master] raised the case of Great Master Yunmen’s visit to Muzhou.
When Muzhou saw him coming, he simply closed the door. The Master said, “What a fine piece of news! Yunmen knocked on the door. Muzhou asked, “Who is it? Yunmen replied, “It is I. Muzhou said—
When Yunmen acted in this manner, he said, "My own matter is not yet clear; I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "What an honest old man you are!
When the gate was opened, as soon as Yunmen saw it, he closed it again. The Master said, "Enter through here. For three days, Yunmen knocked on the gate in this way.
On the third day, as soon as the door was opened, Yun pressed forward. The Master said, "A fine carp surging through the waves.
Zhou seized him and said, "Speak! Speak! Yun was speechless. The Master said, "You nearly lost your scales. Zhou then pushed him out and said, "An axle-pin from the time of Qin!"
He then shut the door, wounding Yun’s leg. Yun immediately attained awakening. The Master said, "You only know how to leap through the Dragon Gate;
you do not know how to burn off your tail. He directed Yun to visit Xuefeng. The Master asked, "How many people truly know this mind?
When Yun arrived at Xuefeng’s manor, he saw a monk there. Yun asked, "Are you going up the mountain today? The monk replied, "Yes. Yun said, "Please give me a message..."
This is the causal condition. He asked the Abbot, "One must simply not say that these are the words of another person. The monk said, "I can do so.

Yun said, "When you, Senior, arrive at the mountain monastery and see the Abbot entering the hall, as soon as the assembly has gathered, you should step forward, clasp your hands behind your back, and stand there, saying:
'Why does this old fellow not cast off the iron cangue upon his neck? The Master said, "Xuefeng had no way out."
The monk followed Yunmen’s teaching exactly as instructed. When Feng saw the monk speak in this manner, he descended from his seat.

The Master said, "The battle clouds shift; the hexagram draws its lines. Feng grabbed the monk by the chest and held him, saying, "Speak! Speak! The Master said, "That is still just Muzhou’s nostrils.
The monk was speechless. Feng pushed him away and said, "Those were not your words. The monk said, "They were my words. Feng—
[The Master] said, "Attendant, bring the rope and staff. The monk said, "This was truly not my words;
it was an elder from Zhejiang on the estate who instructed me to come and say this. Feng said, "Everyone, go to the estate to welcome the five hundred virtuous teachers.
The Master said, "A thief recognizes a thief; a refined person recognizes a refined person. On the following day, Yun went up to Xuefeng. As soon as Feng [saw him],...
Upon seeing him, Yun said, "How did you manage to reach such a state? The Master replied, "There is not even a portion of it that can emerge. Yun then bowed his head.

The Master said, "The lines have been shifted and the images exchanged. From this point on, they reached mutual accord. After years of refined study, the Master secretly transmitted the seal of the lineage to him.
The Master then said, "O Great Assembly, tell me: since he has already realized the truth by tripping over his own feet as he pushed through the door, what further is there to attain?"
Xuefeng possessed such a strategic approach. Now that Xuefeng has passed away, what can be done? Why, then, must one still refine and study it over many years?
As soon as it is sealed with the seal of the school, why not investigate it thoroughly right here? After a long silence, he said:
"Great assembly, this one move of Yunmen comes from Muzhou’s moment of closing the door upon seeing [him].
Muzhou comes from Huangbo’s sticking out his tongue. Huangbo comes from Baizhang and Mazu’s place of great functional power.
Now tell me, what is this one move of Yunmen? *Ei!*” Then he descended from the seat.
From ancient times, those of supreme virtue have responded to the capacities of beings with inexhaustible perfection, like a pearl rolling upon a tray.
Yet, their self-benefit and benefit of others do not at all involve a deliberate engagement with those capacities; it is as if the pearl rolls naturally upon the tray because it is perfectly round.

If one seeks the pearl from above the tray, one will not only lose the substance of the pearl, but will also lose its function. If you wish to find a secure place to dwell and establish your life, you must first relinquish [all grasping].
One loses one’s body and life. If one has not yet reached the point of great death or great life, one still seeks body and life before and after the pivot;
how could every lifting and placing of the feet be within the site of enlightenment? Where would you allow him any chance to show his head? Mazu said:
"The state prior to the pivot is exclusively where you all settle yourselves. That single move prior to the pivot is where you all [reside]."
Regarding the establishment of one’s dwelling for life and destiny: I ask, from where exactly is this body and life established?

If you say that there is nowhere that is not the place to dwell and establish one's life, then how can one distinguish between the "preceding movement" as the dwelling of the body and the "first stroke of the mechanism" as the establishing of destiny?
Now, the mind is the root and dharmas are the dust; the interaction of root and dust is like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another.
When this reed has fallen, that reed follows and topples. If one truly forgets both mind and dharmas, the boundaries of past and future naturally sever.

Where else could one seek a "prior momentum" (ji) that is consistently directed? A single stroke prior to momentum involves many complications; a consistent direction prior to momentum—[where would it be sought?]
It is precisely not permitted to settle the body outside of things; it is merely one move of the initial opportunity. It is precisely not permitted to dwell alone on a solitary peak;
rather, upon the six or seven consciousnesses, one forgets their origin, and within the dharmas of the sense-bases and objects, one forcibly assumes mastery.
The lacquer bucket has not yet been broken. Thus, whether moving left or right, extending or contracting therein, all is accomplished by one's own mind.
Bound and fettered, when have you ever trodden the path of true practice? Naturally, at every step you enter the thorns.
It is also said that the "last word" is the place where all of you emerge from the head; yet if you speak of the "last word," not even a thousand sages have a portion to emerge.
If you claim for yourself to emerge here, you have already buried your head within the shadows and glimmers. Furthermore...
Citing two cases of Yunmen’s study under Muzhou—where Muzhou directed him to visit Xuefeng—I shall provide a commentary for each segment.
To take the words of these ancient worthies as literal or factual speech is entirely to set out snares and nets, merely flaunting their sharp mental triggers (*jīfēng*).

If one interprets the Buddha-dharma through the lens of such mental triggers, this is truly to slander the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. Even Zhuang Zhou was able to say that "those who possess the affairs of the mechanism [of the Dao]... [cannot be fathomed].

The mind harbors a calculating intent. How could it be that those who receive the transmission from Buddha to Buddha and from patriarch to patriarch are all merely things that Zhuang Zhou would have shunned and refused to do?
Furthermore, it is said that Yunmen attained awakening when his leg was broken by a pushing door;
yet at Xuefeng, he also displayed such strategic maneuvers. Once Xuefeng had passed away, what could be done? Why, then, must one refine and study for many years? As soon as—
Seal it with the seal of the fundamental principle (*mudrā*). Why not investigate and examine this very point?

These few words refer to what is called "small awakening" followed by "great awakening," as well as the so-called "great awakening" that occurs after one has awakened and is then able to study the Lesser Vehicle teachings.
The minor laws of the Great Dharma are the root of all manner of erroneous doctrines.

When the virtuous ones of old acted for the sake of others, even if they knew that a person already belonged to the vessel of the Dharma, they would necessarily wait for a long, long time to observe whether their practice and understanding were truly in accord, and whether their liberation was perfectly pure.
Only then would they bestow a prediction of enlightenment. This was because it is truly difficult to find such a person and must not be treated lightly; how much more so now?
From the Tang and Song dynasties onward, the karmic conditions of Nanquan Puyuan and Shoushan Shigong were disseminated among the people. This was different from when Bodhidharma first arrived;
at that time, the single school of "Direct Pointing" had not yet flourished in China, such that one could find resonance through a mere fragment of speech and immediately believe it to be unerring.

There was no need to fear encountering those who merely pick up the spittle of others, or students who play with lumps of clay—those who, by mere chance, borrow the appearance of the Way while remaining empty within.
Regarding the affairs of Confucius, how could they be treated with such negligence as to be handed over merely through a prophetic record?
It is precisely for this reason that one must first refine and investigate them over many years, and only then seal them with the seal of the fundamental principle (*mudrā*).

How could it be that after awakening, one would again allow the karmic winds of ignorance to rise, releasing the conceptualizations of the discriminating consciousness, and through arduous thought and strenuous seeking, attempt to propagate all manner of wild and heterodox views from every quarter?
Fox-slobber and spittle. At first, it is like the pedantic glosses of a scholar, weighing and measuring word by word and phrase by phrase;

later, it becomes like the cunning artifice of a market broker, capable of speaking from between the eyebrows and eyelashes. Only then do they claim that the "essence" (zongzhi) is clear, and only then do they seal it with the "seal of the school" (zongyin).
If this were the case, every single one would become a demon, and the Gate of the School (Zongmen) would utterly perish. As Mazu Daoyi said: [The text continues with the citation of Mazu’s words.]
This move of Yunmen comes from Muzhou’s moment of closing the door upon seeing [him]; Muzhou comes from Huangbo’s sticking out his tongue;
Huangbo comes from Baizhang, Mazu, and the functioning of their great capacity. But tell me, what is this move of Yunmen?
*Ei!* It is simply because of the skillful means with which Yunmen engaged people throughout his life. He looked back at them.
Baizhang immediately perceived this. As soon as [Muzhou] was about to question him, Baizhang uttered an "Ei.

He then took this single instance of "Ei" and, like a faint trail of smoke from a burning snake, traced it all the way back to Mazu’s great function of the spiritual mechanism, thereby clarifying that this Perfect Teaching consists of nothing but a single mechanism.
By doing so, he cast a distant reflection upon what Muzhou called his "primordial mechanism" (*xiānjī*)—that "one move" of the primordial mechanism—thereby deluding and bewitching beginners.
Muzhou, Yunmen, Huangbo, and Baizhang—within the realm of eternal quiescent light—could they not all raise their voices in unison and cry out, "What a grievous suffering!

Yongming said: "To align texts to fixate on a specific meaning, or to follow every word to divide the schools, is to stir up the mental mechanisms within the realm of True Suchness, and to create self-imposed fetters within the unconditioned Dharma. This is truly what is meant by the 'treasury of demons.'"

The *Mozang* states: "I have often seen artists depicting the origins of the Seven Buddhas, beginning with Beiyin (Vipaśyin)."
Regarding the Buddhas of the Seven Ages: once the diagram of the "Great One" (the zero) was established, each of the seven Buddhas had their own verbal explanations.
Although these explanations differ, the essential meaning of the verses of all the Buddhas does not transcend that diagram. Now, "awe" (*wei*) refers to that which lies beyond form;
"sound" (*yin*) refers to that which lies beyond voice. As for the King of Awe-Sound (*Weiyinwang*), he exists beyond both form and sound, and has never been recorded in writing.
There is no basis for textual verification; this is the supreme matter prior to written words.
It was only through Nāgārjuna’s manifestation that we came to revere what is called the signless samādhi (animitta-samādhi), which existed prior to Dīpaṃkara.
Miyun took the "māra-store" (macang) and fabricated the "one-zero" (10) as the progenitor of the thousand buddhas and ten thousand buddhas.

He later regretted that his assembly contained such demonic and heterodox disciples, which would bring disgrace upon future generations; thus, he opened [the gates] once, then twice, up to seven times.
The Mara-Subduer (Mozhi) rescued it later by composing the *Wuzongjiu* (Rescue of the Five Houses). Miyun further composed the *Biwangjiu* (Dispelling Delusions Rescue) to clarify it.

The Mara-Fazang (Mo-zang) refers to the beginning of the Seven Buddhas, which starts with Vipaśyin Buddha (Weiyinwang Fo). After [the Buddha] drew only the great circle symbol (○), the Seven Buddhas [arose].
Each has its own verbal explanation. For now, there is no need to cite the full intent of the verses of the seven Buddhas;
let us simply take the first phrase of the verse of the first Buddha, Vipaśyin. Did the Buddha not say that the body receives birth from within the formless?
Is the "one-zero" (10) hidden by Māra not itself a form? Even as Māra himself speaks, he has never failed to name it "perfect" (yuan).

[This refers to] the "marks" (lakṣaṇa). Regarding these characteristics: the intent of this verse lies within the perfect characteristic (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*). Yet, this perfect characteristic possesses the internal, the external, and that which is between them.
If the perfect characteristic possesses the internal, the external, and that which is between them, then prior to King Bhīṣmagarjitasvara, where would this perfect characteristic be situated?
And after King Bhīṣmagarjitasvara, where would this perfect characteristic be situated? Would this not result in a logical absurdity?

In discussing this, it is further said that "awe" (*wei*) is that which lies beyond form, and "sound" (*yin*) is that which lies beyond voice. "King Awe-Sound" (*Wei-yin-wang*) is that which lies beyond both form and sound;
there has never been a vehicle to convey it, and there is no basis for verification. It is the most supreme matter prior to written characters.
Now, even that which lies beyond form and sound is merely a gateway of this present age; how could it be the realm beyond King Awe-Sound? Furthermore, [it is not].
Regarding the two characters "awe" (wei) and "sound" (yin): if one interprets the meaning based on the text in this manner, they reside precisely within the words themselves.
How, then, can it be said that they exist prior to the words? It is like having "awe" outside of form, yet awe ultimately arises from form;
or having "sound" outside of voice, yet sound ultimately issues from voice. Thus, they likewise reside precisely within form and voice. How, then, can it be said that [they exist] outside of form?

It is beyond both form and sound. As for what was mentioned above regarding the "formless samādhi prior to the lighting of the lamp," could this possibly refer to a majestic presence outside of form or a resonance outside of sound?

If one were to claim that the period before the two polarities (Heaven and Earth) had yet been divided constitutes being "beyond form and sound" as worldly scholars do, then such a person has not yet even recognized the meaning of the two characters "Tathāgata. Furthermore...
From where could one possibly speak of that which lies beyond the limit of Vipaśyin Buddha? For going and staying are simultaneous, and past and present are a single thread.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "I observe the distant past as if it were this very day. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Dharmas have no coming or going, for they never abide.
If one realizes this true mind that abides nowhere and this wondrous nature that is immutable, only then can one [proceed].
Within non-discrimination, one forcibly discriminates between that which lies beyond the era of Wei-yin and the gateway of this present life.
Now, as for what is called "beyond the era of Wei-yin," does it not refer to the vast and formless antiquity? Time arises because of dharmas, yet dharmas are fundamentally non-existent.
The substance of the dharma upon which one relies is like empty space; how could there be any "ancient" or "modern" within that which relies [upon it]?

This very threshold of the present world is itself the other side of the *Viyūha* (Awe-In). If one invokes the other side of the *Viyūha*, one must not again invoke the threshold of the present world.
Only through direct realization can it be known; it cannot be expressed in words. Now, the Dharma-treasury (Dharmakara) refers to the Buddha Vairocana-king (Vaiśvānara-rāja) as the "Great One" alone.
It was only upon reaching the Seven Buddhas that verbal designations (*vyavahāra*) first appeared.

Thus, at the time when Vairocana-king dwelt in the world, this was already the gateway to the present for Vairocana-king himself. What, then, would have been the point of the "signless samādhi" (*animitta-samādhi*)? Therefore, its...
That which is referred to as the "Great One Zero" (10) is precisely the script of King Vaibhiṣaṇa.
Furthermore, what could be more supreme than that which precedes all script? To rely on words to explain meaning is to be at odds with the Buddhas of the three periods.
All the infinite distinctions of names—such as mundane birth-and-death and supramundane nirvana—are known to be established by means of script. If...
There is no knowledge or vision of words and letters; both name and substance are empty. As for the fundamentally wondrous and luminous mind, what else could possibly exist?

It was only because worldly people were deluded regarding the truth and abandoned their fundamental nature, clinging to appearances and pursuing names, that the ancient masters provided alternative expedients to point them toward it beyond words and letters—such as ○, ∴, ●, ◎, and so forth. All of these were employed out of necessity.
Having already done so, you now again employ the methods of speech and written characters to compose commentaries upon it,

even claiming that the seven Buddhas of the Western Heaven once commented upon this "One Circle" (○), and further asserting that this "One Circle" was created by the Buddha King of Awesome Sound (Vibhūṣaṇarāja),
just as Fuxi drew his trigrams. This is truly nothing more than explaining a dream to a fool.

Mofen said: "What is referred to as 'beyond form and sound' does not specifically point to the Vimalacandra mentioned in the *Lotus Sūtra* or the Dīpaṃkara who conferred the prediction upon Śākyamuni.
Looking upward toward our own school, there are three types of Dīpaṃkara: the Dīpaṃkara before, the Dīpaṃkara after, and the Dīpaṃkara of the present—these are they.
This forms a great circle (○) as a symbolic representation, just as the *Taiji tu* (Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate) is used to illustrate Heaven."
At the stage when the myriad things had not yet taken form, it was not that this diagram was definitively held to be the *Tàijí* (Supreme Ultimate).

The *Pìshū* claims that our former teacher arbitrarily fabricated a "one" (○) to cover over Śākyamuni, asserting that since Śākyamuni appeared after Dīpaṃkara, this [diagrammatic] sign could not possibly exist prior to Dīpaṃkara.
Alas! How can such a person know what is meant by the aforementioned Dīpaṃkara?
Ah! Regarding the profound intent within this Dharma, it would be useless to discuss it; let us for now discuss its superficial aspects to clear away the faults of our former teachers.

"Before King Vairocana was enlightened, how could Maitreya be conscious? He also drew this [symbol]. Now, some claim that Caoshan was mistaken.
"Can one clench one's fist to cover over Weiyin and Maitreya? Is this possible? When he heard this, [the Master] said:

"Those who wear felt and coarse wool cannot be discussed regarding the exquisite fineness of pure brocade; those who eat sorrel soup and parched grain are insufficient for deliberating upon the richness of the great ox sacrifice.

People will laugh at such a person; how much more so for one who attempts to practice the Way of Linji and Deshan in this final five-hundred-year period!
In the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta:

"In the distant past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (*Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja*) Tathāgata. The name of that kalpa was..."
Leaving behind decay, there was a land named Mahāsiddhi. In that world, the Buddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvара taught the Dharma.
The lifespan of this Buddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvара was forty quadrillion *nayuta* Ganges-sand eons, and the duration of his True Dharma remaining in the world was for the same number of eons.
The number of kalpas for which the Semblance Dharma remains in the world is equal to the number of atoms in one Jambudvīpa.

After that Buddha has brought great benefit to sentient beings, he then enters parinirvāṇa. Following the total extinction of both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, another Buddha appears in this land, also named Vimalasvararāja Tathāgata. In this manner, there are twenty thousand such Buddhas in succession.

There were two hundred billion Buddhas, all bearing the same name. This is what Migha (Miyun) refers to as the deeds of the World-Honored One Vidyutghoṣarāja (Weiyinwang Buddha) recorded in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Fazang states that Vidyutghoṣarāja lived prior to the Seven Buddhas.
Thus, according to the sequence spoken by the World-Honored One, there were twenty-two thousand billion Buddhas, all bearing the same name; furthermore, he spoke of the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta.
To have personally beheld the majestic power of Vīradhvaja—could he possibly be anyone other than myself? Would such a claim not belong entirely to the realm of fanciful tales?
Yet, "to deviate by even a single word from the Sūtra is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three ages; to depart from even a single word of the Sūtra is the teaching of Māra.

Now, I shall record the life and deeds of Vīradhvaja as set forth in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, alongside the dates and months of the seven Buddhas who were lit by the lamp, Śākyamuni, and Maitreya, compiling them into a chronicle of the Buddhas.
To alter even a single character of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* of a nation—is this not to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three periods?

If you claim that this does not definitively refer to the Vidyottama mentioned in the *Lotus Sūtra*, but rather that there is another Vidyottama Buddha, and furthermore, if you draw a large circle (○) and call it a "symbolic representation," is this not to depart from a single character of the sūtra and thus constitute the teaching of a demon? Ultimately, regarding the Vidyottama spoken of by the World-Honored One...
Regarding these historical accounts: why are they considered words of suchness and truth rather than mere fanciful tales?

If you have not yet clarified this point, to claim that "before the Vipaśyin Buddha there were no written characters" and that "the seven Buddhas have already fallen into the trap of verbal expression" is nothing but arbitrary fabrication and deluded talk, like a blind man describing an elephant.
Since you do not know what the ultimate meaning of the Vipaśyin and seven Buddhas is, you certainly do not understand it.
The prediction of Śākyamuni by Dīpaṃkara refers precisely to what was mentioned above: the period before Dīpaṃkara, after Dīpaṃkara, and during the actual presence of Dīpaṃkara.

Furthermore, within this sutra, since it clearly states that the Bodhisattva Constantly Non-Disparaging is none other than Śākyamuni, even such accounts found in other sutras as the pigeon’s marrow and the goose’s pearl are likewise [identical].

Śākyamuni: here, one should understand this merely as a parable. It is not strange that [the text] refers upward to the three *Dīpaṃkaras*, for it does not mean that there was a single *Dīpaṃkara* who conferred the prophecy upon Śākyamuni.

Furthermore, citing the public case (koan) of "Cao Shan’s Unawareness of Vipaśyin" and "Maitreya’s Lack of Lucidity," which depicts this *bindu* symbol, it explains that Fazang meant Vipaśyin made a great circle (*o*).
This is an error. Yet, when did Caoshan ever say that Vipaśyin and Maitreya created this [seal]? [The opponent] says: "I do not understand. [The master] replies:
"How could they, being already awakened, create such a seal-form to display it? Thus, it is perfectly clear that this was created by Caoshan himself."
How could this compare to the false and fabricated fabrications of Fazang, who claimed that during the Great Kalpa of Weiyin, the Seven Buddhas each used verbal expressions [to describe] it?
Furthermore, Mo Ren even linked this to Zhou Lianxi’s *Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate* (*Taiji tu shuo*) to provide external support for his claims.
This refers to the depiction of the "One" (the zero) in the *Yīguān* (Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate), which illustrates the state before heaven, earth, and the myriad things had taken form.

To interpret it further in such a vulgar and perverse manner is utterly improper. The realm beyond *Vibhāṣin* (Wei-yin-na-pàn) is not the same as the state before heaven, earth, and the myriad things had taken form;
one must not understand it in this way. If it were possible to understand it in this way, then one would simply be describing the state before heaven, earth, and the myriad things had taken form.

At that very moment, one attains it. Why must one speak of "beyond the time of King Wei-yin"? Furthermore, at the moment when heaven, earth, and the myriad things had not yet taken form—how could King Wei-yin Buddha have made his great "one" (○)?
Moreover, prior to the existence of heaven, earth, and the myriad things, what was there?
There is only this one great circle (大○). As for its fruit, who has heard of it and who has transmitted it? For now, let us set aside such debate.
To speak merely in terms of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (太極圖): heaven, earth, and the myriad things share one single Supreme Ultimate, yet each possesses its own individual Supreme Ultimate.
This Great Ultimate (Taiji) is itself the Ultimateless (Wuji). The Great Ultimate is "being," while the Ultimateless is "non-being. This being is a being that is not-being;

therefore it is said that "the Great Ultimate is fundamentally the Ultimateless. This non-being is a non-being that is not-non-being; therefore it is said that "from the Ultimateless comes the Great Ultimate.
Vulgar Confucianists do not understand this, and thus claim that [it refers to] the time before heaven, earth, and the myriad things had taken form.
There are thus the Five Elements. Prior to the distribution of the Five Elements, there are Yin and Yang. Prior to the differentiation of Yin and Yang, there is the Great Ultimate (Taiji).
Prior to the formation of the Great Ultimate, there is the Ultimateless (Wuji).

If one does not know where this Ultimateless, the Great Ultimate, Yin and Yang, and the Five Elements are situated within the interval before heaven, earth, and the myriad things have taken form—where, indeed, do they abide? Furthermore, [The original Chinese text ends here.]
Heaven, earth, and the myriad things had all as yet not yet taken form. Man is but one among these myriad things, and those who harbor such erroneous views are but one among ten thousand men.

Since they themselves had likewise not yet taken form, by what means could they have known that at that time there were such levels of hierarchy or such intricate entanglements? How can they speak such great words without shame and make such judgments?

When one person transmits what is false, it becomes empty; when a thousand people transmit it, it becomes reality. Māra-Endurance (Māradharṣa) picked up this discarded saliva and used these teachings to rescue Dharmagarbha.
Dharmagarbha, in turn, picked up this discarded saliva and used these teachings to imitate the Seven Buddhas beginning with Bhīṣmagarjitasvara.

Their actions were such that the winds of conceptual thoughts—both contrary and compliant—agitated the ocean of awakening, while the waters of greed, delusion, and craving nourished the sprouts of suffering for those with cataracts on their eyes.
They give rise to flowers and further take these flowers as the very nature of their eyes. Confused about their own heads, they recognize only their reflections;
furthermore, they seek their original heads within those reflections. Thus they sink into deep mud and throw themselves into dense thorns—nothing is more pitiable than this.
Mozang said: "The portraits of the patriarchs from the Western Heaven originate [there], and the verses of the Seven Buddhas originate from Bodhidharma;

their transmission surely has its source. Miyun said: "Hanyue, on the contrary, brushes away the accounts of the Buddha Vimalacitra found in the World-Honored One’s Lotus Sutra, claiming that no such records have ever appeared and that there is no basis for verification. This is groundless and arbitrary fabrication."
First, regarding the "ten aspects": you claim that [the Dharma] existed prior to Dīpaṃkara;
yet, having already asserted it existed prior to Dīpaṃkara, how can you then claim that the Perfect Aspect (yuanxiang) originated with the various patriarchs of the Western Heaven?
Furthermore, since those patriarchs of the Western Heaven are all successors of Śākyamuni, by what means could they have existed prior to Dīpaṃkara? Thus, Han Yue’s own words are self-contradictory.
Regarding those whose own characteristics are contradictory: they desire that others not say Han Yue fabricated his words and teachings, yet I, this old monk, do not believe them.
Mo-ren said: "Changsha’s Great Tiger Cen said: 'The Buddhas of the three periods and the sentient beings of the dharma-realm are the light of Mahāprajñā.
Before this light has arisen, there are no Buddhas and no sentient beings; indeed, there is not even [a single thing]...'"
The news of the birth of the Buddha—that which our former master referred to as existing prior to the investigation of written texts—is precisely this meaning.
In the *Zaopo lun* (Peach Pit Treatise) on the Huayan Sūtra and the *Jiyin lun* (Silent Sound Treatise) on the Lotus Sūtra and other scriptures, names and events are mostly indicated through symbols.
How could these be compared to those who seek a sword by marking the spot where it fell from their boat? Now, as for "Vīrasvara" (Wei-yin), he is the mother of all Buddhas.
It is thus. The Patriarchs of the Western Heaven entrusted circular diagrams (*yuánxiàng*) to manifest this.
The Layman Bingshan said: "Before heaven and earth were born, the Sage was in the Dao; after heaven and earth were born, the Dao was in the Sage.
This is the point where one may use symbols to indicate it. To laboriously seek it through the traces of precedence and sequence—is that not wearisome?"
How perplexing! Furthermore, the *Bai shu* (Book of Refutation) states of itself: "Wei-yin is the majestic presence of all sentient beings, evident at a glance.
For now, setting aside the question of whether its reasoning is incorrect, let us tentatively address it by means of two points from the *Bai shu*.
One [aspect] takes the appearance and majesty of sentient beings as its form; the other clings to the historical traces of the *Dharmapada*.
Is this not a contradiction in one's own words? Or is it that the eye of insight has not yet been stabilized? An ancient master said: "The flowing spring is life; the profound stillness is the body.
The thousand waves competing to rise is the realm of Mañjuśrī; the single expanse of the clear sky is the couch of Samantabhadra."
Linji said, "The person of the Way who has no dependence is the mother of all Buddhas.

Zaozang paired Mañjuśrī with the hexagram Gen, making him the 'Youngest Son,' and Samantabhadra with the hexagram Zhen, making him the 'Eldest Son. Such instructions as these are not recorded in the canonical scriptures;
how then can one doubt that the single circle (一○) of Sanfeng is a fabrication?
An ancient worthy said: "If there were even a single dharma to be believed, that would constitute a false view. Only by not believing in anything at all does one truly achieve faith.
Now, if one does not believe in anything at all, what kind of faith is this? Could it be that the ancient worthy’s own words are self-contradictory?"

Only when one’s own realization reaches its ultimate depth does perfect faith (*pariniṣpanna-śraddhā*) finally arise. Once perfect faith has been established, it is natural that not a single dharma is worthy of belief.

When not a single dharma is worthy of belief, it is natural that not a single dharma is worthy of rejection. If there were even one dharma worthy of belief, there would necessarily be various dharmas worthy of rejection.
Since there would then be both rejection and belief, how could this constitute perfect faith? While appearances continue to manifest before one, one still follows along with them.
This shore. If one is truly able to recognize the verse of the Seven Buddhas, then both within and without the circle is entirely the light of Mahāprajñā.
Why inquire as to what its source is? If there were a source, it would be a heterodox teaching; if one takes faith to be the source, it is a false view.
This would be in direct contradiction with what was shown by the patriarchs of the Western Heaven and transmitted by the Seven Buddhas.
Setting this aside, there is no need to further debate whether the *xiang* (characteristics) necessarily originated from the patriarchs of India. The mind is the root;
phenomena (*dharma*) are the dust. Since the mind itself cannot be found even when sought, how much less so can the dust that faces the root or the phenomena that condition the mind?

If one gives rise to views regarding these phenomena, one forms attachments to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), which is precisely what it means to be single-mindedly pursuing external objects while remaining ignorant of returning [to the source].

Regarding the "Original" (Ben): the *Dharmakośa* states that this [text] and its verses have a source; this sufficiently demonstrates that he was deluded regarding the root and pursued only the branches.
When Mìyún meticulously discusses the life and deeds of Wèiyīn, recorded in the *Lotus Sūtra*, one cannot say there is no basis for his evidence.
Since the marks of [Wèiyīn] emerged from the various patriarchs of the Western Heaven, one cannot also claim they existed prior to Dīpaṃkara.
To discard its major errors and expose its minor errors is certainly not worth mentioning; yet Moxien attempted to rescue it, claiming that Fazang’s teaching—
that the Buddhas of the three periods, the dharmadhātu, and sentient beings are the light of the Mahāprajñā,
and that before this light has emerged there are neither Buddhas nor sentient beings, and indeed not even a trace of the arising of a Buddha— is [correct].
Such is the meaning [of his words]. This, however, does not at all rescue the Dharma-treasury; it merely serves to defile the legacy of Changsha Cen to no small degree.

Does this statement by Changsha Cen imply that once the light of the Mahāprajñā has emerged, there are written texts available for consultation, whereas before the light of the Mahāprajñā has emerged, there are no written texts and nothing can be consulted? From antiquity...
Pervading the present; pervading above and below; pervading east and west; pervading south and north—all is the light of Mahāprajñā.
Taking what as "not yet arisen"? There is nothing that is not the light of Mahāprajñā. Taking what as "already arisen"? If you can realize this, you will understand.
Thus, the Buddhas of the three periods and the sentient beings of the dharma-realm are the light of Mahāprajñā.
Before this light has yet arisen, there are no Buddhas and no sentient beings; indeed, there is not even a trace of the arising of a Buddha to be found.

To speak of "the light of Mahāprajñā" is already attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*). To speak of "before the light has arisen" is further to fall into the delusion of what is empty and non-existent.

The Treatise says: How much more so when one demarcates boundaries by taking the period before heaven and earth were born as the time when the light of Mahāprajñā had not yet emerged, and the period after heaven and earth were born as the time when the light of Mahāprajñā had already emerged?
Changsha Cen further added to his own grievance and suffering by citing Pingshan’s statement that "before heaven and earth were born, the Sage was in the Dao."
Once heaven and earth had already come into being, the Way was said to reside in the words of the sages as their commentary; this becomes increasingly untenable.
How could there have been a "Way" at that time before heaven and earth were born, such that it could be said to carry the sages within it?
And once heaven and earth had already come into being, how could this Way then be attributed solely to the sages, while [all else]...?

To claim that sentient and insentient beings cannot be given [as alms] not only greatly contradicts the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, but also greatly contradicts the Confucian discourse on human nature (*xing*) and the Way of Heaven (*tian dao*).

This is a preposterous and absurd argument from the prose essays of scholars written after the Tianqi era of the Ming dynasty; yet it has even been adopted to rescue the Dharma-treasury. How can this be extinguished?
Miyun: Han Yu’s poem on the toad says, "To act without reason is merely to seek clamor"—this is precisely what is meant.
Because Mich’ang (Fa-tsang) fabricated a "Great Circle" (da zuo yīng) based on the name Vipaśyin Buddha (Wei-yin-wang), Miyun used the accounts from the *Lotus Sūtra* to correct him.

Furthermore, because Fazang discussed the seniority and recounted the life histories of King Awesome Sound (Vaiśravaṇa-rāja) and the seven Buddhas, he explained that "Awesome Sound" refers to the majestic appearance of sentient beings, which is immediately apparent to those who look up. Consequently, Mo Ren claimed this was self-contradictory.
How could he have ever grasped Miyun’s intention? If Miyun himself had not yet grasped his own intention, how [could he understand Fazang]?
How much more so regarding the intent of the Buddha King Majestic Sound as spoken by the World-Honored One in the *Lotus Sūtra*. An ancient master said: "If you raise one, you must not raise two;
if you let one pass, you fall into the second. That which lies beyond the realm of King Majestic Sound is precisely the raising of one.
If you let one pass and fall into the second, then that "one" is already contained within it. If you were to exclusively raise one, you would not only lose it, but...

Secondly, because one [aspect] has been lost, the text speaks of the appearance and majesty of sentient beings—of those whose very glance is clear—and yet that majestic sound (Vaiśvānara) is right within it.
This is the Vaiśvānara recorded in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. As for Mōjin’s critique:
"Is this not a contradiction of your own words? Is your vision not yet settled? You cling to the literal text and characters to harshly reproach the Esoteric [teaching]."
Yun: "Miyun, what further explanation can you provide to resolve this? Furthermore, he cited the words of the ancient worthies:
'The flowing spring is life; profound stillness is the body. 'A thousand waves competing to rise is the realm of Mañjuśrī; a single expanse of clear sky is the couch of Samantabhadra.
