The theory that Samantabhadra corresponds to the hexagram Zhen as the eldest son, while Mañjuśrī corresponds to the hexagram Gen as the youngest son,

claims that both are no different from the "one-mark" (*ekalakṣaṇa*) described by Fazang. Now, setting aside Fazang’s assertion that the one-mark is the progenitor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas—
which certainly cannot be discussed on the same level as the other three theories— even among those three theories, furthermore:
How can they be treated as a single, undifferentiated whole? Linji said: "The man who listens to the Dharma before one's eyes, having no dependence, is the mother of all Buddhas.
Thus, the Buddha King Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara) does not depart from the place where sentient beings look up and see clearly.
An ancient worthy said: "Flowing water is life; profound stillness is the body. A thousand waves rising together is the realm of Mañjuśrī; it is a single, continuous expanse."
The clear sky is the bed of Samantabhadra. By making such a statement, one not only directly perceives Wei-yin (Vimalacitra), but also directly perceives the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging.
If Māgarṣa were truly able to awaken to these few phrases, he would certainly not harbor the erroneous view that Wei-yin is a great "one" (the primordial unity) nor engage in groundless speculation.
As for the discourse regarding the *Zao-bo* (Jābāli) and the trigrams *Zhen* and *Gen*, [it is as follows:]...
Even in the discourse on the *Yī* (Book of Changes), this is still untenable; how much more so regarding our fundamental doctrine?

For the meaning of the *Yī* cannot be such that there is no *Gèn* within *Zhèn*, nor no *Zhèn* within *Gèn*. This is because their meanings have distinct attributions; thus, one speaks of *Gèn* when referring to *Gèn*, and of *Zhèn* when referring to *Zhèn*.
*Zhèn* means movement; *Gèn* means cessation. There is no movement that does not involve cessation, nor is there any cessation that does not involve movement. Cessation is...
To stop that which is not stopping, and to move that which is not moving—now, if you take Mañjuśrī as "stopping" and Samantabhadra as "moving," how could this possibly be acceptable?
It would result in a double failure regarding both internal and external scriptures; how then can it be compared or viewed alongside the two previous theories?
Mozang said: "Let us try to examine this. The perfect circle already embodies the essential tenets of the Five Houses.
Each House manifests from one particular aspect, yet there is a primary, foremost source of the orthodox lineage: the tenet of Linji. This circle is cast forth directly to sever the life-root of men.
Within this single zero (○), guest and host roll and roll, entering straight into the eyes of Śiva. As it is said:"
"Following the stream without ceasing, ask how it is; true illumination is boundless—explain it to him thus. Free from characteristics and free from name, people do not receive it;
having used the 'whisking hair' blade, one must immediately polish it. This is it. Next is Yunmen’s Three Statements and the Single-Word Barrier.
The "perfect circles" (yuanxiang) of the Weiyang school originate from this. Fayen discussed doctrinal meanings beyond the six characteristics;
Caodong distinguished between "returning" and "interchanging" at the juncture of black and white. Within a single circle (○), the five schools are fully contained. Moran said:
The five schools each present one aspect; that is, each presents one aspect of the *maṇḍala* (circle) pattern to receive people.

For example, the Caodong school employs the "five ranks" (*wuwei*) through mutual interpenetration: sometimes using the partial to manifest the absolute; sometimes using the absolute to subsume the partial;

sometimes reaching both together where neither "contradiction" nor "contact" applies; and sometimes reaching both together where the entire body is noble. All of these are [expressed] through one aspect.
This is that which penetrates all aspects. Upon reaching the Linji school, however, it is cast off directly and immediately. Therefore, Linji is regarded as the orthodox lineage;
this is not to slight the others, but because he is called the "foremost among the five schools. The *Pibushu* (Book of Opening) states that each of the five schools presents a different aspect;
if this were so, one would have to divide this [circle] sign into five aspects. Since it is already divided into five, how could Linji alone possess it?
Yet, how could one simply cast it aside? Contemplating its intent, one sees that this *maṇḍala* (○) is regarded as a mere inert object.
One does not realize that while hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of faces emerge from this *maṇḍala*, the essence of the *maṇḍala* remains undivided;

and while hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of faces enter this *maṇḍala*, the essence of the *maṇḍala* does not become narrow. Such is the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Thus spoke the former Chan Master Jixiang Yuanshi.

The Master was a disciple of Tianyi Cong. Once, he happened to laugh loudly and disturb the assembly; Tianyi expelled him. He stayed overnight in a village field, where he observed the stars and moon shining brilliantly and attained a realization.
At dawn, he returned to the abbot’s quarters. When Tianyi saw him, he asked, "How do you explain the discourse on the five ranks of ruler and subject?

Shishuang replied, "In my place, there is not even a single rank. Tianyi ordered him to attend the hall and said to his attendant: [The text continues with the subsequent dialogue regarding the five ranks.]

This man possessed a point of insight; yet, alas, he did not recognize the fundamental principle (zongzhi). During the occasion of entering the room, the Master had five attendants arrange themselves in a line beforehand.
When Shishuang Shiqian arrived, the Master summoned him by his title, "Shishangzu" (The Elder Shishuang). At that moment, Shishuang secretly attained the profound essence of the teaching.

The verse states: When a single rank is revealed, the five ranks are distinguished; where ruler and minister meet, purple clouds gather. The night-bright curtain is rolled up, shining without partiality;
the layered golden halls manifest the Most Honored One. Those who know this may be spoken with regarding the opening and closing of the *xiang* (marks/phenomena).
Those who know the opening and closing of the *xiang* may discuss the similarities and differences among the various schools. Alas! The Way is indeed...
There is no contention; yet those who contend do so because their perspectives differ. When Wusheng Gong first attained awakening, could it be called "no-seeing"?
Could it also be called "thorough seeing"? Had it not been for the subtle refinement of Tianyi’s hammering, this would have stood as another formidable adversary to our fundamental tenet.
Nevertheless, this was not out of malice toward the tenet, but simply because he did not realize that the tenet existed.
Furthermore, not understanding [the teachings], they slander them. How could they not consider themselves saviors of the world?
Now, among the seven "Defenses" (*pì*), those that approximate the truth likewise defend against what is called "ignorance.
Among the three "Defenses," those that approximate the truth also defend against what is called "ignorance. Beyond these, there are merely words of reckless contention and violent abuse.
Thus, I have not recorded them in full here, wishing instead to preserve the spirit of profound kindness.
On the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*), not a single speck of dust is established; yet at the gateway of the myriad practices (*sahasra-caryā*), not a single dharma is abandoned.

Only when you have obtained some news from that place where not a single speck of dust is established on the ground of ultimate reality can you then proceed toward the gateway of the myriad practices.

Without abandoning even a single dharma from the head, one proceeds with every step taken and set down. Since one is already within the gateway of the myriad practices, there is naturally a sequence within that which is without sequence, and gradations within that which has no gradations.
If one speaks of the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), then the ten directions are equal and the single path is pure and void;
it does not fall into the realm of words or thought—how could it allow for distinctions? Now, the father [who] endures the treasury...

In your discourse on the Five Houses, you treat Linji as the primary orthodox lineage that appeared first, followed by Yunmen, then Weiyang, then Fayan, and finally Caodong. Does the Perfect School possess such distinctions?
It is merely that you wish to exalt Linji as the foremost of the five houses in order to demonstrate your own [superiority].
He is the legitimate heir of the primary school, reaching the pinnacle of glory and nobility, the most honored and supreme of all.
How could this be a matter of ranking as first or second, or of seniority and excellence, like generals being evaluated for merit or scholars competing in formal examinations?
According to his own theory, the Caodong school would be the very last; yet Dongshan said, "Even this is not it."
How much more so for the Zhangs and Lis, or for emptiness and non-emptiness? What is brought forth will not resemble it; it is as clear as something before one's eyes.
There is no room for even a hair’s breadth of conceptualization. Yongming said: "If even this is still not it, how much less so are the various other frantic faculties and erroneous understandings?
Thus, what is called the "One" (○) is cast down directly to sever the life-root of people. Within this "One" (○)...

That "guest and host roll on and on, straight entering the eye of Śūla" is merely what Dongshan did for "Zhang San and Li Si," and what Yongming did for those of "wild faculties and erroneous understanding.
Even if this were indeed the foremost orthodox tradition, it would still not be this very thing;
how could one use "Zhang San and Li Si" or "wild faculties and erroneous understanding" to distinguish the four?

As for the "Order" (zong): to categorize them horizontally according to a sequence—evaluating the five schools based on one's own realization of the "patience of Māra"—cannot avoid being scrutinized by those with clear eyes.

Consequently, he attempts to defend his position, claiming that taking Linji as the "orthodox school" (zhengzong) is not intended to exclude the others, but rather because it is the "foremost" among the five schools.
This is like using a bearded Zhang San to trade for a dark-complexioned Li Si; if a school could be so easily ranked...

If one were to argue based on seniority and juniority, it would be clear that the junior cannot equal the senior. How does this differ from the saying regarding the partial and the correct within our fundamental tenets?

It is like "the man who retreated fifty paces laughing at the one who retreated a hundred. Since the various schools of our tradition cannot be discussed in terms of right and wrong, how much less can they be debated by means of seniority and juniority?
Mìyún said: "Since each of the five schools has manifested its own particular aspect, one should distinguish these [five] circular aspects as follows..."
As for the "five faces," since they have already been divided into five, how could Linji have simply cast them down?
It was only because the royal treasury lacked such a sword that he spoke thus, unable to restrain his laughter; yet in the end, it merely results in frivolous discourse.

Having spent one's entire life being deceived by the tongue of Linji, one is further deceived by Xuefeng, drinking the drug of madness oneself and then using that same drug to drink others. How truly bitter is this! It is just as the worldly saying goes: [The original Chinese text provided was: 三要轉。遇四喝四賓主。即被四喝四賓主轉。遇三句。又被三句轉。平生受臨濟舌頭瞞不了。又被雪峰瞞自飲狂藥而狂。又復以狂藥飲人。誠何苦耶。正如俗 [The English translation provided above is: Regarding the "three essentials of turning": when encountering the four shouts and the four guest-host dynamics, one is turned by those four shouts and four guest-host dynamics; when encountering the three phrases, one is again turned by those three phrases.

Having spent one's entire life being deceived by the tongue of Linji, one is further deceived by Xuefeng, drinking the drug of madness oneself and then using that same drug to drink others. How truly bitter is this! It is just as the worldly saying goes:

Confucian scholars do not know what the Eight Arrays (*bāzhèn*) actually are. Upon hearing the terms "Heaven, Earth, Wind, Cloud, Dragon, Snake, Bird, and Tiger," they immediately claim that Wind and Cloud belong to Heaven, while Snake and Tiger belong to Earth, and Dragon and Bird reside between Heaven and Earth; thus they produce various interpretations based on the literal text.
They fail to realize that Heaven, Earth, Wind, Cloud, Dragon, Snake, Bird, and Tiger are nothing more than the eight colors of the Imperial Banner today—namely, the Yellow-Striped (*xiānghuáng*).
The colors of the Eight Banners, such as the Correct Yellow and others, are merely used as markers to distinguish military encampments.

Although they are named after Heaven, Earth, Wind, Cloud, Dragon, Snake, Bird, and Tiger, they have no actual connection whatsoever with these eight entities—Heaven, Earth, Wind, Cloud, Dragon, Snake, Bird, and Tiger.
Mo Ren claimed that he had personally traveled through Kuizhou and Xiazhou and seen Zhuge Liang’s battle formations, yet he lamented his ignorance [of them].
Those who examine the calligraphy consider it merely a jumble of stones; even those who understand calligraphy regard it only as a military formation diagram.
No one knows the subtlety of its "entering life and exiting death" and its "capturing and releasing" transformations.

To compare this with our fundamental teaching, there is indeed an "entering life and exiting death" and a "capturing and releasing" transformation, just like Zhuge Liang’s Eight Array Diagrams. This cannot be settled by a single, coarse blow of the staff.
This very patience toward Māra naturally includes its own invitation; it is the point where one acknowledges the karmic offenses of slandering the Great Prajñāpāramitā.
Within the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma, how could taking birth and entering death, or the transformations of capturing and releasing, be considered the ultimate?

It is simply because one does not understand that the patriarchs act for the sake of others—all their words are words of truth and reality. Even the arrangements of their teaching halls are likewise words of truth.
This is the truth. As for those places that cannot be approached, they all arise from what the practitioner brings forth by themselves.

To seize is for you to seize; to release is for you to release. All manner of transformations reside within you. Within your own fundamental nature, how could there be even a hair’s breadth of involvement?
If you first prepare for yourself the mechanism for birth and death, seizing and releasing, and transformation, then...
To wait for students to come while failing to first lose one's own mind—how can such a person act as a teacher? To claim to be acting as a teacher in this way, what benefit is there?
It is nothing more than engaging others in verbal combat. Furthermore, consider all things that are round and capable of revolving.
All must necessarily be without a root. If there were a root even as small as a hair’s breadth, then from that point of the hair’s-breadth root, it would not form a circle;
and if this root, even as small as a hair’s breadth, were not severed, it likewise could not revolve. Not only this:
now that the karma-consciousness of ignorance has been stirred up, one seeks out what are called the "lesser dharmas" and the "great dharma."

The minor dharmas of the Dharma have firm roots and solid foundations; though obscured by dust and buried in earth, once one has already fallen into the Great Iron Ring Mountains (Mahācakravāḍa), how could they ever turn back?
As for what you say regarding being born and dying, capturing and releasing, and manifesting transformations—these are merely empty falsehoods.

Furthermore, even if one were truly able to transcend life and enter death, capturing and releasing with miraculous transformations, and engage in verbal duels with the people of the world—such things would be mere empty words;

they would be nothing but a display of clever rhetoric. When seen in actual practice, they are but a manifestation of a calculating mind. What "fundamental principle" (zongzhi) or what "Buddha-dharma" could there be in such things?
If one must act in this way to be called "clear about the fundamental principle," then that is simply clarity regarding the fundamental principle itself.
Are these all necessarily those who must be executed by the laws of the state? The theory of the Eight Array Diagrams has absolutely no connection with our fundamental tenets.
Furthermore, even Māra’s patience was merely taken as a metaphor; there was originally nothing therein worthy of profound analysis.
However, he delights in using external classics to treat Chan practitioners of the moment with superficiality, and he even treats the illiterate Miyun with arrogance and contempt.
In reality, however, even I myself have never fully understood this; I shall now disclose it all at once to dispel the delusions of Chan practitioners throughout the world and for future generations.
According to tradition, there are three of Zhuge Liang’s Eight Arrays: one at Kuizhou, one at Xindu, and one at Mianyang.
As for the one at Yufu Port in Kuizhou, it is submerged when the waters rise.
When the waters receded, it emerged once more; having endured for thousands of years, it has not crumbled or decayed. The world regards it as divine.
Indeed, among the things of heaven and earth, there are many such inconceivable phenomena. It may also be that this is due to the firm consolidation of sincere devotion.
However, the diagram in question was originally not created by Liang himself; rather, eight [units] formed a square through their emptiness, while seven were solid.

Forming a circle from the center is a natural numerical principle; it is not something that human effort can create. As for the military formation employing the number eight, tradition attributes its origin to Fenghou;
however, it is evident that it did not originate with Zhuge Liang, as Dou Xuan had already employed it prior to him.
Furthermore, arranging stones to form such a diagram merely serves to leave a record for later generations; how could it possibly enable people to understand the art of war?
How could Zhuge Liang have undertaken such a fruitless endeavor merely for the sake of his posthumous reputation?

It was likely nothing more than a temporary training exercise for his soldiers, marked by the ritual ropes and mats (*mianzuo*). Later generations, longing for Zhuge Liang, venerated it as the "Gan Tang" tree of the Duke of Shao;
thus they called it the "Array Diagram of Marquis Wu. Yet within it, how could there ever have been any [strategies for] entering battle to capture the enemy or facing death?
Is this not the marvel of transformation? It is like the case of Duke Shao’s sweet pear tree (*gān táng*).
If a student wishes to seek the beautiful governance of the *Zhōu Nán* within that sweet pear tree, even if they search branch by branch and leaf by leaf, nothing at all can be found.
Furthermore, the Eight Arrays (*bā zhèn*) are merely the formations of soldiers during battle and the layout of encampments during defense; yet—

...finished. As for what is meant by "entering life and entering death," Māra’s patience regarding this so-called "entering life and entering death" stems from being deluded by the heterodox doctrines of the Qimen (Eight Gates) system—namely, Xiu (Rest), Si (Death), Shang (Injury), Du (Obstruction), Kai (Opening), Jing (Alarm), Sheng (Life), and Jing (Scenery). He claims that if an enemy enters the Gate of Death, they will inevitably die.
This is utterly far-fetched, foolish, and laughable. Furthermore, as for Māra’s practice of capturing and releasing [the enemy], it is because...
This recounts the story of Zhuge Liang’s campaign against Meng Huo. Zhuge Liang wished to thoroughly break Meng Huo’s spirit so that he would no longer cause internal disturbances;
thus, he allowed him to escape seven times before capturing him on each occasion. How does this have any connection to the battle formation diagrams at Yufu Ferry in Kuizhou?
The Fish-Return Bay (Yufu Pu) is the site of the Yong'an Palace;

it was there that [Zhuge Liang] established the "mianzuo" (temporary ritual enclosures) for training his troops when he plotted against Wu with Liu Bei. Today, it is ultimately nothing more than a heap of rubble.

Magu Ren considers this to be the place where the Martial Sage used the "seven captures and seven releases" to subdue Meng Huo, which is precisely like mistaking the three phrases of Xuefeng for something else.
The core meaning of this is almost identical. Moran said:
"Those of old who spoke of awakening described it as being like a lotus flower opening, or like suddenly waking from a dream;
I was convinced of this at Mount Mui. Yet Baizhang further preached the Dharma for me, saying: 'This is merely a temporary fork in the road. When the time comes...'"
...and so forth. It is further said: "Awakening is the same as non-awakening; there is no mind and there is no dharma.

At the moment when one deeply brushes away the fire and experiences a sense of joy and liberation, the flower of the mind blossoms with brilliance. Therefore, hearing the principle is most easily penetrated;

within these few words alone, everything is understood once and for all. If one waits until confusion is cast aside and error is embraced, becoming entrenched in habitual patterns, then even with a hundred methods—
Even after polishing and refining it, it is difficult to wash away the stains; this is what is called the grace of the Dharma-milk.
As for Yangshan, he was one who responded from afar to the prediction concerning the circular marks (*maṇḍala*) entrusted by the Western Heaven patriarchs—a true sage of the stage of fruition.

Yet he still said that he had attained the essence under Dayuan and attained its function under Weishan. How could it be that his wisdom was inferior to that of today? It is simply that he did not deceive himself.

Father and son, father and son—each illuminating the other in mutual brilliance. They opened the eyes and ears of humanity, establishing a model to be followed for a hundred generations. It is only fitting, then, that Baizhang said:

"Entering the principle through hearing, when the principle heard is profound and wondrous, the mind becomes naturally perfect and bright, no longer dwelling in the realm of delusion. This is where demons have no foothold.

Ren (Rinzai) subsequently claimed that at the moment Fang (Huangbo) deeply struck out and grasped the fire, experiencing a sense of joy and liberation, the "flower of the mind" blossomed and shone forth;

therefore, he heard the principle most easily and penetrated it deeply. Such discourse is like insects gnawing through wood, accidentally forming patterns, yet ultimately the insects do not recognize characters.
If even Muzhou had remained stuck in the realm of principle when he was with Baizhang while striking out at the fire, then there would have been...
Regarding the point at which awakening occurs: how could Baizhang have so recklessly granted his seal of approval to sentient beings?
Those of antiquity who spoke of awakening said it is "like a lotus blooming" or "like suddenly waking from a dream. When a lotus blooms, not a single speck of dust remains.
If there were still some principle to be thoroughly penetrated, then the lotus would still remain within the mud; how could it ever have blossomed?
It is like suddenly waking from a dream: once awake, where do the objects seen and the deeds performed within the dream actually exist?
If there were still some realm of principle to be thoroughly penetrated, then this would be a dream within a dream; how could one ever truly awaken?

If the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) could be attained through principle alone, the Patriarchs would not have said, "Transmitting mind by means of mind, do not establish written words," nor would Śākyamuni have said, "The Buddha’s words take the mind as their essence; no-gate is the dharma-gate. Why is this?
Principle is manifested through speech, and speech is made clear by means of writing. Although there is a most profound principle, there must necessarily be most explicit writing to [express it].
To bring this forth: if it cannot be elucidated through words as they are, it is simply because the words have not yet reached [the truth].

That the words do not reach it is because the principle (*li*) has not yet been fully clarified. It is absolutely impossible for there to be a principle that has never been clarified and yet lacks the words to convey it.
How can one abandon food because of choking on it? Because words cannot clarify [it], one must not therefore reject the use of words altogether.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the character *li* (principle): it is originally borrowed from the word for the grain or texture of wood to express its usage. When things possess principle, it is like the grain in wood;
"principle" refers to the internal fissures or pores of the wood. Even when it is extremely dense and compact, if one follows its grain, [it can be split].
Then the axe may enter. The place where it enters is precisely its gate. Since there is a principle that can be named, there must be a gate through which one may enter.
If one considers it a hundred times and finds no way, one considers it a thousand times; if one considers it a thousand times and finds no way, one considers it ten thousand times.
Ultimately, by means of the mind’s axe, one can enter the crevices of phenomena and principles. Once one enters those crevices, the bolt and lock are opened. Why?
To attain what is called the "gateless gate" as the Dharma-gate means that the path of speech is cut off, yet no words are established;

the sphere of mental activity ceases, yet the gateless is taken as the Dharma-gate. How could the Buddhas and Patriarchs have spoken empty words? Indeed, this entire earth is the gate, yet it is gateless;
throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they have turned the wondrous Wheel of Dharma, yet there are no characters—this is still [the case].
Where was the word "principle" ever spoken? If the flower of the mind had truly been illuminated, there would already be nothing at all;

how could one then turn back into the consciousness of karma and walk again through the dark alleys of delusion? It is precisely because you have not yet had the flower of your own mind illuminated that you speculate about its state, presuming it must be thus.
Consequently, you have falsely judged Baizhang Huishan; is this not the talk of a common village?
In the inner chambers, they discuss the affairs of the Hall of the Central Secretariat.

It is widely transmitted that Yongming was Maitreya, and Hanshan and Shide were Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra; even in recent times, Yangqi was considered the Buddha Dadao, among many others beyond count.
Not only was Yangshan regarded as the "Little Śākyamuni," but for those who have attained thorough penetration, these matters are indeed real. Minute...
It is not at all refreshing. To speak for those who have not yet attained thorough penetration, one might say that [these claims] are all mere fabrications;

they truly defile the ancients. Now, the demonically stubborn adhere to these doctrines, claiming that Yangshan’s prophetic response regarding the *parikalpa* (circle) bequeathed by the Indian patriarchs proves he was indeed a sage of the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*). This is truly nothing but a delirious dream. Since the *parikalpa* originated from the West...

The Patriarch entrusted [the Dharma] to him; why then did Yangshan burn them? If Yangshan’s entire life had consisted solely of these ninety-seven circular diagrams, then Yangshan would have been a source of delusion for sentient beings.
How could he be deemed worthy of continuing the excellence of Mount Gui (Miaoshan), and how could he be fit to serve as a model for a hundred generations?
Mōrin said: "A small sack cannot hold what is large; a short rope cannot draw from what is deep. How true are the words of the ancient sages!
When Yangshan was a śrāmaṇera, upon seeing this painting once, he immediately understood it clearly in his mind.
Furthermore, he made a duplicate copy without the slightest error. How could this have been possible for one of shallow roots and limited understanding? Thus, [he] refuted..."

The *Shu* (Commentary) cites the two characters "holding the source" (*zhíběn*) with the intent to utterly erase them; this is because it has not yet discerned that the phrase "Danyuan attained it while still a student" refers to this very point.
Furthermore, the existence of the "source" does not involve explanatory glosses or verbal principles that can be transmitted;
rather, it merely intends for the student to lift their mind and intellect beyond all gates and seams, taking yet another step forward. Fengxue said: "If..."

If one grain of dust is established, the family and the state flourish, yet the village elders frown; if not even a grain of dust is established, the family and the state perish, yet the village elders are at peace.
Nowadays, people forcibly create complications within the root of non-abiding, conversely treating the fundamental principle as a superfluous tumor.
It is like a person afflicted with cataracts who, upon taking medicine, becomes dizzy;
instead of blaming their own internal fevers and ailments, they cast the blame upon the medical treatises of the Yellow Emperor and Lu Ban—thus their delusion grows even more profound.
Yangshan’s unsurpassed quality lay in this: upon seeing Dan Yuan’s ninety-seven circular diagrams, he immediately burned them.
Yet, when he later produced a copy for Dan Yuan, it was not a single character out of place. This was merely because he could understand and comprehend; what is there to value in that?
Furthermore, who must necessarily be Yangshan to be able to do this? On that day, Dan Yuan said to Yangshan: [The text continues with the dialogue between Dan Yuan and Yangshan.]
He said: "The National Teacher of Nanyang received the ninety-seven circular diagrams (yuanxiang) of the six ancestral patriarchs at that time and transmitted them to me, saying:
'Thirty years after my passing, a śramaṇa will come from the south.'"
"Greatly promote this teaching and transmit it in succession so that it never be severed. I now entrust it to you; you must uphold it.

At that time, had Yangshan not truly found joy and fulfillment in his life, and had he not realized that not a single dharma could be grasped—such that few would fail to harbor thoughts of wonder—then upon seeing [this teaching] he would have immediately burned it away. Thus, he truly attained mastery through ninety-seven [cases].
It is a perfect circle; one can grasp its meaning at a single glance. I have compiled this single volume again so that not even a hair’s breadth of error remains.

There have been many people throughout the past and present who were of keen intelligence and possessed powerful memories—not only those whose deeds were recorded in writing, but also those whose names and achievements remained within the range of public hearing and sight.
If one were to claim that this is merely the ability of a minor Śākyamuni, then the Buddha-dharma would be swept away from the earth. Yet, as for this—
Individuals who have no connection [to such matters]. During the Song Dynasty, there were two prime ministers at the same time. One ate only half a pancake every day;
he would roll it into a shape as thin as a writing brush handle and eat until it was six-tenths gone, after which he could not swallow any more.

The other ate every day without knowing satiety; his cook secretly kept track of this, and whenever he finished eating one vessel of food and one vessel of drink, he would pour out exactly that amount.
He poured [food] into a large jar; in total, dozens of vessels were emptied until the jar overflowed onto the ground, yet he continued to eat and drink as usual without ceasing.

These two shared the same appearance and the same lifespan, both reaching over eighty years. If even coarse food and longevity have no mutual connection, how much less so is the case for the "Dharma-food" and "right livelihood"?
If one speaks of the marvel of not forgetting what passes before the eyes, then throughout ancient and modern times...
There have been many such individuals whose names at the outset were not well known. To cite briefly those recorded in the historical annals:
for instance, Wang Chong of the Han; Xun Yue of the Wei; Wei Shu, Zhang Xun, and Li Qiao of the Tang; Hu Songnian, Wang Yingchen, He She, and Huang Tingjian of the Song;
and Buhusi of the Yuan. All of them were capable of performing what Yangshan performed; could it be that they, too, had received the Western [Dharma]...?

Is this not the Buddha’s prediction by the Celestial One? To say that those who wish to study must extract their mental consciousness from the "doorless and seamless" state and take another step further is merely a forced intellectual fabrication.

If one wishes to arouse the student's state of doubt so that they may take another step further within that doorless and seamless state, why would it be necessary to rely on the ninety-seven circular diagrams? Only then could it be considered sufficient.

Is it that people employ expedient means? Furthermore, he cites the "Old Man of the Wilds" (Yelao Gong) from the Fengxue lineage as evidence, yet he fails to realize that this particular *gong'an* is the most glaring failure in Fengxue’s entire life.

By treating the "family and state" and the "old man of the wilds" as two separate entities, he contradicts worldly reason and betrays the True Teaching. To establish a distinct "old man of the wilds" outside of the family and state is—
This "rustic old man" is precisely one speck of dust. How can you say that not even a single speck of dust is established?
This is exactly what it means to forcibly create knots where there is no root of dwelling; you have long since become attached to the state of non-dwelling, making it firm and unshakeable.

Such talk, born of a failure to understand, deeply contradicts the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Having not yet attained the eye of insight yourself, you recklessly wish to prescribe medicine for others. This is—
This is the true exposition of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; yet it too would surely turn into a lethal poison, let alone these cases where error is transmitted as error.

Moran said: "It is like casting vessels from gold; whether they be bells, basins, tripods, or cauldrons, they are all gold, yet the tripod is not the bell, and the basin is not the cauldron—their uses differ.
Ganjiang and Moye are employed for cutting and slicing; Linji and Yunmen are close to this."
The precious mirror of the Qin palace was used for its capacity to encompass all things; the Caodong, Shoushan, and Yangqi schools were like this, while the Fayan school was like a tripod.
The *I Ching* says: "The tripod breaks its legs and overturns the lord’s stew. This is because a tripod stands upon three legs; if one is discarded, it tips over.
Yantou said that the three dots of the character "yi" (伊) somewhat resemble the Chan school. Fayan took the six characteristics (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as his school's principle.

The intent [of this teaching] is profound; its concern is that students of future generations might become biased or limited by focusing on only one aspect. The six characteristics (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*) are:

totality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), identity (*sābhāva*), difference (*nānātva*), formation (*utpāda*), and disintegration (*bhaṅga*). Here, totality is not the same as particularity, and difference is not the same as identity;

they act as mother and child to one another, thereby exhausting the vast nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) through the transformations of opening and closing—much like a palindrome poem woven in brocade, where a single character can be recited in a hundred ways.
The complete essence and great function of the Patriarchs were fully manifested by the time the five schools were established.
Linji (Yunmen) succeeded Dizang Chen; Chen succeeded Yuansha Bei; Bei succeeded Xuefeng Cun; Cun succeeded Deshan Jian; Jian succeeded Longtan Xin;
Xin succeeded Tianwang Wu; and Wu succeeded Mazu. Regarding the fundamental principle of Yuansha, there is a point of utility that cannot be shifted from its foundation.
This [teaching] alternates with the meaning of the six characteristics (ṣaḷlakṣaṇa) in its manifestation and concealment; Master Zhancheng was skilled in it.
By the time of Fayan, he exclusively employed this pedagogical device (*upāya*) to receive disciples; thus, the Way of Yuansha only began to flourish with Fayan.

However, students have been unable to investigate it with meticulous care, and before many generations had passed, the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) appeared. That exegetical śramaṇas rely upon it as their primary doctrine is truly lamentable.

Generally, all things that exist in relation to one another possess points of similarity; yet where there is nothing with which they resemble, there must necessarily be something with which they contrast.
Because there is this contrast, there is also this similarity. This is precisely what is meant by the "contrasting categories" (*fàn lèi*) in the *I Ching*. For instance, regarding Yin and Yang:
if one were to attempt to identify which aspect resembles Yin and which resembles Yang, it would be impossible. Nevertheless, Yin and Yang are themselves...
Conversely, the Yin is inherently contrary to the Yang, and the Yang is inherently contrary to the Yin.
If this is so, how could there be any duality within the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvāṇa? Since there is no duality, how could there be any semblance?
Even if one were to take as much ink as the great ocean and as many brushes as Mount Sumeru to record its true semblance, [it would remain unrecorded]. For a hundred...
It does not even approach one hundred-thousand-million-billionth part. Why is this? It is because it is entirely equal to this. To take its opposite as an example:
even if one were to use ink equal in volume to the great ocean and pens piled as high as Mount Sumeru to write it down, it still would not approach one hundred-thousand-million-billionth part.
Why is this? Again, it is because it is entirely equal to that. It is precisely because it is entirely equal...
[They] treat them as such, yet do not grant even a single one [of these] to him; therefore, in general, they cannot be said to be similar.
Now, for Mōrin to attempt to use categories of things as metaphors for his own school’s tenet is already extremely foolish.

How much more so when he divides the tenets of Linji and Yunmen into those "resembling a sword," while categorizing the tenets of Guishan, Yangshan, Caodong, and Fayan as "resembling a mirror"? As for the Fayan school...
The purport [of your words] resembles that of a cauldron. What kind of demonic teaching is this?

Now, while a sword is indeed sharp for cutting, there is such a thing as the "sword that saves people"—how could it possibly have the meaning of cutting? A mirror is indeed useful for reflecting all things, yet a mirror has no self-nature;
who, then, is the one that reflects? As for the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) of the *Avataṃsaka*, they encompass everything in order to eliminate [dualistic attachments].

The views of annihilationism and eternalism are indeed the Buddha’s words; however, failing to realize that the "no-gate" is the true Dharma-gate, one instead clings to the meaning of the six characteristics, thereby falling into the conceptual discrimination of the conscious mind. Furthermore, how could the meaning of the six characteristics constitute three legs?
Even if they were to constitute three legs, what would be seen as the three legs of the tripod? Such forced syntheses and fragmented interpretations are merely verbal gymnastics.

To say that words and letters have not yet been fully perfected is to recklessly attempt to conjecture the essential meaning of the True School, which transcends all language and writing. The Buddha-dharma is vast, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable;
even though Śākyamuni Buddha preached for forty-nine years, and Kāśyapa and Ānanda recorded it from within the Piṭarpaṇa Cave—

The teachings spoken by the Buddha extend from the three piṭakas and twelve divisions of the canon, reaching as far as the four sevens of India and the two threes of this land [China], each recording the Buddha’s intent to provide guidance for future generations.
Furthermore, there are the records of the karmic conditions and pedagogical encounters of the ancestral masters throughout successive dynasties.
As time has passed, these have increased daily until they are so vast that even an elephant could hardly carry them and the Dragon Canon could not contain them all. Nevertheless, it is said:
Having already exhausted all dharma gates, I fear that [the former] does not equal even one hundredth, one thousandth, ten millionth, or one hundred thousand billionth part [of the latter].
If, however, one suddenly realizes one's own mind and goes directly to the precious site, as an ancient worthy said: "When meeting, do not bring it forth."
As soon as an intention arises, one knows it exists. Yongming added a turning word, saying: "Why wait for an intention to arise?
This is indeed a perfect and clear knowing that does not depend on mental thought. The great earth is fully encompassed; nirvana is non-dual.
Therefore, if one speaks of the whole, every word and every silence of the Patriarchs is a total presentation; there is not even a single speck of dust or a single thread remaining.
It is already fully permeated; why wait for the five schools to establish themselves individually before its full expression can be realized?

If one speaks of their distinctions, even if Maitreya were to descend to birth and all the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa were to remain in the world turning the wheel of Dharma, they could not exhaust its vastness.
Although the masters of the five schools are all ancient worthies, how could they possibly surpass Śākyamuni or preemptively transcend Maitreya? And yet...

If, at one moment, he raises his fist and holds up his whisk, responding with words to the capacity of the student, this may be boasted of as the immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable Buddha-dharma.
Is the manifestation of the Dharma exhausted by this alone? Fayan transmitted it to National Teacher Shaokang;
National Teacher Shaokang transmitted it to Chan Master Yongming Youshou. Throughout his life, Yongming’s practice and realization were in accord, being pure and refined to the utmost.
Without the slightest flaw or omission, his spiritual nature was perfectly pure, like the bright sun in the sky, its radiance shining everywhere.
Not only did he surpass Fayen Yi and Tiantai Shaokang, but he truly emerged as one who excelled his teacher;
indeed, since the time of Śākyamuni Buddha and the entry of the Buddha-dharma into China, he was the foremost guide. This was because, at birth, he possessed the unconditioned...

Out of compassion, he gave rise to a sense of empathy that identifies with others' suffering. He unified the teachings of the Sūtras, Śāstras, and Vinaya into a single coherent system, demonstrating the correct path of practice for students of all times and generations.
He gathered the preeminent masters of the three schools—Tiantai, Xianshou, and Cien—and together they expounded upon the essential meanings of the Tripiṭaka texts.
By engaging in mutual inquiry and debate, they compiled these works into a hundred fascicles titled *Zongjing* (The Mirror of the Source).
Record. This enables students of the unsurpassed secret Dharma-gate to see it at a glance and practice it with every step.
It is like a pauper entering the Dragon Treasury: whatever they grasp with their hands brings ten generations of wealth. It is like a sick person encountering divine incense:
as it passes by on the wind, the entire body becomes healthy and peaceful. Among all the texts of the Chan school in China, this is truly the most [excellent].
The Venerable One is most supreme. As for Māra’s patience, when has he ever opened a scroll to even skim its contents?

He instead claims that Yongming could not meticulously investigate the tenets of the Empty Source (Xuanzang) and Sanda (Paramārtha), and thus falsely composed the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source), becoming a śramaṇa of mere intellectual interpretation.

To slander the Buddha and destroy the Patriarchs in such a manner is nothing less than plucking out the eyes of devas and humans and wounding the Compassionate Father of sentient beings; it cuts off the lineage of the Tathāgata.
This burns the medicinal storehouse of the King of Physicians and constitutes the wisdom-life of all Buddhas. Could there be any worldly evil karma greater than this?

Although one possessed of Ānanda’s unimpeded eloquence might exhaust their mental and physical power to explain it through extensive analogies, they could never fully describe the merit of the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Source-Mirror) of the Yongming era.
Such being the case, the sin of Māra and those who tolerate him in destroying the *Zongjing Lu* is beyond measure.
As for karma, even though Ānanda possesses unimpeded eloquence and exhausts his mental power to provide extensive analogies, he cannot fully describe it.
Even if one were to take all the sands in the Ganges River and, using as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand, were to count them, their number could still be exhausted;
for although such sands are exceedingly numerous, their quantity is finite. Yet the karmic offenses of this person are such that they will continue without end.

As for the hells, they have no fixed number from the beginning; how could they ever be exhausted? The mountain of knives and trees of swords, the boiling cauldrons and glowing embers, the iron ropes and hot ashes, and the Avīci Hell of Uninterrupted Suffering—these various hells shall likewise be inexhaustible for them.
Although Bodhidharma came from South India and, while not relying on written words, transmitted the essence of the Mahāyāna’s single mind, he nevertheless [relied upon] the *Laṅkāvatāra*...

The *Ga* is the seal. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The Buddha’s words take the mind as their essence; having no gate is the Dharma-gate. Is the *Laṅkāvatāra* itself not composed of written characters?
"The Buddha’s words take the mind as their essence" means that present speech is precisely the speech of the mind, and the speech of the mind is precisely the speech of the Buddha.
To realize this speech of the mind, there is no separate Buddha-speech. Did Yongming not say: "The nature of written characters is detached from them; this is liberation"?
As soon as one attains the vision of one's nature, one is immediately without mind.

If one is deluded regarding the true nature of all phenomena and, seeking them outside the mind, gives rise to a view based on words and letters, then those very words and letters are used as an antidote to reveal that true reality.
If one awakens to the source of all phenomena, not even a single thread of a word will appear; only then does one truly know all things.
All phenomena are the very nature of mind; thus, object and wisdom are interfused, and form and emptiness both vanish.
At this moment of directly realizing perfect luminosity, at this time of entering the equality of this single dharma, what dharma could there be that is taught and yet to be abandoned?
What dharma is ancestral and thus worthy of reverence? What dharma is sudden and thus worthy of adoption? What dharma is gradual and thus worthy of rejection?
If this is so, what further room is there for intellectual interpretation (*yijie*)? Now, as for the intent of Mazu’s forbearance:

if there were even a single phrase or a single character, it would belong to intellectual interpretation. Yet, transcending both phrases and characters, a single blow does not function as a single blow.
Furthermore, it is said that this is extremely coarse. If so, then only that "one circle" (*o*) squeezed out by Master Yi could truly be called something that covers heaven and earth?
This is exactly like a blind donkey turning a millstone, running around in circles.
For this single great lie, Māra and his son Candra will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell without a doubt.
Māra-ṛṣi said: "The Way of Single Transmission, since the time of Dajian [Huineng], has split into five schools; though their verbal expressions differ,"
There has never been one who established [enlightenment] without relying on a specific event; this can be verified by examining the accounts of their awakenings.

When the Master first met Yunyan, he had already awakened to the principle of "insentient beings preaching the Dharma. Yet, when faced with Yunyan’s long silence, he hesitated and could not resolve it.

Was this not because he had grasped half of the truth while remaining ignorant of its full extent? Therefore, the essential teaching of Yunyan is: "It is like standing before a precious mirror; form and shadow [are reflected together]."
"Look at each other: you are not he; he is precisely you. Later, when the Master was crossing water, he saw his reflection and attained great enlightenment.
He composed a verse, saying: "By all means, do not seek it from another; To do so would distance it from me. I shall now go forth alone; Everywhere I meet him.
He is fundamentally not me; I am now precisely he. One must understand it thus Before one can achieve realization."
Such is the *tathatā*. Caoshan also had a verse that says: "If he has no self, he dies; if I have no him, I am left over.
If he is like me, he is a Buddha; if I am like him, I am a donkey. How similar this is to the words established and the teachings transmitted by fathers and sons, ancestors and descendants!
A venerable elder of recent times has remarked: "Sanfeng exhausted the three peaks by pairing the 'three strikes' and 'three shakes' with the primary essentials.

But as for the Five Ranks of Caodong, how could one possibly find five numbers to pair with them? Alas! This is like being blind oneself and thereby obstructing the vision of the world. Did not Xuefeng say:
"The six lines of the hexagram *Chongli* (the double li) involve the interplay of the biased and the correct; these are layered to form three, and when the transformations are exhausted..."

Wu Chengcheng received the Dharma from Yaoshan; Yaoshan received the Dharma from Shitou. Shitou composed the *Cantong qi*, which extensively clarifies the principle of the mutual interplay of light and darkness.
Chengcheng truly elucidated this, and the father and son of Dongshan further manifested its Way.
The source of their teaching tradition has its origins in antiquity.

The Māra-like father and son [Huangbo and Linji] mistakenly took the scales for granted; they claimed that each of the five houses established its own school, and thus asserted that from Dajian (Huineng) downward, the lineage split into five sects.
This was because they were deluded by the prophetic saying that "one flower opens into five petals" as a sign of the five houses.
Having been deceived themselves, they in turn used those who were already deluded to delude others. They failed to realize that while there are five schools, how could their nature also be five?
There are five [patriarchs]. First, the flower opens into five petals; what connection does this have with the Five Houses?

Furthermore, it is said that although the verbal expressions of the Five Houses differ, there is none that was not established based on specific circumstances. Now, in the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*), not even a single speck of dust is established.
How could there be a principle of establishing a school based on a particular matter? If one matter were to establish one school, how could there be only five schools?

If there were matters as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges Rivers, there would likewise be as many schools as the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges Rivers.
However, the matters of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges-sands are themselves the principles of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges-sands;
these revolve such that the one is all and all is the one—an inexhaustible gate of mutual interpenetration. Even this revolution is not without meaning.
If you claim that one principle is established based on one matter and five principles are established based on five matters, such that once the five schools are established,
the manifestation of their principles is thereby exhausted— such a fallacious argument has never been heard since the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty,
when the Buddha-dharma entered China. This was true even before Bodhidharma came from the West to point directly to the human mind.

Since the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the True Dharma Eye) and the *Nirvāṇa Miaoxin* (Wondrous Mind of Nirvāṇa)—which reveal the seeing of nature and the attainment of Buddhahood—have clearly emerged, one cannot afford such snoring sleep or the prattling of delusions.
Furthermore, [consider] the verses on "I" and "He" composed by Yunyan, Dongshan, and Caoshan.

To claim that the words and teachings established by fathers and sons, or grandfathers and grandchildren, are similar enough to be considered a profound source or a model for emulation—this is truly the "nonsense within nonsense.

If this were so, then the tenets of the Five Houses would be like those who study the *Shijing* speaking of *fu*, *bi*, and *xing*, or those who study the *Yijing* speaking of the *tuan*, *xiang*, and *yao*. Yet, if that were the case, could one not likewise [apply this logic] to the five...?
The imperial edict established the curriculum for the selection of officials, decreeing that those who study Linji should discourse on the "Essential Pivot" (yuanyao);

those who study Yunmen should discourse on the "Mirror and the 'Aha'" (jianyi); those who study Fayan should discourse on "Identity and Difference" (tongyi); those who study Guishan and Yangshan should discourse on "Circular Diagrams" (yuanxiang);

and those who study Caodong should discourse on "Black and White" (heibai). Confucian scholars of the secular world claim that there are five stars in heaven and five elements on earth; thus, they maintain that there are five Confucians.
In the Sūtras, there are now exactly five schools that correspond [to these]. Fazang matched the three strikes and three shakes with the Three Essentials and Three Principles.
If Yi were a true descendant of Caodong, he too would have to take this as the correspondence of the Five Ranks of Ruler and Subject, would he not?
Their deluded views are truly on a par with such [errors]; how could they have ever realized their own minds? They are merely mad dogs.
Chasing after fragments: to let out one's views, hearing, sensations, and cognitions; to chew upon words and letters; to conjecture, deliberate, and calculate;
to weave and carve with artifice—this is to fail to realize that the teachings of the Five Houses are all equally "words devoid of meaning. Why waste such mental effort?

It would be better to change your occupation and exhaust yourself in the study of the Classics; this can still serve as something beneficial to the world. Why suffer within the saliva and spittle of wild foxes?
To engage in false discrimination and pursue with a biased mind is like "climbing a tree to catch fish" in the School of the Patriarchs; one will have no share of it for a lifetime.

It merely allows the Confucian school to know that [Buddhism] has come to lodge beneath its eaves, causing them to laugh until their teeth turn cold. Thus, the ancestral wind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is completely swept away.
Miyun said that Fazang exhausted himself pulling and shaking the staff three times to match the "Original Essentials. If this were the Caodong style...
The five ranks. Furthermore, how could one possibly assign the number five to them? This truly strikes at the very root of the illness.
Yet Mōjin refuses to relinquish his attachments and instead drags in Yunyan’s words to serve as proof; does this not add yet another layer of shackles upon himself?
As for the verses on the "Treasure Mirror Samādhi" from Yunyan, why did Mōjin not look toward that which is neither "contrary" nor "touching"?

Like a great mass of fire, it merely takes on the form of patterns and colors; thus, it belongs to the realm of defiled apprehension. Yet, when directed toward the six lines of the hexagram *Zhònglí* (重離), the biased and the correct intermingle and rotate, layering themselves into three.
When these transformations are exhausted, they form five positions. Is this not striking at the very center? Or is it circling around the periphery?
*Mōjin Shosha Goshū Kyū* (The Five Sectarian Defenses by Māra-Enduring) consists of ten volumes in total.

At the beginning, it lists three general treatises that clarify the demonic doctrines of Yi Shi, who fabricated the "one" and "ten" as the progenitors of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas;

these [treatises] claim that this is the essential teaching transmitted through the patriarchs from the "four sevens" of India to the "two threes" of this land. Next, it enumerates the lineage from the Seven Buddhas down to Huangbo, and subsequently enumerates Linji.
Regarding the Linji (Ji) school: from Linji down to Fazang, there were thirty-one individuals. Next, the remaining four schools are briefly indicated;
only Yunmen, Shoushan (Weiyang), Fayan, and Caodong—six individuals in total—are recorded. Their general intent was all to refute the heterodox arguments of Fazang.
Yet their most essential point of view was that Linji, as the patriarch of the five schools, [was superior], whereas Fazang...
He is the true bone and marrow of Linji; furthermore, he ensures that future generations throughout the world know that he was also the worthy heir of Fazang.
As for Miyun, he is the one through whom Fazang obtained his place within the lineage of Linji.
However, had Miyun refuted Fazang, Fazang’s position would not have been secure; it would have inevitably perished.
Once Miyun had passed away, his followers nevertheless continued to revere the various dragon-pool lineages obtained by Miyun as their ancestral source.
Consequently, those who claimed to be the direct bone-blood descendants of Linji were bound to be viewed with suspicion by the world and future generations.
Thus, from Dongming Haizhou downward, they employed subtle rhetoric to offer pointed criticisms and instead came to revere Gaofeng Yuanmiao.
Fan was the master who transmitted the mind-seal dharma to Fazang. This was because the Linji path transmitted by this father and son had been received separately from Gao Feng Juefan.
As for how he was able to receive it from Gao Feng Juefan, it was because his master was one who had attained the stage of fruition;
it arose from his innate roots and was inconceivable. By means of this...
At that time, the deluded and unwise monastics were like those who merely parrot the words of their patrons to fish for fame in future generations.

They were exactly like Wang Mang, who forged false talismans and edicts; even when the Han troops raised fire to burn them, he still clutched his jade battle-axe and sat facing the cardinal directions, saying, "Heaven has bestowed its virtue upon me;
what can the Han troops do to me? These two individuals were truly [of such a nature].

A rebellious minister of the King of Emptiness and a traitorous son of the Thick Clouds—one who cannot be tolerated in either worldly or world-transcending dharmas—on the eighth day of the fourth month in the eleventh year of the Yongzheng era, a special imperial edict was issued that thoroughly documented his crimes.
Now, from among the "Five Sects' Defenses," I shall select those points most perverse and erroneous, pointing them out one by one to expose [his fallacies]. Ten... [to be continued]

For those Zen practitioners who are like the blind, and who have caused themselves to drink the poison of their mother’s milk, I shall provide this medicine of strong purgatives—turmeric and croton seeds—hoping that those who read it will exhaust the poison and their lives may gradually recover. Perhaps there may be some small benefit therein.
National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang said: "The Dharma of the Zen school should rely upon the definitive meaning of the One Vehicle as taught by the Buddha, thereby realizing its original nature."
The original ground of the mind is transmitted and handed down in succession, identical to the Way of the Buddhas.
One must not rely on deluded sentiments or teachings of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) to form arbitrary views that mislead later students; such actions provide no benefit to either party.

Even if one receives the essential tenets from a master, they may be practiced accordingly only if they accord with the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*). If they accord with teachings of provisional meaning, they are mutually inconsistent [with the ultimate truth].
I agree with this. It is like the worms within a lion’s body that eat the flesh of the lion’s own body;

it is not through celestial Māras or non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) that the Buddha-dharma can be destroyed. Nanyang Zhong understood this statement and definitively established it as early as the Tang dynasty.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The vehicle of the devas and Brahmā, the vehicle of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas."
I have taught these various vehicles as long as the mind continues to function; these vehicles are not ultimate.
When that mind is extinguished, there is neither vehicle nor one who rides it, and no establishment of vehicles exists. This is what I call the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Indeed, even the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddha-Tathāgatas must first be directly realized as having no such establishment before the principle of the One Vehicle can be clarified. How much more so [is this true for others]?

How much more so for the "Māra-Endurance" (Mōjin) father and son, whose private fabrication of the "One Circle," the "Double-Headed Single-Knot" school of thought, and their arbitrarily produced "Discriminating Eye" and "I-Amy" constitute nothing but the wild fox saliva of "Self, Other, Fundamental, Essential, Guest, and Host.
Furthermore, their origins were by no means motivated by a vision to benefit others through the Buddha-dharma; they arose solely from the error of ignorance.

This turmoil arises solely from one’s own attachment to fame and profit, employing a mind of arrogance and conceit as a technique for monopolizing and cornering the market, while feigning the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to indulge in perverse thoughts from one's own breast.

Such slanderers of the Great Prajñāpāramitā and defilers of the life-force of wisdom—these demonic outsiders—how can one bear to listen to their heterodox teachings flowing recklessly? How could one...
I contemplate turning back the surging waves that have already collapsed; therefore, I have composed these words to refute them. It is not that I delight in disputation.
Moreover, protecting the True Dharma takes the discernment of heterodoxy from orthodoxy as its foundation; this is also what I, as an imperial subject, ought to do in repaying my debt of gratitude.
I employ this to demonstrate it to the world and future generations.
Record for Distinguishing and Discerning Demons, Scroll Eight (End)
